drafts.proof_strategy: Adjoin the finitely many coefficients of an integral equation to get a finite R-module containing x.
sketch_steps: setup: Write an integral equation for x with coefficients c_i in C.
derive: R[c_0, ..., c_(n-1)] is a finitely generated R-module because each c_i is integral.
derive: Adjoining x keeps the ring finitely generated as an R-module.
conclude: Cayley-Hamilton shows x is integral over R.

drafts.canonical_statement: If S is an integral domain and the injective ring map R → S makes S integral over R, then R is a field if and only if S is a field.

drafts.proof_strategy: Extract inverses from an integral equation in each direction.
sketch_steps: setup: Assume R is a field and y in S is nonzero.
derive: In a minimal-degree integral equation, the constant term is nonzero, hence a unit of R, which yields an inverse of y.
setup: Conversely assume S is a field and x in R is nonzero.
derive: Multiply an integral equation of x^(-1) by x^(n-1) to express x^(-1) as an element of R.
conclude: Both directions hold.

drafts.canonical_statement: If R → S is an injective ring map making S integral over R, then every prime P of R is the contraction of some prime Q of S (lying over).

drafts.proof_strategy: Localize at P and contract a maximal ideal of the localized extension.
sketch_steps: setup: Localize R and S at the complement of P.
derive: The localization of S is nonzero by injectivity and integral over the local ring R_P.
construct: Take a maximal ideal n of the localized S.
apply_theorem: The contraction of a maximal ideal along an integral extension is maximal, so n contracts to P R_P.
conclude: The contraction Q of n to S satisfies Q ∩ R = P.

sketch_steps: translate: The map R/P_1 → S/Q_1 is injective and integral.
apply_theorem: Lying over gives a prime of S/Q_1 over P_2/P_1.
conclude: Its preimage Q_2 contains Q_1 and lies over P_2.

drafts.proof_strategy: The constant term of a minimal integral equation modulo Q gives an element in J ∩ R outside Q ∩ R.
sketch_steps: setup: Choose x in J outside Q and reduce modulo Q.
derive: The image of x is nonzero and integral over R/(Q ∩ R).
derive: A minimal-degree integral equation has nonzero constant term because S/Q is a domain.
conclude: This constant term is an element of J ∩ R not in Q ∩ R.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a nonzero finitely generated algebra A over a field k there are s and an injective k-algebra map g from k[x_1, ..., x_s] to A making A a finite module over the polynomial ring (Noether normalization).

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on generators, using a change of variables to make a relation monic in the last generator.
sketch_steps: induction: Induct on the number n of algebra generators of A.
case_split: If the generators are algebraically independent, A itself is a polynomial ring.
construct: Otherwise change variables by y_i' = y_i - y_n^(r_i) so that a relation becomes monic in y_n up to a constant.
derive: Then A is finite over the subalgebra generated by y_1', ..., y_(n-1)'.
apply_theorem: The induction hypothesis applies to this subalgebra.
conclude: Finiteness is transitive, which gives the injective finite map from a polynomial ring.

drafts.proof_strategy: Deduce the strong form from the weak form by the Rabinowitsch trick.
sketch_steps: derive: If f^n lies in I, then f vanishes on every common zero of I.
apply_theorem: The weak form says every proper ideal has a common zero, using that maximal ideals are point ideals.
construct: Add a variable t and consider the ideal generated by I and 1 - t f.
derive: It has no common zero, so it is the unit ideal.
derive: Substituting t = 1/f in an expression of 1 and clearing denominators gives f^n in I.
conclude: The two conditions are equivalent.

drafts.proof_strategy: Identify the quotient by a maximal ideal with K via Zariski's lemma.
sketch_steps: derive: The evaluation map at x is surjective onto K, so its kernel is maximal.
setup: Conversely let I be maximal and form the field L = K[x]/I.
apply_theorem: Zariski's lemma makes L algebraic over K, and algebraic closedness gives L = K.
construct: Let a_i be the image of x_i in K.
conclude: I lies in the kernel of evaluation at a, and maximality gives equality.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Artin-Rees to get N = IN, then Nakayama.
sketch_steps: setup: Let N be the intersection of all powers of I.
apply_theorem: The Artin-Rees lemma gives k with I^n ∩ N = I^(n-k) (I^k ∩ N) for n at least k.
derive: Taking n = k + 1 gives N = I N.
apply_theorem: N is finitely generated and I lies in the maximal ideal, so Nakayama's lemma applies.
conclude: Therefore N = 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: A principal ideal domain that is not a field has Krull dimension 1.

drafts.proof_strategy: Exhibit a chain of length one and rule out longer ones because nonzero primes are maximal.
sketch_steps: derive: A nonzero nonunit lies in a nonzero maximal ideal, so the dimension is at least 1.
apply_theorem: Nonzero primes of a principal ideal domain are maximal.
derive: Hence no chain of primes has length 2.
conclude: The Krull dimension equals 1.

drafts.canonical_statement: A field has Krull dimension 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: List the prime ideals of a field.
sketch_steps: derive: The only ideals of a field are 0 and the whole field.
derive: So 0 is the only prime ideal.
conclude: The only chain has length 0.

derive: All irreducibles are associated to ϖ, so a = u ϖ^n with u a unit.
conclude: Therefore s = (ϖ^n).

sketch_steps: setup: Write x = a/b with a, b in R and b nonzero.
apply_theorem: In a valuation ring a divides b or b divides a.
case_split: If b divides a then x lies in R, and if a divides b then x^(-1) lies in R.
conclude: So x or its inverse lies in R.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show nonzero primes are invertible, then run the usual existence and cancellation argument.
sketch_steps: derive: Nonzero primes are maximal and invertible as fractional ideals.
contradiction: A maximal ideal with no prime factorization would factor as P times a larger ideal.
derive: A prime containing a product contains one of the factors and equals it by maximality.
derive: Invertibility allows cancelling the common prime.
conclude: Existence and uniqueness of the factorization follow.

drafts.canonical_statement: For ideals I and J of a Dedekind domain, I divides J if and only if J is contained in I.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use invertibility of nonzero ideals to define the quotient ideal.
sketch_steps: derive: If J = I K, then J is contained in I.
setup: Conversely assume J is contained in I and I is nonzero.
construct: Let K = I^(-1) J, which lies in A because J ⊂ I.
conclude: Then I K = J, so I divides J.

drafts.proof_strategy: In a one-dimensional integrally closed Noetherian local domain, produce a generator of the maximal ideal.
sketch_steps: derive: The localization is a Noetherian local integrally closed domain of dimension 1.
setup: Take nonzero a in the maximal ideal m and the least n with m^n ⊂ (a).
construct: Choose b in m^(n-1) outside (a) and put x = a/b.
derive: Integral closedness gives x^(-1) m = A_P, so m = (x).
conclude: A non-field Noetherian local domain with principal maximal ideal is a discrete valuation ring.

drafts.proof_strategy: Translate a cover by basic opens into the ideal generated being the unit ideal.
sketch_steps: setup: It suffices to refine covers to covers by basic open sets D(f_i).
translate: The D(f_i) cover Spec R exactly when the f_i generate the unit ideal.
derive: The element 1 is a finite combination of the f_i.
conclude: Finitely many D(f_i) already cover Spec R.

drafts.canonical_statement: A point x of Spec R is closed if and only if the corresponding prime ideal is maximal.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prime_spectrum"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closed_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="singleton_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prime_spectrum"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="maximal_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="spectrum_point_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Compute the closure of a point as V(P).
sketch_steps: derive: The closure of {x} is V(P), the set of primes containing P.
translate: Hence {x} is closed exactly when P is the only prime containing P.
apply_theorem: Every proper ideal lies in a maximal ideal, and maximal ideals are prime.
conclude: This condition says P is maximal.

drafts.canonical_statement: A subset Z of Spec R is closed if and only if Z = V(s) for some subset s of R.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="subset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prime_spectrum"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closed_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prime_spectrum"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="subset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="spectrum_zero_locus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Verify the axioms of closed sets for the family V(s), the definition of the topology.
sketch_steps: setup: The Zariski topology is defined by taking the sets V(s) as closed.
derive: Arbitrary intersections and the whole space and empty set are of this form.
derive: V(s) ∪ V(t) = V(st) by primality.
conclude: Thus closed subsets are exactly the V(s).

drafts.canonical_statement: If a commutative ring R is complete and separated for the I-adic topology, then I is contained in the Jacobson radical of R.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="adic_complete"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="subset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="jacobson_radical"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Invert 1 + xy by a convergent geometric series.
sketch_steps: translate: It suffices to show 1 + x y is a unit for x in I and y in R.
construct: The partial sums of the geometric series in -x y form an I-adic Cauchy sequence.
derive: Completeness gives a limit w, and (1 + x y) w - 1 lies in every power of I.
conclude: Separatedness gives (1 + x y) w = 1.

drafts.canonical_statement: The I-adic completion of a Noetherian commutative ring R is a flat R-module.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="noetherian_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="flat_module"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="adic_completion"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Combine exactness of completion on finite modules with the tensor description of completion.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Artin-Rees shows completion is exact on short exact sequences of finitely generated modules.
derive: For finitely generated M, tensoring with the completion of R gives the completion of M.
translate: Flatness reduces to injectivity after tensoring the inclusion of a finitely generated ideal into R.
conclude: That injectivity follows from the two previous facts.

drafts.canonical_statement: For every complex number z, the product of z and its conjugate equals |z|^2.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="C"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="complex_conj"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="abs"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Expand the product in real and imaginary parts and compare with the definition of the modulus.
sketch_steps: setup: Write z = x + iy with real x, y.
derive: Expanding gives z·conj(z) = x^2 + y^2.
conclude: This equals |z|^2 by the definition of the modulus.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a nonzero complex number z, the inverse of z equals conj(z) / |z|^2.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="C"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="divide"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="divide"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="complex_conj"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="abs"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Divide the identity z·conj(z) = |z|^2 by the nonzero number |z|^2.
sketch_steps: setup: Note that |z|^2 is nonzero because z is nonzero.
apply_theorem: Use z·conj(z) = |z|^2.
conclude: Dividing by |z|^2 shows that conj(z)/|z|^2 is the inverse of z.

drafts.canonical_statement: For every complex number z, |Re z| ≤ |z|, |Im z| ≤ |z| and |z| ≤ |Re z| + |Im z|.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="C"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="leq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="abs"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="real_part"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="abs"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="leq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="abs"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="imag_part"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="abs"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="leq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="abs"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="abs"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="real_part"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="abs"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="imag_part"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Compare squares using |z|^2 = x^2 + y^2 and take square roots.
sketch_steps: setup: Write z = x + iy, so |z|^2 = x^2 + y^2.
derive: x^2 and y^2 are each at most x^2 + y^2, which gives the first two bounds.
derive: (|x| + |y|)^2 is at least x^2 + y^2.
conclude: Taking square roots gives |z| ≤ |x| + |y|.

drafts.canonical_statement: For every complex number z, |exp z| = exp(Re z).
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="C"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="abs"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="transc1" name="exp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="transc1" name="exp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="real_part"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Factor exp z into exp(x) and a unimodular factor exp(iy).
sketch_steps: setup: Write z = x + iy and use exp z = exp x · exp(iy).
apply_theorem: Euler's formula gives |exp(iy)| = 1.
conclude: Multiplicativity of the modulus gives |exp z| = exp x.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a complex number z, exp z = 1 if and only if z = 2πin for some integer n.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="C"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="transc1" name="exp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="Z"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="pi"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="complex_imaginary_unit"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Separate modulus and argument of exp z and use the zeros of the real exponential and trigonometric equations.
sketch_steps: derive: If z = 2πin, Euler's formula gives exp z = 1.
setup: Conversely let z = x + iy with exp z = 1.
derive: Taking moduli gives exp x = 1, so x = 0.
derive: Then cos y = 1 and sin y = 0, so y = 2πn for an integer n.
conclude: Hence z = 2πin.

drafts.canonical_statement: For every complex number z, cos z = (exp(iz) + exp(-iz)) / 2.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="C"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="transc1" name="cos"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="divide"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="transc1" name="exp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="complex_imaginary_unit"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="transc1" name="exp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="unary_minus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="complex_imaginary_unit"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Add the exponential series at iz and -iz and compare with the cosine series.
sketch_steps: setup: Substitute iz and -iz in the power series of exp.
derive: Odd-degree terms cancel when the two series are added.
derive: Even-degree terms give twice the cosine series.
conclude: Dividing by 2 yields the formula.

drafts.canonical_statement: For every complex number z, exp(iz) = cos z + i sin z.

drafts.proof_strategy: Split the exponential series at iθ into even and odd degree terms.
sketch_steps: setup: Substitute iθ in the power series of exp.
case_split: Separate even and odd degree terms using powers of i.
derive: The even part is the series of cos θ and the odd part is i times the series of sin θ.
conclude: Adding them gives Euler's formula.

drafts.canonical_statement: For every complex number z and natural number n, (cos z + i sin z)^n = cos(nz) + i sin(nz).

drafts.proof_strategy: Rewrite the base as exp(iz) and apply the law of exponents.
sketch_steps: translate: cos z + i sin z = exp(iz).
apply_theorem: exp(iz)^n = exp(inz) by the law of exponents.
conclude: exp(inz) = cos(nz) + i sin(nz).

drafts.canonical_statement: If z is a complex number with z^n = 1 for a positive integer n, then |z| = 1.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="C"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="gt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="abs"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Take moduli in z^n = 1 and use injectivity of the n-th power on nonnegative reals.
sketch_steps: derive: Multiplicativity of the modulus gives |z|^n = 1.
apply_theorem: The n-th power is injective on nonnegative reals for n > 0.
conclude: Hence |z| = 1.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a complex number ζ satisfies ζ^n = 1 and ζ ≠ 1, then 1 + ζ + ... + ζ^(n-1) = 0.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="C"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="range_sum"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="fns1" name="lambda"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Multiply the sum by ζ - 1 and cancel the nonzero factor.
sketch_steps: setup: Let S be the sum of ζ^k for 0 ≤ k < n.
derive: Telescoping gives S(ζ - 1) = ζ^n - 1 = 0.
conclude: Since ζ - 1 is nonzero, S = 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a positive integer n, the complex solutions of z^n = 1 are exactly the numbers exp(2πik/n) with 0 ≤ k < n.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="gt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="C"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="lt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="transc1" name="exp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="divide"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="pi"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="complex_imaginary_unit"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Verify the forward direction by the law of exponents and reduce the argument modulo 2π for the converse.
sketch_steps: derive: If z = exp(2πik/n), then z^n = exp(2πik) = 1.
setup: Conversely, z^n = 1 gives |z| = 1, so z = exp(iθ) for a real θ.
derive: exp(inθ) = 1 gives nθ = 2πm for an integer m.
construct: Let k be the remainder of m modulo n.
conclude: Periodicity of exp gives z = exp(2πik/n) with 0 ≤ k < n.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every complex number z satisfies z = |z| exp(i Arg z), where Arg is the principal argument.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="C"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="abs"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="transc1" name="exp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="complex_imaginary_unit"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="principal_arg"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Treat z = 0 separately and otherwise use the defining property of the principal argument with Euler's formula.
sketch_steps: case_split: If z = 0 both sides are 0.
setup: For z ≠ 0 the unit vector z/|z| equals cos(Arg z) + i sin(Arg z).
apply_theorem: Euler's formula rewrites this as exp(i Arg z).
conclude: Multiply by |z|.

drafts.canonical_statement: For every nonzero complex number z, exp(Log z) = z, where Log is the principal logarithm.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="C"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="transc1" name="exp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="principal_log"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Expand the definition of the principal logarithm and use the polar form.
sketch_steps: setup: Log z = ln|z| + i Arg z, which makes sense because z ≠ 0.
derive: exp(Log z) = |z| exp(i Arg z) by the law of exponents.
conclude: The polar form gives exp(Log z) = z.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a complex number z satisfies -π < Im z ≤ π, then Log(exp z) = z.

drafts.proof_strategy: Identify the modulus and the principal argument of exp z.
sketch_steps: setup: Write z = x + iy, so |exp z| = exp x.
derive: Since y lies in (-π, π], Arg(exp z) = y.
conclude: Log(exp z) = x + iy = z.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a complex number z is not a nonpositive real number, the principal logarithm is complex differentiable at z with derivative 1/z.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="C"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="or"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="gt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="real_part"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="imag_part"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="has_complex_deriv_at"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="principal_log_fn"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="divide"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the inverse function rule to exp on the slit plane, where Log is a continuous inverse.
sketch_steps: setup: On the slit plane Log is continuous and is a right inverse of exp.
derive: The derivative of exp at Log z is exp(Log z) = z, which is nonzero.
apply_theorem: The inverse function rule gives a derivative of 1/z at z.
conclude: Hence Log has derivative 1/z at z.

drafts.proof_strategy: Restrict the difference quotient to the real and imaginary directions and compare real and imaginary parts.
sketch_steps: setup: Write f'(z) = a + ib.
derive: Restricting h to real values gives f_x = f'(z).
derive: Restricting h to imaginary values gives f_y = i f'(z).
translate: Taking real and imaginary parts gives u_x = a, v_x = b, u_y = -b and v_y = a.
conclude: Hence u_x = v_y and u_y = -v_x.

drafts.canonical_statement: A function f on the complex plane is complex differentiable at z if and only if it is real differentiable at z and its real differential satisfies Df(z)(i) = i·Df(z)(1).

drafts.proof_strategy: Show that the real linear differential is complex linear exactly under the stated condition.
sketch_steps: derive: A complex derivative makes the differential multiplication by f'(z), which is complex linear.
setup: Conversely let L be the real differential with L(i) = iL(1).
derive: For h = a + ib, linearity gives L(h) = hL(1).
translate: The real differentiability expansion becomes f(z+h) - f(z) = hL(1) + o(|h|).
conclude: Hence f is complex differentiable with derivative L(1).

drafts.canonical_statement: The conjugation map z ↦ conj(z) is not complex differentiable at any point.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="C"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="complex_conj"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="not"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="holomorphic_at"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Compute the difference quotient along the real and imaginary directions.
sketch_steps: setup: The difference quotient at z equals conj(h)/h.
derive: Along real h it is identically 1.
derive: Along imaginary h it is identically -1.
conclude: The limit does not exist, so conjugation is not complex differentiable at z.

drafts.canonical_statement: If f is holomorphic on a connected open set U and f' vanishes identically on U, then f is constant on U.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show that f is locally constant by integrating along segments and then use connectedness.
sketch_steps: derive: On a disc in U, integrating f' along a segment shows that f is constant on the disc.
setup: Fix z in U and consider the level set of f through z.
derive: The level set is open by the local step and closed in U by continuity.
conclude: Connectedness makes the level set all of U.

drafts.canonical_statement: If w lies in the open disc |z-c| < R, then the integral of 1/(z-w) over the positively oriented circle |z-c| = R equals 2πi.

drafts.proof_strategy: Expand 1/(z-w) as a geometric series around c, integrate termwise and evaluate each term by parametrization.
sketch_steps: derive: On the circle, |w-c|/|z-c| < 1 gives a uniformly convergent geometric series for 1/(z-w).
apply_theorem: Uniform convergence allows termwise integration.
derive: Parametrizing z = c + Re^(iθ) gives 2πi for the term n = 0.
derive: The terms with n ≥ 1 have primitives on the circle and integrate to 0.
conclude: The integral equals 2πi.

drafts.canonical_statement: For an integer n ≠ -1, R > 0 and a point w not on the circle |z-c| = R, the integral of (z-w)^n over that circle is 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Exhibit an explicit primitive near the circle and use that the path is closed.
sketch_steps: construct: Since n ≠ -1, (z-w)^(n+1)/(n+1) is a single-valued function.
derive: Since w is off the circle, it is a primitive of (z-w)^n near the circle.
apply_theorem: The integral along a path equals the difference of the primitive at the endpoints.
conclude: The circle is closed, so the integral is 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Parametrize the circle and bound the modulus of the integrand.
sketch_steps: translate: Parametrize the circle by z = c + Re^(iθ).
derive: The integrand has modulus at most CR.
apply_theorem: The modulus of an integral is at most the integral of the modulus.
conclude: Integrating over an interval of length 2π gives 2πRC.

derive: Uniform continuity on the closed disc shows that these integrals converge as r tends to R.
conclude: The integral over the circle of radius R is 0.

conclude: A holomorphic function with zero derivative on the plane is constant.

drafts.canonical_statement: If f is holomorphic on the whole complex plane and f(z) tends to c as |z| tends to infinity, then f is identically c.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="entire_function"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="tends_to_at_infinity"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Prove boundedness from the limit and compactness, then apply Liouville's theorem.
sketch_steps: derive: Outside a large disc, |f - c| ≤ 1.
derive: On the closed disc, f is bounded by continuity.
apply_theorem: f is bounded and entire, so Liouville's theorem makes it constant.
conclude: The limit at infinity identifies the constant as c.

drafts.canonical_statement: If f is holomorphic on the whole complex plane and |f(z)| ≥ m for all z with a constant m > 0, then f is constant.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="entire_function"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="gt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="geq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="abs"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Liouville's theorem to the reciprocal of f.
sketch_steps: derive: The bound shows that f has no zeros.
construct: Hence g = 1/f is entire and bounded by 1/m.
apply_theorem: Liouville's theorem makes g constant.
conclude: Taking reciprocals, f is constant.

drafts.canonical_statement: The fundamental theorem of algebra: a complex polynomial of positive degree has a complex root.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="polynomial_over"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="C"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="gt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="poly_degree"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="C"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="poly_eval"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Assume no root and apply Liouville's theorem to 1/p.
sketch_steps: contradiction: Suppose that p has no complex root.
construct: Then 1/p is entire.
derive: Positive degree gives |p(z)| → ∞, so 1/p(z) → 0 as |z| → ∞.
apply_theorem: Liouville's theorem forces 1/p to be identically 0.
conclude: This is impossible, so p has a root.

drafts.canonical_statement: A function holomorphic on an open set U is analytic on U, that is, near each point of U it is the sum of a convergent power series.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="open_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="holomorphic_on"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="analytic_on"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Expand the Cauchy kernel into a geometric series on a circle around each point.
sketch_steps: setup: Choose a closed disc about a inside U.
apply_theorem: Cauchy's integral formula represents f(w) by a circle integral.
derive: The kernel 1/(z-w) is a uniformly convergent geometric series on the circle.
derive: Termwise integration gives a power series in w - a.
conclude: f is analytic near a.

drafts.canonical_statement: If f is holomorphic on the open disc |z-c| < r, then at each z in the disc the Taylor series of f at c converges to f(z).
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="holomorphic_on"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="open_disc"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="open_disc"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="series_has_sum"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="fns1" name="lambda"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="divide"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="iterated_complex_deriv"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="factorial"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="minus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use Cauchy's formula on an intermediate circle to get a series and identify the coefficients by termwise differentiation.
sketch_steps: setup: Choose ρ with |z-c| < ρ < r.
apply_theorem: Cauchy's integral formula on the circle of radius ρ applies.
derive: Expanding the kernel and integrating termwise gives a power series at c.
derive: Termwise differentiation identifies the coefficients as f^(n)(c)/n!.
conclude: The series converges to f(z) on the whole disc.

drafts.canonical_statement: The derivative of a function holomorphic on an open set U is again holomorphic on U.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="open_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="holomorphic_on"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="complex_deriv"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="holomorphic_on"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use the power series expansion of f near each point and differentiate it termwise.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Near a point a of U, f is the sum of a convergent power series.
derive: Termwise differentiation shows that f' is a convergent power series near a.
derive: A convergent power series is complex differentiable.
conclude: Since a is arbitrary, f' is holomorphic on U.

drafts.canonical_statement: If f and g are holomorphic on a connected open set U and the set where f = g has an accumulation point in U, then f = g on U.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="open_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="connected_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="holomorphic_on"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="holomorphic_on"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="accumulation_point_of_agreement"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Show that h = f - g vanishes near z₀ by its power series, then use a connectedness argument on the set where h vanishes locally.
sketch_steps: setup: Let h = f - g.
contradiction: If the power series of h at z₀ were nonzero, z₀ would be an isolated zero of h.
derive: So h vanishes identically near z₀.
construct: Let A be the set of points of U near which h vanishes identically.
derive: A is open, nonempty and closed in U.
conclude: By connectedness A = U, so f = g on U.

drafts.canonical_statement: A function holomorphic on an open set either vanishes identically near a given point z₀ of the set or has no zeros in a punctured neighbourhood of z₀.

drafts.proof_strategy: Factor out the lowest nonzero term of the power series at z₀.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Expand f in a power series at z₀.
case_split: If all coefficients vanish, f is identically zero near z₀.
construct: Otherwise write f(z) = (z-z₀)^k u(z) with u(z₀) ≠ 0.
derive: Continuity of u keeps it nonzero near z₀.
conclude: f has no zeros near z₀ other than z₀.

sketch_steps: setup: Assume that f is not constant and fix z₀ in an open subset s of U.
derive: Isolated zeros give a small circle about z₀ on which |f - f(z₀)| ≥ 2δ.
setup: For |w - f(z₀)| < δ consider h = f - w.
contradiction: If h had no zero inside, the maximum modulus principle for 1/h would fail at the centre.
conclude: Hence w is attained, and the image contains a disc about f(z₀).

drafts.proof_strategy: Multiply by (z-c)^2 to obtain a holomorphic function with a double zero and divide it out.
sketch_steps: construct: Define h(z) = (z-c)^2 f(z) with h(c) = 0.
derive: Boundedness of f gives h(z) = o(|z-c|), so h is complex differentiable at c with h'(c) = 0.
apply_theorem: The power series of h at c starts at degree 2.
construct: So h(z) = (z-c)^2 g(z) with g holomorphic near c.
conclude: g agrees with f off c and gives the extension.

sketch_steps: construct: Define g(z) = f(z)/(z-c) for z ≠ c and g(c) = f'(c).
derive: g is holomorphic off c and continuous at c by the definition of the derivative.
apply_theorem: The removable singularity theorem makes g holomorphic on U.
conclude: Since f(c) = 0, f(z) = (z-c)g(z) on U.

sketch_steps: setup: Take a closed disc D in U; the F_n converge uniformly on its boundary circle.
derive: Cauchy's formula passes to the limit f inside D.
derive: The integral representation shows that f is holomorphic inside D.
apply_theorem: On a smaller concentric closed disc, the derivative formula bounds |F_n' - f'| by a constant times the maximum of |F_n - f| on the circle.
conclude: Covering compact sets by finitely many discs gives locally uniform convergence of the derivatives.

sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The M-test gives uniform convergence of the partial sums on U.
derive: Each partial sum is a finite sum of holomorphic functions.
apply_theorem: The locally uniform limit of holomorphic functions is holomorphic.
conclude: The sum of the F_n is holomorphic on U.

conclude: Termwise differentiation gives g' = f on the disc.

drafts.canonical_statement: The real number √2 + √3 is irrational.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="notin"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="root"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="root"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>3</n1:OMI><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="Q"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Square the assumed rational value to force √6 to be rational.
sketch_steps: setup: Assume √2 + √3 = q with q rational.
derive: Squaring gives √6 = (q² - 5)/2, so √6 would be rational.
apply_theorem: 6 is not a perfect square, so √6 is irrational.
conclude: This contradiction shows √2 + √3 is irrational.

drafts.canonical_statement: The real number log_10 2 = log 2 / log 10 is irrational.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="notin"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="divide"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="transc1" name="ln"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="transc1" name="ln"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>10</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="Q"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Clear denominators to get an equation between powers and compare divisibility by 5.
sketch_steps: setup: Assume log_10 2 = a/b with positive integers a and b.
translate: Exponentiating gives 10^a = 2^b.
derive: Since a ≥ 1, 5 divides the left side.
contradiction: A power of 2 is not divisible by 5.

drafts.canonical_statement: Both sin 1° and cos 1° are irrational, where 1° = π/180.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="notin"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="transc1" name="sin"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="divide"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="pi"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>180</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="Q"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="notin"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="transc1" name="cos"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="divide"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="pi"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>180</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="Q"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Propagate rationality of cos θ to cos nθ by the three-term recurrence and reach cos 30°.
sketch_steps: induction: If cos θ is rational, then cos nθ is rational for all n by cos(n+1)θ = 2cos θ cos nθ - cos(n-1)θ.
case_split: Treat cos 1° and sin 1° separately.
derive: If cos 1° is rational, take θ = 1° and n = 30 to make cos 30° rational.
derive: If sin 1° is rational, then cos 2° = 1 - 2sin²1° is rational; take θ = 2° and n = 15.
contradiction: cos 30° = √3/2 is irrational.

drafts.canonical_statement: The real number cos 20° = cos(π/9) is irrational.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="notin"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="transc1" name="cos"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="divide"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="pi"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>9</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="Q"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use the triple-angle formula to get a cubic with integer coefficients and test its rational roots.
sketch_steps: derive: The triple-angle formula gives 4c³ - 3c = 1/2 for c = cos 20°.
translate: Then x = 2c is a root of x³ - 3x - 1.
setup: Write a rational x as p/q in lowest terms and clear denominators.
derive: Coprimality forces q = 1 and p = ±1.
contradiction: Neither 1 nor -1 is a root.

drafts.canonical_statement: The real cube root 2^(1/3) is irrational.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="notin"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="root"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI><n1:OMI>3</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="Q"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Assume a reduced fraction and derive that numerator and denominator are both even.
sketch_steps: setup: Assume 2^(1/3) = p/q in lowest terms.
derive: Then p³ = 2q³, so p is even.
derive: Writing p = 2r gives 4r³ = q³, so q is even.
contradiction: p and q were coprime.

drafts.canonical_statement: If rational numbers a, b, c satisfy a + b·2^(1/3) + c·(2^(1/3))² = 0, then a = b = c = 0.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="Q"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="Q"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="Q"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="root"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI><n1:OMI>3</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="root"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI><n1:OMI>3</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Eliminate t² between the relation and its multiple by t, then use irrationality of t twice.
sketch_steps: setup: Let t = 2^(1/3), so t³ = 2 and t is irrational.
derive: Multiply the relation by t and eliminate t² to get (ac - b²)t + (2c² - ab) = 0.
apply_theorem: Irrationality of t gives ac = b² and 2c² = ab.
derive: These imply b³ = 2c³.
contradiction: If c ≠ 0 then b/c = t would be rational.
conclude: Hence c = 0, then b = 0, then a = 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: Euler's number satisfies e > 2.7.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="lt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="divide"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>27</n1:OMI><n1:OMI>10</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="transc1" name="exp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Bound e from below by a partial sum of its exponential series.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: For the exponential series with positive terms, e is at least any partial sum.
derive: The sum of the first six terms is 163/60.
conclude: Since 163/60 > 2.7, we get e > 2.7.

drafts.canonical_statement: The circle constant satisfies 3.1 < π < 3.2.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="lt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="divide"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>31</n1:OMI><n1:OMI>10</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="pi"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="lt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="pi"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="divide"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>32</n1:OMI><n1:OMI>10</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Apply sin x < x at π/12 and x < tan x at π/24 with explicit surds.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Use sin x < x < tan x for 0 < x < π/2.
derive: The half-angle formula gives tan 7.5° = √6 + √2 - √3 - 2 < 0.133.
conclude: At x = π/24, π < 24 tan 7.5° < 3.2.

drafts.canonical_statement: The common logarithm of 2 satisfies 3/10 < log_10 2 < 1/3.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="lt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="divide"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>3</n1:OMI><n1:OMI>10</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="divide"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="transc1" name="ln"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="transc1" name="ln"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>10</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="lt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="divide"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="transc1" name="ln"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="transc1" name="ln"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>10</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="divide"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI><n1:OMI>3</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Compare integer powers of 2 and 10 and take logarithms.
sketch_steps: derive: 2^10 > 10³ gives 10 log 2 > 3 log 10.
derive: 2³ < 10 gives 3 log 2 < log 10.
conclude: Dividing by log 10 > 0 gives both bounds.

drafts.canonical_statement: The inequality π^e < e^π holds.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="lt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="pi"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="transc1" name="exp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="transc1" name="exp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="pi"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Apply log x < x - 1 at x = π/e and exponentiate.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: log x < x - 1 for x > 0 with x ≠ 1.
setup: Take x = π/e, which is not 1 because π > 3 > e.
derive: This gives e log π < π.
conclude: Exponentiating yields π^e < e^π.

drafts.canonical_statement: For every integer n ≥ 2, n⁴ + 4 is not prime.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="geq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="notin"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>4</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>4</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="P"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Factor by completing the square and check both factors exceed 1.
sketch_steps: derive: n⁴ + 4 = (n² + 2n + 2)(n² - 2n + 2).
derive: For n ≥ 2 the factor n² - 2n + 2 = (n-1)² + 1 is at least 2.
derive: The other factor is also at least 2.
conclude: A product of two integers at least 2 is not prime.

drafts.canonical_statement: The value n² + n + 41 is prime for all natural numbers n < 40, but it is not prime for n = 40.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="lt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>40</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>41</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="P"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="notin"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>40</n1:OMI><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>40</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>41</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="P"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Check the forty values by finite computation and factor the value at n = 40.
sketch_steps: derive: For n < 40 the value is at most 1601, which is below 41².
case_split: Check each of the forty values against primes up to 40.
derive: At n = 40 the value equals 41².
conclude: The value at n = 40 is composite.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime p, the number p² + 2 is prime if and only if p = 3.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="P"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="P"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>3</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Work modulo 3 to show p² + 2 is a multiple of 3 for p ≠ 3.
sketch_steps: case_split: Separate p = 3 from p ≠ 3.
derive: If p = 3 then p² + 2 = 11 is prime.
derive: If p ≠ 3 then p² ≡ 1 mod 3, so 3 divides p² + 2.
conclude: Since p² + 2 > 3, it is composite.

drafts.canonical_statement: If n ≥ 1 and 2^n + 1 is prime, then n is a power of 2.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="geq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="P"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Split off the odd part of n and factor x^m + 1 by x + 1.
sketch_steps: setup: Write n = 2^k m with m odd and let x = 2^(2^k).
contradiction: Assume m ≥ 3.
derive: For odd m, x + 1 divides x^m + 1 = 2^n + 1.
derive: The divisor x + 1 is strictly between 1 and 2^n + 1.
conclude: So m = 1 and n is a power of 2.

drafts.canonical_statement: If 2^n - 1 is prime, then n is prime.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the addition formula and coprimality of neighbours to transfer the Euclidean algorithm to indices.
sketch_steps: induction: Prove F_{m+n} = F_m F_{n+1} + F_{m-1} F_n.
derive: Consecutive Fibonacci numbers are coprime.
derive: Therefore gcd(F_{m+n}, F_n) = gcd(F_m, F_n).
induction: Run the Euclidean algorithm on the indices.
conclude: The algorithm ends at F_gcd(m,n).

drafts.canonical_statement: For n ≥ 1, the sum 1! + 2! + ... + n! is a perfect square if and only if n = 1 or n = 3.

drafts.proof_strategy: Check small n directly and use residues modulo 5 for n ≥ 4.
sketch_steps: case_split: Check n = 1, 2, 3 directly.
induction: For n ≥ 4 the sum is 3 modulo 5, since k! is divisible by 5 for k ≥ 5.
derive: Squares modulo 5 are 0, 1 or 4.
conclude: No sum with n ≥ 4 is a square.

drafts.canonical_statement: For every positive integer n, the product n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3) is not a perfect square.

drafts.proof_strategy: Trap the product strictly between two consecutive squares.
sketch_steps: setup: Let s = n² + 3n, so s ≥ 1.
derive: The product equals s(s + 2).
derive: Hence s² < s(s + 2) < (s + 1)².
conclude: No square lies strictly between consecutive squares.

drafts.canonical_statement: For positive integers a and b with a < b, a^b = b^a holds if and only if a = 2 and b = 4.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show a divides b, reduce to a^(k-1) = k and compare growth.
sketch_steps: derive: a^a divides b^a, so a divides b.
setup: Write b = ak with k ≥ 2.
derive: Taking a-th roots gives a^k = ak, so a^(k-1) = k.
derive: a = 1 is impossible, so a ≥ 2 and 2^(k-1) ≤ k.
conclude: Thus k = 2 and a = 2, which gives b = 4, and indeed 2⁴ = 4².

drafts.canonical_statement: For every natural number N there is a prime p > N with p ≡ 3 mod 4.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take a prime factor of 4·N! - 1 that is 3 modulo 4.
sketch_steps: construct: Let M = 4·N! - 1, which is 3 modulo 4.
derive: A product of primes that are 1 modulo 4 is 1 modulo 4, so M has a prime factor q ≡ 3 mod 4.
contradiction: If q ≤ N then q divides both M and M + 1.
conclude: Therefore q > N.

drafts.canonical_statement: For n ≥ 2, the harmonic sum 1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/n is not an integer.

drafts.proof_strategy: Isolate the unique term with the largest power of 2 in its denominator.
sketch_steps: setup: Take the largest e with 2^e ≤ n, so e ≥ 1.
derive: Among 1, ..., n only 2^e is divisible by 2^e.
construct: Multiply the sum by 2^(e-1)m, where m is the lcm of the odd parts.
derive: Every term becomes an integer except m/2.
conclude: The sum cannot be an integer.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use a - b | P(a) - P(b) with b = 0 or 1 according to the parity of n.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: For integers a, b, a - b divides P(a) - P(b).
case_split: Split on the parity of a hypothetical root n.
derive: If n is even, P(0) is even.
derive: If n is odd, P(1) is even.
conclude: Both contradict the hypotheses.

drafts.canonical_statement: If complex numbers x and y have integer sum and integer product, then x^n + y^n is an integer for every natural number n.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the three-term recurrence for power sums and induct on consecutive pairs.
sketch_steps: setup: Let S_n = x^n + y^n, so S_0 = 2 and S_1 = x + y.
derive: S_{n+2} = (x + y)S_{n+1} - xy S_n.
induction: If S_n and S_{n+1} are integers, then so is S_{n+2}.
conclude: Every S_n is an integer.

drafts.canonical_statement: For every natural number n, the floor of (2 + √3)^n is odd.

drafts.proof_strategy: Add the conjugate power to get an even integer and read off the floor.
sketch_steps: induction: S_{n+2} = 4S_{n+1} - S_n with S_0 = 2, S_1 = 4 shows S_n is even.
derive: For n ≥ 1, 0 < (2-√3)^n < 1.
derive: Therefore the floor of (2+√3)^n is S_n - 1.
conclude: S_n - 1 is odd, and n = 0 is checked directly.

drafts.canonical_statement: For every natural number n there is a natural number m with (√2 - 1)^n = √(m+1) - √m.

drafts.proof_strategy: Track (1+√2)^n = x + y√2 and use the norm equation x² - 2y² = (-1)^n.
sketch_steps: induction: Write (1+√2)^n = x + y√2 with natural numbers x and y.
derive: Then x² - 2y² = (-1)^n and (√2-1)^n = (-1)^n (x - y√2).
case_split: Split on the parity of n.
construct: For even n take m = 2y²; for odd n take m = x².
conclude: In each case the value equals √(m+1) - √m.

drafts.canonical_statement: For every natural number n, the product over k from 1 to n of |1 - exp(2πik/(n+1))| equals n + 1.

drafts.proof_strategy: Factor x^(n+1) - 1 over the roots of unity, divide by x - 1 and evaluate at 1.
sketch_steps: setup: Let ζ = exp(2πi/(n+1)).
derive: x^(n+1) - 1 = (x - 1) times the product of (x - ζ^k).
derive: Dividing by x - 1 gives 1 + x + ... + x^n as that product.
derive: Setting x = 1 gives a product equal to n + 1.
conclude: Taking absolute values gives the chord product.

drafts.canonical_statement: For every natural number n and real number x, |sin nx| ≤ n|sin x|.

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on n using the addition formula and |cos| ≤ 1.
sketch_steps: induction: The case n = 0 is trivial.
derive: Expand sin((n+1)x) by the addition formula.
derive: The triangle inequality and |cos| ≤ 1 give |sin((n+1)x)| ≤ |sin nx| + |sin x|.
conclude: The induction hypothesis gives the bound.

drafts.canonical_statement: For every n ≥ 1, the sum of 1/k² for 1 ≤ k ≤ n is at most 2 - 1/n.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare with a telescoping sum.
sketch_steps: derive: For k ≥ 2, 1/k² ≤ 1/(k-1) - 1/k.
derive: Summing from 2 to n telescopes to 1 - 1/n.
conclude: Adding the first term 1 gives 2 - 1/n.

drafts.canonical_statement: For every n ≥ 1, log(n+1) ≤ 1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/n ≤ 1 + log n.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare the sum with the integral of 1/x on unit intervals.
sketch_steps: derive: Monotonicity gives 1/(k+1) ≤ ∫_k^(k+1) dx/x ≤ 1/k.
derive: Summing the upper bound for 1 ≤ k ≤ n gives log(n+1) ≤ H_n.
derive: Summing the lower bound for 1 ≤ k ≤ n-1 gives H_n - 1 ≤ log n.
conclude: Both bounds hold.

drafts.canonical_statement: The integrals of x^n/(1+x) over [0,1] tend to 0 as n tends to infinity.

drafts.proof_strategy: Bound the integrand by x^n and squeeze.
sketch_steps: derive: On [0,1], 0 ≤ x^n/(1+x) ≤ x^n.
derive: Integrating gives 0 ≤ I_n ≤ 1/(n+1).
apply_theorem: The squeeze theorem applies since 1/(n+1) tends to 0.
conclude: I_n tends to 0.

sketch_steps: derive: Polynomial division gives x⁶ - 4x⁵ + 5x⁴ - 4x² + 4 - 4/(1+x²).
construct: An antiderivative is x⁷/7 - 2x⁶/3 + x⁵ - 4x³/3 + 4x - 4 arctan x.
apply_theorem: Apply the fundamental theorem of calculus on [0,1].
derive: arctan 1 = π/4 gives the value 22/7 - π.

drafts.proof_strategy: Expand the inner product of a sum and a difference.
sketch_steps: derive: H - a = b + c.
derive: (b + c)·(b - c) = ‖b‖² - ‖c‖² = 0.
derive: The other two pairs follow by the same calculation.
conclude: All three inner products vanish.
