drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the triangle inequality for integrals and use that the exponential kernel has modulus one.
sketch_steps: derive: The absolute value of the integral is at most the integral of the absolute value.
translate: The kernel has modulus 1, so the integrand's modulus is |f(v)|.
conclude: This gives the uniform bound independent of w.

drafts.proof_strategy: Periodize f, compute the Fourier coefficients of the periodization, and use convergence for summable coefficients.
sketch_steps: construct: Define the periodization g(x) = Σ f(x+n), which is continuous by the decay of f.
derive: Interchanging sum and integral gives that the m-th Fourier coefficient of g is Ff(m).
derive: The decay of Ff makes the coefficients summable.
apply_theorem: A continuous function with summable coefficients equals its Fourier series at every point.
conclude: This is the stated identity.

drafts.canonical_statement: A linear map f between normed spaces over ℝ or ℂ is continuous if and only if there is a constant C with ‖f x‖ ≤ C‖x‖ for all x.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use continuity at 0 to get a bound by scaling, and linearity to turn the bound into a Lipschitz estimate.
sketch_steps: setup: Assume f is continuous and pick δ > 0 with ‖f x‖ ≤ 1 whenever ‖x‖ ≤ δ.
derive: Scale a nonzero x to norm δ and use linearity to get ‖f x‖ ≤ (1/δ)‖x‖.
translate: Conversely, a bound C gives ‖f x - f y‖ = ‖f(x-y)‖ ≤ C‖x-y‖.
conclude: So f is Lipschitz, hence continuous, and the two conditions are equivalent.

drafts.canonical_statement: A linear map between normed spaces that is continuous at 0 is continuous everywhere.

drafts.proof_strategy: Translate continuity at a point to continuity at 0 using additivity.
sketch_steps: translate: For any a, write f(a+h) - f(a) = f(h).
apply_theorem: Continuity at 0 and f(0) = 0 give f(h) → 0 as h → 0.
conclude: Hence f is continuous at every a.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a bounded linear operator T and every vector x, ‖T x‖ ≤ ‖T‖‖x‖.

drafts.proof_strategy: The operator norm is the least admissible constant, and the infimum is attained because the condition is closed.
sketch_steps: setup: Recall that ‖T‖ is the infimum of the constants C ≥ 0 with ‖T x‖ ≤ C‖x‖ for all x.
derive: The inequality is preserved under limits of C, so the infimum is admissible.
conclude: Thus ‖T x‖ ≤ ‖T‖‖x‖ for every x.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a bounded linear operator T and M ≥ 0, ‖T‖ ≤ M if and only if ‖T x‖ ≤ M‖x‖ for all x.

drafts.proof_strategy: One direction uses the basic bound; the other uses that the norm is the infimum of admissible constants.
sketch_steps: derive: If ‖T‖ ≤ M, then ‖T x‖ ≤ ‖T‖‖x‖ ≤ M‖x‖.
translate: If the inequality holds for all x, then M is an admissible constant.
conclude: The infimum ‖T‖ of admissible constants is at most M.

drafts.canonical_statement: For bounded linear operators T from E to F and S from F to G, ‖S∘T‖ ≤ ‖S‖‖T‖.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the basic bound twice and use the characterization of the operator norm.
sketch_steps: derive: For every x, ‖S(T x)‖ ≤ ‖S‖‖T x‖ ≤ ‖S‖‖T‖‖x‖.
conclude: Hence ‖S‖‖T‖ is an admissible constant, so ‖S∘T‖ ≤ ‖S‖‖T‖.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare the supremum with the norm in both directions, normalizing vectors for the harder direction.
sketch_steps: setup: Let s be the supremum of ‖T x‖ over ‖x‖ ≤ 1.
derive: The bound ‖T x‖ ≤ ‖T‖‖x‖ gives s ≤ ‖T‖.
derive: Applying the definition of s to x/‖x‖ gives ‖T x‖ ≤ s‖x‖.
conclude: Thus ‖T‖ ≤ s and the two values agree.

drafts.canonical_statement: If F is a Banach space and E is a normed space, the space of bounded linear operators from E to F is complete in the operator norm.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="banach_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="complete_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="bounded_operator_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Build the limit pointwise from completeness of F, then upgrade to operator-norm convergence.
sketch_steps: setup: Take a Cauchy sequence T_n in operator norm.
derive: For each x, (T_n x) is Cauchy in F, so define T x as its limit.
derive: Linearity passes to the limit, so T is linear.
derive: Letting m → ∞ in ‖T_n x - T_m x‖ ≤ ε‖x‖ gives ‖T_n x - T x‖ ≤ ε‖x‖.
conclude: T is bounded and T_n → T in operator norm.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a Banach space, if the series of norms of a sequence converges, then the series itself converges unconditionally.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="banach_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="series_abs_summable"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="series_summable"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: The triangle inequality makes the sums over finite index sets a Cauchy net, and completeness gives the limit.
sketch_steps: setup: For a finite index set S, bound the norm of the sum over S by the sum of the norms.
derive: A tail of the convergent series of norms makes this bound small for every finite S beyond some N.
derive: So the sums over finite index sets form a Cauchy net.
conclude: Completeness of E gives unconditional convergence of the series.

drafts.canonical_statement: A normed space is complete if and only if for every sequence whose series of norms converges, the partial sums converge.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="complete_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="series_abs_summable"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="partial_sums_converge"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: For the converse, extract a rapidly converging subsequence of a Cauchy sequence and sum its differences.
sketch_steps: derive: Completeness makes partial sums of an absolutely summable sequence Cauchy, hence convergent.
setup: Conversely, take a Cauchy sequence u and a subsequence with consecutive differences at most 2^{-k}.
apply_theorem: The difference series is absolutely summable, so its partial sums converge by assumption.
derive: The partial sums telescope, so the subsequence converges.
conclude: A Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges, so E is complete.

drafts.canonical_statement: A finite-dimensional normed space over ℝ or ℂ is complete.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_dim_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="complete_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Transfer completeness from the coordinate space along a bicontinuous linear isomorphism.
sketch_steps: setup: Choose a basis and form the linear isomorphism with the coordinate space.
apply_theorem: Equivalence of norms makes this isomorphism continuous in both directions.
derive: A Cauchy sequence in E has Cauchy coordinates, which converge.
conclude: Applying the inverse gives a limit in E.

drafts.canonical_statement: Closed balls in a finite-dimensional normed space over ℝ or ℂ are compact; in particular the space is locally compact.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_dim_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="locally_compact_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="compact_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closed_ball"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Transport the Heine-Borel theorem from the coordinate space.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix the bicontinuous linear isomorphism between E and the coordinate space.
derive: A closed ball maps to a closed bounded set.
apply_theorem: Heine-Borel makes that image compact.
conclude: Pull compactness back; closed balls are compact neighbourhoods, so E is locally compact.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every linear map from a finite-dimensional normed space to a normed space is continuous.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_dim_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="linear_operator"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="continuous_map"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Bound f on a basis and compare the coordinate norm with the given norm.
sketch_steps: setup: Expand x in a basis as a sum of c_i e_i.
derive: The triangle inequality gives ‖f x‖ ≤ (max ‖f e_i‖) Σ|c_i|.
apply_theorem: Equivalence of norms gives Σ|c_i| ≤ C‖x‖.
conclude: So f is bounded and hence continuous.

drafts.canonical_statement: A finite-dimensional subspace of a normed space over ℝ or ℂ is closed.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="subspace_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_dim_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closed_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Finite-dimensional subspaces are complete, and complete subsets of a metric space are closed.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: K is complete because it is a finite-dimensional normed space.
setup: Take a sequence in K converging to x in E.
derive: The sequence is Cauchy in K, so it has a limit in K.
conclude: By uniqueness of limits x lies in K, so K is closed.

drafts.canonical_statement: Any two norms p and q on a finite-dimensional real vector space are equivalent, that is, there are positive constants C and D with p(x) ≤ C q(x) and q(x) ≤ D p(x) for all x.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare every norm with a fixed coordinate norm, using compactness of the unit sphere for the lower bound.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix a basis and the sup norm on coordinates.
derive: The triangle inequality gives r(x) ≤ a‖x‖, so r is continuous for the sup norm.
apply_theorem: The unit sphere is compact, so r attains a positive minimum m on it.
derive: Homogeneity gives m‖x‖ ≤ r(x).
conclude: Chain the comparisons for p and q to get the constants C and D.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a proper closed subspace F of a normed space and r < 1, there is x with ‖x‖ = 1 and ‖x - y‖ ≥ r for all y in F.

drafts.proof_strategy: Pick a near-best approximation of a point outside F and normalize the difference.
sketch_steps: setup: Assume r > 0, take z outside F and set d = dist(z, F) > 0.
construct: Choose y₀ in F with ‖z - y₀‖ < d/r and let x be the normalized difference.
derive: For y in F, ‖x - y‖‖z - y₀‖ is the distance from z to a point of F, so it is at least d.
conclude: Thus ‖x - y‖ ≥ d/‖z - y₀‖ > r.

drafts.canonical_statement: If the closed unit ball of a normed space is compact, then the space is finite dimensional.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="compact_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="unit_closed_ball"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_dim_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use the Riesz lemma to build a separated sequence in the unit ball when the dimension is infinite.
sketch_steps: contradiction: Assume E is infinite dimensional.
derive: The span of finitely many vectors is a proper closed subspace.
construct: Apply the Riesz lemma inductively to get unit vectors x_n with ‖x_n - x_m‖ ≥ 1/2.
derive: This sequence has no convergent subsequence.
conclude: This contradicts compactness of the closed unit ball.

drafts.canonical_statement: Hahn-Banach theorem. A bounded linear functional f on a subspace p of a normed space E over ℝ or ℂ extends to a bounded linear functional g on E with ‖g‖ = ‖f‖.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="subspace_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dual_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dual_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="restricts_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="norm"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="norm"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Extend one dimension at a time under a norm bound, then use Zorn's lemma; reduce the complex case to the real part.
sketch_steps: setup: Treat the real case with the sublinear bound p(x) = ‖f‖‖x‖.
construct: For x outside the domain, choose a value c compatible with the bound on the larger subspace.
apply_theorem: Zorn's lemma gives a maximal norm-bounded extension.
contradiction: A maximal extension with proper domain could be extended further.
case_split: For complex scalars, apply the real case to the real part and rebuild g.
conclude: The resulting g extends f and satisfies ‖g‖ = ‖f‖.

drafts.canonical_statement: Open mapping theorem. A surjective bounded linear operator between Banach spaces is an open map.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="banach_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="banach_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="bounded_operator"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="surjective_on"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="open_map"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the Baire category theorem to get an interior point of the closure of an image, then remove the closure by successive approximation.
sketch_steps: setup: Write F as the union of closures of T(nB), where B is the unit ball of E.
apply_theorem: The Baire category theorem gives a closure with nonempty interior.
derive: By symmetry and linearity, a ball around 0 lies in the closure of T(B).
construct: Solve T x = y by a geometric series of approximate preimages using completeness of E.
conclude: A ball around 0 lies in T(B), and translation gives openness of T.

drafts.canonical_statement: Closed graph theorem. A linear map between Banach spaces whose graph is closed in the product is continuous.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="banach_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="banach_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="linear_operator"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closed_graph"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="continuous_map"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the bounded inverse theorem to the projection from the graph onto E.
sketch_steps: setup: The closed graph G is a closed subspace of the Banach space E×F, hence a Banach space.
derive: The first projection is a bounded linear bijection from G to E.
apply_theorem: The bounded inverse theorem makes x ↦ (x, f x) continuous.
conclude: Composing with the second projection shows f is continuous.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the Baire category theorem to find a ball on which the family is uniformly bounded, then translate it to the origin.
sketch_steps: setup: Define closed sets A_n of points where all g_i are bounded by n.
apply_theorem: Pointwise boundedness gives E as the union of A_n, so Baire yields a ball inside some A_n.
derive: For small h, g_i h = g_i(a+h) - g_i a has norm at most 2n.
conclude: Scaling gives ‖g_i‖ ≤ 2n/r for all i.

drafts.proof_strategy: Embed the dual ball into a product of compact discs and apply Tychonoff's theorem.
sketch_steps: construct: Map f to the family of values (f(x)) in the product of discs of radius r‖x‖.
apply_theorem: Tychonoff's theorem makes the product compact.
translate: The weak-* topology on the ball coincides with the product topology.
derive: Linearity is a closed condition, so the image is closed.
conclude: The ball is homeomorphic to a closed subset of a compact space, hence compact.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the orthogonal complement of the kernel to produce the representing vector, then compare norms via Cauchy-Schwarz.
sketch_steps: case_split: The case f = 0 is settled by y = 0.
apply_theorem: For f ≠ 0, the projection theorem gives a unit vector z orthogonal to the closed kernel.
derive: f(x)z - f(z)x lies in the kernel, so its inner product with z vanishes.
construct: This gives f(x) = ⟨conj(f z) z, x⟩.
derive: Uniqueness follows by testing the difference of two representers on itself.
conclude: Cauchy-Schwarz and f(y) = ‖y‖² give ‖f‖ = ‖y‖.

drafts.proof_strategy: Get the lower bound from the spectral mapping of powers and the upper bound from holomorphy of the resolvent via the power series radius.
sketch_steps: derive: λ ∈ σ(a) implies λ^n ∈ σ(a^n), so |λ| ≤ ‖a^n‖^{1/n}.
derive: Hence r(a) ≤ liminf ‖a^n‖^{1/n}.
apply_theorem: The map z ↦ (1 - z a)^{-1} is holomorphic on |z| < 1/r(a).
translate: Its power series is the sum of z^n a^n.
apply_theorem: The Cauchy-Hadamard formula gives limsup ‖a^n‖^{1/n} ≤ r(a).
conclude: Liminf and limsup agree with r(a).

apply_theorem: By the open mapping theorem T is an open map.
translate: For open U, the preimage of U under S equals T(U), which is open.
conclude: So S is continuous, that is, bounded.

derive: Then x = (‖y‖/δ) z satisfies T x = y and ‖x‖ ≤ (1/δ)‖y‖.
conclude: C = 1/δ works, with x = 0 for y = 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: The pointwise limit of a sequence of bounded linear operators from a Banach space to a normed space is a bounded linear operator.

sketch_steps: derive: Linearity of f follows by passing to the limit.
derive: Each sequence (g_n x) converges, so it is bounded.
apply_theorem: The Banach-Steinhaus theorem gives ‖g_n‖ ≤ C for all n.
conclude: Taking limits in ‖g_n x‖ ≤ C‖x‖ gives ‖f x‖ ≤ C‖x‖.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a nonzero vector x of a normed space over ℝ or ℂ there is a bounded linear functional g with ‖g‖ = 1 and g(x) = ‖x‖.

drafts.proof_strategy: Define the functional on the line through x and extend it by Hahn-Banach.
sketch_steps: construct: On the span of x, set f(c x) = c‖x‖.
derive: Since |f(c x)| = ‖c x‖, f has norm 1.
apply_theorem: The Hahn-Banach theorem extends f to g on E with ‖g‖ = 1.
conclude: Then g(x) = f(x) = ‖x‖.

drafts.canonical_statement: The canonical map J from a normed space E to its double dual, given by J(x)(f) = f(x), is isometric, that is ‖J(x)‖ = ‖x‖.

drafts.proof_strategy: The upper bound is immediate, and a norming functional gives the lower bound.
sketch_steps: derive: |J(x)(f)| = |f(x)| ≤ ‖f‖‖x‖ gives ‖J(x)‖ ≤ ‖x‖.
apply_theorem: For x ≠ 0, Hahn-Banach provides g with ‖g‖ = 1 and g(x) = ‖x‖.
derive: Evaluating J(x) at g gives ‖J(x)‖ ≥ ‖x‖.
conclude: Hence ‖J(x)‖ = ‖x‖ for all x.

drafts.proof_strategy: Subtract from y its component along x and use nonnegativity of the squared norm.
sketch_steps: case_split: The case x = 0 is trivial.
construct: For x ≠ 0, let c = ⟨x, y⟩/‖x‖² so that y - c x is orthogonal to x.
derive: Expanding 0 ≤ ‖y - c x‖² gives |⟨x, y⟩|² ≤ ‖x‖²‖y‖².
conclude: Take square roots.

derive: Therefore (v_n) is Cauchy.
derive: Completeness and closedness give a limit v in K with ‖u - v‖ = d.
conclude: The same inequality for two minimizers shows they coincide.

construct: Set z = x - y.

conclude: A vector orthogonal to itself is 0, so the decomposition is unique.

drafts.proof_strategy: Expand the squared distance along directions of K for one implication and use Pythagoras for the other.
sketch_steps: derive: Expand ‖u - v - t w‖² for w in K and scalars t.
derive: Minimality forces ⟨u - v, w⟩ = 0 by letting t be small.
apply_theorem: Conversely, orthogonality and Pythagoras give ‖u - w‖² = ‖u - v‖² + ‖v - w‖².
conclude: Hence v is a best approximation exactly when u - v is orthogonal to K.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a closed subspace K of a Hilbert space, the orthogonal complement of the orthogonal complement of K equals K.

drafts.proof_strategy: Decompose an element of the double complement by the projection theorem and show the orthogonal part vanishes.
sketch_steps: derive: The inclusion of K in the double complement follows from the definition.
apply_theorem: Decompose x in the double complement as y + z with y in K and z in K⊥.
derive: ‖z‖² = ⟨x, z⟩ - ⟨y, z⟩ = 0.
conclude: Thus x = y lies in K.

sketch_steps: construct: For a finite S, let y be the sum of ⟨v_i, x⟩ v_i over S.
derive: Orthonormality makes x - y orthogonal to y.
apply_theorem: Pythagoras gives ‖x‖² ≥ ‖y‖² = Σ_S |⟨v_i, x⟩|².
conclude: Nonnegative terms with bounded finite sums are summable with sum at most ‖x‖².

derive: x - y is orthogonal to every b_i, so completeness of the family gives x = y.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take a maximal orthonormal subset by Zorn's lemma and use the projection theorem to rule out a proper closed span.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Zorn's lemma gives a maximal orthonormal subset w.
setup: Let K be the closure of the span of w and suppose K is proper.
apply_theorem: The projection theorem gives a unit vector orthogonal to K.
contradiction: Adding this vector to w contradicts maximality.
conclude: Hence the span of w is dense.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the Riesz representation theorem to x ↦ ⟨y, T x⟩ for each fixed y.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix y and consider the bounded functional x ↦ ⟨y, T x⟩.
apply_theorem: The Riesz representation theorem gives a unique S y.
derive: Uniqueness forces S to be linear.
derive: ‖S y‖² = ⟨y, T S y⟩ ≤ ‖y‖‖T‖‖S y‖ gives boundedness.
conclude: Uniqueness of S again follows from uniqueness of representers.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a bounded linear operator T between Hilbert spaces, ‖T*‖ = ‖T‖.

drafts.proof_strategy: Estimate ‖T* y‖² by the defining identity and use T** = T for the reverse inequality.
sketch_steps: derive: ‖T* y‖² = ⟨y, T T* y⟩ ≤ ‖y‖‖T‖‖T* y‖.
derive: Hence ‖T*‖ ≤ ‖T‖.
apply_theorem: Since T** = T, the same inequality gives ‖T‖ ≤ ‖T*‖.
conclude: The norms agree.

drafts.proof_strategy: Combine submultiplicativity with the identity ‖T x‖² = ⟨T*T x, x⟩.
sketch_steps: derive: ‖T*T‖ ≤ ‖T*‖‖T‖ = ‖T‖².
derive: ‖T x‖² = ⟨T*T x, x⟩ ≤ ‖T*T‖‖x‖².
conclude: Taking the supremum over unit vectors gives ‖T‖² ≤ ‖T*T‖.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a bounded linear operator T between Hilbert spaces, the orthogonal complement of the range of T equals the kernel of T*.

drafts.proof_strategy: Rewrite orthogonality to the range through the adjoint identity.
sketch_steps: translate: y in (ran T)⊥ means ⟨y, T x⟩ = 0 for all x.
derive: The adjoint identity turns this into ⟨T* y, x⟩ = 0 for all x.
conclude: This holds exactly when T* y = 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: If compact operators from a normed space to a Banach space converge in operator norm, then the limit is a compact operator.

drafts.proof_strategy: Approximate the image of the unit ball by images under compact operators and use total boundedness.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix ε and choose n with ‖T_n - T‖ < ε.
apply_theorem: Compactness of T_n covers its image of the unit ball by finitely many ε-balls.
derive: The same centres with radius 2ε cover the image under T.
conclude: Total boundedness and completeness of F give relative compactness.

drafts.canonical_statement: The composition S∘T of bounded linear operators is compact whenever S or T is compact.

drafts.proof_strategy: A continuous image of a compact set is compact, and a bounded operator sends bounded sets to bounded sets.
sketch_steps: case_split: Treat compact T and compact S separately.
derive: If T is compact, S maps the compact set containing T(ball) to a compact set.
derive: If S is compact, T(ball) is bounded and S sends it to a relatively compact set.
conclude: In both cases S∘T is compact.

drafts.canonical_statement: A bounded linear operator with finite-dimensional range is compact.

drafts.proof_strategy: The image of the unit ball is inside a closed ball of the finite-dimensional range, which is compact.
sketch_steps: derive: ‖x‖ ≤ 1 gives ‖T x‖ ≤ ‖T‖, so T(ball) lies in a closed ball of the range R.
apply_theorem: Closed balls in a finite-dimensional normed space are compact.
conclude: The inclusion of R into F preserves compactness, so T is compact.

drafts.proof_strategy: Absolute convergence from the geometric bound and the telescoping identity for partial sums.
sketch_steps: derive: ‖t^n‖ ≤ ‖t‖^n for n ≥ 1 makes the series absolutely convergent.
apply_theorem: Completeness gives a sum S.
derive: Partial sums satisfy (1 - t) S_n = S_n (1 - t) = 1 - t^{n+1}.
conclude: Since t^{n+1} → 0, taking limits gives (1 - t) S = S (1 - t) = 1.

drafts.canonical_statement: The set of bounded linear operators from a Banach space E to a normed space F that have a bounded inverse is open in the operator norm.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="banach_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="open_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="invertible_operators"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Factor a nearby operator through T₀ and apply the Neumann series.
sketch_steps: setup: Let T₀ be invertible and T satisfy ‖T - T₀‖ < 1/‖T₀⁻¹‖.
translate: Write T = T₀(I - T₀⁻¹(T₀ - T)).
apply_theorem: The Neumann series inverts I - T₀⁻¹(T₀ - T).
conclude: T is invertible, so a ball about T₀ consists of invertible operators.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a bounded linear operator T on a Banach space, λ is in the spectrum of T if and only if λI - T is not bijective.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the bounded inverse theorem to identify invertibility with bijectivity.
sketch_steps: translate: λ is outside the spectrum when λI - T is invertible in the ring of bounded operators.
derive: An invertible operator is bijective.
apply_theorem: The bounded inverse theorem gives a bounded inverse for a bijective operator.
conclude: Taking the contrapositive gives the stated equivalence.

drafts.canonical_statement: The spectrum of an element of a complex Banach algebra is compact.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="complex_banach_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="compact_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="spectrum_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Closedness from openness of the units and boundedness from the Neumann series.
sketch_steps: derive: The resolvent set is the preimage of the open set of units under a continuous map, so σ(a) is closed.
apply_theorem: The Neumann series makes z1 - a invertible when |z| is larger than ‖a‖‖1‖.
derive: Hence σ(a) is bounded.
conclude: A closed bounded subset of ℂ is compact.

drafts.canonical_statement: The spectrum of every element of a nontrivial complex Banach algebra is nonempty.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Liouville's theorem to the resolvent composed with functionals.
sketch_steps: contradiction: Suppose σ(a) is empty, so the resolvent is defined on all of ℂ.
derive: The resolvent is entire and tends to 0 at infinity.
apply_theorem: By Liouville and Hahn-Banach the resolvent vanishes identically.
conclude: An invertible element would be 0, which contradicts nontriviality of A.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show any λ with |λ| > ‖a‖ lies in the resolvent set via the Neumann series.
sketch_steps: setup: Take |λ| > ‖a‖.
apply_theorem: The Neumann series inverts 1 - a/λ because ‖a/λ‖ < 1.
derive: Then λ1 - a is invertible, so λ is not in σ(a).
conclude: Elements of σ(a) satisfy |λ| ≤ ‖a‖, and the supremum is at most ‖a‖.

derive: Summing, the inner product terms cancel.
conclude: The sum equals 3 PG² + GA² + GB² + GC².

sketch_steps: translate: The vertices lie on the circumcircle, so each is at distance R from O.
apply_theorem: Points equidistant from two points are exactly the perpendicular bisector.
conclude: O lies on each perpendicular bisector.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a plane, a point on the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC of a triangle ABC also lies on that of CA and equals the circumcenter.

drafts.proof_strategy: Transitivity of equal distances gives the third bisector; two non-parallel lines in a plane meet in one point.
sketch_steps: translate: Membership in the two bisectors means PA = PB and PB = PC.
derive: Hence PA = PC, so P lies on the third bisector.
derive: The two bisectors are not parallel because AB and BC are not parallel.
conclude: They meet in one point, which is the circumcenter, so P = O.

sketch_steps: setup: Let D be the point antipodal to B, so BD = 2R.
case_split: Treat D = C, D on the same side of BC as A, and D on the opposite side.
apply_theorem: The inscribed angle theorem gives sin∠BDC = sin∠BAC.
derive: In right triangle BCD, BC = 2R sin∠BDC.
conclude: Divide by the nonzero value sin∠BAC.

sketch_steps: setup: Put u = AB and w = AC with u·w = 0.
derive: |u + w| = |w - u|, so MA = BC/2.
derive: MB = MC = BC/2 since M is the midpoint.
conclude: M lies in the plane of the triangle and is equidistant from the vertices, so it is the circumcenter.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the angle bisector theorem twice to locate I on the cevian AD.
sketch_steps: setup: Let D be the intersection of line AI and side BC.
apply_theorem: The angle bisector theorem gives BD:DC = c:b and BD = ac/(b+c).
apply_theorem: In triangle ABD it gives AI:ID = (b+c):a.
derive: Hence OI = (a OA + b OB + c OC)/(a+b+c) for any O.
conclude: Taking O = I gives the identity.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the bisector characterisation for equal distances and acute angles on the external bisectors for positions.
sketch_steps: translate: I_a lies on the internal bisector at A and external bisectors at B and C.
derive: A point on a bisector is equidistant from the two lines, so the three distances agree.
derive: On the side of AB containing C, the internal bisector ray at A and the external bisector ray at B make angles with AB summing to less than π, so they meet there at I_a.
derive: The external bisector makes acute angles with ray BC and the extension of AB, which fixes D and F; symmetrically at C.
derive: I_a is inside angle A, which gives the two same-side statements.
contradiction: If I_a were on A's side of BC it would be inside angle B.
conclude: All claimed positions hold.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use symmetry of the two tangents from each vertex, and the reversal of ray BA and ray BF.
sketch_steps: setup: Take the circle touching side BC and the extensions of AB and AC at D, F, E.
derive: Tangents from A are symmetric about AI_a, which gives the internal bisector.
derive: Tangents from B are symmetric about BI_a, so ∡FBI_a = ∡I_aBC.
derive: Rays BA and BF are opposite, adding π.
conclude: The same argument applies at C.

sketch_steps: derive: Line AI is the internal bisector at A because the tangents from A are AB and AC.
derive: Line AI_a is the same bisector for the excircle.
conclude: The internal bisector line through A is unique, so the three points are collinear.

derive: Likewise BD = BF and CD = CE.
derive: AF = AB + BF, AE = AC + CE and BC = BD + DC by the positions of the touchpoints.
conclude: 2 AF = AB + BC + CA.

drafts.proof_strategy: Construct H from the circumcenter as the sum of the three vertex vectors and check perpendicularity.
sketch_steps: setup: Put O at the circumcenter so the three vertex vectors have equal length.
construct: Define H by OH = a + b + c.
derive: AH·BC = |c|² - |b|² = 0, and cyclically.
conclude: H lies on all three altitudes, which therefore concur.

drafts.proof_strategy: The three inner products sum to zero identically.
sketch_steps: setup: Write all vectors from P as x, y, z.
derive: x·(z-y) + y·(x-z) + z·(y-x) = 0 identically.
conclude: Two vanishing terms force the third to vanish.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a plane, a point P with (P - A)·(B - C) = 0 and (P - B)·(C - A) = 0 for a triangle ABC is the orthocenter.

drafts.proof_strategy: Two altitudes are non-parallel lines in the plane, so they meet in one point.
sketch_steps: translate: The two conditions place P on the altitudes from A and B.
derive: H lies on the same two altitudes.
derive: The altitudes are not parallel because BC and CA are not parallel.
conclude: P = H.

drafts.canonical_statement: If ∠BAC = π/2 in a triangle ABC, then the orthocenter equals A.

drafts.proof_strategy: The two legs are themselves altitudes.
sketch_steps: derive: Since AB ⟂ AC, the altitude from B is line BA.
derive: The altitude from C is line CA.
conclude: These altitudes meet at A, so H = A.

derive: AH = OB + OC.
derive: OM = (OB + OC)/2.
conclude: AH = 2 OM, and lengths follow.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the parallelogram law to the vectors from the circumcenter.
sketch_steps: derive: AH = OB + OC and BC = OC - OB.
apply_theorem: The parallelogram law gives |OB + OC|² + |OC - OB|² = 2|OB|² + 2|OC|².

derive: NM = -OA/2 and NK = OA/2, so M and K lie on the circle and are antipodal.
derive: DK ⟂ BC and DM is parallel to BC, so DK·DM = 0.
apply_theorem: Thales' theorem puts D on the circle with diameter MK.
conclude: Permute the vertices for all nine points.

drafts.canonical_statement: Let S be a sphere (circle in the plane) whose centre lies in the plane of triangle ABC and which passes through the midpoints of the three sides. Then its centre is the midpoint of the circumcenter O and the orthocenter H, and its radius is R/2 where R is the circumradius.

drafts.proof_strategy: Express the points in the basis AB, AC and turn collinearity into a vanishing determinant.
sketch_steps: setup: Let u = AB and w = AC, which are linearly independent.
derive: FD = (1-r-t)u + r w and FE = -t u + (1-s) w.
translate: Collinearity gives FD = p v and FE = q v, hence two scalar equations.
derive: Not both p and q vanish, so (1-r-t)(1-s) + rt = 0.
conclude: Expanding gives rst + (1-r)(1-s)(1-t) = 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Rewrite the hypothesis as a vanishing determinant and exhibit the proportionality case by case.
sketch_steps: setup: Compute FD and FE in terms of u = AB and w = AC.
translate: The hypothesis is (1-r-t)(1-s) + rt = 0.
case_split: Treat t ≠ 0, then t = 0 with s = 1, then t = 0 with s ≠ 1.
derive: In each case FD and FE are multiples of one vector.
conclude: D, E, F are collinear.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use barycentric coordinates of p, turn each incidence into an equation, and multiply.
sketch_steps: setup: Write p = λA + αB + γC with λ + α + γ = 1.
translate: The three incidences give αr = γ(1-r), λ(1-s) = γs, λt = α(1-t).
contradiction: If any of λ, α, γ vanishes, then one of r, s, t vanishes.
derive: Hence none of r, s, t equals 1.
conclude: Multiplying and cancelling λαγ gives the product 1.

sketch_steps: derive: The product condition forces r, s, t and the denominators to be nonzero and rst = (1-r)(1-s)(1-t).
setup: Write p = λA + αB + γC with sum 1.
translate: The two incidences give αr = γ(1-r) and λ(1-s) = γs.
derive: γ ≠ 0, and substitution gives λt = α(1-t).
conclude: p = γC + (λ+α)F, so p lies on line CF.

drafts.proof_strategy: Convert the signed Ceva identity to lengths by taking absolute values.
sketch_steps: setup: Parametrise D, E, F by r, s, t, none equal to 0 or 1.
derive: BD/DC = |r/(1-r)|, and likewise for the other two ratios.
apply_theorem: Signed Ceva gives the product of signed ratios equal to 1.
conclude: Taking absolute values gives the product of lengths equal to 1.

drafts.proof_strategy: Chase directed angles modulo π through the circles with diameters XB and XC.
sketch_steps: case_split: If X is a vertex, or D = F, or D = E, at most two distinct points remain.
setup: Otherwise X lies on no side line, and we measure directed angles between lines modulo π.
derive: D and F lie on the circle with diameter XB, so (DF, DX) = (BA, BX); the cases D = B and F = B are checked directly.
derive: The same argument at C gives (DE, DX) = (CA, CX).
apply_theorem: Since A, X, B, C are concyclic, (BA, BX) = (CA, CX).
conclude: Lines DF and DE pass through D and make the same directed angle with DX, so they coincide.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a Euclidean plane, if A, B, X, Y lie on a circle, A ≠ B, and X, Y lie strictly on the same side of line AB, then ∠AXB = ∠AYB.

drafts.proof_strategy: Isosceles triangles on the radii give the central angle relation in every position of the center; the inscribed angle then depends only on the side of AB.
sketch_steps: setup: Let U be X or Y and let U' be the other end of the diameter through U.
derive: The isosceles triangle OUP gives angle POU' = 2 angle PUO for P on the circle, P ≠ U.
case_split: If O lies on AB, the triangle angle sum gives angle AUB = π/2.
case_split: If A, B lie on opposite sides of UO, the point where AB meets UO decides between angle AOB = 2 angle AUB and angle AOB + 2 angle AUB = 2π.
case_split: If A, B lie on one closed side of UO, differences of angles give angle AOB = 2 angle AUB, and O, U lie on the same side of AB.
conclude: X and Y have the same position relative to O and AB, so their angles are equal.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a Euclidean plane, if A ≠ B, X and Y lie strictly on the same side of line AB, and ∠AXB = ∠AYB, then A, B, X, Y lie on a common circle.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare Y with the point where the ray from the midpoint of AB through Y meets the circle ABX; a point inside a triangle sees the opposite side under a larger angle.
sketch_steps: setup: Take the circle through A, B, X and the midpoint M of AB.
construct: The ray from M through Y meets the circle at one point Z on the same side as X.
apply_theorem: The inscribed angle theorem gives angle AZB = angle AXB = angle AYB.
derive: A point inside a triangle ABQ sees AB under a larger angle than Q does, by two exterior angles.
contradiction: If Y ≠ Z, one of them lies inside the triangle formed with the other, so the two angles differ.
conclude: Y = Z, so the four points are concyclic.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a Euclidean plane, if A, B, X lie on a circle with center O, A ≠ B, and O, X lie strictly on the same side of line AB, then ∠AOB = 2∠AXB.

drafts.proof_strategy: Draw the diameter through X; isosceles triangles on the radii give a doubling relation on each side, and the position of A, B relative to the diameter decides whether to add or subtract.
sketch_steps: setup: Let X' be the other end of the diameter through X.
derive: The isosceles triangle OXP gives angle POX' = 2 angle PXO for P on the circle, P ≠ X.
case_split: If A, B lie on one closed side of XO, both angles are differences, so angle AOB = 2 angle AXB.
derive: If A, B lie on opposite sides of XO, the crossing point D of AB and XO lies between O and X' because O, X are on the same side of AB.
conclude: Then both angles are sums, so again angle AOB = 2 angle AXB.

drafts.proof_strategy: The segment OX crosses the chord AB, so the diameter through X splits both angles; isosceles triangles on the radii relate the parts.
sketch_steps: setup: Let X' be the other end of the diameter through X and D the point where segment OX meets line AB.
derive: D lies inside the circle, so it lies strictly between A and B.
derive: The isosceles triangles on OA and OB give angle AOX' = 2 angle AXO and angle BOX' = 2 angle BXO.
derive: Since D lies on AB, angle AOB and angle AXB split along XO.
conclude: Using angle AOX = π - angle AOX' gives angle AOB + 2 angle AXB = 2π.

drafts.canonical_statement: If AB is a diameter of a sphere (a circle in the plane) in a real inner product affine space and X ≠ A, B, then ∠AXB = π/2 if and only if X lies on the sphere.

drafts.proof_strategy: Expand the inner product of XA and XB from the center; it equals |XO|^2 - r^2.
sketch_steps: setup: Let O be the midpoint of AB and write a = A-O, x = X-O, so B-O = -a.
derive: The inner product of A-X and B-X equals |x|^2 - r^2.
translate: For nonzero vectors, a right angle means inner product zero.
conclude: This holds exactly when |x| = r.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a Euclidean plane, if A, B, X lie on a circle, X ≠ A, B and ∠AXB = π/2, then AB is a diameter of the circle.

drafts.proof_strategy: The midpoint of AB is equidistant from A, B, X, and in the plane the circumcenter is unique.
sketch_steps: setup: Let M be the midpoint of AB.
derive: The right angle gives |MX| = |MA| = |MB|.
derive: A, B, X are not collinear, so the plane contains only one point equidistant from them.
conclude: The center equals M, so AB is a diameter.

derive: This inner product is cos of angle AXB times a positive number.
translate: The sign of the cosine on [0,π] decides acute or obtuse.

apply_theorem: The inscribed angle theorem transfers the four parts to angles of triangles ABC and ACD.

apply_theorem: The opposite angle theorem gives angle ABC + angle CD'A = π.
derive: The hypothesis then gives angle CD'A = angle CDA.
apply_theorem: The converse of the inscribed angle theorem puts D on the circle through A, C, D'.
conclude: That circle is the circle through A, B, C.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare X with the point A' opposite A; the right triangle ABA' gives the formula at A', and the inscribed angle theorem transfers the sine to X.
sketch_steps: setup: Let A' be the other end of the diameter through A.
case_split: If B = A', then AB = 2r and Thales gives a right angle at X.
derive: Otherwise Thales makes ABA' a right triangle, so |AB| = 2r sin of angle AA'B.
case_split: X and A' on the same side give equal angles; on opposite sides they give supplementary angles.
conclude: In both cases the sines agree, so |AB| = 2r sin of angle AXB.

drafts.canonical_statement: If A, B lie on a sphere with center O (a circle in the plane) and M is the midpoint of AB, then the inner product of O-M and B-A is zero.

drafts.proof_strategy: Expand the inner product from the center using equal radii.
sketch_steps: setup: Write a = A-O, b = B-O with equal norms.
derive: O-M = -(a+b)/2 and B-A = b-a.
conclude: The inner product equals (|a|^2-|b|^2)/2 = 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: If A ≠ B lie on a sphere with center O (a circle in the plane), H lies on line AB, and O-H is orthogonal to B-A, then H is the midpoint of AB.

drafts.proof_strategy: The midpoint already satisfies the orthogonality, and two such points on the line must coincide.
sketch_steps: derive: The midpoint M satisfies that M-O is orthogonal to B-A.
derive: Subtracting gives that M-H is orthogonal to B-A.
derive: M-H is a multiple k(B-A), so k|B-A|^2 = 0.
conclude: A ≠ B forces k = 0, so H = M.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the parallelogram law to the two radius vectors.
sketch_steps: setup: Write a = A-O, b = B-O, both of norm r.
translate: M-O = (a+b)/2 and A-B = a-b.
apply_theorem: The parallelogram law gives |a+b|^2 + |a-b|^2 = 4r^2.
conclude: Dividing by 4 gives the claim.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the law of cosines at the center and injectivity of cosine on [0,π].
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The law of cosines gives each squared chord as 2r^2 - 2r^2 cos of the central angle.
derive: Equal angles give equal squared chords.
derive: Equal chords and r > 0 give equal cosines.
conclude: Cosine is injective on [0,π].

drafts.canonical_statement: For points A, B on a sphere of radius r (a circle in the plane), |AB| ≤ 2r, and |AB| = 2r if and only if AB is a diameter.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="on_circle"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="on_circle"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="leq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dist_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dist_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="is_diameter"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use the triangle inequality for the bound and the parallelogram law for the equality case.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The triangle inequality through O gives |AB| ≤ 2r.
derive: A diameter has length 2r.
derive: If |AB| = 2r, the parallelogram law gives |a+b| = 0 for a = A-O, b = B-O.
conclude: Then O is the midpoint of AB.

drafts.canonical_statement: If A ≠ B lie on a sphere with center O and radius r (a circle in the plane) and H lies on line AB, then H is strictly between A and B if and only if |HO| < r.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="on_circle"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="on_circle"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="on_line"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="strictly_between"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="lt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dist_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Compute |HO|^2 - r^2 as (t^2-t)|B-A|^2 along the line.
sketch_steps: setup: Write H = A + t(B-A).
derive: Equal radii give 2<x,u> + |u|^2 = 0 for x = A-O, u = B-A.
derive: Hence |HO|^2 - r^2 = (t^2-t)|u|^2.
conclude: This is negative exactly when 0 < t < 1.

drafts.canonical_statement: If T lies on a sphere with center O and radius r > 0 (a circle in the plane) and X ≠ T, then line TX is tangent at T if and only if ∠XTO = π/2.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="gt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="on_circle"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="tangent_to_circle_at"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="euclid_angle"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="divide"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="pi"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Translate the right angle into orthogonality of X-T and T-O and scale along the line.
sketch_steps: translate: The angle is π/2 exactly when X-T is orthogonal to T-O.
derive: Tangency gives this by taking U = X.
derive: Conversely every point of the line has the form T + t(X-T).
conclude: So all points of the line satisfy the orthogonality.

drafts.canonical_statement: If T lies on a sphere with center O (a circle in the plane) and X ≠ T, then line TX is orthogonal to the radius at T if and only if T is the only common point of the line and the sphere.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="on_circle"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="tangent_to_circle_at"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="on_line"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="on_circle"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Solve the quadratic for the parameter of the common points of the line and the sphere.
sketch_steps: setup: Parametrize the line as T + tv with v = X-T.
derive: Common points correspond to t(2<x,v> + t|v|^2) = 0 with x = T-O.
derive: The only solution is t = 0 exactly when <x,v> = 0.
conclude: That condition is the same as orthogonality of the line to the radius.

drafts.canonical_statement: If lines QA and QB are tangent to a sphere (a circle in the plane) at A and B with Q ≠ A, B, then |QA| = |QB|.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the Pythagorean theorem to the two right triangles with hypotenuse QO.
sketch_steps: derive: Tangency at A gives |QO|^2 = |QA|^2 + r^2.
derive: Tangency at B gives |QO|^2 = |QB|^2 + r^2.
conclude: So |QA| = |QB|.

drafts.canonical_statement: If T lies on a sphere with center O and radius r (a circle in the plane) and Q ≠ T, then line QT is tangent at T if and only if |QT|^2 = |QO|^2 - r^2.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="on_circle"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="tangent_to_circle_at"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dist_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="minus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dist_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Expand |QO|^2 through T; the cross term vanishes exactly at tangency.
sketch_steps: derive: |QO|^2 = |QT|^2 + 2<Q-T,T-O> + r^2.
translate: The stated equation means <Q-T,T-O> = 0.
conclude: That orthogonality is equivalent to tangency of the line QT at T.

drafts.canonical_statement: If lines QA and QB are tangent at A and B to a sphere with center O (a circle in the plane) and Q ≠ A, B, then ∠AQO = ∠BQO and ∠AOQ = ∠BOQ.

drafts.proof_strategy: The triangles AQO and BQO are congruent by three sides.
sketch_steps: derive: Equal tangent lengths give |QA| = |QB|.
derive: |OA| = |OB| = r and QO is common.
apply_theorem: The triangles AQO and BQO are congruent by SSS.
conclude: Corresponding angles are equal.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a Euclidean plane, if lines QA and QB are tangent at distinct points A and B to a circle with center O and radius r > 0, and Q ≠ A, B, then QO is perpendicular to AB and the midpoint of AB lies on line QO.

drafts.proof_strategy: Q, O and the midpoint are all equidistant from A and B, and in the plane the set of such points is a line.
sketch_steps: derive: Equal tangent lengths give |QA| = |QB|.
derive: Any point equidistant from A and B has Z-M orthogonal to B-A.
derive: So Q-O is orthogonal to B-A.
translate: In the plane, vectors orthogonal to B-A form a line.
conclude: Since Q ≠ O, the midpoint lies on line QO.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a Euclidean plane, if A, B, C lie on a circle, A ≠ B, line AT is tangent at A, and T, C lie strictly on opposite sides of line AB, then ∠TAB = ∠ACB.

drafts.proof_strategy: Draw the diameter through A; the tangent makes a right angle with it, the triangle ABA' has a right angle at B, and the inscribed angle theorem moves the angle at A' to C.
sketch_steps: setup: Let A' be the other end of the diameter through A; tangency gives angle TAA' = π/2.
case_split: If B = A', both angles equal π/2.
derive: Otherwise Thales gives angle BAA' + angle AA'B = π/2.
case_split: If A', C lie on the same side of AB, then angle ACB = angle AA'B and the rays give angle TAB = π/2 - angle BAA'.
case_split: If A', C lie on opposite sides, then angle ACB = π - angle AA'B and the rays give angle TAB = π/2 + angle BAA'.
conclude: In every case angle TAB = angle ACB.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare AT with the true tangent at A; the tangent chord theorem gives the same angle with AB on the same side, so the rays coincide.
sketch_steps: setup: Let l be the line through A orthogonal to A-O; it is tangent at A.
derive: B is not on l, so l has a point T' on the side of T.
apply_theorem: The tangent chord theorem gives angle T'AB = angle ACB = angle TAB.
derive: T and T' lie on the same side of AB with equal angles, so the rays AT and AT' coincide.
conclude: Line AT equals l, so it is tangent at A.

drafts.canonical_statement: If X ≠ Y and H is the foot of the perpendicular from the center O of a sphere of radius r (a circle in the plane) to line XY, then the line is tangent at H if and only if |OH| = r.

drafts.proof_strategy: Being the foot already gives orthogonality, so only membership of H in the sphere remains.
sketch_steps: derive: Tangency at H puts H on the sphere, so |OH| = r.
derive: Conversely |OH| = r puts H on the sphere.
derive: Any U on the line has U-H a multiple of Y-X.
conclude: Hence U-H is orthogonal to H-O and the line is tangent at H.

drafts.canonical_statement: Inside form. If A, B lie on a sphere with center O and radius r (a circle in the plane) and H is strictly between A and B, then |HA||HB| = r^2 - |HO|^2.

drafts.proof_strategy: Parametrize H on the chord and compute |HO|^2 - r^2.
sketch_steps: setup: Write H = A + tu with u = B-A and 0 < t < 1.
derive: Equal radii give 2<x,u> + |u|^2 = 0 for x = A-O.
derive: So |HO|^2 - r^2 = -t(1-t)|u|^2.
conclude: Also |HA||HB| = t(1-t)|u|^2.

sketch_steps: setup: Write B-Q = λ(A-Q) with λ > 1.

derive: Expanding |QO|^2 through T gives <Q-T,T-O> = 0.
conclude: The line QT is orthogonal to the radius at T, so it is tangent.

sketch_steps: setup: A, B, C are not collinear, so they lie on a circle with center O and radius r.

derive: With D-H = -λ(C-H), the hypothesis gives |HO|^2 - r^2 = -λ|C-H|^2.
derive: Substituting the equation for C factors |DO|^2 - r^2 as (1+λ)(w+λ|v|^2).
conclude: Therefore D lies on the same sphere.

sketch_steps: setup: A, B, C are not collinear, so they lie on a circle with center O and radius r.
derive: The two equations for A and B give |QO|^2 - r^2 = |QA||QB|.

drafts.proof_strategy: Common points satisfy a linear equation, so they lie on a line, and a line meets a circle at most twice.
sketch_steps: derive: Different circles through A have different centers.
derive: Subtracting the circle equations gives a linear equation for common points.
derive: So A, B, Q lie on one line.
conclude: The line AB meets a circle only at A and B.

drafts.canonical_statement: Two spheres (circles in the plane) with centers O1, O2 and radii r1, r2 are externally tangent, meaning that some common point lies on segment O1O2, if and only if |O1O2| = r1 + r2 and r1, r2 ≥ 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Add distances along the segment, and conversely divide the segment in the ratio r1 to r2.
sketch_steps: derive: A common point on the segment gives |O1O2| = r1 + r2.
construct: Conversely take the point dividing the segment in the ratio r1 to r2.
case_split: The case r1 + r2 = 0 is the point circle.
conclude: This point is a common point on the segment.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a nonzero real inner product affine space, the sphere with center O1 and radius r1 is internally tangent to the sphere with center O2 and radius r2, meaning that some common point T has O1 on segment O2T, if and only if |O1O2| = r2 - r1 and r1, r2 ≥ 0. Coincident spheres and spheres of radius 0 count as internally tangent under this definition.

drafts.proof_strategy: Add distances along O2, O1, T, and conversely extend the ray from O2 through O1 to distance r2.
sketch_steps: derive: A common point T with O1 on segment O2T gives |O1O2| = r2 - r1.
case_split: If O1 = O2 the spheres coincide and any point of them works.
construct: Otherwise extend the ray from O2 through O1 to distance r2.
conclude: That point lies on both spheres and has O1 on segment O2T.

drafts.canonical_statement: If two spheres (circles in the plane) with radii r1, r2 > 0 have center distance r1 + r2, then they have exactly one common point.

drafts.proof_strategy: A common point attains equality in Cauchy-Schwarz, which determines it.
sketch_steps: construct: The point dividing the segment in the ratio r1 to r2 is a common point.
derive: For a common point Q, the inner product of Q-O1 and O2-O1 equals the product of norms.
apply_theorem: The equality case of Cauchy-Schwarz gives Q-O1 = (r1/d)(O2-O1).
conclude: Hence Q is that point.

sketch_steps: construct: The point on the ray from O2 through O1 at distance r2 is a common point.
derive: For a common point Q, the inner product of Q-O1 and O1-O2 equals the product of norms.
apply_theorem: The equality case of Cauchy-Schwarz gives Q-O1 = (r1/d)(O1-O2).

drafts.canonical_statement: If two spheres (circles in the plane) with centers O1, O2 and r1 > 0 share a point T on line O1O2, X ≠ T, and line TX is tangent to the first at T, then line TX is tangent to the second at T.

drafts.proof_strategy: Both radii at T are multiples of O2-O1, so orthogonality to one gives orthogonality to the other.
sketch_steps: setup: Write T-O1 = kw and T-O2 = (k-1)w with w = O2-O1.
derive: r1 > 0 forces k ≠ 0.
derive: Tangency to the first sphere gives that U-T is orthogonal to w.
conclude: So U-T is orthogonal to T-O2.

drafts.canonical_statement: If two spheres (circles in the plane) with centers O1, O2 and radii r1, r2 have a common point, then |r1 - r2| ≤ |O1O2| ≤ r1 + r2.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the triangle inequality to the triangle with vertices O1, O2, T.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The triangle inequality gives |O1O2| ≤ r1 + r2.
apply_theorem: It also gives r1 ≤ r2 + |O1O2| and r2 ≤ r1 + |O1O2|.
conclude: These are the stated bounds.

sketch_steps: setup: Let y = O2-O1 and let Jy be its rotation by a right angle.
construct: Set a = (d^2+r1^2-r2^2)/(2d).
derive: The hypotheses make r1^2 - a^2 a nonnegative product over 4d^2.
construct: Let b be its square root and T = O1 + (a/d)y + (b/d)Jy.
conclude: The Pythagorean theorem gives |TO1| = r1 and |TO2| = r2.

drafts.proof_strategy: The tangent lengths from H to both spheres equal the square root of |HA||HB|.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The tangent-secant theorem for each sphere gives |HT1|^2 = |HA||HB| = |HT2|^2.
setup: Write H = T1 + t(T2-T1).
derive: The equal distances give |t| = |1-t|.
conclude: So t = 1/2 and H is the midpoint.

drafts.proof_strategy: Decompose O2-O1 into the tangent segment and the radii; on the same side the radii point the same way.
sketch_steps: setup: Write u = T1-O1, v = T2-O2, w = T2-T1; then u and v are orthogonal to w.
translate: The same-side condition gives α(aw-u) = β(bw-v) with α, β > 0.
derive: The inner product with w gives αa = βb, hence αu = βv.
derive: So <u,v> = r1 r2.
conclude: Expanding O2-O1 = u+w-v gives the formula.

sketch_steps: construct: For reflexivity take H(t,x) = f(x).
construct: For symmetry reverse time, H'(t,x) = H(1-t,x).
construct: For transitivity run H on [0,1/2] and K on [1/2,1], each at double speed.
derive: The two pieces agree at t = 1/2, so the pasting lemma gives continuity.
conclude: The three properties make homotopy an equivalence relation.

drafts.canonical_statement: A topological space Y is contractible if and only if its identity map is homotopic to a constant map on Y.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare the composites of the maps between Y and a one-point space with the identity.
sketch_steps: setup: Define contractible as homotopy equivalent to a one-point space.
derive: A homotopy equivalence Y to a point has a composite Y to Y that is constant and homotopic to the identity.
construct: Conversely, from id homotopic to the constant map at c, take f to the point and g sending the point to c.
derive: The composite g after f is the constant map at c, homotopic to id, and f after g is the identity of the point.
conclude: So f and g form a homotopy equivalence.

sketch_steps: setup: Choose c in Y and a homotopy from the identity of Y to the constant map at c.
derive: Precomposing with f shows f is homotopic to the constant map X to c.
derive: The same argument applies to g.
conclude: By symmetry and transitivity f and g are homotopic.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use identities, swap the inverse pair, and compose while using that homotopy respects composition.
sketch_steps: construct: The identity with itself gives reflexivity.
construct: Swapping f and its homotopy inverse g gives symmetry.
construct: For transitivity take h after f with homotopy inverse g after k.
derive: Since k after h is homotopic to the identity, g k h f is homotopic to g f, hence to the identity.
derive: The other composite is handled the same way.
conclude: So the composite is a homotopy equivalence.

drafts.canonical_statement: A nonempty convex subset of a real topological vector space is contractible in the subspace topology.

sketch_steps: setup: Pick c in S, which is possible since S is nonempty.
construct: Define H(t,x) = (1-t)x + tc on [0,1] times S.
derive: Convexity keeps H(t,x) in S, and the vector space operations make H continuous.
conclude: H is a homotopy from the identity of S to the constant map at c.

drafts.proof_strategy: Glue the two path homotopies along the midpoint of the parameter.
sketch_steps: setup: Let F and G be the given endpoint-fixing homotopies.
construct: Define H(t,s) = F(t,2s) for s ≤ 1/2 and H(t,s) = G(t,2s-1) for s ≥ 1/2.
derive: Both formulas give y at s = 1/2, so H is continuous by the pasting lemma.
conclude: H fixes the endpoints and joins the two concatenations.

drafts.canonical_statement: For composable paths p, q, r, the concatenations (p·q)·r and p·(q·r) are path homotopic.

drafts.proof_strategy: Exhibit one concatenation as a reparametrization of the other and interpolate the reparametrization.
sketch_steps: setup: Let γ = p·(q·r).
construct: Find a piecewise linear φ of [0,1] with φ(0)=0, φ(1)=1 and (p·q)·r = γ∘φ.
construct: Define H(t,s) = γ((1-t)s + tφ(s)).
derive: H is continuous, fixes the endpoints, and joins γ to γ∘φ.
conclude: Hence the two concatenations are path homotopic.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use reparametrization for the unit laws and a run-out-and-back homotopy for the inverse laws.
sketch_steps: derive: p·c_y and c_x·p are reparametrizations of p, so linear interpolation of parameters gives homotopies to p.
construct: For inverses define H(t,s) = p(2ts) for s ≤ 1/2 and p(t(2-2s)) for s ≥ 1/2.
derive: The two formulas agree at s = 1/2, and H fixes the endpoints at x.
derive: H joins c_x at t = 0 to p·p⁻¹ at t = 1.
conclude: Replacing p by p⁻¹ gives the last homotopy.

drafts.proof_strategy: Conjugate loops by a path joining the two base points.
sketch_steps: setup: Choose a path γ from x to y by path-connectedness.
construct: Send the class of a loop α at x to the class of γ⁻¹·α·γ.
derive: The map is well defined because concatenation respects path homotopy.
derive: It is multiplicative because γ·γ⁻¹ is homotopic to the constant path.
conclude: Conjugating by γ⁻¹ gives the inverse, so the map is an isomorphism.

drafts.proof_strategy: Check both identities on a representative loop.
sketch_steps: setup: Represent p by a loop α at x.
derive: f_*(p) is the class of f∘α, so g_*(f_*(p)) is the class of g∘(f∘α).
derive: Associativity of composition identifies this with (g∘f)∘α.
conclude: The identity map fixes α, hence fixes its class.

drafts.canonical_statement: A space Y is simply connected if and only if it is path-connected and every loop at any base point is path homotopic to the constant path.

drafts.proof_strategy: Reduce comparison of two paths to the loop formed by one path and the inverse of the other.
sketch_steps: derive: Simply connected spaces are path-connected and any two paths with the same endpoints are homotopic.
derive: Applying this to a loop and the constant path gives the forward direction.
setup: For the converse take paths p and q from x to y.
derive: The loop p·q⁻¹ is homotopic to c_x, so p ≃ p·q⁻¹·q ≃ q.
conclude: Path-connectedness and uniqueness of path classes give simple connectivity.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every contractible space is simply connected.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="contractible_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="simply_connected_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Transfer simple connectivity from a point along a homotopy equivalence.
sketch_steps: setup: Y is homotopy equivalent to a one-point space.
derive: A homotopy equivalence induces an equivalence of fundamental groupoids.
derive: The fundamental groupoid of a point has one object and one morphism.
conclude: So Y is nonempty with exactly one path class between any two points.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a simply connected space, any two paths with the same endpoints are path homotopic and every fundamental group is trivial.

sketch_steps: setup: Simple connectivity means exactly one path class between any two points.
derive: Two paths from x to y lie in the same class, so they are homotopic.
conclude: Taking y = x shows the fundamental group has only one element.

drafts.proof_strategy: Subdivide the interval so each piece lies in an evenly covered set, lift step by step, and use connectedness for uniqueness.
sketch_steps: setup: Cover X by evenly covered open sets.
derive: Compactness of [0,1] gives a subdivision with each γ([t_i,t_{i+1}]) inside one such set.
construct: Inductively extend Γ using the local inverse of p on the sheet containing Γ(t_i).
derive: The resulting Γ is continuous with p∘Γ = γ and Γ(0) = e.
derive: The agreement set of two lifts is open and closed in [0,1] and contains 0.
conclude: Connectedness of [0,1] gives uniqueness.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show that the agreement set is open and closed using sheets over an evenly covered neighborhood.
sketch_steps: setup: Let S be the set where g₁ and g₂ agree; it contains a.
derive: If g₁(b) = g₂(b), both maps stay in one sheet near b, where p is injective, so b is interior to S.
derive: If g₁(b) ≠ g₂(b), the values lie in different sheets, so b is interior to the complement.
conclude: S is nonempty, open and closed in a connected space, so S = A.

sketch_steps: setup: The structure assigns to each x a chart whose source contains x.
derive: A chart is a homeomorphism between open sets, so source and target are open.
