drafts.proof_strategy: Show every right end bounds every left end, then take the supremum of the left ends.
sketch_steps: derive: For any m and n, a_m ≤ a_k ≤ b_k ≤ b_n with k = max(m, n).
apply_theorem: The left ends are bounded above, so they have a supremum x.
derive: a_n ≤ x because x is an upper bound, and x ≤ b_n because b_n is one.
conclude: x lies in every interval.

drafts.canonical_statement: For every positive real a and every real b there is a natural number n with b < n a.

drafts.proof_strategy: Assume all multiples are bounded and contradict the supremum of the multiples.
sketch_steps: contradiction: Suppose n a ≤ b for all natural n.
apply_theorem: The multiples of a have a supremum s.
derive: Since s - a is not an upper bound, s - a < n a for some n.
conclude: Then s < (n+1) a contradicts s being an upper bound.

drafts.canonical_statement: If reals a and b satisfy a ≤ b + ε for every ε > 0, then a ≤ b.

drafts.proof_strategy: Argue by contradiction with half of the supposed gap.
sketch_steps: contradiction: Suppose a > b.
derive: Taking ε = (a-b)/2 in the hypothesis gives a ≤ (a+b)/2.
conclude: This forces a ≤ b, a contradiction.

drafts.canonical_statement: For reals a < b there is a rational q with a < q < b.

drafts.proof_strategy: Clear denominators with the Archimedean property and take the least integer above n a.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Choose a positive integer n with n(b-a) > 1.
construct: Let m be the least integer greater than n a.
derive: Then n a < m ≤ n a + 1 < n b.
conclude: Dividing by n gives a < m/n < b.

drafts.proof_strategy: Approximate an arbitrary real by rationals and pass to the limit on both sides.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix a real x.
construct: Choose rationals q_n converging to x by density.
derive: Continuity gives f(q_n) → f(x) and g(q_n) → g(x).
conclude: Since f(q_n) = g(q_n), uniqueness of limits gives f(x) = g(x).

sketch_steps: translate: Neighbourhoods of L are generated by the intervals (L-ε, L+ε).
translate: Membership in the interval means |a_n - L| < ε.
conclude: Being eventually in each interval is the ε-N condition.

drafts.proof_strategy: Split the error with the triangle inequality, using boundedness of a for the product.
sketch_steps: derive: |a_n + b_n - L - M| ≤ |a_n - L| + |b_n - M|.
derive: a_n b_n - L M = a_n (b_n - M) + M (a_n - L).
apply_theorem: The convergent sequence a is bounded by some K.
conclude: Both error bounds tend to 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a_n ≤ b_n for all n, a converges to L and b converges to M, then L ≤ M.

drafts.proof_strategy: Separate L and M by a gap of 2ε and contradict the termwise inequality.
sketch_steps: contradiction: Suppose L > M and set ε = (L-M)/2.
derive: For large n, a_n > L - ε and b_n < M + ε.
derive: The two bounds coincide, so a_n > b_n.
conclude: This contradicts a_n ≤ b_n, so L ≤ M.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every convergent real sequence is bounded.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_tends_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="leq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="abs"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Bound the tail with ε = 1 and take a maximum with the finitely many initial terms.
sketch_steps: setup: Choose N with |a_n - L| < 1 for n ≥ N.
derive: The tail satisfies |a_n| < |L| + 1.
construct: Let M be the maximum of |L| + 1 and the first N absolute values.
conclude: M bounds every term.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a real sequence a is bounded and b converges to 0, then a_n b_n converges to 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Dominate the product by M times |b_n| and squeeze.
sketch_steps: derive: |a_n b_n| ≤ M |b_n| for every n.
derive: M |b_n| → 0 because b_n → 0.
conclude: Squeezing gives a_n b_n → 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: A nondecreasing real sequence that is bounded above converges to the supremum of its values.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_monotone"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="is_lub"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_tends_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Take the supremum of the values and use monotonicity to keep the tail near it.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The set of values has a supremum s.
setup: Fix ε > 0 and pick N with s - ε < a_N.
derive: Monotonicity gives s - ε < a_n ≤ s for n ≥ N.
conclude: Hence a_n → s.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every bounded real sequence has a convergent subsequence.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="leq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="abs"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="strict_mono_index"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_fn_tends_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="fns1" name="lambda"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Bisect the bounding interval, always keeping a half containing infinitely many terms.
sketch_steps: setup: All terms lie in [-M, M].
construct: Repeatedly bisect, keeping a half with infinitely many terms.
apply_theorem: The nested closed intervals share a point x.
construct: Choose increasing indices with terms in successive intervals.
conclude: The widths tend to 0, so the subsequence converges to x.

drafts.canonical_statement: A real sequence is a Cauchy sequence if and only if it converges.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_cauchy"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_tends_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: The triangle inequality gives one direction; a convergent subsequence of a bounded Cauchy sequence gives the other.
sketch_steps: derive: A convergent sequence is Cauchy by the triangle inequality.
setup: Conversely let a be Cauchy, hence bounded.
apply_theorem: Bolzano-Weierstrass gives a subsequence converging to L.
derive: Compare a_n with a far term of the subsequence.
conclude: Hence a_n → L.

drafts.canonical_statement: A real sequence a is Cauchy if and only if for every ε > 0 there is N with |a_m - a_n| < ε for all m, n ≥ N.

drafts.proof_strategy: Unfold the Cauchy condition using the metric on ℝ.
sketch_steps: translate: Entourages of ℝ are generated by pairs at distance less than ε.
translate: The distance of a_m and a_n is |a_m - a_n|.
conclude: The Cauchy condition becomes the ε-N statement.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every real Cauchy sequence is bounded.

drafts.proof_strategy: Bound the tail by comparing with one fixed far term, then take a maximum.
sketch_steps: setup: Choose N with |a_m - a_n| < 1 for m, n ≥ N.
derive: For n ≥ N, |a_n| < |a_N| + 1.
construct: Let M be the maximum of this bound and the first N absolute values.
conclude: M bounds all terms.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a and b are the suprema of sets S and T of reals, then a + b is the supremum of the set of all sums x + y with x in S and y in T.

drafts.proof_strategy: Fix one summand at a time and use the least-upper-bound property twice.
sketch_steps: derive: x + y ≤ a + b, so a + b is an upper bound.
setup: Let c be any upper bound of the sums.
derive: For fixed y, x ≤ c - y for all x in S, so a ≤ c - y.
derive: Then y ≤ c - a for all y in T, so b ≤ c - a.
conclude: Hence a + b ≤ c.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a real sequence a converges to L, then both its limit superior and its limit inferior equal L.

drafts.proof_strategy: Trap the tail suprema and infima in an ε-band around L.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix ε > 0 and N with L - ε < a_n < L + ε for n ≥ N.
derive: Tail suprema and infima beyond N lie in [L-ε, L+ε].
derive: Their limits, limsup and liminf, lie in the same interval.
conclude: Since ε is arbitrary both equal L.

drafts.canonical_statement: A bounded real sequence whose limit superior and limit inferior both equal L converges to L.

drafts.proof_strategy: Translate limsup and liminf into eventual upper and lower bounds.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix ε > 0.
derive: limsup a = L < L + ε gives a_n < L + ε eventually.
derive: liminf a = L > L - ε gives a_n > L - ε eventually.
conclude: Hence |a_n - L| < ε eventually.

sketch_steps: translate: limsup a is the infimum of the tail suprema s_m.
derive: Since it is below c, some s_N < c.
conclude: For n ≥ N, a_n ≤ s_N < c.

derive: a_N = S_{N+1} - S_N.
conclude: The right side tends to S - S = 0.

apply_theorem: Monotone convergence gives convergence.

conclude: Passing to the limit gives the inequality.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare the tail with a geometric series whose ratio lies between l and 1.
sketch_steps: setup: Pick r strictly between l and 1.
derive: Eventually |a_{n+1}| ≤ r |a_n| when l < 1.
induction: Hence |a_{N+k}| ≤ |a_N| r^k.
apply_theorem: Compare with the geometric series.
case_split: When l > 1, eventually |a_{n+1}| ≥ r |a_n| with r > 1.
conclude: The terms do not tend to 0, so the series diverges.

drafts.canonical_statement: If the n-th root of |a_n| converges to some l < 1, then the series of a_n converges absolutely.

drafts.proof_strategy: Eventually bound |a_n| by r^n for some r in (l, 1) and compare with a geometric series.
sketch_steps: setup: Choose r with l < r < 1.
derive: For large n, |a_n|^(1/n) < r.
derive: Raising to the n-th power gives |a_n| ≤ r^n.
apply_theorem: Compare with the convergent geometric series.
conclude: The series converges absolutely.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a real sequence a is nonincreasing and converges to 0, then the partial sums of the alternating series of (-1)^k a_k converge.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show even and odd partial sums are monotone and bounded with a vanishing difference.
sketch_steps: derive: a_k ≥ 0 since a is nonincreasing with limit 0.
derive: Even partial sums increase and odd partial sums decrease.
derive: The even ones stay below the odd ones, so both are bounded.
apply_theorem: Monotone convergence gives limits of both.
conclude: The difference a_{2m} tends to 0, so the limits coincide.

drafts.canonical_statement: If |r| < 1, then the geometric series of r^n converges to 1/(1-r).

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the closed form for the partial sums and the limit of r^N.
sketch_steps: derive: S_N (1-r) = 1 - r^N by telescoping.
derive: r^N → 0 because |r| < 1.
conclude: S_N → 1/(1-r), and the same computation for |r| gives absolute convergence.

drafts.proof_strategy: Group terms into dyadic blocks each contributing at least one half.
sketch_steps: construct: Group the terms with 2^m < k ≤ 2^(m+1).
derive: Each block sums to at least 1/2.
derive: The partial sum of the first 2^m terms is at least m/2.
conclude: Partial sums are monotone and unbounded, so they diverge to plus infinity.

sketch_steps: setup: Fix ε > 0 and K with absolute tail below ε/2 and partial sum within ε/2 of S.
construct: Choose N with σ(0), ..., σ(N-1) containing 0, ..., K-1.
derive: The rearranged partial sum differs from the K-th partial sum only by terms with index at least K.
derive: This difference is at most the absolute tail.
conclude: The rearranged partial sum is within ε of S.

sketch_steps: derive: The family a_k b_l over pairs is absolutely summable, bounded by the product of the absolute sums.
apply_theorem: Absolutely summable families can be regrouped freely.
derive: Summing over k + l = n gives the Cauchy product terms.
derive: Summing over k and l separately gives the product of sums.
conclude: The two results agree.

drafts.proof_strategy: Unfold uniform convergence through the metric of ℝ, keeping N independent of x.
sketch_steps: translate: Uniform convergence means that for each ε eventually all x in S are within ε.
translate: Eventually along the naturals means there is a threshold N.
conclude: Writing the distance as an absolute value gives the stated condition.

drafts.canonical_statement: If functions continuous on S converge uniformly on S to f, then f is continuous on S.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the three-epsilon argument with one sufficiently late continuous function.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix x in S and ε > 0.
apply_theorem: Uniform convergence gives N with |F_N - f| < ε/3 on S.
derive: Continuity of F_N gives |F_N(y) - F_N(x)| < ε/3 for y near x.
derive: The triangle inequality bounds |f(y) - f(x)| by three terms.
conclude: Thus f is continuous at x.

drafts.proof_strategy: Assume a uniform threshold and let x tend to 1 in the single power x^N.
sketch_steps: derive: For 0 ≤ x < 1, x^n → 0, giving pointwise convergence.
contradiction: Suppose x^N < 1/2 for all x in [0,1) and some N.
derive: Continuity of x^N at 1 gives 1 ≤ 1/2.
conclude: The convergence is not uniform.

sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Each series at x converges absolutely by comparison.
derive: The error at x is at most the sum of M_n over n ≥ N.
derive: This tail is independent of x and tends to 0.
conclude: The partial sums converge uniformly on S.

conclude: The derivative of the sum is the sum of the derivatives.

derive: The limit is continuous, so its integral exists.

derive: Linearity turns the integral of a partial sum into a sum of integrals.
conclude: The series of integrals converges to the integral of the sum.

sketch_steps: derive: f is continuous as a uniform limit, so it is integrable.
setup: Fix ε > 0 and put δ = ε/(b-a+1).
apply_theorem: Uniform convergence gives N with |F_n - f| < δ on [a,b] for n ≥ N.
derive: The integral of the difference is at most δ(b-a).
conclude: This is less than ε.

derive: The U_n are relatively open, increasing and cover S.
apply_theorem: Compactness gives a single U_N equal to S.
derive: Monotonicity gives 0 ≤ f - F_n < ε on S for n ≥ N.
conclude: The convergence is uniform.

sketch_steps: derive: The terms a_n x_0^n tend to 0, so they are bounded by some M.
setup: Put r = |x|/|x_0| < 1.
derive: |a_n x^n| = |a_n x_0^n| r^n ≤ M r^n.
apply_theorem: Compare with the geometric series.
conclude: The series converges absolutely at x.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take the supremum of |x| over points of convergence and apply Abel's lemma.
sketch_steps: construct: Let R be the supremum in [0, ∞] of |x| over points where the series converges.
derive: If |x| < R, there is a point x_0 of convergence with |x| < |x_0|.
apply_theorem: Abel's lemma gives absolute convergence at x.
contradiction: If |x| > R and the series converged at x, then |x| ≤ R.
conclude: R has the required properties.

sketch_steps: derive: For |x| ≤ r, |a_n x^n| ≤ |a_n| r^n.
apply_theorem: The bounds are summable and independent of x, so the M-test applies.

drafts.canonical_statement: A real function f is uniformly continuous if and only if for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 with |f(x) - f(y)| < ε whenever |x - y| < δ.

drafts.proof_strategy: Unfold uniform continuity through the metric of ℝ.
sketch_steps: translate: Uniformity on ℝ is generated by pairs at distance below a positive number.
translate: Uniform continuity pulls pairs at distance below ε back to pairs at distance below δ.
conclude: Writing distances as absolute values gives the stated condition.

drafts.canonical_statement: A map between metric spaces that is continuous on a compact set is uniformly continuous on that set.

drafts.proof_strategy: Cover the compact set by half-radius balls from pointwise continuity and take the minimum radius.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix ε > 0 and choose δ_x from continuity at each x in S.
apply_theorem: Finitely many balls of radius δ_x/2 cover S.
construct: Let δ be the smallest of the finitely many half radii.
derive: Points y, z with d(y,z) < δ both lie in one ball of radius δ_x around a centre.
conclude: The triangle inequality gives d(f(y), f(z)) < ε.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show total boundedness in the sup norm from equicontinuity on a finite cover, then use compactness.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix ε > 0 and cover X by finitely many open sets where all f_n vary by less than ε.
construct: Sample each f_n at one point of each set.
derive: Boundedness makes the samples range in a compact box, so finitely many patterns suffice.
derive: Therefore the family is totally bounded in the sup norm.
apply_theorem: The closure of the family is compact in the complete space.
conclude: The sequence has a subsequence converging uniformly.

drafts.canonical_statement: A ring homomorphism f between commutative rings is injective if and only if its kernel is the zero ideal.

drafts.proof_strategy: Translate equality of images into membership of the difference in the kernel.
sketch_steps: setup: Suppose f is injective and x lies in the kernel.
derive: Then f(x) = 0 = f(0), so x = 0.
translate: Conversely, f(x) = f(y) gives f(x - y) = 0.
conclude: A zero kernel forces x - y = 0, so f is injective.

drafts.canonical_statement: The preimage of a prime ideal P of S under a ring homomorphism f from R to S is a prime ideal of R.

drafts.proof_strategy: Check properness through f(1) = 1 and transport the prime property along multiplicativity.
sketch_steps: setup: The preimage of an ideal under f is an ideal of R.
derive: Since f(1) = 1 is not in P, the preimage is proper.
translate: If ab is in the preimage, then f(a)f(b) lies in P.
conclude: Primality of P puts f(a) or f(b) in P, so a or b is in the preimage.

drafts.canonical_statement: An ideal I of a commutative ring equals the whole ring if and only if I contains a unit.

drafts.proof_strategy: Multiply a unit by its inverse to place 1 in the ideal.
sketch_steps: setup: If I = R then 1 is a unit in I.
derive: If u in I is a unit, then 1 = u⁻¹u lies in I.
conclude: Then x = x·1 lies in I for every x, so I = R.

drafts.canonical_statement: If ideals I and J of a commutative ring satisfy I + J = R, then their intersection equals their product.

drafts.proof_strategy: Write 1 = i + j and split an element of the intersection into two products.
sketch_steps: setup: The inclusion IJ ⊆ I ∩ J holds for any ideals.
construct: Choose i in I and j in J with i + j = 1.
derive: For x in I ∩ J, x = xi + xj.
conclude: Both xi and xj lie in IJ, so x lies in IJ.

drafts.canonical_statement: For elements a and b of a commutative ring, the principal ideal (a) is contained in (b) if and only if b divides a.

drafts.proof_strategy: Unfold membership in a principal ideal as divisibility.
sketch_steps: translate: Membership of a in (b) means a = bc for some c.
derive: If b divides a, every multiple of a is a multiple of b.
conclude: Hence (a) ⊆ (b) is equivalent to b dividing a.

sketch_steps: translate: Equal cosets means x lies in y + I.
derive: Then x - y lies in I.
conclude: Conversely, x = y + i with i in I gives x + I = y + I.

conclude: Every element of R/I is a residue class, so the condition determines g uniquely.

sketch_steps: translate: f(x) = f(y) holds exactly when x - y lies in ker f.
construct: Define the map on residue classes by x + ker f ↦ f(x).
derive: The equivalence shows the map is well defined and injective.
derive: It is a ring homomorphism because f is.
conclude: It is onto the image by definition, hence an isomorphism.

sketch_steps: construct: Since I ⊆ J, define R/I → R/J by x + I ↦ x + J.

derive: Its kernel is the image of J in R/I.
apply_theorem: The first isomorphism theorem gives the claimed isomorphism.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare residue classes and use I ⊆ J to absorb the difference.
sketch_steps: setup: The inclusion J ⊆ π⁻¹(π(J)) is immediate.
translate: For x in π⁻¹(π(J)), choose j in J with π(x) = π(j).
derive: Then x - j lies in I, hence in J.
conclude: So x = (x - j) + j lies in J.

derive: Its kernel is I ∩ J.
construct: Choose i in I and j in J with i + j = 1.
derive: The element aj + bi reduces to a mod I and b mod J, so the map is surjective.
apply_theorem: The first isomorphism theorem gives the isomorphism.

drafts.canonical_statement: If ideals I and J satisfy I + J = R, then for all a and b there is an x with x - a in I and x - b in J.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_sum"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="unit_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="minus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="minus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use the decomposition of 1 to interpolate a and b explicitly.
sketch_steps: construct: Choose i in I and j in J with i + j = 1, and put x = aj + bi.
derive: Then x - a = (b - a)i lies in I.
conclude: Likewise x - b = (a - b)j lies in J.

drafts.canonical_statement: For an ideal I of a commutative ring R, the quotient R/I is an integral domain if and only if I is a prime ideal.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="integral_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="quotient_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prime_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Translate zero products in the quotient into memberships in I.
sketch_steps: translate: R/I is nonzero exactly when I ≠ R.
translate: (a + I)(b + I) = 0 means ab lies in I.
translate: a + I = 0 means a lies in I.
conclude: Absence of zero divisors in R/I is the prime condition on I.

drafts.canonical_statement: For an ideal I of a commutative ring R, the quotient R/I is a field if and only if I is a maximal ideal.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="is_field"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="quotient_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="maximal_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Convert maximality into invertibility of nonzero residue classes, in both directions.
sketch_steps: setup: Assume I is maximal and a is not in I.
derive: Then I + (a) = R, so ab + i = 1 with i in I.
translate: Thus b + I inverts a + I, and R/I is a field.
setup: Conversely assume R/I is a field and J strictly contains I.
derive: Taking a in J outside I, ab - 1 lies in I for some b.
conclude: So 1 lies in J, J = R, and I is maximal.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every maximal ideal of a commutative ring is a prime ideal.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="maximal_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prime_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Pass through the quotient, which is a field and therefore a domain.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: R/M is a field because M is maximal.
derive: Every field is an integral domain.
conclude: R/M being a domain means M is prime.

drafts.canonical_statement: Krull's theorem. Every proper ideal I of a commutative ring is contained in a maximal ideal.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="unit_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="maximal_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="subset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Zorn's lemma to proper ideals containing I.
sketch_steps: setup: Order proper ideals containing I by inclusion.
derive: The union of a chain is an ideal.
derive: The union does not contain 1, so it is proper.
apply_theorem: Zorn's lemma gives a maximal element M.
conclude: M is a maximal ideal containing I.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every non-unit of a commutative ring lies in some maximal ideal.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="not"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="unit_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="maximal_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Enlarge the principal ideal generated by a to a maximal ideal.
sketch_steps: derive: Since a is not a unit, (a) does not contain 1.
apply_theorem: The proper ideal (a) lies in a maximal ideal M.
conclude: Therefore a lies in M.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a prime ideal P contains the product IJ of two ideals, then P contains I or J.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prime_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="subset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_product"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="or"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="subset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="subset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Pick an element of I outside P and apply the prime condition to its products with J.
sketch_steps: case_split: Assume I is not contained in P and take a in I outside P.
derive: For b in J, ab lies in IJ and hence in P.
derive: Primality of P forces b into P.
conclude: Thus J is contained in P.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every finite integral domain is a field.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="integral_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="is_field"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Multiplication by a nonzero element is injective, hence surjective on a finite set.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix a nonzero element a of R.
derive: Cancellation makes x ↦ ax injective.
derive: Finiteness makes the map surjective.
conclude: Some b satisfies ab = 1, so a is a unit.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a commutative ring, the sum of a unit and a nilpotent element is a unit.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="unit_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nilpotent_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="unit_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Factor out u and invert 1 - m by the finite geometric series.
sketch_steps: setup: Put m = -u⁻¹n, which is nilpotent by commutativity.
derive: Then u + n = u(1 - m).
construct: If m^k = 0, the sum 1 + m + ... + m^(k-1) inverts 1 - m.
conclude: So u + n is a product of units.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every prime element of an integral domain is irreducible.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="integral_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prime_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="irreducible_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use primality on a factorization and cancel p.
sketch_steps: setup: Suppose p = ab.
derive: Primality gives p | a or p | b.
case_split: If a = pc, then p = pcb.
derive: Cancelling p shows b is a unit.
conclude: The other case is symmetric, so p is irreducible.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every irreducible element of a principal ideal domain is prime.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="principal_ideal_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="irreducible_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prime_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Generate the ideal (p, a) by one element and extract a Bezout identity.
sketch_steps: setup: Suppose p divides ab but not a.
construct: Write the ideal (p, a) as (d).
derive: Since d divides p and p does not divide a, irreducibility makes d a unit.
derive: Hence 1 = px + ay.
conclude: Multiplying by b shows p divides b.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a unique factorization domain, an element is irreducible if and only if it is prime.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="unique_factorization_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="irreducible_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prime_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Compare the factorizations of ab and pc using uniqueness.
sketch_steps: derive: Prime elements are irreducible in any domain.
setup: Let p be irreducible with p | ab, and write ab = pc.
case_split: The case a = 0 or b = 0 is immediate.
derive: Uniqueness of factorization makes p an associate of an irreducible factor of a or b.
conclude: So p divides a or b.

drafts.canonical_statement: In the ring Z[√-5], the element 2 is irreducible but not prime.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="irreducible_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="int_adjoin_sqrt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>-5</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="not"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prime_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="int_adjoin_sqrt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>-5</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use the multiplicative norm for irreducibility and the factorization of 6 for non-primality.
sketch_steps: setup: Use the multiplicative norm N(a + b√-5) = a² + 5b².
derive: A factorization of 2 gives norms multiplying to 4.
derive: The equation a² + 5b² = 2 has no integer solution, so one factor has norm 1 and is a unit.
derive: The element 2 divides (1 + √-5)(1 - √-5) = 6.
contradiction: Neither factor is divisible by 2 because its √-5 coefficient is odd.
conclude: So 2 is irreducible but not prime.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every Euclidean domain is a principal ideal domain.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="euclidean_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="principal_ideal_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Generate the ideal by a nonzero element of minimal Euclidean size.
sketch_steps: setup: Let I be a nonzero ideal.
construct: Pick a nonzero d in I of minimal Euclidean size.
derive: For x in I, divide to get x = dq + r with r in I.
contradiction: A nonzero r would have smaller size than d.
conclude: So r = 0 and I = (d).

drafts.canonical_statement: Every principal ideal domain is a unique factorization domain.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="principal_ideal_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="unique_factorization_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Get existence from the ascending chain condition and uniqueness from irreducible elements being prime.
sketch_steps: derive: Every ascending chain of principal ideals stabilizes because its union is principal.
derive: A nonzero non-unit therefore factors into irreducibles in finitely many steps.
apply_theorem: Irreducible elements of a principal ideal domain are prime.
induction: Cancel prime factors one at a time to compare two factorizations.
conclude: The factorization is unique up to order and associates.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every nonzero prime ideal of a principal ideal domain is maximal.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="principal_ideal_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prime_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="zero_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="maximal_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Write P = (p), factor p through any larger ideal, and use primality with cancellation.
sketch_steps: setup: Write P = (p) with p nonzero and take (a) containing P.
derive: Then p = ab for some b.
case_split: Primality puts a or b in P.
derive: If a is in P then (a) = P.
derive: If b = pc then cancelling p gives ac = 1, so (a) = R.
conclude: Hence P is maximal.

drafts.canonical_statement: Gauss's theorem. If R is a unique factorization domain, then the polynomial ring R[X] is also a unique factorization domain.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="unique_factorization_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="unique_factorization_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="polynomial_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Reduce to the Euclidean ring K[X] and to R through contents and Gauss's lemma.
sketch_steps: setup: Let K be the field of fractions of R.
derive: Write a polynomial as its content times a primitive polynomial.
apply_theorem: Factor the primitive part in the unique factorization domain K[X].
apply_theorem: Gauss's lemma brings the factorization back to R[X].
conclude: Uniqueness in R and K[X] gives uniqueness in R[X].

drafts.canonical_statement: For a polynomial f and a monic polynomial g over a nontrivial commutative ring, there are polynomials q and r with f = gq + r and deg r < deg g.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nontrivial_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="polynomial_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="or"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="lt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="poly_degree"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="poly_degree"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on the degree of f and remove the leading term using the monic divisor.
sketch_steps: induction: Induct on the degree of f.
case_split: If deg f < deg g, take q = 0 and r = f.
derive: Otherwise subtract aX^(n-m)g, which lowers the degree because g is monic.
conclude: Add aX^(n-m) to the quotient from the induction hypothesis.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a polynomial f over a commutative ring and an element a, there is a polynomial q with f = (X - a)q + f(a).
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="polynomial_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="minus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="poly_var"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="poly_const"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="poly_const"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="poly_eval"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Divide by the monic polynomial X - a and substitute X = a.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Divide f by the monic polynomial X - a.
derive: The remainder r has degree below 1, so it is a constant.
conclude: Substituting X = a shows r = f(a).

drafts.canonical_statement: Factor theorem. For a polynomial f over a commutative ring and an element a, X - a divides f if and only if f(a) = 0.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="polynomial_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dvd"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="minus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="poly_var"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="poly_const"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="poly_eval"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Substitute in one direction and use the remainder theorem in the other.
sketch_steps: derive: If f = (X - a)g, substituting a gives f(a) = 0.
apply_theorem: The remainder theorem gives f = (X - a)q + f(a).
conclude: If f(a) = 0 this says X - a divides f.

drafts.canonical_statement: A nonzero polynomial over an integral domain has at most as many distinct roots as its degree.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="integral_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="polynomial_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="subset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="poly_eval"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="leq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="poly_degree"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Peel off one root by the factor theorem and use that a domain has no zero divisors.
sketch_steps: induction: Induct on the degree of f.
apply_theorem: If a is a root, the factor theorem gives f = (X - a)g.
derive: For another root b, 0 = (b - a)g(b), so g(b) = 0.
conclude: The remaining roots are roots of g, so the bound follows.

drafts.canonical_statement: Gauss's lemma. Over a GCD domain, which includes every unique factorization domain, the product of two primitive polynomials is primitive.

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on the total degree, showing the content of fg is coprime to both leading coefficients.
sketch_steps: setup: Let d be the content of fg, which divides the product of the leading coefficients a and b.
derive: Remove the leading term of f, write the rest as a content times a primitive polynomial, and apply the induction hypothesis.
derive: Coefficients of fg and of the shorter product differ by multiples of a, so gcd(d, a) = 1.
derive: Swapping f and g gives gcd(d, b) = 1.
conclude: Since d divides ab and is coprime to a, it divides b, so d is a unit.

drafts.canonical_statement: A primitive polynomial with integer coefficients is irreducible in Z[X] if and only if it is irreducible in Q[X].

drafts.proof_strategy: Clear denominators to primitive factors and apply Gauss's lemma.
sketch_steps: setup: Suppose f = gh in Q[X] with both factors of positive degree.
construct: Rescale g and h to primitive integer polynomials g₀ and h₀, so f = c g₀ h₀.
apply_theorem: Gauss's lemma makes g₀h₀ primitive.
derive: Since f is primitive, c = ±1, which factors f in Z[X].
derive: Conversely, non-unit factors of primitive f in Z[X] are nonconstant.
conclude: So such a factorization remains proper in Q[X].

drafts.proof_strategy: Reduce modulo P, where the polynomial becomes a monomial, and deduce that both constant terms lie in P.
sketch_steps: setup: Suppose f = gh with non-units g and h.
derive: Primitivity forces both factors to have positive degree.
translate: Modulo P the image of f is a nonzero monomial cXⁿ.
derive: Over the fraction field of R/P, the images of g and h are monomials of positive degree.
derive: Hence the constant terms of g and h both lie in P.
contradiction: The constant term of f then lies in P².

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Eisenstein at the ideal (p), then transfer irreducibility to Q[X] by Gauss.
sketch_steps: derive: A monic polynomial is primitive.
translate: The divisibility conditions say the coefficients lie in (p) and the constant term is not in (p²).
apply_theorem: Eisenstein's criterion gives irreducibility in Z[X].
apply_theorem: Gauss's lemma transfers irreducibility to Q[X].

drafts.canonical_statement: Let φ from R to S be a ring homomorphism between integral domains and f in R[X] monic. If the polynomial obtained by applying φ to the coefficients is irreducible in S[X], then f is irreducible in R[X].

drafts.proof_strategy: Use that a monic factorization preserves degrees under reduction.
sketch_steps: setup: Suppose f = gh.
derive: The leading coefficients of g and h multiply to 1, so they are units.
derive: Hence φ preserves the degrees of g and h.
apply_theorem: Irreducibility of φ(f) makes one image a unit of degree 0.
conclude: The corresponding factor has degree 0 and unit leading coefficient, so it is a unit.

drafts.canonical_statement: A polynomial of degree 2 or 3 over a field K is irreducible if and only if it has no root in K.

drafts.proof_strategy: Link roots to linear factors and use the small degree to force a linear factor.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: A root a gives f = (X - a)g by the factor theorem.
derive: Since deg g ≥ 1, f is reducible.
setup: Conversely suppose f = gh with non-units g and h.
derive: Degrees are at least 1 and sum to at most 3, so one factor is linear.
conclude: A linear factor over a field has a root, which is a root of f.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a polynomial f over a field K, the quotient K[X]/(f) is a field if and only if f is irreducible.

drafts.proof_strategy: Reduce to maximality of (f) in the principal ideal domain K[X], treating f = 0 separately.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The quotient is a field exactly when (f) is maximal.
case_split: If f = 0, both sides fail because K[X] is not a field and 0 is not irreducible.
derive: If f ≠ 0 and (f) is maximal, then (f) is prime, so f is prime and irreducible.
derive: If f is irreducible and (f) ⊆ (g), then g is a unit or an associate of f.
conclude: Hence (f) is maximal exactly when f is irreducible.

drafts.canonical_statement: The characteristic of an integral domain is either zero or a prime number.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="integral_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ring_characteristic"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="or"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="P"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Factor the characteristic and use the absence of zero divisors.
sketch_steps: setup: Assume p ≠ 0; since 1 ≠ 0, also p ≠ 1.
case_split: Suppose p = ab with 1 < a, b < p.
derive: Then (a·1)(b·1) = 0 in R.
contradiction: One factor vanishes, against minimality of p.
conclude: So p is prime.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a commutative ring of prime characteristic p, one has (x + y)^p = x^p + y^p.

drafts.proof_strategy: Expand by the binomial theorem and kill the middle binomial coefficients.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Expand (x + y)^p by the binomial theorem.
derive: For 0 < k < p, the prime p divides the binomial coefficient C(p, k).
conclude: In characteristic p only x^p and y^p remain.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a reduced commutative ring of prime characteristic p, the Frobenius map is injective, that is, x^p = y^p implies x = y.

drafts.proof_strategy: Turn equal p-th powers into nilpotence of the difference.
sketch_steps: derive: In characteristic p, (x - y)^p = x^p - y^p.
translate: The hypothesis gives (x - y)^p = 0, so x - y is nilpotent.
conclude: Reducedness gives x = y.

sketch_steps: translate: An element of K is a class of a pair (a, b) with b nonzero.
conclude: This class equals the quotient of the images of a and b.

sketch_steps: derive: Injectivity gives g(b) ≠ 0 for b ≠ 0.
construct: Set h(a/b) = g(a)/g(b).
derive: The cross-multiplication relation shows h is well defined.
derive: Fraction arithmetic shows h is a ring homomorphism.
conclude: Any extension must satisfy the same formula, so it is unique.

drafts.canonical_statement: The nilradical of a commutative ring, that is, the set of its nilpotent elements, equals the intersection of all prime ideals.

drafts.proof_strategy: The easy inclusion uses primality; the other builds a prime ideal avoiding the powers of x by Zorn's lemma.
sketch_steps: derive: If x^n = 0, then x lies in every prime ideal.
setup: Conversely, let x be non-nilpotent.
apply_theorem: Zorn's lemma gives an ideal P maximal among those missing all powers of x.
derive: If a, b are outside P, then P + (a) and P + (b) contain powers of x.
contradiction: If ab were in P, a power of x would lie in P.
conclude: So P is a prime ideal not containing x.

drafts.canonical_statement: An element x lies in the Jacobson radical of a commutative ring if and only if xy + 1 is a unit for every y.

drafts.proof_strategy: Put a non-unit into a maximal ideal for one direction and use M + (x) = R for the other.
sketch_steps: setup: Assume x is in every maximal ideal.
contradiction: A non-unit xy + 1 lies in a maximal ideal containing x, which would contain 1.
setup: Conversely, suppose x is not in a maximal ideal M.
derive: Then M + (x) = R, so m + xz = 1 with m in M.
conclude: With y = -z, xy + 1 = m is not a unit.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take a minimal generating set and eliminate one generator using that 1 - a is a unit.
sketch_steps: setup: Suppose N ≠ 0 and choose a generating set of minimal size.
derive: Since N ⊆ IN, the last generator is an I-combination of all generators.
derive: Moving terms gives (1 - a) uₙ as a combination of the others.
apply_theorem: The element 1 - a is a unit because a lies in the Jacobson radical.
contradiction: Then uₙ is redundant, against minimality.

sketch_steps: derive: The hypothesis gives e(e - 1) = 0.
conclude: With no zero divisors, e = 0 or e = 1.

sketch_steps: derive: AB = E gives det A · det B = 1.
apply_theorem: The adjugate satisfies A adj A = adj A A = (det A) E.
conclude: If det A is a unit, then (det A)⁻¹ adj A inverts A.

derive: All generators appear at some stage of the chain.
conclude: The chain stabilizes there.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take the union, which is finitely generated, and locate its generators.
sketch_steps: derive: The union I of the chain is an ideal.
apply_theorem: Since R is Noetherian, I is finitely generated.
derive: The generators all lie in some I_N, so I = I_N.
conclude: For m ≥ N, I_N ⊆ I_m ⊆ I = I_N.

drafts.canonical_statement: Hilbert's basis theorem. If R is a Noetherian ring, then the polynomial ring R[X] is Noetherian.

drafts.proof_strategy: Choose generators of minimal degree and use finite generation of the ideal of leading coefficients.
sketch_steps: setup: Suppose an ideal I of R[X] is not finitely generated.
construct: Pick f_{k+1} of minimal degree in I outside (f_1, ..., f_k).
apply_theorem: The ideal of leading coefficients of the f_i is finitely generated.
derive: So some leading coefficient a_{k+1} is an R-combination of the earlier ones.
contradiction: Subtracting the matching combination gives an element of smaller degree outside (f_1, ..., f_k).

drafts.proof_strategy: Rewrite both fractions over the common denominator bd.
sketch_steps: setup: Note that bd is nonzero because b and d are nonzero.
derive: Expand a/b to ad/(bd) and c/d to bc/(bd).
conclude: Add the numerators over the common denominator.

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on n using the recursive definition of powers.
sketch_steps: setup: Define powers by x^0 = 1 and x^(k+1) = x^k x.
induction: Check each identity for n = 0.
derive: Assuming the case n, extract one factor to get the case n+1.
conclude: All three identities hold for every n.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a nonzero real a and natural numbers n ≤ m, a^m / a^n = a^(m-n).

drafts.proof_strategy: Write m = n + k and cancel a^n.
sketch_steps: setup: Put k = m - n, a natural number since n ≤ m.
derive: The exponent law gives a^m = a^n a^k.
conclude: Divide by the nonzero number a^n.

drafts.canonical_statement: For real a and b, ab = 0 if and only if a = 0 or b = 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Multiply by the inverse of a when a is nonzero.
sketch_steps: derive: A zero factor makes the product zero.
case_split: For the converse, consider whether a is zero.
derive: If a ≠ 0, multiplying ab = 0 by 1/a gives b = 0.
conclude: Hence one of the factors is zero.

drafts.canonical_statement: For real a and b, a² = b² if and only if a = b or a = -b.

drafts.proof_strategy: Factor a² - b² and use the zero product property.
sketch_steps: translate: Rewrite a² = b² as (a-b)(a+b) = 0.
apply_theorem: A product of reals is zero exactly when a factor is zero.
conclude: This gives a = b or a = -b.

drafts.canonical_statement: Difference of squares. For real a and b, a² - b² = (a + b)(a - b).

sketch_steps: derive: Distributivity gives a² - ab + ba - b².
conclude: The cross terms cancel, leaving a² - b².

sketch_steps: derive: Expand (a+b)(a²-ab+b²); the mixed terms cancel to give a³+b³.
derive: Expand (a-b)(a²+ab+b²); the mixed terms cancel to give a³-b³.
conclude: Both identities hold for all real a and b.

drafts.proof_strategy: Multiply the sum by a and by b, then telescope.
sketch_steps: setup: Let S be the sum of a^k b^(n-k) for k from 0 to n.
derive: Reindex aS and bS over the same terms a^j b^(n+1-j).
derive: The terms with j from 1 to n cancel in the difference.
conclude: Only a^(n+1) and b^(n+1) remain, so (a-b)S = a^(n+1) - b^(n+1).

sketch_steps: derive: From ax = b, divide by a to get x = b/a.
derive: From x = b/a, multiply by a to get ax = b.
conclude: The two conditions are equivalent.

drafts.proof_strategy: Split into the three exhaustive cases on a and b.
sketch_steps: case_split: Consider a ≠ 0, then a = b = 0, then a = 0 with b ≠ 0.
derive: If a ≠ 0, the only solution is x = b/a.
derive: If a = b = 0, the equation reads 0 = 0 for every x.
derive: If a = 0 and b ≠ 0, the left side is always 0, which differs from b.
conclude: The cases are exhaustive and the outcomes exclusive, so each implication is an equivalence.

drafts.proof_strategy: Eliminate each variable by a linear combination, then substitute back.
sketch_steps: setup: Put D = ad - bc, which is nonzero.
derive: d times the first equation minus b times the second gives Dx = ed - bf.
derive: a times the second equation minus c times the first gives Dy = af - ec.
derive: Dividing by D gives the stated values of x and y.
conclude: Substituting those values back verifies both equations.

drafts.canonical_statement: For real a, b, c, d, e, f, the system ax + by = e, cx + dy = f has exactly one real solution (x, y) if and only if ad - bc ≠ 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the explicit formula one way and shift a solution along kernel directions the other way.
sketch_steps: derive: If ad - bc ≠ 0, elimination forces one value of (x, y), which does solve the system.
contradiction: Suppose a unique solution (x, y) exists and ad - bc = 0.
construct: The points (x-b, y+a) and (x-d, y+c) are also solutions.
derive: Uniqueness forces a = b = c = d = 0.
conclude: Then (x+1, y) is another solution, a contradiction.

drafts.canonical_statement: Let a, b, c, d, e, f be real with ad - bc = 0 and with a or b nonzero. The system ax + by = e, cx + dy = f has a real solution if and only if af - ce = 0 and bf - de = 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compute the two quantities from a solution, and build a solution on a coordinate axis for the converse.
sketch_steps: derive: From a solution, af - ce = (ad - bc)y = 0.
derive: Likewise bf - de = -(ad - bc)x = 0.
case_split: For the converse, consider whether a or b is nonzero.
construct: Take (e/a, 0) or (0, e/b) respectively.
conclude: The conditions make the second equation hold, so a solution exists.

drafts.canonical_statement: Let ad - bc = 0 with a or b nonzero, and let (x0, y0) solve ax + by = e, cx + dy = f. Then (x, y) is a solution if and only if x = x0 - bt and y = y0 + at for some real t.

drafts.proof_strategy: Verify the parametrized points directly, and recover t from the first equation for the converse.
sketch_steps: derive: Points x0 - bt, y0 + at solve the first equation identically.
derive: The second equation changes by (ad - bc)t = 0, so it still holds.
setup: For a solution (x, y), put u = x - x0 and v = y - y0, so au + bv = 0.
construct: Since a² + b² ≠ 0, define t = (av - bu)/(a² + b²).
derive: Using au + bv = 0, check u = -bt and v = at.
conclude: Every solution has the stated form.

drafts.proof_strategy: Split on the signs for the product, then apply the product rule to a = (a/b)b.
sketch_steps: case_split: Consider the signs of a and b.
derive: In each case |ab| = |a||b|.
derive: Applying this to a = (a/b)b gives |a| = |a/b||b|.
conclude: Dividing by |b| gives the quotient rule.

drafts.canonical_statement: Triangle inequality. For real a and b, |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|.

drafts.proof_strategy: Bound both a + b and its negative by |a| + |b|.
sketch_steps: derive: From a ≤ |a| and b ≤ |b| we get a + b ≤ |a| + |b|.
derive: From -a ≤ |a| and -b ≤ |b| we get -(a + b) ≤ |a| + |b|.
conclude: |a + b| is one of these two numbers, so the bound follows.

drafts.canonical_statement: For real a and b, |a + b| = |a| + |b| if and only if ab ≥ 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Split on whether a and b have the same sign.
sketch_steps: case_split: Consider ab ≥ 0 and ab < 0.
derive: If a and b have the same sign, both sides equal the sum of their sizes.
derive: If a > 0 > b, both a + b and -(a + b) are strictly less than a - b.
conclude: So equality holds exactly when ab ≥ 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: For real a and b, ||a| - |b|| ≤ |a - b|.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the triangle inequality to a = (a - b) + b and to its swap.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The triangle inequality gives |a| ≤ |a - b| + |b|.
derive: Swapping a and b gives |b| - |a| ≤ |a - b|.
conclude: Both signs of |a| - |b| are bounded by |a - b|.

drafts.canonical_statement: For real x and a, with no sign assumption on a, |x| = a if and only if a ≥ 0 and (x = a or x = -a).

drafts.proof_strategy: Use nonnegativity of the absolute value and split on the sign of x.
sketch_steps: derive: |x| = a forces a ≥ 0 because absolute values are nonnegative.
case_split: The sign of x gives x = a or x = -a.
conclude: Conversely, a ≥ 0 gives |±a| = a.

drafts.canonical_statement: For real x and a, |x| < a if and only if -a < x < a, and |x| > a if and only if x < -a or x > a.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use x ≤ |x|, -x ≤ |x| and the fact that |x| equals x or -x.
sketch_steps: setup: Record x ≤ |x|, -x ≤ |x|, and that |x| equals x or -x.
derive: Hence |x| < a holds exactly when both x < a and -x < a.
derive: If |x| > a, then x > a or -x > a according to the value of |x|.
conclude: Conversely, either alternative gives |x| > a by the first bounds.

drafts.proof_strategy: Determine the sign of x - a and x - b in each of the three ranges.
sketch_steps: case_split: Consider x < a, a ≤ x ≤ b and x > b.
derive: Determine the signs of x - a and x - b in each range.
conclude: Remove the absolute values and simplify.

drafts.canonical_statement: For real a ≤ b and x, |x - a| + |x - b| = b - a if and only if a ≤ x ≤ b.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compute the sum in each range of x and compare with b - a.
sketch_steps: derive: For a ≤ x ≤ b the sum equals b - a.
derive: For x < a the sum equals (b - a) + 2(a - x), which is larger.
derive: For x > b the sum equals (b - a) + 2(x - b), which is larger.
conclude: Equality holds exactly on the interval.

drafts.canonical_statement: For every real a, with no sign assumption, √(a²) = |a|.

drafts.proof_strategy: Check that |a| is the nonnegative number whose square is a².
sketch_steps: derive: |a| is nonnegative and |a|² = a².
apply_theorem: The nonnegative square root of a² is unique.
conclude: Therefore √(a²) = |a|.

drafts.canonical_statement: For real x ≥ 0 and real a, √x = a if and only if a ≥ 0 and a² = x.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the definition one way and factor the difference of squares the other way.
sketch_steps: derive: By definition, √x = a gives a ≥ 0 and a² = x.
derive: Conversely, (a - √x)(a + √x) = a² - x = 0.
case_split: Consider whether the factor a + √x vanishes.
conclude: In both cases a = √x.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show the product is the nonnegative square root of ab.
sketch_steps: derive: The product √a √b is nonnegative.
derive: Its square is ab.
conclude: By uniqueness of the nonnegative root it equals √(ab).

drafts.canonical_statement: For real a, b ≥ 0, √a < √b if and only if a < b.

drafts.proof_strategy: Factor b - a for one direction and argue by contradiction for the other.
sketch_steps: derive: b - a = (√b - √a)(√b + √a).
derive: If √a < √b, both factors are positive, so a < b.
contradiction: If a < b but √b ≤ √a, then squaring nonnegative numbers gives b ≤ a.
conclude: The two inequalities are equivalent.

sketch_steps: derive: The square of √a + √b is a + b + 2√a√b.
derive: This is at least a + b, which gives the inequality.
translate: Equality of nonnegative numbers means equality of their squares.
conclude: So equality holds exactly when √a√b = 0, that is ab = 0.

sketch_steps: derive: The product of the two conjugates is a - b, which is nonzero.
derive: So neither conjugate vanishes.
conclude: Multiplying top and bottom by the other conjugate gives both formulas.

sketch_steps: derive: The conjugate product is p² - q²r.
derive: The hypothesis makes this nonzero, so p + q√r ≠ 0.
conclude: Multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate gives the formula.

sketch_steps: contradiction: Suppose q ≠ t.
derive: Solving for √r gives (s - p)/(q - t), a rational number.
derive: This contradicts the irrationality of √r, so q = t.
conclude: Cancelling the surd term gives p = s.

sketch_steps: derive: The radicand equals (√a + √b)².

conclude: Taking the square root returns √a + √b.

drafts.proof_strategy: Introduce u and v as the claimed radicals and write each radicand as a square.
sketch_steps: setup: Put s = √(p² - q), noting 0 ≤ s ≤ p.
construct: Put u = √((p+s)/2) and v = √((p-s)/2), so u ≥ v ≥ 0.
derive: Then u² + v² = p and (2uv)² = p² - s² = q.
derive: Since 2uv ≥ 0, this gives √q = 2uv.
derive: So p + √q = (u + v)² and p - √q = (u - v)².
conclude: Take square roots using u + v ≥ 0 and u - v ≥ 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: If real x, y, s, p satisfy x + y = s and xy = p, then x³ + y³ = s³ - 3ps.

sketch_steps: derive: Expand s³ = (x + y)³.
derive: The mixed terms equal 3xy(x + y) = 3ps.
conclude: Rearranging gives x³ + y³ = s³ - 3ps.

sketch_steps: derive: From a real pair, s² - 4p = (x - y)², which is nonnegative.
construct: Conversely, put d = √(s² - 4p), x = (s + d)/2 and y = (s - d)/2.
derive: Then x + y = s.
conclude: Also xy = (s² - d²)/4 = p.

sketch_steps: translate: Multiply by the nonzero number abc(a + b + c).
derive: The equation becomes (ab + bc + ca)(a + b + c) = abc.
derive: Expansion gives (a+b)(b+c)(c+a) = (a+b+c)(ab+bc+ca) - abc.
conclude: So the equation is equivalent to (a+b)(b+c)(c+a) = 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: Fundamental theorem of symmetric polynomials. For a natural number n, every symmetric polynomial in n variables with real coefficients is a polynomial with real coefficients in the elementary symmetric polynomials e_1, ..., e_n.

drafts.proof_strategy: Remove the lexicographically leading term with a product of elementary symmetric polynomials and induct.
sketch_steps: setup: Order monomials lexicographically, which is a well-ordering of exponent tuples.
derive: Symmetry forces the leading exponents to satisfy d_1 ≥ ... ≥ d_n.
construct: Let h be the product of e_k^(d_k - d_(k+1)), with d_(n+1) = 0.
derive: The polynomial h has the same leading monomial as f.
induction: Subtracting c h gives a symmetric polynomial with a smaller leading monomial.
conclude: By well-founded induction, f is a polynomial in e_1, ..., e_n.

drafts.canonical_statement: For reals a, r, x, |x-a| ≤ r if and only if a-r ≤ x ≤ a+r.

sketch_steps: setup: Put y = x - a.
derive: |y| ≤ r holds exactly when y ≤ r and -y ≤ r.
conclude: Rewriting both gives a-r ≤ x ≤ a+r.

conclude: The distance equals √((x1-x2)^2+(y1-y2)^2).

conclude: Taking square roots of nonnegative quantities gives the inequality.

sketch_steps: derive: Write x1-x2=(x1-x3)-(x2-x3) and likewise for y, then expand.
translate: AB^2 equals AC^2+BC^2 minus twice the dot product of CA and CB.
conclude: The Pythagorean relation holds exactly when the dot product vanishes.
