drafts.proof_strategy: Approximate by Urysohn functions and sum a uniformly convergent series (outline).
sketch_steps: setup: Reduce to a bounded function with |f| ≤ 1.
apply_theorem: Urysohn's lemma on {f ≤ -1/3} and {f ≥ 1/3} gives a first approximation g_1.
induction: Repeat on the remainder, shrinking by 2/3 at each step.
derive: The series of approximations converges uniformly to a continuous function.
conclude: Its sum extends f; the unbounded case follows through a homeomorphism of ℝ with (-1,1).

drafts.canonical_statement: In a metric space, open balls are open and closed balls are closed.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="metric_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="open_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="open_ball"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closed_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closed_ball"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use the triangle inequality with the margin r - d(x,y).
sketch_steps: setup: Take y in the ball and let s = r - d(x,y).
derive: The triangle inequality gives B(y,s) ⊆ B(x,r).
derive: For y outside the closed ball, s = d(x,y) - r gives a ball missing it.
conclude: Open balls are open and closed balls are closed.

drafts.canonical_statement: A Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges to the same limit.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="metric_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="cauchy_seq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="strictly_increasing_index"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_tends_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="function_compose_map"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_tends_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Combine Cauchy estimates with one far term of the subsequence.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix ε > 0 and N from the Cauchy condition at ε/2.
derive: Choose k with φ(k) ≥ N and a_{φ(k)} within ε/2 of L.
conclude: The triangle inequality gives d(a_n, L) < ε for n ≥ N.

drafts.canonical_statement: A closed subset of a complete metric space is complete as a subspace.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="complete_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closed_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="complete_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="subspace_topology_on"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Take the limit in X and use closedness to stay in C.
sketch_steps: setup: Take a Cauchy sequence in C.
derive: It is Cauchy in X, so it converges in X by completeness.
derive: Closedness of C puts the limit in C.
conclude: The subspace C is complete.

drafts.canonical_statement: A complete subset of a metric space is closed.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="metric_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="complete_subset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closed_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use the limit in S and uniqueness of limits.
sketch_steps: setup: Take a sequence in S converging to L in X.
derive: The sequence is Cauchy, so it converges to some L' in S.
apply_theorem: Limits in a metric space are unique, so L = L'.
conclude: S contains the limits of its sequences, so it is closed.

drafts.canonical_statement: A uniform limit of continuous maps from a topological space into a metric space is continuous.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="metric_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="continuous_between"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="tends_uniformly"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="continuous_between"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: The ε/3 argument.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix a point a and ε > 0.
derive: Choose n with F_n uniformly within ε/3 of f.
derive: Continuity of F_n gives a neighborhood of a with variation below ε/3.
conclude: The triangle inequality gives d(f(x), f(a)) < ε on it.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show iterates are Cauchy by a geometric estimate; contraction gives uniqueness.
sketch_steps: construct: Fix z and define the iterates a_n = f^n(z).
derive: d(a_{n+1}, a_n) ≤ K^n d(a_1, a_0) makes the sequence Cauchy.
apply_theorem: Completeness gives a limit x.
derive: Continuity of f gives f(x) = x.
derive: Two fixed points satisfy d(x,y) ≤ K d(x,y), so x = y.
conclude: Iteration from any point converges to the unique fixed point.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a complete metric space, a countable intersection of dense open sets is dense.

drafts.proof_strategy: Build nested closed balls with radii shrinking to zero.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix a nonempty open set V.
construct: Choose nested closed balls B_n with B_n ⊆ U_n and radii tending to 0.
derive: The centers form a Cauchy sequence.
apply_theorem: Completeness gives a limit point.
derive: The limit lies in every B_n, so in V and every U_n.
conclude: The intersection meets every nonempty open set.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a nonempty complete metric space is a countable union of closed sets, then one of them has nonempty interior.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Baire to the complements.
sketch_steps: contradiction: Assume every C_n has empty interior.
derive: The complements are open and dense.
apply_theorem: The Baire category theorem makes their intersection dense.
conclude: A dense subset of a nonempty space is nonempty, contradicting the cover.

drafts.proof_strategy: Read the uniform definition of total boundedness on the distance basis.
sketch_steps: translate: The uniformity of a metric space has basis the sets d(x,y) < ε.
derive: Covers at each entourage scale correspond to covers by ε-balls.
conclude: Total boundedness is equivalent to finite ε-nets.

drafts.canonical_statement: A subset of a metric space is compact if and only if it is totally bounded and complete.

drafts.proof_strategy: Forward via covers and sequential compactness; backward by a diagonal Cauchy subsequence.
sketch_steps: derive: A finite subcover of ε-balls shows total boundedness.
derive: A Cauchy sequence has a convergent subsequence, so it converges in K.
construct: Conversely use finite 1/k-covers and a diagonal argument to extract a Cauchy subsequence.
apply_theorem: Completeness gives its limit in K.
conclude: K is sequentially compact, hence compact in a metric space.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a group G acting on a set X, elements g, h of G and a point x, h fixes gx if and only if g⁻¹hg fixes x; hence Stab(gx) = g Stab(x) g⁻¹.

drafts.proof_strategy: Act on the fixing equation by g⁻¹ and use compatibility of the action.
sketch_steps: setup: Write the condition h(gx) = gx.
derive: Apply g⁻¹ to both sides and use compatibility to get (g⁻¹hg)x = x.
conclude: Applying g reverses the step, so the two conditions are equivalent.

drafts.canonical_statement: The kernel of the homomorphism from G to Sym(X) given by an action of G on X is the intersection of the stabilizers of all points of X.

drafts.proof_strategy: Unfold membership in the kernel as pointwise equality of permutations.
sketch_steps: translate: g is in the kernel exactly when the permutation of g is the identity.
derive: Equality of permutations means gx = x for every x.
conclude: This is membership in every stabilizer.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a group G of order p^n, with p prime, acts on a finite set X, then |X| ≡ |X^G| modulo p, where X^G is the set of points fixed by all of G.

drafts.proof_strategy: Split X into orbits and observe that non-singleton orbits have size divisible by p.
sketch_steps: setup: Write |X| as the sum of the orbit sizes.
apply_theorem: By orbit-stabilizer every orbit size divides p^n.
derive: Orbits of size 1 are exactly the points of X^G.
derive: Every other orbit has size divisible by p.
conclude: Reducing modulo p gives |X| ≡ |X^G|.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a group G acts on a finite set X, then |X| is the sum of the sizes of the orbits.

drafts.proof_strategy: Orbits are the classes of an equivalence relation, so they partition X.
sketch_steps: setup: Define x ~ y when y lies in the orbit of x.
derive: The group axioms make this an equivalence relation whose classes are the orbits.
conclude: Counting a partition gives the sum of the orbit sizes.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a subgroup H of a group G has finite index n, then H contains a normal subgroup N of G whose index [G:N] divides n!.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take the kernel of the left multiplication action on the cosets of H.
sketch_steps: construct: Let G act on the n left cosets of H, giving a homomorphism to a symmetric group of order n!.
setup: Let N be the kernel, which is normal.
derive: An element of N fixes the coset H, so it lies in H.
apply_theorem: The first isomorphism theorem gives [G:N] = |im|.
conclude: Lagrange shows that |im| divides n!.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare the prime factors of [H:N] with p for the kernel N of the action on cosets.
sketch_steps: construct: Let N be the kernel of the action of G on the p cosets of H.
derive: Then [G:N] divides p!, and writing [G:N] = pk gives k | (p-1)!.
contradiction: A prime factor q of k would satisfy q < p and q | |G|, against minimality of p.
conclude: So k = 1, H = N, and H is normal.

drafts.canonical_statement: For elements a, b of a group, bab⁻¹ and a have the same order, and ab and ba have the same order, including the case of infinite order.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="element_order"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group_mul"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group_mul"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group_inv"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="element_order"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="element_order"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group_mul"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="element_order"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group_mul"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Conjugation preserves the set of exponents killing an element, and ab is a conjugate of ba.
sketch_steps: derive: Compute (bab⁻¹)^n = b a^n b⁻¹.
translate: So the exponents n killing bab⁻¹ and a coincide.
derive: Write ab = a(ba)a⁻¹.
conclude: Apply the conjugation claim to ba.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a group homomorphism f from G to H and an element g of finite order, the order of f(g) divides the order of g.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group_hom"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_order_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dvd"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="element_order"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="element_order"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: A homomorphism sends the relation g^m = 1 to f(g)^m = 1.
sketch_steps: derive: f(g)^m = f(g^m) = 1 for m the order of g.
derive: Division with remainder shows the order of any element killing by m divides m.
conclude: Hence the order of f(g) divides m.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime p, a natural number n and a group element g, if g^(p^(n+1)) = 1 and g^(p^n) ≠ 1, then g has order p^(n+1).

cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="element_order"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: The order divides a prime power, so it is a smaller prime power unless the top exponent occurs.
sketch_steps: derive: The order divides p^(n+1), so it equals p^k with k ≤ n+1.
contradiction: If k ≤ n, then g^(p^n) = 1, against the hypothesis.
conclude: So k = n+1.

drafts.canonical_statement: For elements a and b of finite order in groups G and H, the order of (a, b) in G × H is the least common multiple of the orders of a and b.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_order_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_order_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="element_order"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ordered_pair"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="lcm"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="element_order"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="element_order"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Powers are computed componentwise, and common multiples are the multiples of the lcm.
sketch_steps: derive: (a,b)^n = (a^n, b^n).
translate: This is the identity exactly when both orders divide n.
conclude: The least such positive n is the lcm of the orders.

drafts.canonical_statement: A finite abelian group G has an element g whose order is divisible by the order of every element h of G.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="abelian_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dvd"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="element_order"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="element_order"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: If a maximal order fails to absorb some order, build a larger order from coprime parts.
sketch_steps: setup: Take g of maximal order m and suppose ord(h) = k does not divide m.
derive: Choose a prime q with larger exponent b in k than exponent a in m.
construct: Form g^(q^a) of order m' and h^(k') of order q^b, which are coprime.
apply_theorem: Commuting elements of coprime orders have product of order m'q^b.
contradiction: m'q^b exceeds m.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a finite group G has at most n solutions of x^n = 1 for every positive integer n, then G is cyclic.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="gt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="leq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="power_root_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="cyclic_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Count elements by order and compare with the totient sum over divisors.
sketch_steps: setup: Let ψ(d) be the number of elements of order d for d dividing N = |G|.
derive: If an element a of order d exists, the solutions of x^d = 1 are exactly ⟨a⟩, so ψ(d) = φ(d).
derive: Thus ψ(d) ≤ φ(d) for every d.
apply_theorem: The sums of ψ and of φ over divisors of N both equal N.
conclude: ψ(N) = φ(N) ≥ 1 gives a generator.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a permutation σ of a set X and points a, b of X, σ (a b) σ⁻¹ = (σ(a) σ(b)), where (a a) denotes the identity.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="permutation_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group_mul"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group_mul"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="transposition_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group_inv"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="transposition_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Compare both permutations pointwise, separating σ(a), σ(b) and the other points.
sketch_steps: case_split: Treat x = σ(a), x = σ(b) and the remaining points.
derive: On the first two, the conjugate exchanges σ(a) and σ(b).
derive: Otherwise σ⁻¹(x) is fixed by (a b), so x is fixed.
conclude: The two permutations agree everywhere.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a permutation of a finite set is written in two ways as a product of transpositions, the numbers of transpositions have the same parity.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="list_of_transpositions"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="list_of_transpositions"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="list_product"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="list_product"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nat_mod"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="list_length"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nat_mod"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="list_length"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Define the sign as a product over unordered pairs, show it is multiplicative with value -1 on transpositions, and apply it to both products.
sketch_steps: construct: Number X and let ε(σ) be the product of (σ(i)-σ(j))/(i-j) over unordered pairs {i,j}.
derive: Each permutation permutes the pairs, so ε(σρ) = ε(σ)ε(ρ).
derive: A direct computation gives ε((1 2)) = -1.
derive: Every transposition is a conjugate of (1 2), so ε takes the value -1 on it.
conclude: The two products have values (-1)^|l| and (-1)^|m|, so equal products force equal parity.

drafts.proof_strategy: Conjugation relabels the entries of cycles, and a matching of equal-length cycles defines the conjugator.
sketch_steps: derive: ρ(a_1 ... a_k)ρ⁻¹ = (ρ(a_1) ... ρ(a_k)).
conclude: Conjugate permutations therefore have the same cycle type.
setup: Conversely, include fixed points as cycles of length 1 and match cycles of equal length.
construct: Define ρ by sending the entries of each cycle of σ to those of the matched cycle of τ.
conclude: Then ρσρ⁻¹ = τ.

drafts.canonical_statement: The order of a permutation of a finite set is the least common multiple of the lengths of the cycles in its disjoint cycle decomposition, with value 1 for the identity.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="symmetric_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="element_order"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="multiset_lcm"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="cycle_type"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Disjoint cycles commute and act on separate supports, so a power vanishes exactly when each factor does.
sketch_steps: setup: Decompose σ = c_1...c_r into disjoint cycles of lengths ℓ_i.
derive: Commutativity gives σ^n = c_1^n...c_r^n.
derive: Disjoint supports give σ^n = 1 exactly when each c_i^n = 1.
translate: This means ℓ_i divides n for every i.
conclude: The order is the lcm of the ℓ_i.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every permutation of a finite set is a finite product of pairwise disjoint cycles, the identity being the empty product.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="symmetric_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="list_product"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="list_of_cycles"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="pairwise_disjoint_permutations"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Restrict σ to each nontrivial orbit of the cyclic group it generates.
sketch_steps: setup: Take the orbits of ⟨σ⟩ of size at least 2.
derive: Each orbit has the form a, σ(a), ..., σ^(k-1)(a).
construct: Let c_i equal σ on the i-th orbit and the identity elsewhere.
derive: The c_i are cycles with disjoint supports.
conclude: Their product agrees with σ at every point.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a subgroup H and a normal subgroup N of a group G, an element lies in the subgroup generated by H and N if and only if it has the form hn with h in H and n in N; in other words the product set HN is a subgroup.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="subgroup_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normal_subgroup"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="subgroup_join"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group_mul"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Check that HN is closed under products and inverses by moving elements of N past elements of H.
sketch_steps: setup: Let S be the set of products hn.
derive: (hn)(h'n') = (hh')((h')⁻¹nh')n' lies in S because N is normal.
derive: (hn)⁻¹ = h⁻¹(hn⁻¹h⁻¹) lies in S for the same reason.
derive: So S is a subgroup containing H and N.
conclude: Any subgroup containing H and N contains S, so S is the generated subgroup.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a subgroup H of a finite group G is the only subgroup of its order, then H is normal.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="subgroup_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="subgroup_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normal_subgroup"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: A conjugate of H is a subgroup of the same order.
sketch_steps: derive: Conjugation by g is an automorphism, so gHg⁻¹ is a subgroup with |gHg⁻¹| = |H|.
derive: Uniqueness gives gHg⁻¹ = H.
conclude: H is normal.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a normal subgroup N of finite index in a group G and an element g of G, the power g^[G:N] lies in N.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the fact that the group order kills every element to the quotient G/N.
sketch_steps: setup: G/N is a finite group of order [G:N].
apply_theorem: Hence (gN)^[G:N] is the identity coset.
conclude: This says g^[G:N] lies in N.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a group homomorphism f from a finite group G to a group H, |G| = |ker f|·|im f|.

drafts.proof_strategy: Combine the first isomorphism theorem with Lagrange's theorem.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The first isomorphism theorem gives [G:ker f] = |im f|.
apply_theorem: Lagrange gives |G| = |ker f|·[G:ker f].
conclude: Substitute.

drafts.proof_strategy: Define φ on cosets, check well-definedness with N ⊆ ker f, and note that cosets exhaust G/N.
sketch_steps: construct: Set φ(gN) = f(g).
derive: gN = g'N gives g⁻¹g' in ker f, so φ is well defined.
derive: φ is a homomorphism because f is.
conclude: Any other such map agrees with φ on every coset.

drafts.canonical_statement: For subgroups H and K of finite index in a group G, the intersection H ∩ K has finite index and [G:H∩K] ≤ [G:H][G:K].

drafts.proof_strategy: Inject the cosets of H ∩ K into pairs of cosets of H and of K.
sketch_steps: construct: Send g(H∩K) to the pair (gH, gK).
derive: The map is well defined and injective because g⁻¹g' lies in H∩K exactly when it lies in both.
conclude: The target has [G:H][G:K] elements.

drafts.canonical_statement: If G is a solvable group, then every subgroup H of G is solvable and the target K of every surjective homomorphism from G is solvable.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="solvable_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="subgroup_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group_hom"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="surjective_function"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="solvable_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="solvable_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Compare derived series by induction, using inclusion for H and surjectivity for K.
sketch_steps: setup: Choose m with G^(m) trivial.
induction: H^(i) is contained in G^(i) for all i.
induction: f(G^(i)) = K^(i), using surjectivity at i = 0 and f([A,A]) = [f(A),f(A)].
conclude: H^(m) and K^(m) are trivial.

drafts.canonical_statement: A nontrivial group G with [G,G] = G is not solvable.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="trivial_subgroup"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="commutator_subgroup"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="not"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="solvable_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: The derived series is constant equal to G, so it never reaches the trivial group.
sketch_steps: induction: G^(i) = G for every i.
contradiction: Solvability would give G^(m) = 1, while G is nontrivial.

drafts.canonical_statement: If the quotient G/Z(G) of a group G by its center is nilpotent, then G is nilpotent.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nilpotent_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="quotient_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group_center"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nilpotent_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Pull the upper central series of G/Z(G) back to G, shifted by one step.
sketch_steps: setup: Define the upper central series Z_i and fix c with Z_c(G/Z) = G/Z.
induction: π(x) in Z_i(G/Z) implies x in Z_(i+1)(G).
derive: The step uses π([x,y]) = [π(x),π(y)].
conclude: Z_(c+1)(G) = G.

drafts.canonical_statement: A proper subgroup H of a nilpotent group G is properly contained in its normalizer N_G(H).
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nilpotent_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="subgroup_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="prsubset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="subgroup_normalizer"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Choose an element in the first term of the upper central series outside H; it normalizes H.
sketch_steps: setup: Use the upper central series with Z_c = G.
derive: There is i with Z_i inside H and Z_(i+1) not inside H.
construct: Take x in Z_(i+1) outside H.
derive: [x,h] in Z_i gives xhx⁻¹ in H, and likewise for x⁻¹.
conclude: x normalizes H and is not in H.

drafts.canonical_statement: A finite group G is nilpotent if and only if, for every prime p, every Sylow p-subgroup of G is normal.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nilpotent_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="P"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="sylow_subgroup"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normal_subgroup"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use the normalizer condition for one direction and the internal direct product of Sylow subgroups for the other.
sketch_steps: setup: For nilpotent G and a Sylow subgroup T, put L = N_G(T).
derive: T is the unique Sylow p-subgroup of L, so any g normalizing L normalizes T, giving N_G(L) = L.
apply_theorem: The normalizer condition forces L = G.
setup: Conversely, list the normal Sylow subgroups T_1, ..., T_r.
derive: Coprime orders make distinct T_i commute, and the product map from their direct product to G is an injective homomorphism between groups of equal order.
conclude: Finite p-groups and finite products of nilpotent groups are nilpotent.

drafts.canonical_statement: For f with values in a commutative additive monoid and a natural number n, the sum over i < n of the sum over j < i of f(i,j) equals the sum over j < n of the sum over j < i < n of f(i,j).

drafts.proof_strategy: Describe both iterated ranges as the single set of pairs with j < i < n.
sketch_steps: translate: The left side sums over pairs with 0 ≤ i < n and 0 ≤ j < i.
derive: This set equals the set of pairs with 0 ≤ j < n and j < i < n.
conclude: Finite sums do not depend on the order of the terms.

drafts.canonical_statement: If finite sets s and t and a map φ satisfy φ(x) ∈ t for all x in s, then the sum over y in t of the sum over x in s with φ(x) = y of f(x) equals the sum over x in s of f(x).

drafts.proof_strategy: The fibers of φ over t partition s.
sketch_steps: setup: Let s_y be the fiber of φ over y in t.
derive: The fibers are disjoint, and they cover s because φ maps s into t.
conclude: Summing over a disjoint union gives the identity.

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on s, splitting subsets of s ∪ {c} by whether they contain c.
sketch_steps: induction: Empty s gives 1 on both sides.
setup: For a new index c, multiply the identity for s by a_c + b_c.
derive: Terms with a_c correspond to subsets containing c.
derive: Terms with b_c correspond to subsets not containing c.
conclude: These two kinds exhaust the subsets of s ∪ {c}.

setup: Add a_(n+1) b_(n+1) to the identity for n.
derive: Replace b_(n+1) by B_(n+1) - B_n.
conclude: Collect (a_(n+1) - a_n) B_n into the difference sum.

drafts.proof_strategy: Remove a pair {c, φ(c)} with f(c) ≠ 0 and induct on the size of s.
sketch_steps: case_split: If f vanishes on s the sum is 0.
setup: Otherwise pick c with f(c) ≠ 0 and set d = φ(c), so d ≠ c.
derive: φ preserves s minus {c, d} because φ is an involution.
induction: The sum over the smaller set is 0.
conclude: f(c) + f(d) = 0 finishes the sum.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a subset s and a submodule p of a module M over a ring S, the submodule generated by s is contained in p if and only if s ⊆ p.

drafts.proof_strategy: One direction uses s ⊆ ⟨s⟩ and the other uses closure of p under linear combinations.
sketch_steps: derive: s lies in the generated submodule, which gives the forward implication.
derive: Elements of the generated submodule are finite linear combinations of s.
conclude: p is closed under these combinations.

sketch_steps: setup: Take x = y + z in (p+q) ∩ r with y in p and z in q.
derive: z = x - y lies in r because y lies in p ⊆ r.
derive: So x lies in p + (q∩r).
conclude: The reverse inclusion follows from p ⊆ r directly.

derive: A nonzero kernel element gives a nonzero element of some A_i ∩ sum of the others.
conclude: Injectivity and independence are equivalent.
