drafts.proof_strategy: The ultrametric inequality makes every point a center; complementary points have disjoint balls.
sketch_steps: derive: The ultrametric inequality shows B(x, r) is contained in B(y, r), and conversely.
derive: Two balls of the same radius are either equal or disjoint.
conclude: The complement is a union of open balls, so the ball is closed.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime p, the subset of x in Q_p with |x|_p ≤ 1 is open and compact.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="P"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="open_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="padic_unit_ball"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="compact_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="padic_unit_ball"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="padic_field"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: The ultrametric inequality shows the closed unit ball contains an open ball around each of its points.
sketch_steps: derive: The set is Z_p, which is compact.
derive: Points within distance below 1 of a point of the set stay in the set.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime p, the maximal ideal of Z_p is (p), and every nonzero ideal of Z_p has the form (p^n) for some natural number n.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="P"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="padic_integers"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="maximal_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="principal_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="padic_integers"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="principal_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Divide by powers of p according to the norm; the element of largest norm generates the ideal.
sketch_steps: derive: Nonunits are the elements of norm at most 1/p, that is, multiples of p.
construct: In a nonzero ideal choose an element of largest norm p^(-n).
derive: Dividing by a unit shows p^n lies in the ideal.
conclude: Every other element is a multiple of p^n.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime p and a nonzero x in Q_p, there are u in Q_p with |u|_p = 1 and an integer n such that x = u p^n.

drafts.proof_strategy: Divide x by the power of p that has the same norm.
sketch_steps: setup: Write |x|_p = p^(-n) with n an integer.
construct: Let u = x p^(-n).
conclude: Multiplicativity of the norm gives |u|_p = 1.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime p and a natural number n, the reduction homomorphism from Z_p to Z/p^n Z, sending x to the class of a natural number a with |x - a|_p ≤ p^(-n), is surjective with kernel (p^n).

sketch_steps: construct: Define the reduction using natural approximations of x.
derive: Natural numbers map onto Z/p^n Z, so the map is surjective.
derive: x lies in the kernel iff |x|_p ≤ p^(-n), iff x is in (p^n).

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime p and x in Z_p, there is exactly one integer n with 0 ≤ n < p and |x - n|_p < 1.

sketch_steps: construct: Take a natural number close to x and reduce it modulo p.
derive: The ultrametric inequality preserves the closeness.
derive: Two valid digits differ by a multiple of p of absolute value below p.

drafts.proof_strategy: Define g as the limit of compatible representatives and use that an element of Z_p is determined by its residues.
sketch_steps: construct: Take representatives a_n of f_n(r) in the range 0 to p^n - 1.
derive: Compatibility makes (a_n) converge, and the limit reduces to f_n(r).
derive: Additivity and multiplicativity hold modulo every p^n, hence exactly.
conclude: Uniqueness follows since the intersection of (p^n) is zero.

drafts.proof_strategy: Run Newton's iteration from a, which converges quadratically because the derivative stays a unit on the residue disk.
sketch_steps: derive: Taylor expansion over Z_p gives F(x+h) = F(x) + F'(x)h + h^2 G(x,h), and |F'(x)| = 1 whenever |x-a| < 1.
construct: Define a_(n+1) = a_n - F(a_n)/F'(a_n).
induction: |a_n - a| ≤ c and |F(a_n)| ≤ c^(2^n), where c = |F(a)| < 1.
derive: The sequence converges in Z_p to a root z with |z - a| < 1.
conclude: If w is another root in the disk, then h = w - z satisfies h(F'(z) + hG) = 0 with the second factor nonzero, so h = 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Hensel's lemma to X² - u at a, whose derivative has norm 1 for odd p.
sketch_steps: derive: The hypotheses force |a|_p = 1.
derive: For odd p, |2a|_p = 1.
apply_theorem: Hensel's lemma for simple roots gives z.

drafts.canonical_statement: If u in Z_2 satisfies |u - 1|_2 ≤ 1/8, that is u ≡ 1 mod 8, then u = z^2 for some z in Z_2.

sketch_steps: setup: Take F = X² - u and a = 1.
apply_theorem: Hensel's inequality holds, which gives a root.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Hensel's lemma to X^(p-1) - 1, using Fermat's little theorem at a.
sketch_steps: derive: Fermat's little theorem gives |a^(p-1) - 1|_p < 1.
derive: The derivative (p-1) a^(p-2) has norm 1.
apply_theorem: Hensel's lemma for simple roots gives a unique lift.

drafts.canonical_statement: For an odd prime p, there is z in Z_p with z^2 = -1 if and only if p ≡ 1 mod 4.

drafts.proof_strategy: Reduce modulo p for one direction and lift a square root by Hensel's lemma for the other.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: -1 is a square mod p iff p ≡ 1 mod 4.
derive: A square root in Z_p reduces to one mod p.
apply_theorem: Hensel's lemma lifts a square root mod p to Z_p.

drafts.canonical_statement: Ostrowski's theorem. A nontrivial absolute value f on Q is equivalent to the usual absolute value or to the p-adic absolute value for exactly one prime p, where equivalence means that f^c equals the other for some c > 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Separate the unbounded case, handled by base expansions, from the bounded case, where the absolute value is ultrametric and determined by one prime.
sketch_steps: case_split: Some natural number has f(n) > 1, or none does.
derive: In the first case base expansions give f(b) = f(a)^(log_a b), so f = |·|^s.
derive: In the second case f is ultrametric, and the integers with f < 1 form a prime ideal (p).
derive: Then f(n) = f(p)^(v_p(n)), so f is a power of the p-adic absolute value.
conclude: Different primes give inequivalent absolute values.

drafts.canonical_statement: Mahler's theorem. For a prime p, a complete ultrametric normed Z_p-module E with bounded scalar action and a continuous f from Z_p to E, with Δf(x) = f(x+1) - f(x), the elements Δ^n f(0) tend to 0, and f is the uniformly convergent sum of binomial(x, n) Δ^n f(0).

drafts.proof_strategy: Show iterated differences tend to 0 using (T-1)^(p^s) ≡ T^(p^s) ± 1 mod p and uniform continuity, then compare with f on the dense set of natural numbers.
sketch_steps: derive: Modulo p the operator Δ^(p^s) is T^(p^s) ± 1.
derive: Uniform continuity makes (T^(p^s) - 1)g small, so differences of high order have small norm.
derive: Hence Δ^n f(0) tends to 0 and the series converges uniformly since binomials have norm at most 1.
conclude: Newton's formula gives equality on N, and density gives equality on Z_p.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime p and a commutative ring R, every p-typical Witt vector x over R satisfies F(V(x)) = x p, where F is Frobenius and V is Verschiebung.

sketch_steps: translate: Components of F(V(x)) - xp are universal integer polynomials.
derive: It suffices to work over a polynomial ring over Z, where the ghost map is injective.
derive: Ghost components satisfy w_n(FV(x)) = p w_n(x).
conclude: Hence F(V(x)) = xp.

sketch_steps: derive: In characteristic p, F and V commute, so V(F(y)) = y p.
induction: Peel off one V and F and use additivity of V^n.

sketch_steps: apply_theorem: In characteristic p, x p = V(F(x)).
derive: F raises components to the p-th power, and V shifts them.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime p and a field k of characteristic p, x in W(k) is a unit if and only if its zeroth component x_0 is nonzero.

drafts.proof_strategy: The zeroth component is a ring homomorphism; conversely solve for the inverse component by component.
sketch_steps: derive: Taking the zeroth component is a ring homomorphism, so units map to units.
construct: Solve (xy)_n recursively for y_n, which appears linearly with coefficient x_0^(p^n).
conclude: Since x_0 is nonzero, the recursion defines an inverse.

drafts.proof_strategy: Identify truncated Witt vectors with Z/p^n Z by counting and pass to the inverse limit.
sketch_steps: derive: The truncation W_n has p^n elements, and p^n = V^n(1) over F_p.
derive: So Z/p^n Z maps isomorphically to W_n.
conclude: Pass to the inverse limit over n.

sketch_steps: setup: Fix ε > 0 and put ε' = ε/(2K), which is positive because K > 0.
apply_theorem: The hypothesis for ε' gives N with |a_n - L| ≤ Kε' for n ≥ N.
conclude: Since Kε' = ε/2 < ε, the strict bound holds for n ≥ N.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take ε = |L|/2 in the definition and use the triangle inequality.
sketch_steps: setup: Since L ≠ 0, ε = |L|/2 is positive; take the corresponding N.
derive: For n ≥ N, |L| ≤ |L - a_n| + |a_n| < |L|/2 + |a_n|.
conclude: Rearranging gives |L|/2 < |a_n|.

drafts.canonical_statement: If real sequences satisfy a_n → L and b_n → M with M ≠ 0 and b_n ≠ 0 for all n, then a_n/b_n → L/M.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_tends_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_tends_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_fn_tends_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="fns1" name="lambda"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="divide"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="divide"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Bound the denominator away from zero, then estimate the difference by the two errors.
sketch_steps: derive: Eventually |b_n| > |M|/2 because b_n → M and M ≠ 0.
translate: Write a_n/b_n - L/M = (M(a_n - L) - L(b_n - M))/(b_n M).
derive: For large n the difference is at most 2|a_n - L|/|M| + 2|L||b_n - M|/|M|².
conclude: Choose N so that each of the two terms is below ε/2.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a real sequence a converges to L and p from the naturals to the naturals is strictly increasing, then the subsequence a_{p(n)} converges to L.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="strict_mono_index"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_tends_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_fn_tends_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="fns1" name="lambda"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Show p(n) ≥ n by induction, so the same N works for the subsequence.
sketch_steps: induction: A strictly increasing p on the naturals satisfies p(n) ≥ n.
setup: Fix ε > 0 and take N for the sequence a.
conclude: For n ≥ N we have p(n) ≥ N, hence |a_{p(n)} - L| < ε.

drafts.canonical_statement: If the even-indexed and the odd-indexed terms of a real sequence both converge to L, then the sequence converges to L.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_fn_tends_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="fns1" name="lambda"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_fn_tends_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="fns1" name="lambda"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_tends_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Choose N large enough for both parities and split on the parity of n.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix ε > 0 and take N₁, N₂ for the even and odd subsequences.
case_split: Write n = 2k or n = 2k + 1 for n ≥ 2N₁ + 2N₂ + 1.
conclude: In each case k is beyond the corresponding threshold, so |a_n - L| < ε.

drafts.canonical_statement: A real sequence a converges to L if and only if for every strictly increasing p there is a strictly increasing q such that a_{p(q(n))} converges to L.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_tends_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="strict_mono_index"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="strict_mono_index"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_fn_tends_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="fns1" name="lambda"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: The forward direction takes q to be the identity; for the converse, extract a subsequence staying ε away from L.
sketch_steps: derive: If a_n → L then every subsequence converges to L, so q = id works.
contradiction: If a_n does not tend to L, some ε > 0 has |a_n - L| ≥ ε for arbitrarily large n.
construct: Choose a strictly increasing p with |a_{p(k)} - L| ≥ ε for all k.
conclude: No further subsequence of a_{p(n)} can converge to L.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a real sequence a converges to L, then the arithmetic means (a_0 + ... + a_n)/(n+1) converge to L.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_tends_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_fn_tends_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="fns1" name="lambda"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="divide"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="real_partial_sum"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="fns1" name="lambda"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Reduce to limit 0 and split the sum into a fixed head and a small tail.
sketch_steps: translate: With b_n = a_n - L, the mean minus L equals the mean of the b_i.
setup: Fix ε > 0 and take N with |b_n| < ε/2 for n ≥ N.
derive: The first N terms contribute at most A/(n+1), which is below ε/2 for large n.
derive: The remaining terms contribute at most ε/2.
conclude: The mean differs from L by less than ε for large n.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a_{n+1} = f(a_n) for all n, a_n → L and f is continuous at L, then f(L) = L.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_tends_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_continuous_at"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="fns1" name="lambda"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: The sequence a_{n+1} = f(a_n) has both limits L and f(L), and limits are unique.
sketch_steps: derive: Continuity at L gives f(a_n) → f(L).
derive: Shifting the index gives f(a_n) = a_{n+1} → L.
conclude: Uniqueness of limits gives f(L) = L.

drafts.canonical_statement: For natural numbers n, the (n+1)-th root of n+1 converges to 1 as n tends to infinity.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_fn_tends_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="fns1" name="lambda"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="divide"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Write the root as 1 + h and bound h with one term of the binomial expansion.
sketch_steps: setup: Put h_m = m^(1/m) - 1, which is nonnegative.
derive: The binomial theorem gives m ≥ m(m-1)h_m²/2 for m ≥ 2.
derive: Hence h_m ≤ √(2/(m-1)).
conclude: The right side tends to 0, so m^(1/m) → 1.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a natural number k and real r with |r| < 1, the sequence n^k r^n converges to 0.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="lt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="abs"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_fn_tends_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="fns1" name="lambda"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Take a (k+1)-th root of |r| and reduce to n s^n → 0, which follows from the binomial theorem.
sketch_steps: setup: Treat r = 0 directly and otherwise put s = |r|^(1/(k+1)) in (0,1).
derive: The binomial theorem gives n s^n ≤ 2/((n-1)h²) with s = 1/(1+h), so n s^n → 0.
translate: |n^k r^n| = (n s^n)^k s^n.
conclude: For large n this is at most n s^n, which tends to 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: If |a_{n+1} - a_n| ≤ C r^n for all n with 0 ≤ r < 1, then a converges to some L and |a_n - L| ≤ C r^n/(1-r) for all n.

drafts.proof_strategy: Sum the increments as a geometric series to get a Cauchy bound, then pass to the limit.
sketch_steps: derive: For m > n, |a_m - a_n| ≤ C r^n/(1-r) by the triangle inequality.
apply_theorem: Since r^n → 0 the sequence is Cauchy, so it converges to some L.
conclude: Letting m → ∞ gives |a_n - L| ≤ C r^n/(1-r).

drafts.proof_strategy: Factor x^n - a^n and bound the cofactor after restricting to |x - a| < 1.
sketch_steps: case_split: The case n = 0 is immediate since the difference vanishes.
translate: Factor x^n - a^n as (x - a) times a sum of n products.
derive: For |x - a| < 1 each product is at most B^(n-1) with B = |a| + 1.
construct: Take δ = min(1, ε/(n B^(n-1))).
conclude: Then |x - a| < δ gives |x^n - a^n| < ε.

drafts.proof_strategy: Assume y ≤ x, compare the square of the difference with x - y, and take roots.
sketch_steps: setup: By symmetry assume y ≤ x and put s = √x, t = √y.
derive: Since t² ≤ st, (s - t)² ≤ s² - t² = |x - y|.
conclude: Taking square roots gives the bound.

conclude: Taking the smaller δ gives |f(x)g(x) - LM| < ε.

conclude: The denominator exceeds |M|²/2, so the difference is below ε.

apply_theorem: The sequence f(x_n) is Cauchy, so it converges to some L.
conclude: For x near a, compare f(x) with f(x_n) and f(x_n) with L.

apply_theorem: The interval (a, a+δ) contains a rational q and an irrational u.
derive: Then |1 - f(a)| < 1/2 and |f(a)| < 1/2.
conclude: The triangle inequality gives 1 < 1.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply uniform continuity at level e to a pair (x_n, y_n) closer than δ.
sketch_steps: contradiction: Assume f is uniformly continuous on S and take δ for ε = e.
derive: Since x_n - y_n → 0, some n has |x_n - y_n| < δ.
conclude: Then |f(x_n) - f(y_n)| < e, against the hypothesis.

drafts.proof_strategy: Outside a large interval both values are near L; on the interval use uniform continuity on a compact set.
sketch_steps: setup: Choose R with |f(x) - L| < ε/2 for |x| ≥ R.
apply_theorem: f is uniformly continuous on [-R-1, R+1], which gives δ₀.
construct: Put δ = min(δ₀, 1).
case_split: If x, y lie in the interval use δ₀; otherwise both have absolute value at least R.
conclude: In either case |f(x) - f(y)| < ε.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a < b and f is uniformly continuous on the open interval (a,b), then the right limit of f at a exists.

drafts.proof_strategy: Uniform continuity sends a sequence decreasing to a to a Cauchy sequence, whose limit is the right limit.
sketch_steps: construct: Let x_n = a + (b-a)/(n+2), a sequence in (a,b) tending to a.
apply_theorem: Uniform continuity makes f(x_n) Cauchy, so it converges to some L.
setup: Fix ε > 0 and take δ for ε/2 and n with x_n within δ/2 of a and f(x_n) within ε/2 of L.
conclude: For a < x < a + min(b - a, δ/2), comparing with f(x_n) gives |f(x) - L| < ε.

drafts.canonical_statement: A function f has derivative u at a if and only if for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 with |f(x) - f(a) - u(x-a)| ≤ ε|x-a| whenever |x - a| < δ.

drafts.proof_strategy: Multiply or divide the difference quotient estimate by |x - a|.
sketch_steps: translate: The derivative condition is the ε-δ limit of the difference quotient.
derive: Multiplying by |x - a| gives the linear approximation bound, and x = a is trivial.
derive: Conversely, dividing the bound for ε/2 by |x - a| gives the quotient estimate.
conclude: The two conditions are equivalent.

sketch_steps: setup: Apply the definition of the derivative with ε = u/2 to get δ.
derive: For 0 < |x - a| < δ the difference quotient is greater than u/2 > 0.
case_split: Split on the sign of x - a.
conclude: f(x) - f(a) has the same sign as x - a.

sketch_steps: setup: Fix ε > 0 and take δ with |g(t) - u| < ε for 0 < |t - a| < δ.
apply_theorem: For 0 < |x - a| < δ the mean value theorem gives c between a and x with difference quotient g(c).
derive: Since 0 < |c - a| < δ, the difference quotient is within ε of u.
conclude: Therefore the derivative at a exists and equals u.

sketch_steps: induction: Induct on n over all sequences of functions.
derive: For n = 0, F_0 has zero derivative and is constant by the mean value theorem.
derive: For the step, the induction hypothesis gives F_1 as a polynomial.
construct: Let P be the termwise antiderivative of F_1.
conclude: F_0 - P has zero derivative, so F_0 is P plus a constant.

sketch_steps: translate: For m ≤ n, the block sum equals S_n - S_m.
derive: A convergent sequence of partial sums is Cauchy, which gives the condition.

apply_theorem: Completeness of the reals gives convergence.

sketch_steps: setup: Take N with c/2 < a_n/b_n < 3c/2 for n ≥ N.
derive: Hence (c/2)b_n < a_n < (3c/2)b_n for n ≥ N.
apply_theorem: Comparison on the tails gives each implication.
conclude: Convergence of the two series is equivalent.

drafts.canonical_statement: For real p, the series of 1/(n+1)^p over natural numbers n converges if and only if p > 1.

drafts.proof_strategy: Group terms in dyadic blocks and compare with a geometric series or with a constant lower bound.
sketch_steps: setup: Positive terms converge if and only if the partial sums are bounded.
derive: For p > 1 the block 2^k ≤ m < 2^(k+1) sums to at most (2^(1-p))^k, a convergent geometric series.
derive: For 0 < p ≤ 1 each block 2^k < m ≤ 2^(k+1) sums to at least 1/2.
derive: For p ≤ 0 the terms do not tend to 0.
conclude: The series converges exactly when p > 1.

sketch_steps: setup: Both series have nonnegative terms, so convergence is boundedness of partial sums.
derive: On 2^k ≤ i < 2^(k+1), f(i) ≤ f(2^k), so the sum up to 2^K is at most T_K.

conclude: The two sequences of partial sums are bounded together.

drafts.proof_strategy: Choose s between |x| and r, bound the differentiated terms by a summable sequence, and differentiate term by term.
sketch_steps: setup: Put s = (|x|+r)/2 and q = s/r, so |x| < s < r and q < 1.
derive: The sequence (n+1)q^n is bounded by some K, so u_n = |a_(n+1)|(n+1)s^n is summable.
apply_theorem: The term-by-term differentiation theorem applies to a_(n+1) y^(n+1) on (-s, s).
derive: The differentiated series converges absolutely at x.
conclude: Adding the constant a_0 gives the derivative of the original power series near x.

drafts.canonical_statement: Abel's limit theorem. If the partial sums of a real series a converge to l, then the series of a_n x^n converges absolutely for |x| < 1 and its sum tends to l as x tends to 1 from the left.

drafts.proof_strategy: Rewrite the power series with partial sums via Abel summation, then split into a finite head and a small tail.
sketch_steps: derive: The partial sums A_n and the terms a_n are bounded, so both power series converge absolutely for |x| < 1.
translate: The sum of a_n x^n minus l equals (1-x) times the sum of (A_n - l) x^n.
setup: Fix ε > 0 and take N with |A_n - l| < ε/2 for n ≥ N.
derive: The head contributes at most (1-x)D and the tail at most ε/2.
conclude: Choosing x close to 1 makes the difference smaller than ε.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a nonempty subset S of a metric space X, with d(x,S) the infimum of d(x,s) over s in S, |d(x,S) - d(y,S)| ≤ d(x,y) for all x, y in X.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the triangle inequality for each s and take the infimum, then swap x and y.
sketch_steps: derive: For s in S, d(x,S) ≤ d(x,y) + d(y,s).
derive: Taking the infimum over s gives d(x,S) ≤ d(x,y) + d(y,S).
conclude: Swapping x and y gives the absolute value bound.

drafts.proof_strategy: Choose a point in each set; they form a Cauchy sequence whose limit lies in every closed set.
sketch_steps: construct: Pick p_n in F_n for each n.
derive: The shrinking condition makes (p_n) a Cauchy sequence, so it converges to some x.
derive: For fixed n, p_m lies in the closed set F_n for m ≥ n, so x lies in F_n.
contradiction: A second common point y would give d(y,x) < d(y,x).
conclude: The common point exists and is unique.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a is the supremum of a set S of reals and c > 0, then c a is the supremum of the set of all c x with x in S.

drafts.proof_strategy: Check the upper bound directly and divide an arbitrary upper bound of cS by c to compare it with a.
sketch_steps: derive: For x in S, x ≤ a gives c x ≤ c a, so c a is an upper bound of cS.
setup: Let b be any upper bound of cS.
derive: Then x ≤ b/c for all x in S, so b/c is an upper bound of S.
conclude: Hence a ≤ b/c, that is, c a ≤ b.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a set S of reals, a is the infimum of S if and only if -a is the supremum of the set of all -x with x in S.

drafts.proof_strategy: Translate lower bounds of S into upper bounds of -S with the order-reversing map x ↦ -x.
sketch_steps: translate: b ≤ x is equivalent to -x ≤ -b.
derive: So b is a lower bound of S exactly when -b is an upper bound of -S.
conclude: Greatest lower bounds correspond to least upper bounds under this bijection.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a nonempty closed subset S of the reals has supremum a, then a belongs to S.

derive: Then x_n converges to a.
conclude: Since S is closed, a belongs to S.

derive: b_n = (b_n - a_n) + a_n converges to x as well.
derive: Monotonicity gives a_n ≤ x ≤ b_n for all n.
conclude: Any y in all the intervals satisfies x ≤ y ≤ x in the limit, so y = x.

drafts.canonical_statement: For every real ε > 0 there is a natural number n with 1/(n+1) < ε.

sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The Archimedean property gives a natural number n with 1/ε < n.
conclude: Then 1/ε < n + 1, and taking reciprocals gives 1/(n+1) < ε.

drafts.canonical_statement: For reals a < b there is an irrational number x with a < x < b.

drafts.proof_strategy: Translate the interval by √2 and apply density of the rationals.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Choose a rational q between a - √2 and b - √2.
construct: Put x = q + √2, so that a < x < b.
contradiction: If x were rational, then √2 = x - q would be rational.
conclude: So x is an irrational number in the interval.

drafts.proof_strategy: Split on whether infinitely many indices dominate all later terms.
sketch_steps: setup: Call n a peak if x_m < x_n for all m > n.
case_split: With infinitely many peaks, listing them gives a decreasing subsequence.
case_split: With finitely many peaks, start after the last one.
construct: Each non-peak index has a later index with a term at least as large, which gives a nondecreasing subsequence.
conclude: In both cases a monotone subsequence exists.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take c to be the supremum of A; each element of B is an upper bound of A.
sketch_steps: derive: Every element of B is an upper bound of A, so A is bounded above.
apply_theorem: The nonempty set A has a supremum c.
conclude: a ≤ c for a in A, and c ≤ b for b in B because c is the least upper bound.

sketch_steps: derive: If a_{p(n)} → c, then p(m) ≥ m provides arbitrarily late terms close to c.
construct: Conversely choose p(k+1) > p(k) with |a_{p(k+1)} - c| < 1/(k+2).
conclude: The radii tend to 0, so the subsequence converges to c.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the definition with ε = L - c.
sketch_steps: setup: Put ε = L - c > 0 and take the corresponding K.
derive: For n ≥ K, a_n - L > -(L - c).
conclude: Hence a_n > c.

drafts.canonical_statement: General form of limit monotonicity with the inequality only for large n. If a_n → L, b_n → M and a_n ≤ b_n for all n ≥ K, then L ≤ M.

drafts.proof_strategy: If L > M, an ε-band of half the gap separates the two sequences for large n.
sketch_steps: setup: Suppose L > M and put ε = (L - M)/2.
derive: For large n, b_n < M + ε = L - ε < a_n.
contradiction: This contradicts a_n ≤ b_n for n ≥ K.

drafts.canonical_statement: Let a and b be real sequences and L a real. If |a_n - L| ≤ b_n for all n and b_n → 0, then a_n → L.

drafts.proof_strategy: The ε-N condition for b transfers directly to a.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix ε > 0 and take K with |b_n| < ε for n ≥ K.
conclude: For n ≥ K, |a_n - L| ≤ b_n ≤ |b_n| < ε.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a real sequence satisfies a_n → L, then |a_n| → |L|.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the reverse triangle inequality.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix ε > 0 and take K with |a_n - L| < ε for n ≥ K.
conclude: The reverse triangle inequality gives ||a_n| - |L|| ≤ |a_n - L| < ε.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a real sequence a and a natural number k, a_{n+k} → L if and only if a_n → L.

drafts.proof_strategy: Shift the threshold by k in each direction.
sketch_steps: derive: If a_n → L with threshold K, then the same K works for a_{n+k}.
derive: If a_{n+k} → L with threshold K, then K + k works for a_m.
conclude: The two limits are equivalent.

drafts.proof_strategy: Treat L = 0 directly and rationalize the difference when L > 0.
sketch_steps: derive: The limit L is nonnegative.
case_split: If L = 0, a_n < ε² gives √(a_n) < ε.
case_split: If L > 0, rationalizing gives |√(a_n) - √L| ≤ |a_n - L|/√L.
conclude: In both cases √(a_n) → √L.

drafts.proof_strategy: First bound |a_n| below by |L|/2, then control the difference of reciprocals.
sketch_steps: setup: Take K for both |L|/2 and ε|L|²/2.
derive: For n ≥ K, |a_n| > |L|/2, so a_n ≠ 0.
conclude: The bounds give a value below ε.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a positive real sequence satisfies a_{n+1}/a_n → r with r < 1, then a_n → 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Eventually compare with a geometric sequence of ratio s between r and 1.
sketch_steps: setup: Choose s with r < s < 1.
derive: For n ≥ K, a_{n+1} < s a_n.
induction: Hence 0 < a_n ≤ s^(n-K) a_K for n ≥ K.
conclude: The squeeze theorem gives a_n → 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a > 0, then a^(1/(n+1)) → 1 as n tends to infinity.

drafts.proof_strategy: Bound the excess over 1 with Bernoulli's inequality and reduce a < 1 to 1/a > 1.
sketch_steps: case_split: If a ≥ 1, put h_n = a^(1/(n+1)) - 1 ≥ 0.
apply_theorem: Bernoulli gives a ≥ 1 + (n+1) h_n.
derive: So h_n ≤ (a-1)/(n+1), which tends to 0.
case_split: If a < 1, apply the first case to 1/a and take reciprocals.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a positive real sequence, a_n → +∞ if and only if 1/a_n → 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Exchange M and ε = 1/M by taking reciprocals of positive numbers.
sketch_steps: derive: If a_n > 1/ε for n ≥ K, then 0 < 1/a_n < ε.
derive: If 1/a_n < 1/(|M|+1) for n ≥ K, then a_n > |M| + 1 > M.
conclude: The two conditions are equivalent.

sketch_steps: setup: Fix a real M.
derive: Since M is not an upper bound, a_K > M for some K.
conclude: Monotonicity gives a_n > M for all n ≥ K.

derive: Since p(n) ≥ n, the subsequence a_{p(n)} converges to A; likewise for q.
contradiction: Uniqueness of limits gives L = A = M.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a nondecreasing real sequence converges to L, then a_n ≤ L for all n.

drafts.proof_strategy: A term above L would keep all later terms away from L by monotonicity.
sketch_steps: setup: Suppose a_n > L and put ε = a_n - L.
derive: For large m ≥ n, a_m < L + ε = a_n.
contradiction: Monotonicity gives a_n ≤ a_m.

drafts.proof_strategy: Telescope the increments of c_n = a_n - L b_n after a threshold and divide by b_n.
sketch_steps: setup: Put c_n = a_n - L b_n and fix ε > 0.
derive: For n ≥ K, |c_{n+1} - c_n| ≤ (ε/2)(b_{n+1} - b_n) and b_n > 0.
induction: Summing gives |c_n - c_K| ≤ (ε/2)(b_n - b_K).
derive: Since b_n → +∞, |c_K| < (ε/2) b_n for large n.
conclude: So |c_n| < ε b_n, that is, |a_n/b_n - L| < ε.

sketch_steps: setup: Let l be the limit superior and s_n the supremum of a_k over k ≥ n.
derive: For large n, s_n < l + ε, and s_n ≥ l gives some k ≥ n with a_k > l - ε.
construct: Choose p inductively with |a_{p(k)} - l| < 1/(k+1).
conclude: The subsequence converges to l.

drafts.proof_strategy: Monotonicity follows from shrinking tails, and the two bounds on s_n come directly from the definition of l as an infimum.
sketch_steps: derive: Shrinking the tail shrinks the supremum, so s_n is nonincreasing.
derive: l is an infimum, so some u < l + ε bounds all terms from some K on; hence s_n ≤ u for n ≥ K.
derive: Each s_n bounds all terms from n on, so l ≤ s_n.
conclude: |s_n - l| < ε for n ≥ K.

drafts.proof_strategy: If all terms from K on were at most c, then c would bound the limit superior.
sketch_steps: setup: Suppose a_n ≤ c for all n ≥ K.
derive: Then c bounds all sufficiently late terms, so the limit superior is at most c.
contradiction: This contradicts c < limsup a.

sketch_steps: setup: Put A, B for the two limit superiors and fix ε > 0.
derive: For large n, a_n + b_n < A + B + ε.
derive: Hence the limit superior of the sum is at most A + B + ε.
conclude: ε is arbitrary, which gives the inequality.

derive: All sufficiently late terms are at most s, so a_{p(n)} ≤ s for large n.
contradiction: Passing to the limit gives c ≤ s < c.

derive: The partial sum up to m + k equals A plus the partial sum of the shifted series.
apply_theorem: Shifting the index of a sequence does not change its limit.
conclude: Each series converges exactly when the other does.

conclude: Since S_m → s, the tail tends to 0.

sketch_steps: derive: For m ≥ K, the partial sum of |a_i| is at most a finite sum plus the sum of b_i from K to m.
derive: The latter is bounded because the series of b_n converges and b_n ≥ 0 for n ≥ K.
conclude: A monotone bounded sequence of partial sums converges.

sketch_steps: induction: For n ≥ K, |a_n| ≤ |a_K| r^(n-K).
apply_theorem: The geometric series with ratio r converges.
conclude: The comparison test gives absolute convergence.

apply_theorem: The geometric series of r^n converges.
conclude: The comparison test gives absolute convergence.

derive: S_{2k} is nondecreasing and S_{2k+1} is nonincreasing, both with limit s.

case_split: For n = 2k+1, S_{2k+1} - a_{2k+1} ≤ s ≤ S_{2k+1}.
conclude: In both cases |s - S_n| ≤ a_n.

sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The bounded monotone sequence b converges to some B.
setup: Put c_n = b_n - B, which is monotone and tends to 0.
apply_theorem: Partial sums of a are bounded, so Dirichlet's test applies to a_n c_n.
conclude: Adding B times the partial sums of a gives convergence of the series of a_n b_n.

sketch_steps: apply_theorem: 1/(n+1) is nonincreasing and tends to 0, so the alternating series converges.
derive: The absolute values form the harmonic series.

sketch_steps: setup: Put F(t) for the integral of f over [0, t] and S_m for the partial sums; both are nondecreasing.
derive: Monotonicity on unit intervals gives Σ_{i=1}^m f(i) ≤ F(m) ≤ S_m.
case_split: If S_m converges, F is bounded and monotone, hence convergent.
case_split: If F converges, S_{m+1} ≤ f(0) + lim F, hence S_m converges.

sketch_steps: setup: Put d_n for the difference and recall x/(1+x) ≤ log(1+x) ≤ x for x > 0.
derive: With x = 1/n, d_{n+1} - d_n ≤ 0.
derive: Summing 1/k ≥ log(k+1) - log k gives d_n > 0.
conclude: A nonincreasing sequence bounded below converges.

drafts.proof_strategy: Bound the partial sums of the sines by telescoping and apply Dirichlet's test with 1/(n+1).

apply_theorem: Dirichlet's test applies with the nonincreasing null sequence 1/(n+1).
conclude: The series converges.

drafts.proof_strategy: Far on either side both values are near the corresponding limit; on the compact middle use uniform continuity.
sketch_steps: setup: Choose A and B with f within ε/2 of M left of A and within ε/2 of L right of B.
apply_theorem: f is uniformly continuous on [A-1, B+1], which gives δ₀.
construct: Put δ = min(δ₀, 1).
case_split: If x, y ≥ B compare through L; if x, y ≤ A compare through M.
derive: Otherwise |x - y| < 1 forces both points into [A-1, B+1].
conclude: In every case |f(x) - f(y)| < ε.

sketch_steps: derive: Monotonicity and the intermediate value theorem show that f maps [a, b] onto [f(a), f(b)].
derive: g is the inverse on this interval and is strictly increasing.
construct: Around x_0 = g(y_0) take endpoints x_1, x_2 within ε of x_0 inside [a, b].
derive: Near y_0 in the interval, f(x_1) ≤ y ≤ f(x_2).
conclude: Monotonicity of g gives |g(y) - x_0| ≤ ε.

drafts.proof_strategy: Assign a rational number to each jump interval; distinct jumps have disjoint intervals.
sketch_steps: derive: One-sided limits exist at each point and f is discontinuous at x exactly when f(x-) < f(x+).
construct: Choose a rational q(x) in each jump interval.
derive: For x < y, f(x+) ≤ f(y-), so jump intervals are disjoint and q is injective.
conclude: The discontinuity set injects into the rationals.

sketch_steps: setup: Take δ_1 and δ_2 for ε/2 on the two intervals and put δ as their minimum.

case_split: If x ≤ b ≤ y, both |x - b| and |b - y| are at most |x - y|.

drafts.proof_strategy: Split the difference of products into two terms and bound the factors by K.
sketch_steps: setup: Put η = ε/(2(K+1)) and take δ for η for both functions.
derive: f(x)g(x) - f(y)g(y) = f(x)(g(x) - g(y)) + (f(x) - f(y))g(y).
conclude: The bound is at most 2Kη < ε.

drafts.canonical_statement: A continuous function on the reals with period T > 0 is uniformly continuous.

drafts.proof_strategy: Translate the two points by a multiple of the period into a fixed compact interval.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: f is uniformly continuous on [-T, 2T], which gives δ₀.
construct: Put δ = min(δ₀, T) and choose n with nT ≤ x < (n+1)T.
derive: The translates u = x - nT and v = y - nT lie in [-T, 2T] at the same distance.
conclude: Periodicity gives |f(x) - f(y)| = |f(u) - f(v)| < ε.

drafts.proof_strategy: Prove the formula on rationals from additivity and extend by density and continuity.
sketch_steps: derive: Additivity gives f(0) = 0, f(-x) = -f(x) and f(nx) = n f(x) for integers n.
derive: For rational q = m/n, n f(q) = m f(1), so f(q) = f(1) q.
apply_theorem: Rationals are dense, so choose rational q_k → x.
conclude: Continuity gives f(x) = f(1) x.

conclude: K = max(C, |L|+1, |M|+1) bounds f everywhere.

sketch_steps: setup: Choose A < 0 < B with f(x) > f(0) outside [A, B].
apply_theorem: f attains a minimum on [A, B] at some x_0, and f(x_0) ≤ f(0).
conclude: Outside the interval f(x) > f(0) ≥ f(x_0), so x_0 is a global minimum.

drafts.proof_strategy: Walk from 0 to x in steps shorter than δ; each step changes f by at most 1.
sketch_steps: setup: Take δ for ε = 1.
induction: For |x| ≤ nδ/2, |f(x) - f(0)| ≤ n, using the intermediate point n x/(n+1).
construct: Take n as the ceiling of 2|x|/δ.

sketch_steps: derive: g(x)/(x-a) tends to v ≠ 0, so g(x) ≠ 0 near a with x ≠ a.
derive: f(x)/g(x) is the quotient of the two difference quotients.
conclude: The limit of the quotient is u/v.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Cauchy's mean value theorem on [x, y] and let y tend to infinity.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix ε and N beyond which f'/g' is within ε of L.
derive: g is injective by Rolle, hence strictly monotone, so g(x) ≠ 0.
apply_theorem: Cauchy's mean value theorem bounds (f(y)-f(x))/(g(y)-g(x)) within ε of L.
conclude: Letting y → +∞ gives |f(x)/g(x) - L| ≤ ε for x > N.

drafts.proof_strategy: Fix a base point N, compare increments with Cauchy's mean value theorem and absorb the constant terms by the divergence of g.
sketch_steps: setup: Choose N with f'/g' within ε/2 of L beyond N and put A = |f(N) - L g(N)| + (ε/2)|g(N)|.
apply_theorem: Cauchy's mean value theorem on [N, x] gives f(x) - f(N) = q (g(x) - g(N)) with |q - L| < ε/2.
derive: Hence |f(x) - L g(x)| ≤ A + (ε/2)|g(x)|.
conclude: For large x, A < (ε/2) g(x), so |f(x)/g(x) - L| < ε.

sketch_steps: construct: Define F(t) as the Taylor polynomial at x with base point t.
derive: The derivative of F telescopes to f^(n+1)(t)(x-t)^n/n!.
apply_theorem: The mean value theorem between a and x gives c with F(x) - F(a) = F'(c)(x-a).
conclude: F(x) = f(x) and F(a) is the Taylor polynomial, which gives the formula.

drafts.proof_strategy: Regard the Taylor polynomial as a function of its base point and apply the fundamental theorem of calculus.
sketch_steps: construct: Define F(t) as the Taylor polynomial at x with base point t.
derive: The derivative of F telescopes to f^(n+1)(t)(x-t)^n/n!, which is continuous.
apply_theorem: The fundamental theorem of calculus gives F(x) - F(a) = ∫_a^x F'.
conclude: F(x) = f(x), and F(a) is the Taylor polynomial.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the Lagrange remainder of order n-1 and the continuity of the n-th derivative.
sketch_steps: case_split: For n = 0 the claim is continuity of f.
apply_theorem: For n ≥ 1 the Lagrange form of order n-1 gives a point c_x between a and x.
derive: The quotient equals (f^(n)(c_x) - f^(n)(a))/n!.
conclude: c_x → a and f^(n) is continuous, so the quotient tends to 0.

apply_theorem: For x > a the Lagrange remainder equals f^(n+1)(c)(x-a)^(n+1)/(n+1)!.
conclude: C = M/(n+1)! works.

sketch_steps: construct: y = λx + μz with λ = (z-y)/(z-x) and μ = (y-x)/(z-x).
apply_theorem: Convexity gives (z-x) f(y) ≤ (z-y) f(x) + (y-x) f(z).
derive: Rearranging gives each of the two inequalities between slopes.

drafts.canonical_statement: If f is convex on [a, b], then f(x) ≤ max(f(a), f(b)) for all x in [a, b].

drafts.proof_strategy: If f(x) < f(y), extending the chord beyond y forces f to exceed any bound.
sketch_steps: setup: Suppose f(x) < f(y) and take t large and w = y + t(y-x).
derive: y is a convex combination of w and x, so f(w) ≥ f(y) + t(f(y) - f(x)).
contradiction: With t = (K - f(y))/(f(y) - f(x)) + 1, this gives f(w) > K.
conclude: Hence f(y) ≤ f(x) for all x, y, and f is constant.

drafts.proof_strategy: Monotonicity of slopes makes f Lipschitz on compact subintervals.
sketch_steps: setup: Around x_0 choose a < c < p < x_0 < q < d < b.
apply_theorem: Monotonicity of slopes bounds the slope between any s < t in [p, q] by the slopes on [c, p] and [q, d].
derive: So f is Lipschitz on [p, q].
conclude: f is continuous at x_0.

drafts.proof_strategy: The integral of (t f + g)^2 is a nonnegative quadratic in t.
sketch_steps: setup: Put A, B, C for the integrals of f², f g and g².
derive: For all t, 0 ≤ A t² + 2 B t + C.
case_split: If A > 0, take t = -B/A.
case_split: If A = 0, a nonnegative affine function has slope 0, so B = 0.
conclude: In both cases B² ≤ A C.

conclude: Bounding the integrand by M gives at most M|x - y|.

derive: Convergence of F gives the condition by the triangle inequality.
construct: Conversely F(a+n) is a Cauchy sequence with a limit L.
conclude: The condition extends this limit to all t → ∞.

conclude: The same bound gives F(t) → L.

sketch_steps: derive: Nonnegativity of f makes the primitive F nondecreasing.
construct: Let L be the supremum of F on [a, ∞).
conclude: For t ≥ T with F(T) > L - ε, |F(t) - L| < ε.

sketch_steps: setup: Take N for ε = 1 and put K as the sum of the first bounds plus 2.

sketch_steps: setup: Choose N so that derivatives are uniformly within ε/3 of each other and F_N'(x) is within ε/3 of g(x).
apply_theorem: The mean value theorem for F_m - F_N bounds the difference of quotients by ε/3.
derive: Let m → ∞ to compare the quotient of f with that of F_N.
apply_theorem: Differentiability of F_N at x gives δ.
conclude: The quotient of f is within ε of g(x) for 0 < |y - x| < δ.

sketch_steps: derive: f is continuous as a uniform limit of continuous functions.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a metric space, if d(y, x) < r, then the open ball B(y, r - d(y, x)) is contained in the open ball B(x, r).

sketch_steps: setup: Take z in the smaller ball.
conclude: d(z, x) ≤ d(z, y) + d(y, x) < r.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a metric space, the closure of the open ball B(x, r) is contained in the closed ball of center x and radius r.

sketch_steps: setup: Let y be in the closure and fix ε > 0.
derive: Some z in the ball has d(y, z) < ε, so d(y, x) < ε + r.
conclude: Since ε is arbitrary, d(y, x) ≤ r.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a metric space, if x_n → x and y_n → y, then d(x_n, y_n) → d(x, y).

sketch_steps: derive: Two triangle inequalities give |d(x_n, y_n) - d(x, y)| ≤ d(x_n, x) + d(y_n, y).
conclude: The right side tends to 0.

sketch_steps: construct: For each k cover S by finitely many balls of radius 1/(k+1).
derive: The pigeonhole principle gives nested infinite index sets N_k with x_n in one ball B_k.
construct: Choose increasing p(k) in N_k.
conclude: For i, j ≥ k, d(x_{p(i)}, x_{p(j)}) < 2/(k+1), so the subsequence is Cauchy.

sketch_steps: construct: Choose preimages x_n in S of the given points y_n.
apply_theorem: Sequential compactness gives x_{p(n)} → a in S.
conclude: Continuity gives y_{p(n)} → f(a), which lies in f(S).

drafts.proof_strategy: If the intersection were empty, the complements would form an increasing open cover of K_0, and a finite subcover contradicts nonemptiness.
sketch_steps: setup: The complements U_n of K_n are open and increasing.
derive: If the intersection is empty, the U_n cover K_0.
apply_theorem: Compactness gives a finite subcover, hence K_0 ⊂ U_N for some N.
contradiction: A point of the nonempty set K_N ⊂ K_0 would lie outside U_N.

conclude: So every ball around x meets S.

drafts.proof_strategy: The fixed point of T^m is mapped by T to another fixed point of T^m, so uniqueness forces it to be fixed by T.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Banach's fixed point theorem gives a unique fixed point a of T^m.
derive: T^m(T a) = T(T^m a) = T a, so T a is also fixed by T^m.
derive: Uniqueness gives T a = a.
conclude: Every fixed point of T is fixed by T^m, so it equals a.

sketch_steps: setup: Take K for ε = c.
contradiction: If x_n ≠ x_K with n ≥ K, then d(x_n, x_K) ≥ c, against the Cauchy condition.
conclude: The sequence is constant from K on.

sketch_steps: setup: Write the coefficient of X^n as a sum over pairs (i, j) with i + j = n.
derive: Every coefficient of the second factor equals 1.
conclude: The pairs are (i, n - i) for i = 0, ..., n, which gives the partial sum.

derive: The constant terms of both sides equal a_0.
derive: The coefficient of X^(n+1) on both sides equals a_{n+1} - a_n.
conclude: Two power series with equal coefficients are equal.

conclude: The recurrence makes those coefficients zero.

drafts.proof_strategy: Separate the constant term and shift the index by one for the other coefficients.
sketch_steps: case_split: Treat n = 0 and n = m + 1 separately.
derive: The constant term of X F' is zero.
derive: The coefficient of X^(m+1) in X F' equals the coefficient of X^m in F'.
conclude: That coefficient is (m+1) a_{m+1}.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compute the Cauchy product coefficient and rewrite the reciprocal factorials with a binomial coefficient.
sketch_steps: setup: Write the coefficient of X^n of the product as a sum over i from 0 to n.
translate: Replace 1/(i!(n-i)!) with C(n,i)/n!.
derive: Pull out the factor 1/n!.
conclude: The coefficient equals c_n/n! for each n.

drafts.canonical_statement: For elements a, b of a commutative algebra over the rationals, let E_c = sum c^n X^n / n!. Then E_a E_b = E_{a+b}; the case b = -a is E_a E_{-a} = 1.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare coefficients with the Cauchy product and apply the binomial theorem.
sketch_steps: setup: Compute the coefficient of X^n in E_a E_b.
translate: Rewrite reciprocal factorials as C(n,i)/n!.
apply_theorem: Use the binomial theorem in the commutative algebra.
conclude: The coefficient equals (a+b)^n/n!.

drafts.canonical_statement: The generating function F = sum C_n X^n of the Catalan numbers, defined by C_0 = 1 and C_{n+1} = sum_{i=0}^n C_i C_{n-i}, satisfies F = 1 + X F^2.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare coefficients, using that the coefficient of X^n in F^2 is the convolution in the recurrence.
sketch_steps: setup: Let F be the generating function of the Catalan numbers.
derive: The constant term of 1 + X F^2 is C_0.
derive: The coefficient of X^(n+1) in X F^2 is the convolution sum, equal to C_{n+1}.
conclude: All coefficients agree with those of F.

drafts.canonical_statement: For every natural number n, the Catalan number satisfies C_n + C(2n, n+1) = C(2n, n), that is, C_n = C(2n, n) - C(2n, n+1).

drafts.proof_strategy: Multiply by n+1 and use the closed form of C_n together with the ratio of adjacent binomial coefficients.
sketch_steps: setup: Recall (n+1) C_n = C(2n, n).
derive: The ratio of adjacent binomial coefficients gives (n+1) C(2n, n+1) = n C(2n, n).
derive: Multiply the claimed identity by n + 1 and simplify.
conclude: Cancel the nonzero factor n + 1.

derive: Prefix conditions for u and v follow from the height of w.
derive: Any decomposition U u' D v' has first return exactly after u'.
conclude: Hence the decomposition is unique, and counting U gives the semilength formula.

drafts.canonical_statement: The first letter of a nonempty Dyck word is U and its last letter is D.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dyck_word"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="empty_dyck_word"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="word_first_letter"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dyck_up_step"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="word_last_letter"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dyck_down_step"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the prefix condition to the prefix of length one and to the word without its last letter.
sketch_steps: derive: The prefix of length one contains at least as many U as D, so it is U.
contradiction: If the last letter were U, removing it would leave more D than U.
conclude: Therefore the last letter is D.

drafts.canonical_statement: The number of Dyck words of semilength n is the Catalan number C_n, where C_0 = 1 and C_{n+1} = sum_{i=0}^n C_i C_{n-i}.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dyck_words"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="catalan_number"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use the first-return decomposition to derive the Catalan recurrence for the counts.
sketch_steps: setup: Let d_n be the number of Dyck words of semilength n, so d_0 = 1.
construct: Map a word of semilength n+1 to the pair (u, v) from its first-return decomposition.
derive: This map is a bijection onto pairs of Dyck words with total semilength n.
derive: Classifying by the semilength of u gives the convolution recurrence.
induction: The sequences d_n and C_n coincide.

drafts.canonical_statement: The number of rooted binary trees with n internal nodes is the Catalan number C_n, where a binary tree is either empty or a root with an ordered pair of binary subtrees, and C_0 = 1, C_{n+1} = sum_{i=0}^n C_i C_{n-i}.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="binary_trees_with_nodes"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="catalan_number"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Decompose a tree at its root to obtain the Catalan recurrence.
sketch_steps: setup: Let t_n count binary trees with n nodes, so t_0 = 1.
construct: A tree with n+1 nodes corresponds to a pair of subtrees with total n nodes.
derive: Classifying by the size of the left subtree gives the convolution.
induction: Conclude t_n = C_n.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a natural number n, the number of compositions of n+1, that is, ordered sequences of positive integers with sum n+1, is 2^n.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="compositions_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Biject compositions with the subsets of the n gaps between n+1 points in a row.
sketch_steps: setup: Arrange n+1 points in a row, with n gaps between neighbours.
construct: A subset of gaps cuts the row into blocks whose sizes form a composition.
construct: Partial sums of a composition recover the subset of gaps.
conclude: The number of subsets of n gaps is 2^n.

drafts.canonical_statement: Euler's partition theorem. For a natural number n, the number of partitions of n into odd parts equals the number of partitions of n into distinct parts.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="partitions_odd_parts"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="partitions_distinct_parts"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Build a bijection using binary expansions of multiplicities.
sketch_steps: setup: Write each positive integer uniquely as 2^j r with r odd.
construct: Expand each multiplicity of an odd part in binary and replace copies by the parts 2^j r.
construct: Conversely, collect distinct parts with the same odd factor into copies of that factor.
derive: The sum n is preserved in both directions.
conclude: Uniqueness of binary expansion makes the maps mutually inverse.

drafts.canonical_statement: Glaisher's theorem. For a positive integer m and a natural number n, the number of partitions of n with no part divisible by m equals the number of partitions of n in which every part occurs fewer than m times.

drafts.proof_strategy: Build a bijection using base m expansions of multiplicities.
sketch_steps: case_split: For m = 1 both families contain only the empty partition of 0.
setup: For m at least 2, write each positive integer uniquely as m^j r with m not dividing r.
construct: Expand each multiplicity of r in base m and create parts m^j r with those digits as multiplicities.
construct: Reverse the map by collecting parts with the same factor r.
conclude: Uniqueness of base m digits gives a bijection preserving the sum.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a predicate p on positive integers, let a_n be the number of partitions of n with all parts satisfying p. In Z[[X]] with the coefficientwise topology, sum a_n X^n is the limit of the infinite product over i ≥ 1 of f_i, where f_i = sum_j X^(ij) if p(i) holds and f_i = 1 otherwise.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="partition_euler_factor_product_tends_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="partition_count_series_restricted"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Show that each coefficient of the partial products stabilizes and counts partitions through multiplicities.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix n and a finite index set I containing 1, ..., n.
derive: The coefficient of X^n in the partial product counts tuples (j_i) with sum of i j_i equal to n.
construct: Such a tuple corresponds to the partition with part i repeated j_i times.
derive: Parts of a partition of n are at most n, so all partitions occur.
conclude: The partial products converge coefficientwise.

drafts.canonical_statement: For integers k put ω(k) = k(3k-1)/2. Then ω is injective, ω(k) < ω(-k) for k > 0, and ω(-k) < ω(k+1) for k ≥ 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compute the two consecutive differences and read injectivity from the resulting strictly increasing enumeration.
sketch_steps: derive: For k > 0, the difference ω(-k) - ω(k) equals k.
derive: For k ≥ 0, the difference ω(k+1) - ω(-k) equals 2k + 1.
translate: These inequalities chain ω(0), ω(1), ω(-1), ω(2), ω(-2), ... increasingly.
conclude: Each integer occurs once in the chain, so ω is injective.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use that swapping coordinates is an involutive bijection between the cells of μ and μ'.
sketch_steps: derive: Swapping twice gives back μ.
derive: The swap is a bijection of cells, so the sizes agree.
derive: Cells in row i of μ' correspond to cells in column i of μ.
conclude: Applying the same fact to μ' handles the columns.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the lower-set property to see that each row and column is an initial segment.
sketch_steps: setup: A Young diagram is a finite lower set of cells.
derive: Each row is an initial segment, so membership is j < μ_i.
derive: The same argument works for columns.
derive: Moving a cell up within the lower set gives the monotonicity of the lengths.
conclude: All four statements follow.

drafts.canonical_statement: The number of cells of a Young diagram μ equals the sum of its row lengths over i from 0 to r-1, where r is the length of column 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Partition the cells by their row index, which is smaller than the length of column 0.
sketch_steps: derive: Every cell (i,j) forces (i,0) to be a cell, so i < r.
translate: The cells are the disjoint union of the rows 0, ..., r-1.
conclude: Summing the row sizes gives the number of cells.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a semistandard tableau T of shape μ with natural number entries, weakly increasing in rows and strictly increasing in columns, every cell (i,j) of μ satisfies T_{i,j} ≥ i, with rows indexed from 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on the row index using strict increase in each column.
sketch_steps: induction: Induct on the row index i.
derive: The case i = 0 is trivial for natural numbers.
derive: The cell above (i+1, j) belongs to μ, and the column increases strictly.
conclude: Hence the entry grows by at least one per row.

drafts.canonical_statement: Define the unsigned Stirling numbers of the first kind by c(0,0) = 1, c(0,k+1) = c(n+1,0) = 0 and c(n+1,k+1) = n c(n,k+1) + c(n,k). For x in a commutative semiring, the product of (x+i) over i < n equals the sum of c(n,k) x^k over k ≤ n.

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on n, multiply by x+n and shift the index in the second sum.
sketch_steps: induction: Induct on n, the case n = 0 being trivial.
derive: Multiply the expansion for n by x + n and split the sum.
derive: The boundary terms n c(n,0) and c(n,n+1) vanish, so the index can be shifted.
derive: Combine the sums with the recurrence for c(n+1,k+1).
conclude: Since c(n+1,0) = 0, this is the expansion for n+1.

drafts.canonical_statement: The unsigned Stirling numbers of the first kind, with c(n+1,k+1) = n c(n,k+1) + c(n,k), satisfy sum_{k=0}^n c(n,k) = n!.

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on n using the recurrence and the vanishing boundary terms.
sketch_steps: induction: Induct on n with base c(0,0) = 1.
derive: Split the row sum for n+1 with the recurrence.
derive: The boundary terms vanish, so the first sum equals n times the row sum for n.
conclude: The total is n n! + n! = (n+1)!.

drafts.canonical_statement: The unsigned Stirling numbers of the first kind satisfy c(n+1,1) = n! and c(n+1,n) = C(n+1,2).

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on n using the recurrence and Pascal's rule.
sketch_steps: derive: Note c(n,n) = 1 and c(n,k) = 0 for k > n.
induction: For column 1, c(n+2,1) = (n+1) c(n+1,1).
induction: For the subdiagonal, c(n+2,n+1) = (n+1) + c(n+1,n).
conclude: Pascal's rule gives the binomial coefficient.

drafts.canonical_statement: Define the Stirling numbers of the second kind by S(0,0) = 1, S(0,k+1) = S(n+1,0) = 0 and S(n+1,k+1) = (k+1) S(n,k+1) + S(n,k). For x in a commutative ring, x^n = sum_{k=0}^n S(n,k) x(x-1)...(x-k+1).

drafts.proof_strategy: Use x f_k = f_{k+1} + k f_k and induct on n.
sketch_steps: setup: Let f_k be the falling product and note x f_k = f_{k+1} + k f_k.
induction: Multiply the expansion for n by x.
derive: The boundary terms vanish, so the second sum can be reindexed.
derive: The recurrence for S(n+1,k+1) combines the two sums.
conclude: Since S(n+1,0) = 0, this is the expansion for n+1.

drafts.canonical_statement: The Stirling numbers of the second kind, with S(n+1,k+1) = (k+1) S(n,k+1) + S(n,k), satisfy S(n+2,2) + 1 = 2^(n+1).

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on n using the recurrence and the value S(m+1,1) = 1.
sketch_steps: derive: Column one is constant, S(m+1,1) = 1.
induction: The base case is S(2,2) = 1.
derive: The recurrence gives S(n+3,2) = 2 S(n+2,2) + 1.
conclude: Adding one doubles the previous value.

drafts.canonical_statement: The Stirling numbers of the second kind satisfy S(n+1,1) = 1 and S(n+1,n) = C(n+1,2).
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="stirling_second"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="stirling_second"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="binom"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on n using the recurrence and Pascal's rule.
sketch_steps: derive: Note S(n,n) = 1 and S(n,k) = 0 for k > n.
induction: Column one is constant by the recurrence.
induction: The subdiagonal satisfies S(n+2,n+1) = (n+1) + S(n+1,n).
conclude: Pascal's rule gives C(n+2,2).

drafts.canonical_statement: With Bell numbers B_0 = 1, B_{n+1} = sum_i C(n,i) B_{n-i}, and Stirling numbers of the second kind S(n+1,k+1) = (k+1) S(n,k+1) + S(n,k), one has sum_{k=0}^n S(n,k) = B_n.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="sum"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="integer_range"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="fns1" name="lambda"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="stirling_second"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="bell_number"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Prove the column recurrence S(n+1,k+1) = sum_j C(n,j) S(j,k) by induction, then sum over k and compare with the Bell recurrence.
sketch_steps: setup: Claim S(n+1,k+1) = sum_j C(n,j) S(j,k) for all n and k.
induction: Pascal's rule splits the sum for n+1 into two sums.
case_split: Treat k = 0 and k = l + 1 with the Stirling recurrence.
derive: Summing over k gives T_{n+1} = sum_j C(n,j) T_j for the row sums T_n.
induction: Strong induction and the symmetry of binomial coefficients give T_n = B_n.

drafts.canonical_statement: The exponential generating function F of the Bell numbers in Q[[X]] satisfies the formal differential equation F' = E F, where E = sum X^n/n!.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare coefficients; the Cauchy product with E reproduces the Bell recurrence.
sketch_steps: setup: The coefficient of X^n in F' is B_{n+1}/n!.
derive: The coefficient of X^n in E F is a sum with reciprocal factorials.
translate: Rewrite it with C(n,i)/n!.
conclude: The Bell recurrence gives equality.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a positive integer n and natural number m, the product over p < m of C(pn+n-1, n-1), times (n!)^m m!, equals (mn)!. The product counts partitions of an mn-element set into m blocks of size n.
