drafts.proof_strategy: Adjoin the finitely many coefficients of an integral equation, so that x lies in a finitely generated R-module.
sketch_steps: setup: Let x in B satisfy a monic equation with coefficients a_i in A.
derive: The subring A' generated by the images of the a_i is a finite R-module.
derive: A'[x] is a finite A'-module, hence a finite R-module.
apply_theorem: An element acting on a finite R-module containing 1 is integral over R.
conclude: So x is integral over R.

drafts.canonical_statement: Let A be a commutative R-algebra and N a finitely generated R-submodule of A containing 1. If x in A satisfies xN ⊆ N, then x is integral over R.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the determinant trick to multiplication by x on N and evaluate at 1.
sketch_steps: setup: Write xy_i as a combination of generators y_j of N with coefficients in R.
derive: Multiplying (xE - C)y = 0 by the adjugate gives det(xE - C)y_i = 0.
construct: p(X) = det(XE - C) is monic and p(x)N = 0.
conclude: Since 1 lies in N, p(x) = 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: Let R be an integral domain, A a commutative R-algebra and z in A algebraic over R. Then yz is integral over R for some nonzero y in R.

drafts.proof_strategy: Multiply the equation by a power of the leading coefficient to make it monic in a_n z.
sketch_steps: setup: Take p of degree n with leading coefficient a_n and p(z) = 0.
case_split: If n = 0, then a_0 z = 0, which is integral.
derive: For n ≥ 1, multiplying by a_n^(n-1) gives a monic equation for a_n z.
conclude: So y = a_n works.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show that p is contracted from the localization S_Q, using minimal polynomials over the fraction field of R.
sketch_steps: translate: It suffices that p S_Q ∩ R lies in p.
apply_theorem: The minimal polynomial over K of an element of pS has coefficients in p, by the determinant trick, integral closedness and lying over.
setup: Take x in R outside p with x = y/s, y in pS and s outside Q.
derive: The minimal polynomial of s = y/x has coefficients v_i = u_i/x^i in R.
derive: From x^i v_i in p and x outside p, each v_i lies in p.
contradiction: Then s^r lies in pS ⊆ Q, so s lies in Q.
conclude: Hence p is a contraction from S_Q, and pulling back to S gives P.

drafts.canonical_statement: Going down for flat algebras. If S is a flat R-algebra, p ⊆ q are primes of R and Q is a prime of S over q, then there is a prime P ⊆ Q of S over p.

drafts.proof_strategy: Pass to the flat local homomorphism R_q → S_Q, which is faithfully flat, and lift the prime.
sketch_steps: derive: R_q → S_Q is a local homomorphism.
derive: S_Q is flat over R_q because localization and composition preserve flatness.
apply_theorem: A flat local homomorphism is faithfully flat, so primes of R_q have primes of S_Q above them.
construct: Take a prime of S_Q above p R_q and pull it back to S.
conclude: The pullback P lies in Q and lies over p.

drafts.canonical_statement: If R → S is an injective homomorphism of commutative rings and S is integral over R, then S and R have the same Krull dimension.

drafts.proof_strategy: Contract chains using incomparability and lift chains using lying over and going up.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Incomparability makes contraction strictly increasing on chains of primes of S.
derive: So dim S ≤ dim R.
apply_theorem: Lying over gives a prime over the bottom of a chain in R.
apply_theorem: Going up lifts the rest of the chain.
conclude: So dim R ≤ dim S.

drafts.canonical_statement: Zariski's lemma. If a field L is finitely generated as an algebra over a field K, then L is a finite-dimensional K-vector space.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Noether normalization and use that a domain integral over a polynomial ring cannot be a field unless there are no variables.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Noether normalization gives a finite injective map from K[x_1, ..., x_s] to L.
apply_theorem: Since L is a field and integral over K[x_1, ..., x_s], that polynomial ring is a field.
derive: x_1 is not a unit, so s = 0.
conclude: L is finite over K.

drafts.proof_strategy: For f outside the radical, take a maximal ideal of the localization at f and use Zariski's lemma to see that its contraction is maximal.
sketch_steps: derive: The radical lies in every maximal ideal containing I.
setup: Let f be outside rad(I), and let B = A/I.
derive: B_f is a nonzero finitely generated K-algebra; take a maximal ideal n.
apply_theorem: By Zariski's lemma, B_f/n is finite over K.
derive: The contraction m to A has A/m a finite-dimensional domain over K, hence a field.
conclude: m is a maximal ideal containing I and omitting f.

drafts.proof_strategy: Enlarge I to a maximal ideal and use Zariski's lemma to read off a point from the residue field.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: A proper ideal lies in a maximal ideal m.
apply_theorem: By Zariski's lemma, A/m is finite over K, so K → A/m is an isomorphism because K is algebraically closed.
construct: Let a_i in K correspond to the image of x_i, so x_i - a_i lies in m.
derive: For every polynomial p, p - p(a) lies in m.
conclude: If p lies in I, the constant p(a) lies in the proper ideal m, so p(a) = 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: A valuation ring is integrally closed: if R is a domain with fraction field K such that x or its inverse lies in R for every nonzero x in K, then every element of K integral over R lies in R.

drafts.proof_strategy: Divide the integral equation by a power of x, using that the inverse of x lies in R.
sketch_steps: setup: Let x in K satisfy a monic equation over R and suppose x is not in R.
derive: Then the inverse of x lies in R.
derive: Dividing by x^(n-1) writes x as an element of R.
contradiction: So x lies in R.

drafts.canonical_statement: A commutative Artinian ring has only finitely many maximal ideals.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="artinian_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="maximal_ideals_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Take a minimal finite intersection of maximal ideals and compare any maximal ideal with it.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The set of finite intersections of maximal ideals has a minimal element.
setup: Let m be a maximal ideal.
derive: By minimality, m contains the minimal intersection.
derive: A prime containing a finite intersection contains a member, so m = m_i.
conclude: There are finitely many maximal ideals.

drafts.canonical_statement: A Noetherian local ring R with maximal ideal m is Artinian if and only if m^n = 0 for some n.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare with the characterization of Artinian rings as Noetherian rings in which primes are maximal.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Artinian is equivalent to Noetherian with all primes maximal.
derive: If R is Artinian, m is the only prime, so it is the nilradical.
derive: A finitely generated nil ideal is nilpotent.
derive: Conversely, m^n = 0 forces every prime to contain m.
conclude: So all primes equal m and R is Artinian.

drafts.proof_strategy: Combine nilpotence of the Jacobson radical with the Chinese remainder theorem, and identify the local factors with localizations.
sketch_steps: derive: Primes are maximal, so there are finitely many: m_1, ..., m_n.
apply_theorem: The Jacobson radical is nilpotent, so J^k = 0.
apply_theorem: The Chinese remainder theorem gives R isomorphic to the product of R/m_i^k.
derive: Each factor is local with unique prime m_i/m_i^k, and equals R localized at m_i.
conclude: The canonical map to the product of localizations is bijective with Artinian local factors.

drafts.canonical_statement: If R is an Artinian local ring whose maximal ideal is principal, generated by t, then every ideal of R is principal.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show every element is a unit times a power of t, then generate an ideal by the smallest power of t it contains.
sketch_steps: derive: t is nilpotent because the maximal ideal is the Jacobson radical.
induction: Downward induction shows each element is zero or a unit times a power of t.
setup: For an ideal I, take the least k with t^k in I.
derive: Any nonzero x = ut^a in I has t^a in I, so a ≥ k.
conclude: Hence I = (t^k).

drafts.canonical_statement: A Noetherian local domain R that is not a field is a discrete valuation ring, that is, a local principal ideal domain that is not a field, if and only if its maximal ideal is principal.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use Krull's intersection theorem to write every nonzero element as a unit times a power of the generator.
sketch_steps: derive: A principal ideal domain has principal maximal ideal.
setup: Suppose m = (t) with t nonzero.
apply_theorem: Krull's intersection theorem gives a largest a with x in (t^a).
derive: So x = ut^a with u a unit.
conclude: Every nonzero ideal is (t^k), so R is a principal ideal domain.

sketch_steps: derive: A DVR is a UFD, hence integrally closed, and m is its only nonzero prime.
setup: Take a nonzero a in m, so rad(a) = m and m^n ⊆ (a) for a least n.
construct: Choose b in m^(n-1) outside (a) and let y = b/a.
derive: y is outside R and ym lies in R.
derive: If ym ⊆ m, the determinant trick makes y integral, so y lies in R, a contradiction.
derive: So ym = R, which makes m principal.
conclude: A principal maximal ideal gives a DVR.

drafts.proof_strategy: Factor numerator and denominator in R, where the only prime up to units is t.
sketch_steps: setup: Write x = a/b with a, b nonzero in R.
apply_theorem: In a DVR, every nonzero element is a unit times a power of t.
derive: So a = ut^m and b = vt^k.
conclude: Then x = (u/v) t^(m-k).

drafts.canonical_statement: A Noetherian integral domain whose localization at every nonzero prime is a discrete valuation ring is a Dedekind domain, where a Dedekind domain means a Noetherian integrally closed domain in which every nonzero prime is maximal, fields included.

drafts.proof_strategy: Rule out chains of primes by localizing and check integral closedness at maximal ideals.
sketch_steps: setup: Suppose there is a chain of nonzero primes q ⊊ p.
derive: Localizing at a maximal ideal containing p gives a chain of length 2 in a DVR.
contradiction: A DVR has only one nonzero prime, so nonzero primes are maximal.
derive: Each R_m is a DVR or R is a field, so each R_m is integrally closed.
apply_theorem: Integral closedness is checked at maximal ideals.
conclude: R is a Dedekind domain.

drafts.canonical_statement: Let I be an ideal of a Dedekind domain and x a nonzero element of I. Then I = (x, y) for some y. In particular, every ideal of a Dedekind domain is generated by at most two elements.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use unique factorization and the Chinese remainder theorem to choose y with the exact exponents of I at the primes dividing x.
sketch_steps: setup: Factor I and (x) over the primes p_i dividing x, with exponents e_i ≤ f_i.
construct: Choose y_i in p_i^(e_i) outside p_i^(e_i+1).
apply_theorem: The Chinese remainder theorem gives y with y ≡ y_i modulo p_i^(e_i+1).
derive: y lies in I and has exponent exactly e_i at p_i.
conclude: The exponents of (x, y) agree with those of I, so (x, y) = I.

drafts.canonical_statement: A module M over a Dedekind domain is flat if and only if it is torsion free.

drafts.proof_strategy: Flat implies torsion free by multiplication maps; the converse is checked locally over principal ideal domains.
sketch_steps: derive: Tensoring the injection given by multiplication by a shows M has no torsion.
setup: Conversely let M be torsion free and m maximal.
derive: R_m is a principal ideal domain and M_m is torsion free.
apply_theorem: Finitely generated torsion free modules over a PID are free, so M_m is a directed union of free modules, hence flat.
apply_theorem: Flatness is checked at maximal ideals.
conclude: M is flat.

drafts.proof_strategy: Pass to the Rees algebra, which is Noetherian, and take the top degree of generators of N*.
sketch_steps: setup: Let R* be the Rees algebra of I and M* the direct sum of the I^n M.
apply_theorem: R* is Noetherian by the Hilbert basis theorem, and M* is finitely generated.
derive: N*, the direct sum of the I^n M ∩ N, is a finitely generated submodule.
construct: Let k be the largest degree of homogeneous generators of N*.
derive: For n ≥ k, the degree n part of N* lies in I^(n-k)(I^k M ∩ N).
conclude: The reverse inclusion is immediate.

drafts.canonical_statement: Krull's intersection theorem, general form. For a Noetherian ring R, an ideal I, a finitely generated module M and x in M, x lies in I^n M for all n if and only if rx = x for some r in I. The local form is a corollary.

sketch_steps: derive: If rx = x, then x = r^n x lies in I^n M for every n.
setup: Let N be the intersection of the I^n M.
apply_theorem: Artin-Rees with n = k + 1 gives N = IN.
apply_theorem: N is finitely generated, so Nakayama's lemma gives r in I with (1 - r)N = 0.
conclude: Hence rx = x for x in N.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the general intersection theorem and use that 1 - r is a unit.
sketch_steps: setup: Let x lie in the intersection.
apply_theorem: The general intersection theorem gives r in I with rx = x.
derive: r lies in the Jacobson radical, so 1 - r is a unit.
conclude: From (1 - r)x = 0, x = 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the general intersection theorem with M = R and cancel 1 - r in the domain.
sketch_steps: setup: Let x lie in the intersection of the powers of I.
apply_theorem: The general intersection theorem gives r in I with rx = x.
derive: 1 - r is nonzero because I is proper.
conclude: Since R is a domain, x = 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take inverse limits of the exact sequences modulo I^n, and use Artin-Rees to compare the induced and I-adic filtrations on L.
sketch_steps: setup: Let L_n = L ∩ I^n M, so 0 → L/L_n → M/I^n M → N/I^n N → 0 is exact.
derive: Surjectivity of L/L_(n+1) → L/L_n allows inductive lifting of compatible sequences.
derive: The inverse limit sequence is exact.
apply_theorem: Artin-Rees gives L_n ⊆ I^(n-k) L for n ≥ k.
derive: The filtrations (L_n) and (I^n L) define the same limit.
conclude: So the completed sequence is exact.

drafts.proof_strategy: Run Newton's iteration and use completeness to take the limit.
sketch_steps: derive: I lies in the Jacobson radical, so f'(c) is a unit whenever c ≡ a modulo I.
construct: Define c_(n+1) = c_n - f(c_n)/f'(c_n).
induction: The Taylor expansion gives f(c_n) in I^(2^n) and c_n ≡ a modulo I.
apply_theorem: The Cauchy sequence c_n has a limit b by completeness.
conclude: f(b) lies in every power of I, so f(b) = 0 by separatedness, and b - a lies in I.

drafts.canonical_statement: Krull's height theorem. If R is a Noetherian ring, s a finite subset and p a prime minimal over the ideal (s), then the height of p is at most the number of elements of s. The case of one element is Krull's principal ideal theorem.

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on the number of generators, replacing generators by elements of a prime just below p and applying the principal ideal theorem in a quotient.
sketch_steps: setup: Induct on n and localize so that p is the maximal ideal.
setup: Take a prime q just below p; it suffices to bound ht q by n - 1.
derive: Some x_n is outside q, so p is the radical of q + (x_n).
construct: Write x_i^m = y_i + a_i x_n with y_i in q, and let J = (y_1, ..., y_(n-1)).
apply_theorem: p/J is minimal over a principal ideal, so its height is at most 1.
derive: Thus q is minimal over J.
conclude: The induction hypothesis gives ht q ≤ n - 1, so ht p ≤ n.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime p of a Noetherian ring there is a finite subset s such that p is minimal over (s) and the number of elements of s equals the height of p. This is the converse of Krull's height theorem.

drafts.proof_strategy: Choose elements of p inductively by prime avoidance so that minimal primes over the partial ideals have growing height.
sketch_steps: setup: Let h be the height of p, finite by Krull's height theorem.
induction: Assume a_1, ..., a_i chosen so that minimal primes over them have height at least i.
apply_theorem: Prime avoidance gives a_(i+1) in p outside the minimal primes of height exactly i.
derive: Minimal primes over (a_1, ..., a_(i+1)) then have height at least i + 1.
derive: For s = {a_1, ..., a_h}, a minimal prime over (s) inside p has height at least h.
conclude: It equals p, so p is minimal over (s).

drafts.canonical_statement: For a local ring R with maximal ideal m, the Krull dimension of R equals the height of m.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="local_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_height"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="unique_maximal_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ring_krull_dim"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Every chain of primes can be extended to end at the maximal ideal.
sketch_steps: setup: Take a chain of primes in R.
derive: Its top lies in m, so the chain can be extended to end at m.
conclude: So the supremum of lengths of chains equals the supremum for chains ending at m.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime ideal p of a commutative ring R, the Krull dimension of the localization R_p equals the height of p.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prime_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="localization_at_prime"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ring_krull_dim"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_height"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use the order-preserving correspondence between primes of R_p and primes contained in p.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Primes of R_p correspond to primes of R contained in p, preserving inclusions.
derive: Chains correspond with the same length.
conclude: dim R_p is the supremum of lengths of chains ending inside p, which is ht p.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime ideal p of a commutative ring R, the height of p plus the dimension of R/p is at most the dimension of R.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prime_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="leq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_height"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ring_krull_dim"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="quotient_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ring_krull_dim"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Concatenate a chain ending at p with a chain starting at p.
sketch_steps: setup: Take a chain of primes ending at p of length h and a chain of primes of R/p of length d.
derive: Primes of R/p correspond to primes of R containing p, and the chain can be taken to start at p.
derive: Concatenating gives a chain of length h + d in R.
conclude: Taking suprema gives the inequality.

drafts.canonical_statement: If R is a Noetherian local ring whose maximal ideal is generated by a finite set s, then dim R is at most the number of elements of s. In particular a Noetherian local ring has finite dimension.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="noetherian_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="local_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="subset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_generated_by"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="unique_maximal_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="leq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ring_krull_dim"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: The dimension is the height of m, which Krull's height theorem bounds by the number of generators.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: In a local ring, dim R = ht m.
derive: m is trivially minimal over (s) = m.
apply_theorem: Krull's height theorem gives ht m ≤ |s|.
conclude: So dim R ≤ |s|.

drafts.canonical_statement: If x is a nonunit nonzerodivisor of a Noetherian ring, then the height of the ideal (x), the least height of a prime minimal over (x), equals 1.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="noetherian_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="not"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="unit_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_height"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="principal_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: The principal ideal theorem gives the upper bound and a nonzerodivisor avoids minimal primes.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Primes minimal over (x) exist and have height at most 1.
setup: Suppose such a prime p has height 0.
derive: Then p is a minimal prime of R, whose elements are zero divisors.
contradiction: x is a nonzerodivisor in p.
conclude: So every such prime has height exactly 1.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a Noetherian commutative ring R, the Krull dimension of R[X] equals dim R + 1, the zero ring having dimension minus infinity.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="noetherian_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ring_krull_dim"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="polynomial_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ring_krull_dim"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Lift chains for the lower bound; for the upper bound, express a prime of R[X] as minimal over h + 1 elements after localizing at its contraction.
sketch_steps: construct: A chain in R of length d gives a chain in R[X] of length d + 1.
setup: Let P be a prime of R[X] with contraction p of height h.
apply_theorem: p is minimal over h elements x_1, ..., x_h.
derive: Modulo p the prime P becomes 0 or a principal ideal (f̄) in the PID k[X].
apply_theorem: So P is minimal over at most h + 1 elements of the Noetherian ring R_p[X], and Krull's height theorem applies.
conclude: ht P ≤ h + 1 ≤ dim R + 1.

drafts.canonical_statement: The Krull dimension of the polynomial ring in n variables over a field is n.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="is_field"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ring_krull_dim"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="mv_polynomial_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="variable_family"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on n using the dimension formula for polynomial rings over Noetherian rings.
sketch_steps: derive: For n = 0, a field has dimension 0.
apply_theorem: k[x_1, ..., x_(n-1)] is Noetherian by Hilbert's basis theorem.
apply_theorem: The dimension formula adds 1 for each new variable.
conclude: So the dimension is n.

drafts.proof_strategy: Extend chains below using that minimal primes consist of zero divisors, and bound the height of m by generators using Krull's height theorem.
sketch_steps: setup: Let d = dim R/(x), with a chain of primes of R containing x.
derive: The bottom prime contains the nonzerodivisor x, so it is not minimal, and the chain extends by one.
derive: So d + 1 ≤ dim R.
apply_theorem: m/(x) is minimal over d elements, so m is minimal over d + 1 elements.
apply_theorem: Krull's height theorem gives dim R = ht m ≤ d + 1.
conclude: Equality holds.

drafts.canonical_statement: If r_1, ..., r_k is a regular sequence on a Noetherian local ring R, meaning each r_i is a nonzerodivisor on R/(r_1, ..., r_(i-1)) and (r_1, ..., r_k) ≠ R, then dim R/(r_1, ..., r_k) + k = dim R.

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on k, dividing by r_1 and using the drop of dimension by a regular element.
sketch_steps: derive: All r_i lie in the maximal ideal because the ideal they generate is proper.
apply_theorem: dim R/(r_1) + 1 = dim R since r_1 is a nonzerodivisor in m.
derive: The images of r_2, ..., r_k form a regular sequence on R/(r_1).
induction: The hypothesis applied to R/(r_1) gives dim R/(r_1, ..., r_k) + k - 1 = dim R/(r_1).
conclude: Combining the two equalities gives the claim.

drafts.canonical_statement: Over a Noetherian local ring, any permutation of a regular sequence on a finitely generated module is again a regular sequence.

drafts.proof_strategy: Reduce to swapping two adjacent elements, and use Nakayama's lemma for the kernel of multiplication by b.
sketch_steps: derive: All r_i lie in m, by Nakayama's lemma and properness.
setup: Reduce to swapping a and b on M' = M/(r_1, ..., r_(i-1))M.
derive: The kernel K of b on M' satisfies K = aK.
apply_theorem: Nakayama's lemma gives K = 0, so b is a nonzerodivisor on M'.
derive: If az = by on M', then y = ay' and z = by', so a is a nonzerodivisor on M'/bM'.
conclude: Later quotients do not change, so the swapped sequence is regular.

drafts.canonical_statement: Let B be a faithfully flat A-algebra, meaning flat with B ⊗ N = 0 only for N = 0. For every ideal I of A, the preimage in A of the extension IB equals I.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show N → B ⊗ N is injective for every N, using faithful flatness, and apply it to N = A/I.
sketch_steps: setup: Let K be the kernel of N → B ⊗ N.
derive: Flatness identifies B ⊗ K with the kernel of id ⊗ ι.
derive: id ⊗ ι has a left inverse given by multiplication, so B ⊗ K = 0.
apply_theorem: Faithful flatness gives K = 0.
conclude: For N = A/I, the map A/I → B/IB is injective, so the contraction of IB is I.

drafts.canonical_statement: If B is a faithfully flat A-algebra and p is a prime ideal of A, then there is a prime ideal of B lying over p; that is, Spec B → Spec A is surjective.

drafts.proof_strategy: The contraction of pB is p, so pB misses the image of the complement of p, and a prime separates them.
sketch_steps: derive: The contraction of pB is p by faithful flatness.
derive: So pB does not meet the image T of the complement of p.
apply_theorem: There is a prime P containing pB and disjoint from T.
conclude: The contraction of P is p.

drafts.proof_strategy: Find a finitely generated J inside I with JS = IS, then contract using faithful flatness.
sketch_steps: setup: Each of finitely many generators of IS involves finitely many elements of I.
construct: Let J be the finitely generated ideal generated by those elements, so JS = IS.
apply_theorem: Faithful flatness gives that the contraction of JS is J.
conclude: So I lies in J, hence I = J is finitely generated.

derive: B ⊗ Ax is B/aB, which is nonzero.
apply_theorem: Flatness makes B ⊗ Ax inject into B ⊗ N.
conclude: So B ⊗ N is nonzero.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the chain rule for a complex differentiable function along the radial and angular curves.
sketch_steps: derive: A complex differentiable f composed with a real curve γ has derivative f'(γ(t))γ'(t).
apply_theorem: For γ(s) = s e^(iθ) the velocity at r is e^(iθ).
apply_theorem: For γ(t) = r e^(it) the velocity at θ is i r e^(iθ).
conclude: Multiplying by a gives both formulas.

drafts.canonical_statement: If f has complex derivative a ≠ 0 at z, then its real differential at z preserves the unoriented angle between any two plane vectors, the angle with the zero vector being π/2 by convention.

drafts.proof_strategy: The real differential is multiplication by a, which scales the inner product by |a|^2 and each norm by |a|.
sketch_steps: translate: The real differential at z is w ↦ a w.
derive: ⟨au, av⟩ = |a|^2 ⟨u, v⟩ and |au| = |a||u|.
conclude: The cosine of the angle is unchanged, so the angle is unchanged.

drafts.canonical_statement: If f has complex derivative a at z, then g(w) = conj(f(conj w)) has complex derivative conj(a) at conj z.

drafts.proof_strategy: Write the difference quotient of g as the conjugate of a difference quotient of f.
sketch_steps: derive: The difference quotient of g at conj z is the conjugate of that of f at z.
apply_theorem: Conjugation is continuous, so the limit exists.
conclude: The derivative is conj a.

sketch_steps: setup: Write f = u + iv.
translate: The Cauchy-Riemann equations for f and for conj f hold together.
derive: All first partial derivatives of u and v vanish, so f' = 0.
apply_theorem: A holomorphic function with zero derivative on a connected open set is constant.

sketch_steps: case_split: If the common modulus is 0, f vanishes on U.
derive: Otherwise conj f = k^2/f is holomorphic on U.
derive: The Cauchy-Riemann equations for f and conj f force f' = 0.
conclude: f is constant on the connected set U.

conclude: Both inequalities give 1/ρ = limsup.

drafts.proof_strategy: Factor out the lowest nonzero term of the difference series and use continuity at the centre.
sketch_steps: setup: Let h be the difference series with coefficients d_n.
contradiction: Assume some d_n is nonzero and let m be the least such index.
derive: h(w) = (w-c)^m g(w) with g continuous and g(c) ≠ 0.
conclude: Then h(s_k) ≠ 0 for large k, a contradiction.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the Cauchy estimate for f' on a large circle centred at an arbitrary point.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix c and ε; choose T with |f(z)| ≤ ε|z| for |z| > T.
derive: On a large circle about c, |f| ≤ 2εR.
apply_theorem: The Cauchy estimate gives |f'(c)| ≤ 2ε.
conclude: f' = 0, so f is constant.

sketch_steps: derive: Factor z^n out of p(z).
derive: The remaining factor tends to a_n ≠ 0.
conclude: |p(z)| ≥ |a_n||z|^n/2 for large |z|.

drafts.canonical_statement: Generalizing the fundamental theorem of algebra from the value 0 to any value, a complex polynomial of positive degree is surjective onto the complex plane.

sketch_steps: construct: q = p - w has the same positive degree.
apply_theorem: q has a root by the fundamental theorem of algebra.
conclude: That root solves p(z) = w.

sketch_steps: case_split: A root of P' that is also a root of P lies in the hull.
derive: Otherwise the logarithmic derivative gives Σ 1/(z-r_j) = 0.
derive: Conjugating gives Σ (z-r_j)/|z-r_j|^2 = 0.
conclude: z is a convex combination of the r_j.

sketch_steps: derive: Forward, divide the power series of f by (z-c)^n.
derive: Backward, multiply the power series of g by (z-c)^n.
apply_theorem: Uniqueness of power series coefficients concludes.

apply_theorem: The identity theorem gives g = 0 on U.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take an analytic n-th root of the nonvanishing factor g via the logarithm.
sketch_steps: setup: Write f = (z-c)^n g with g(c) ≠ 0.
construct: An analytic n-th root φ of g near c, using the principal logarithm of g/g(c).
construct: h = (z-c) φ.
conclude: h(c) = 0, h'(c) = φ(c) ≠ 0 and h^n = f.

sketch_steps: construct: h(z) = (z-c)^2 f(z), h(c) = 0.

derive: h has a zero of order at least 2 at c, so h = (z-c)^2 g.
conclude: g extends f.

construct: h = 1/(f-a) is bounded on the punctured disc.
apply_theorem: Riemann's theorem extends h to G.
conclude: f = a + 1/G is meromorphic at c.

derive: On the circle |f - v| > ε/2.
apply_theorem: The maximum principle for 1/(f-v) at the centre.
conclude: |f(c) - v| ≥ ε/2, a contradiction.

sketch_steps: construct: The difference quotient g extends holomorphically to the disc.
derive: On |w-c| = r, |g| ≤ R_2/r.
apply_theorem: The maximum principle gives |g(z)| ≤ R_2/r.
conclude: Let r tend to R_1.

apply_theorem: The maximum principle for 1/F_n gives |F_n(c)| ≥ m/2.

sketch_steps: derive: e^(g-h) = 1 makes φ = (g-h)/(2πi) integer valued.
apply_theorem: A continuous integer-valued function on a connected set is constant.

drafts.proof_strategy: Subdivide the path so each piece stays in a right half-plane after dividing, and glue principal logarithms.
sketch_steps: setup: Choose a partition with |γ(t) - γ(t_j)| < min |γ| on each piece.
construct: Define Γ inductively using the principal logarithm of γ(t)/γ(t_j).
derive: e^Γ = γ by induction.
conclude: For a closed path, e^(Γ(1)) = e^(Γ(0)) gives an integer multiple of 2πi.

drafts.canonical_statement: The first step of the Riemann mapping theorem, surjectivity not included. If U ≠ ℂ is a simply connected open set, there is f holomorphic and injective on U with nonvanishing derivative and f(U) contained in the open unit disc.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take a square root of z - a, whose image misses a disc, and invert around that disc.
sketch_steps: construct: A holomorphic square root s of z - a on U, with a outside U.
derive: s is injective and s' ≠ 0.
derive: The image of s contains a disc, whose reflection the image misses.
construct: f = (ε/2)/(s + s(z_0)) maps U into the unit disc.

drafts.canonical_statement: If f is analytic at z, then Re f and Im f are harmonic at z, that is, C^2 near z with vanishing Laplacian near z as functions of two real variables.

drafts.proof_strategy: The function u_x - i u_y is holomorphic; a primitive of it has real part u up to a constant.
sketch_steps: construct: g = u_x - i u_y.
derive: Harmonicity gives the Cauchy-Riemann equations for g.
apply_theorem: g has a primitive G on the disc.
conclude: Re G and u have the same gradient, so they differ by a constant.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take real parts of the mean value property of a holomorphic function with real part u, then let the radius grow.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: u = Re F on the open disc.
derive: The mean value property on radius r < R gives the formula for u.
derive: Uniform continuity on the closed disc lets r tend to R.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Cauchy's formula to F(ζ)/(1 - conj(w) ζ/R^2), simplify the kernel on the circle, take real parts and let the radius grow.
sketch_steps: construct: h(ζ) = F(ζ)/(1 - conj(w) ζ/R^2).
apply_theorem: Cauchy's formula for h at w.
derive: On the circle the kernel simplifies to R^2/|z-w|^2.
derive: Take real parts for u = Re F on smaller radii.
conclude: Uniform continuity gives the formula at radius R.

drafts.proof_strategy: The maximum set is open by the maximum modulus principle for exp F and closed by continuity.
sketch_steps: setup: Let V be the set where u equals its maximum.
derive: On a disc about x in V, u = Re F and |e^F| = e^u has a maximum at x.
apply_theorem: The maximum modulus principle makes u constant on the disc.
conclude: V is open and closed in U, so V = U.

drafts.proof_strategy: Write u locally as Re F, so u∘g = Re(F∘g) near z.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: u = Re F on a disc about g(z).
derive: u∘g = Re(F∘g) near z.
apply_theorem: Real parts of analytic functions are harmonic.

drafts.canonical_statement: Harnack's inequality. If u is harmonic on |z-c| < R, continuous on the closed disc and nonnegative there, then for |w-c| = ρ < R, ((R-ρ)/(R+ρ)) u(c) ≤ u(w) ≤ ((R+ρ)/(R-ρ)) u(c).

sketch_steps: setup: Choose m with A = (z-c)^m f analytic at c.
derive: A is not locally zero, so A = (z-c)^k g with g(c) ≠ 0.
construct: Put n = k - m.
contradiction: Two different exponents would force g_1(c) = 0.

sketch_steps: case_split: An infinite order summand does not change the sum near c.
derive: With m ≤ n, f+g = (z-c)^m H with H analytic at c.
derive: So the order of f+g is at least m.
derive: If m < n then H(c) = F(c) ≠ 0, so equality holds.

conclude: A_(m-1) = g(c) ≠ 0.

derive: Handle a or b equal to 0 by a limit.

drafts.proof_strategy: Map the half-plane Re g ≤ A into the unit disc and apply the Schwarz lemma.
sketch_steps: setup: Put g = f - f(0) and A = M + |f(0)|.
construct: ω = g/(2A-g) maps the disc into the closed unit disc with ω(0) = 0.
apply_theorem: The Schwarz lemma gives |ω(z)| ≤ |z|/R.
derive: Invert to bound |g(z)| and add |f(0)|.

drafts.canonical_statement: If R > 0 and a lies in the closed disc |z-c| ≤ R, then the mean of log|z-a| over the circle |z-c| = R equals log R, using the known value of the integral of log sin s over [0, π].

derive: The triangle inequality gives Π(1 + |a_i|) - 1.
apply_theorem: 1 + x ≤ e^x finishes.

sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Pointwise convergence follows from Σ|F_n(z)| ≤ Σ u_n.
derive: The finite product bound gives uniform convergence of partial products.
apply_theorem: The Weierstrass theorem gives holomorphy of the limit.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a real number s > 0, the improper integral of e^(-x) x^(s-1) over (0, ∞) converges absolutely, and its value is Γ(s).

drafts.proof_strategy: Split the integral at 1 and compare with x^(s-1) near 0 and with x^(-2) near infinity.
sketch_steps: setup: Split (0, ∞) into (0, 1] and [1, ∞).
derive: On (0, 1] the integrand is at most x^(s-1), which is integrable because s > 0.
derive: On [1, ∞) the integrand is at most M x^(-2), because x^(s+1) e^(-x) is bounded.
conclude: Both pieces are finite, so the integral converges absolutely and defines Γ(s).

drafts.canonical_statement: For a real number s > 0, Γ(s+1) = s Γ(s).

drafts.proof_strategy: Integrate by parts on [ε, R] and pass to the limit, the boundary terms vanishing.
sketch_steps: setup: Write Γ(s+1) as the limit of the integral of e^(-x) x^s over [ε, R].
derive: Integrate by parts, differentiating x^s and integrating e^(-x).
derive: The boundary terms tend to 0 as ε → 0 and R → ∞.
conclude: The limit gives Γ(s+1) = s Γ(s).

drafts.canonical_statement: For a nonnegative integer n, Γ(n+1) = n!.

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on n using Γ(1) = 1 and the recurrence.
sketch_steps: setup: Compute Γ(1) as the integral of e^(-x) over (0, ∞), which equals 1.
induction: If Γ(n+1) = n!, the recurrence gives Γ(n+2) = (n+1) n!.
conclude: Hence Γ(n+1) = n! for all n.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a real number s > 0 and a nonnegative integer n, Γ(s+n) = (∏_{k=0}^{n-1} (s+k)) Γ(s), with the empty product equal to 1. For s = 1 this gives Γ(n+1) = n!.

drafts.proof_strategy: Iterate the recurrence by induction on n.
sketch_steps: setup: The case n = 0 is trivial with the empty product.
induction: Apply Γ(t+1) = t Γ(t) at t = s + n, which is positive.
conclude: The product gains the factor s + n, so the formula holds for n + 1.

drafts.canonical_statement: Define Γ by its integral for s > 0 and extend it to negative non-integers by Γ(s) = Γ(s+1)/s. For a nonnegative integer n and a real s with -(n+1) < s < -n, one has (-1)^(n+1) Γ(s) > 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on n, moving s to s + 1 with the functional equation and tracking one sign change.
sketch_steps: setup: Γ is positive on (0, ∞).
derive: For -1 < s < 0, Γ(s) = Γ(s+1)/s is negative.
induction: For -(n+1) < s < -n, the point s + 1 lies in the previous interval.
derive: Dividing by the negative number s changes the sign once.
conclude: Hence (-1)^(n+1) Γ(s) > 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Substitute x = t^2 to reduce the definition to the Gaussian integral.
sketch_steps: setup: Write Γ(1/2) as the integral of e^(-x) x^(-1/2) over (0, ∞).
translate: Substitute x = t^2, so the integral becomes twice the Gaussian integral over (0, ∞).
apply_theorem: The Gaussian integral over the real line equals √π.
conclude: Hence Γ(1/2) = √π.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a nonnegative integer n, Γ(n + 1/2) = (2n)! √π / (4^n n!).

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on n from Γ(1/2) = √π using the recurrence.
sketch_steps: setup: The case n = 0 is Γ(1/2) = √π.
induction: Apply Γ(s+1) = s Γ(s) at s = n + 1/2.
derive: Multiply numerator and denominator by 2n + 2 to obtain (2n+2)! and 4^(n+1) (n+1)!.
conclude: The formula holds for n + 1.

drafts.canonical_statement: For s, t > 0 and a, b > 0 with a + b = 1, Γ(as + bt) ≤ Γ(s)^a Γ(t)^b. Equivalently, log Γ is convex on (0, ∞).

sketch_steps: setup: Write e^(-x) x^(as+bt-1) as the product of the a-th power of e^(-x) x^(s-1) and the b-th power of e^(-x) x^(t-1).
apply_theorem: Apply Hölder's inequality with exponents 1/a and 1/b.
derive: This gives Γ(as+bt) ≤ Γ(s)^a Γ(t)^b.
conclude: Taking logarithms of positive values gives the convexity of log Γ.

drafts.proof_strategy: Squeeze f(x) between expressions independent of f using the increasing slopes of the convex function log f.
sketch_steps: setup: Let φ = log f; the recurrence and f(1) = 1 give f(n+1) = n!.
derive: For 0 < x ≤ 1, the slopes of φ give x log n ≤ φ(n+1+x) - φ(n+1) ≤ x log(n+1).
derive: Using f(n+1+x) = f(x) ∏_{j≤n}(x+j), obtain G_n(x) ≤ f(x) ≤ (1+1/n)^x G_n(x) with G_n independent of f.
derive: Hence f(x) is the limit of G_n(x), and the same holds for Γ.
conclude: So f = Γ on (0, 1], and the recurrence extends this to (0, ∞).

drafts.canonical_statement: Gauss's limit formula. If a real s is not a nonpositive integer, then Γ(s) is the limit as n → ∞ of n^s n! / ∏_{j=0}^{n} (s+j), where Γ at negative non-integers is defined by Γ(s) = Γ(s+1)/s.

drafts.proof_strategy: Prove the limit on (0, 1] by log-convexity, then transfer it to other s by the shift relation for G_n.
sketch_steps: setup: Let G_n(s) = n^s n! / ∏_{j≤n}(s+j).
derive: For 0 < s ≤ 1, log-convexity of Γ gives G_n(s) ≤ Γ(s) ≤ (1+1/n)^s G_n(s).
derive: Reindexing gives G_n(s) = (1/s) ((s+n+1)/n) G_n(s+1).
induction: This shift transfers the limit to all s > 0.
conclude: The same shift reaches every negative non-integer, so G_n(s) → Γ(s).

drafts.canonical_statement: Reflection formula. For a complex number z that is not an integer, Γ(z) Γ(1-z) = π / sin(πz), where Γ is the analytic continuation of the integral on Re s > 0 to the complex plane minus the nonpositive integers.

drafts.proof_strategy: Multiply the Gauss limit expressions for z and 1 - z and compare with Euler's sine product.
sketch_steps: setup: Let G_n(s) = n^s n! / ∏_{j≤n}(s+j), which converges to Γ(s).
derive: The product G_n(z) G_n(1-z) simplifies to (n/(n+1-z)) / (z ∏_{k≤n}(1 - z²/k²)).
apply_theorem: Euler's sine product gives the limit of z ∏_{k≤n}(1 - z²/k²) as sin(πz)/π.
derive: Since z is not an integer, this limit is nonzero.
conclude: Passing to the limit gives Γ(z) Γ(1-z) = π / sin(πz).

drafts.canonical_statement: For a real number t, |Γ(1/2 + it)|² = π / cosh(πt).

drafts.proof_strategy: On Re z = 1/2 one has 1 - z = conj z, so the reflection formula computes the squared modulus.
sketch_steps: setup: Let z = 1/2 + it, so that 1 - z is the conjugate of z.
derive: Conjugating the integral gives Γ(conj z) = conj Γ(z), hence Γ(z) Γ(1-z) = |Γ(z)|².
apply_theorem: The reflection formula gives π / sin(πz).
conclude: Since sin(π/2 + iπt) = cosh(πt), the claim follows.

drafts.canonical_statement: Legendre duplication formula. For a real number s > 0, Γ(s) Γ(s + 1/2) = 2^(1-2s) √π Γ(2s).

drafts.proof_strategy: Check that 2^(x-1) Γ(x/2) Γ((x+1)/2) / √π satisfies the hypotheses of the Bohr–Mollerup theorem.
sketch_steps: setup: Define f(x) = 2^(x-1) Γ(x/2) Γ((x+1)/2) / √π for x > 0.
derive: Γ(1/2) = √π gives f(1) = 1.
derive: The recurrence for Γ gives f(x+1) = x f(x).
derive: log f is convex as a sum of an affine function and convex functions of affine functions.
apply_theorem: The Bohr–Mollerup theorem gives f = Γ.
conclude: Putting x = 2s gives the formula.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the strict convexity of Γ together with Γ(1) = Γ(2) = 1.
sketch_steps: setup: Pointwise strict convexity of u ↦ x^u for x ≠ 1 gives strict convexity of Γ after integrating.
derive: Chord slopes increase, and the chord over [1, 2] has slope 0.
derive: So Γ is strictly decreasing on (0, 1] and strictly increasing on [2, ∞).
derive: Γ has a minimum on [1, 2], with value below 1 because Γ(3/2) < 1, so the minimizer lies in (1, 2).
conclude: Outside [1, 2] the values are at least 1, so this point is the global minimizer.

sketch_steps: setup: Put t = u/r, so dt = du/r.
derive: The powers of r combine to r^(-a).
conclude: The remaining integral is Γ(a).

sketch_steps: setup: Put t = b x^p, a monotone change of variable on (0, ∞).
derive: Then dx = (1/p) b^(-1/p) t^(1/p-1) dt and x^q = b^(-q/p) t^(q/p).
derive: The integrand becomes t^((q+1)/p - 1) e^(-t) times a constant.
conclude: Since (q+1)/p > 0, the integral equals Γ((q+1)/p).

drafts.canonical_statement: As a complex number s ≠ 0 tends to 0, s Γ(s) tends to 1.

drafts.proof_strategy: Rewrite s Γ(s) as Γ(s+1) and use continuity at 1.
sketch_steps: setup: For s ≠ 0 the recurrence gives s Γ(s) = Γ(s+1).
apply_theorem: Γ is holomorphic on Re s > 0, hence continuous at 1.
conclude: So s Γ(s) tends to Γ(1) = 1.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a complex number s is not a nonpositive integer, then Γ(s) ≠ 0.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="C"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="unary_minus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="complex_gamma_fn"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Separate positive integers from non-integers and use the reflection formula for the latter.
sketch_steps: case_split: Either s is a positive integer or s is not an integer.
derive: At a positive integer, Γ(s) = (s-1)! is nonzero.
apply_theorem: For non-integer s, the reflection formula gives Γ(s) Γ(1-s) = π / sin(πs), which is nonzero.
conclude: Hence Γ(s) ≠ 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: The reciprocal 1/Γ, with value 0 at each nonpositive integer -m, is holomorphic on the whole complex plane.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="holomorphic_fn_on"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="fns1" name="lambda"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="divide"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="complex_gamma_fn"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="C"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Extend holomorphy from the right half plane to the left using h(s) = s h(s+1).
sketch_steps: setup: Define h = 1/Γ away from the poles and h(-m) = 0.
derive: h is holomorphic on Re s > 0 because Γ is holomorphic and nonvanishing there.
derive: The recurrence gives h(s) = s h(s+1) for every complex s.
induction: If h is holomorphic on Re s > -k, this identity makes it holomorphic on Re s > -k-1.
conclude: Hence h is entire.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a nonnegative integer n, Γ'(n+1) = n! (-γ + Σ_{k=1}^{n} 1/k), where γ is the limit of Σ_{k=1}^{m} 1/k - log m as m → ∞. In particular Γ'(1) = -γ.

drafts.proof_strategy: Trap the derivative of log Γ at integers between chord slopes of the convex function log Γ.
sketch_steps: setup: Let f = log Γ, which is convex and differentiable on (0, ∞).
derive: Differentiating f(s+1) = f(s) + log s gives f'(m+1) = f'(1) + H_m.
derive: Convexity gives log m ≤ f'(1) + H_m ≤ log(m+1).
derive: Letting m → ∞ gives f'(1) = -γ.
conclude: Then Γ'(n+1) = Γ(n+1) f'(n+1) = n! (-γ + H_n).

drafts.canonical_statement: Let n be a positive integer and r > 0. The volume of an open ball of radius r in ℝ^n is π^(n/2) r^n / Γ(n/2 + 1).

drafts.proof_strategy: Evaluate the n-dimensional Gaussian integral in two ways using Tonelli's theorem.
sketch_steps: setup: Let V be the volume of the unit ball; scaling gives volume V r^n for radius r.
derive: The product of Gaussian integrals gives the integral of e^(-|x|²) over ℝ^n as π^(n/2).
derive: Writing e^(-|x|²) as the integral of e^(-t) over t > |x|² and using Tonelli gives V times the integral of t^(n/2) e^(-t).
conclude: This equals V Γ(n/2 + 1), so V = π^(n/2) / Γ(n/2 + 1).

drafts.canonical_statement: For real numbers u, v > 0, the function x^(u-1) (1-x)^(v-1) is integrable on (0, 1), and B(u,v), its integral over (0, 1), equals Γ(u) Γ(v) / Γ(u+v).

drafts.proof_strategy: Write Γ(u) Γ(v) as a double integral and change variables to x = rt, y = r(1-t).
sketch_steps: setup: Express Γ(u) Γ(v) as a double integral of a nonnegative function over the quadrant.
translate: Change variables by x = rt and y = r(1-t), with Jacobian r.
apply_theorem: Tonelli's theorem separates the integrals in r and t.
derive: The factor in r equals Γ(u+v).
conclude: Finiteness of Γ(u) Γ(v) gives integrability, and dividing gives the identity.

drafts.canonical_statement: For complex numbers u, v with positive real parts, u B(u, v+1) = v B(u+1, v), where B(u,v) is the integral of x^(u-1) (1-x)^(v-1) over (0, 1).

drafts.proof_strategy: Integrate the derivative of x^u (1-x)^v over (0, 1).
sketch_steps: setup: Let F(x) = x^u (1-x)^v.
derive: F' equals u x^(u-1) (1-x)^v - v x^u (1-x)^(v-1).
derive: F tends to 0 at both endpoints because the real parts of u and v are positive.
conclude: Integrating F' over (0, 1) gives u B(u, v+1) = v B(u+1, v).

drafts.canonical_statement: For a complex number u with positive real part and a nonnegative integer n, B(u, n+1) = n! / ∏_{j=0}^{n} (u+j), where B(u,v) is the integral of x^(u-1) (1-x)^(v-1) over (0, 1).

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on n for all u, using the recurrence for B.
sketch_steps: setup: The case n = 0 is the integral of x^(u-1), which equals 1/u.
induction: Apply u B(u, n+2) = (n+1) B(u+1, n+1) and the hypothesis at u + 1.
conclude: Dividing by u, which is nonzero, gives the formula for n + 1.

drafts.canonical_statement: For nonnegative integers m and n, the integral of x^m (1-x)^n over [0, 1] equals m! n! / (m+n+1)!.

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on n by integrating by parts, raising the exponent of x each time.
sketch_steps: setup: The case n = 0 is the integral of x^m.
induction: Integrate by parts, the boundary terms vanishing.
derive: Apply the hypothesis with m + 1 and simplify.
conclude: This gives m! (n+1)! / (m+n+2)!.

drafts.canonical_statement: Stirling's formula. As n → ∞, n! is asymptotically equivalent to √(2πn) (n/e)^n; that is, the ratio of the two sides tends to 1.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show that n!/(√(2n) (n/e)^n) decreases to a positive limit and identify the limit by Wallis's product.
sketch_steps: setup: Let a_n = n! / (√(2n) (n/e)^n).
derive: The series for log((1+t)/(1-t)) with t = 1/(2n+1) gives 0 ≤ log a_n - log a_(n+1) ≤ 1/(12n(n+1)).
derive: So a_n decreases to a positive limit a.
apply_theorem: Wallis's product gives a_n^4 / a_(2n)^2 → π.
derive: The left side tends to a², so a = √π.
conclude: Hence n! / (√(2πn) (n/e)^n) tends to 1.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare consecutive logarithms using the series of log((1+t)/(1-t)).
sketch_steps: setup: Compute log a_n - log a_(n+1) = (n + 1/2) log(1 + 1/n) - 1.
derive: With t = 1/(2n+1), log(1 + 1/n) = log((1+t)/(1-t)) ≥ 2t.
derive: Hence (n + 1/2) log(1 + 1/n) ≥ 1.
conclude: So a_(n+1) ≤ a_n.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a positive integer n, √(2πn) (n/e)^n ≤ n!.

drafts.proof_strategy: The decreasing sequence n!/(√(2n) (n/e)^n) stays above its limit √π.
sketch_steps: setup: Let a_n = n! / (√(2n) (n/e)^n).
apply_theorem: a_n is decreasing and tends to √π by Stirling's formula.
derive: So a_n ≥ √π for every n ≥ 1.
conclude: Rewriting gives the inequality.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a positive integer n, (n/e)^n ≤ n! ≤ e n (n/e)^n.

drafts.proof_strategy: Keep one term of the exponential series for the lower bound, and induct with (1+1/n)^(n+1) ≥ e for the upper bound.
sketch_steps: setup: Keep the term k = n of the series of e^n to get e^n ≥ n^n / n!.
derive: Rearranging gives the lower bound.
induction: The upper bound holds at n = 1.
derive: From log(1+1/n) ≥ 1/(n+1), obtain e n^(n+1) ≤ (n+1)^(n+1).
conclude: Combining with the hypothesis gives the upper bound for n + 1.

drafts.canonical_statement: As n → ∞, C(2n, n) √(πn) / 4^n tends to 1; that is, C(2n, n) is asymptotically equivalent to 4^n / √(πn).
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_fn_tends_to"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="fns1" name="lambda"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="divide"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="binomial"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="root"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="pi"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>4</n1:OMI><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Substitute the Stirling sequence into (2n)!/(n!)² and take the limit.
sketch_steps: setup: Let a_n = n! / (√(2n) (n/e)^n), which tends to √π.
derive: Substituting gives C(2n, n) = (a_(2n) / a_n²) 4^n / √n.
derive: Hence C(2n, n) √(πn) / 4^n = √π a_(2n) / a_n².
conclude: The right side tends to 1.

drafts.canonical_statement: Wallis's product. The limit as n → ∞ of ∏_{k=1}^{n} (2k/(2k-1)) (2k/(2k+1)) is π/2.

drafts.proof_strategy: Express the partial product as (π/2) I_(2n+1)/I_(2n) for the sine power integrals and squeeze the ratio.
sketch_steps: setup: Let I_m be the integral of sin^m over [0, π/2].
derive: Integration by parts gives I_m = ((m-1)/m) I_(m-2).
derive: This yields the partial product W_n = (π/2) I_(2n+1) / I_(2n).
derive: Monotonicity of I_m gives 2n/(2n+1) ≤ I_(2n+1)/I_(2n) ≤ 1.
conclude: The squeeze theorem gives W_n → π/2.

drafts.canonical_statement: Euler's sine product. For every complex number z, sin(πz) = πz times the limit as n → ∞ of ∏_{k=1}^{n} (1 - z²/k²).

drafts.proof_strategy: Use a recursion for the integrals of cos(2zx) cos^n x and the concentration of cos^(2n) x near 0.
sketch_steps: setup: Let J_n be the integral of cos(2zx) cos^n x over [0, π/2] and B_n the integral of cos^n x.
derive: Two integrations by parts give (n² - 4z²) J_n = n(n-1) J_(n-2), and n B_n = (n-1) B_(n-2).
derive: For R_k = J_(2k)/B_(2k), this gives (1 - z²/k²) R_k = R_(k-1).
derive: Since R_0 = sin(πz)/(πz), one has sin(πz)/(πz) = R_n ∏_{k≤n} (1 - z²/k²).
derive: The mass of cos^(2n) x concentrates near 0, so R_n → 1.
conclude: Hence πz ∏_{k≤n} (1 - z²/k²) → sin(πz).

drafts.canonical_statement: For a complex number z that is not an integer, the series Σ_{n≥1} (1/(z-n) + 1/(z+n)) converges absolutely, and π cot(πz) = 1/z + Σ_{n≥1} (1/(z-n) + 1/(z+n)).

drafts.proof_strategy: Logarithmically differentiate Euler's sine product, using locally uniform convergence.
sketch_steps: setup: The general term equals 2z/(z² - n²), which is O(1/n²), so the series converges absolutely.
apply_theorem: The partial products of Euler's sine product converge locally uniformly away from the integers.
derive: Locally uniform convergence passes to derivatives, so the logarithmic derivatives converge to π cot(πw).
derive: The logarithmic derivative of the partial product is 1/w + Σ_{k≤n} (1/(w-k) + 1/(w+k)).
conclude: Letting n → ∞ gives the partial fraction expansion.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use linearity of the integral, the integrands being integrable because |e_(-n)| = 1.
sketch_steps: setup: Since |e_(-n)| = 1, the functions e_(-n) f and e_(-n) g are integrable.
derive: Expand e_(-n)(cf + g) as c e_(-n) f + e_(-n) g.
conclude: Linearity of the integral gives the formula.

drafts.proof_strategy: Change variables by translation invariance and factor the exponential.
sketch_steps: setup: Write c_n(f_a) as the integral of e_(-n)(x) f(x+a).
translate: Invariance of μ allows the substitution y = x + a.
derive: The exponential factors as e_(-n)(y-a) = e_(-n)(y) e_n(a).
conclude: Hence c_n(f_a) = e_n(a) c_n(f).

drafts.proof_strategy: Conjugate the integral for real f, and substitute x ↦ -x for even or odd f.
sketch_steps: case_split: Treat the real, even and odd cases separately.
derive: For real f, conjugating the integral replaces e_(-n) by e_n.
translate: The substitution x ↦ -x gives c_(-n)(f) as the integral of e_(-n)(x) f(-x).
conclude: Evenness or oddness of f gives the stated relations.

drafts.canonical_statement: Let T > 0, s a finite set of integers and a_k complex numbers. For the trigonometric polynomial P(x) = Σ_{k∈s} a_k e^(2πikx/T), the coefficient c_n(P), which is (1/T) times the integral of P(x) e^(-2πinx/T) over [0, T], equals a_n if n is in s and 0 otherwise.

sketch_steps: setup: Interchange the finite sum and the integral.
derive: For k = n the factor equals 1.
derive: For k ≠ n the antiderivative is T-periodic, so the factor equals 0.
conclude: Only the term k = n survives.

sketch_steps: setup: Euler's formula gives e^(-inx) = cos(nx) - i sin(nx).
derive: The products of f with cos(nx) and sin(nx) are integrable.
conclude: Linearity of the integral gives c_n = (a_n - i b_n)/2.

drafts.canonical_statement: Let a < b, T = b - a and c_n(f) = (1/T) ∫_a^b f(x) e^(-2πinx/T) dx. If f is differentiable at each point of [a, b] with integrable derivative f' and f(a) = f(b), then c_n(f') = (2πin/T) c_n(f) for every integer n. This is the periodic form of the integration by parts formula with boundary terms.

drafts.proof_strategy: Integrate by parts; the boundary terms cancel since f and the exponential agree at the endpoints.
sketch_steps: case_split: Treat n = 0 and n ≠ 0 separately.
derive: For n = 0, the fundamental theorem gives c_0(f') = (f(b) - f(a))/T = 0.
derive: For n ≠ 0, integrate by parts against e(x) = e^(-2πinx/T).
derive: The boundary terms cancel because f(a) = f(b) and e(a) = e(b).
conclude: Dividing by T gives c_n(f') = (2πin/T) c_n(f).

If g_0, ..., g_k are functions such that for j < k, g_j is differentiable at each point of [a, b] with g_j' = g_(j+1), g_(j+1) is integrable and g_j(a) = g_j(b), then c_n(g_k) = (2πin/T)^k c_n(g_0) for every integer n.

derive: Apply the rule to g_k and use the induction hypothesis.
conclude: The power of 2πin/T increases by one.

sketch_steps: setup: Integration by parts gives c_n(f') = (2πin/T) c_n(f), the boundary terms cancelling.
derive: So |c_n(f)| = (T/(2π|n|)) |c_n(f')|.
derive: Since the exponential has modulus 1, |c_n(f')| ≤ (1/T) ∫|f'|.
conclude: Combining gives the bound.

sketch_steps: setup: The exponentials are orthonormal for the normalized inner product and c_n(f) = ⟨f, e_n⟩.
construct: Let g = f - Σ_{n∈s} c_n(f) e_n.
derive: Expanding gives ⟨g, g⟩ = ⟨f, f⟩ - Σ_{n∈s} |c_n(f)|².
conclude: Nonnegativity of ⟨g, g⟩ gives the inequality.

drafts.canonical_statement: Riemann–Lebesgue lemma on an interval. Let a ≤ b and let f be an integrable complex function on [a, b]. As the real number λ satisfies |λ| → ∞, the integral of f(x) e^(iλx) over [a, b] tends to 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Approximate f in L¹ by step functions and integrate the exponential explicitly on intervals.
sketch_steps: setup: Choose a step function g with ∫|f - g| < ε.
derive: Since the exponential has modulus 1, replacing f by g changes the integral by less than ε.
derive: On each interval, the integral of e^(iλx) has modulus at most 2/|λ|.
conclude: So the integral of f e^(iλx) is below 2ε for large |λ|.

drafts.canonical_statement: Let a < b, T = b - a and c_n(f) = (1/T) ∫_a^b f(x) e^(-2πinx/T) dx. If f is integrable on [a, b], then c_n(f) → 0 as |n| → ∞.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma on the interval with λ = -2πn/T.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The Riemann–Lebesgue lemma on an interval gives decay of the integral of f e^(iλx) as |λ| → ∞.
derive: Take λ = -2πn/T, which tends to infinity in absolute value with n.
conclude: Hence c_n(f) → 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Polarize Parseval's identity for the orthonormal basis of exponentials.
sketch_steps: setup: The exponentials form a complete orthonormal system of L²(μ) with c_n(f) = ⟨e_n, f⟩.
derive: Parseval makes the coefficient sequences square summable, so the product series converges absolutely.
apply_theorem: Polarization expresses ⟨f, g⟩ through the norms of f + i^k g.
derive: The same identity holds for the coefficients.
conclude: Applying Parseval to each f + i^k g gives the formula.

drafts.canonical_statement: Let T > 0, μ the invariant probability measure on ℝ/Tℤ, c_n(f) the integral of e_(-n) f and e_n(x) = e^(2πinx/T). For f in L²(μ), the Fourier series Σ_{n∈ℤ} c_n(f) e_n converges unconditionally to f in the norm of L²(μ). No pointwise convergence is claimed.

drafts.proof_strategy: Bessel's inequality gives convergence, and density of trigonometric polynomials identifies the limit with f.
sketch_steps: setup: The exponentials are orthonormal, so Bessel's inequality and completeness give convergence of the series to some g.
derive: The difference h = f - g is orthogonal to every e_n.
apply_theorem: Stone–Weierstrass makes trigonometric polynomials dense in continuous functions, hence in L²(μ).
conclude: So h = 0 and the series converges to f.

drafts.canonical_statement: Let T > 0. If continuous functions f, g on ℝ/Tℤ satisfy c_n(f) = c_n(g) for all integers n, then f = g. Here c_n(f) is the integral of e_(-n) f, μ is the invariant probability measure and e_n(x) = e^(2πinx/T).

drafts.proof_strategy: Show the difference is orthogonal to itself by uniform approximation with trigonometric polynomials.
sketch_steps: setup: Let h = f - g, which is continuous and has all Fourier coefficients zero.
derive: So h is orthogonal to all trigonometric polynomials.
apply_theorem: Stone–Weierstrass gives trigonometric polynomials P_k converging uniformly to h.
derive: Taking limits gives the integral of |h|² equal to 0.
conclude: Continuity forces h = 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: Let T > 0. For a continuous function f on ℝ/Tℤ and ε > 0, there is a trigonometric polynomial P(x) = Σ_{k∈s} a_k e^(2πikx/T), with s a finite set of integers, such that |f(x) - P(x)| < ε for all x.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the complex Stone–Weierstrass theorem to the algebra of trigonometric polynomials.
sketch_steps: setup: The circle is compact Hausdorff.
derive: Trigonometric polynomials form a subalgebra containing constants, closed under conjugation.
derive: The mode e_1 separates points.
apply_theorem: The complex Stone–Weierstrass theorem gives uniform density.
conclude: Hence the required polynomial exists.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a nonnegative integer N and a real x with sin(x/2) ≠ 0, the Dirichlet kernel satisfies 1 + 2 Σ_{k=1}^{N} cos(kx) = sin((N + 1/2) x) / sin(x/2).

drafts.proof_strategy: Multiply by sin(x/2) and telescope with the product-to-sum formula.
sketch_steps: setup: Multiply the left side by sin(x/2).
derive: The product-to-sum formula gives 2 cos(kx) sin(x/2) = sin((k+1/2)x) - sin((k-1/2)x).
derive: The sum telescopes to sin((N+1/2)x) - sin(x/2).
conclude: Adding sin(x/2) and dividing gives the formula.

derive: The product-to-sum formula gives D_n(x) sin²(x/2) = (cos(nx) - cos((n+1)x))/2.
derive: The sum over n telescopes to (1 - cos(Nx))/2 = sin²(Nx/2).
derive: Dividing by sin²(x/2) gives the square, which is nonnegative.

drafts.proof_strategy: Two integrations by parts give O(1/n²) coefficients; uniform convergence and uniqueness identify the sum.
sketch_steps: setup: Since f' is also T-periodic, two integrations by parts give c_n(f) = (T/(2πin))² c_n(f'').
derive: Hence |c_n(f)| ≤ T² M / (4π² n²), which is summable.
apply_theorem: The M-test gives a uniformly convergent series with continuous sum g.
derive: Term-by-term integration gives c_n(g) = c_n(f).
conclude: Uniqueness for continuous periodic functions gives g = f.

drafts.proof_strategy: Substitute u = -v for the reflection, and move the conjugation inside the integral.
sketch_steps: translate: Substitute u = -v, using invariance of Lebesgue measure under reflection.
derive: This gives g^(w) = f^(-w).
derive: Conjugating the integral for f^(-w) gives the integral of e^(-2πivw) conj f(v).
conclude: Hence h^(w) = conj f^(-w).

drafts.canonical_statement: If f on ℝ is integrable, then its Fourier transform f^(w) = ∫ e^(-2πivw) f(v) dv is continuous on ℝ.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the dominated convergence theorem with the dominating function |f|.
sketch_steps: setup: Take a sequence w_k converging to w.
derive: The integrands converge pointwise and are dominated by |f|.
apply_theorem: The dominated convergence theorem gives f^(w_k) → f^(w).
conclude: Sequential continuity gives continuity.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Fubini's theorem to e^(-2πivw) f(v) g(w).
sketch_steps: setup: Let F(v,w) = e^(-2πivw) f(v) g(w).
derive: Since |F| = |f||g|, Tonelli shows F is integrable on the plane.
apply_theorem: Fubini's theorem allows exchanging the order of integration.
conclude: The two iterated integrals are the two sides.

drafts.canonical_statement: Fourier inversion. Let V be a finite-dimensional real inner product space with Lebesgue measure, F f(w) = ∫ e^(-2πi⟨v,w⟩) f(v) dv and F⁻¹ g(v) = ∫ e^(2πi⟨v,w⟩) g(w) dw. If f and F f are integrable and f is continuous at v, then F⁻¹(F f)(v) = f(v).

drafts.proof_strategy: Insert a Gaussian factor, apply Fubini, and let the Gaussian kernels concentrate at the point v.
sketch_steps: setup: Define I_ε by inserting e^(-πε|w|²) in the inverse transform of F f.
apply_theorem: Dominated convergence gives I_ε → F⁻¹(F f)(v), since F f is integrable.
apply_theorem: Fubini and the Gaussian Fourier transform give I_ε = ∫ f(x) G_ε(v-x) dx.
derive: G_ε is a positive kernel of integral 1 that concentrates at 0 as ε → 0.
derive: Continuity of f at v and integrability give I_ε → f(v).
conclude: Uniqueness of limits gives the inversion formula.

drafts.canonical_statement: If f on ℝ is continuous and integrable and f^(w) = ∫ e^(-2πivw) f(v) dv is also integrable, then the transform of f^ at x equals f(-x) for every real x.

sketch_steps: setup: Write the double transform at x as an integral of e^(-2πiwx) f^(w).
translate: This equals the inverse Fourier transform of f^ at -x.
apply_theorem: The inversion formula applies since f is continuous and f, f^ are integrable.
conclude: The value is f(-x).

drafts.canonical_statement: For a complex number b with Re b > 0, the function f(x) = e^(-πbx²) has Fourier transform f^(t) = ∫ e^(-2πixt) f(x) dx = b^(-1/2) e^(-πt²/b), with the principal branch of b^(-1/2). In particular, for b = 1 the function e^(-πx²) is its own transform.

drafts.proof_strategy: Derive a first-order differential equation in t and determine the initial value by analytic continuation in b.
sketch_steps: setup: Let I(t) be the transform of e^(-πbx²), which converges absolutely.
derive: Differentiating under the integral and integrating by parts gives I'(t) = -(2πt/b) I(t).
derive: So I(t) = I(0) e^(-πt²/b).
apply_theorem: For real b > 0 the Gaussian integral gives I(0) = b^(-1/2), and the identity theorem extends this to Re b > 0.
conclude: Hence the formula.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a complex b with Re b < 0 and complex c, d, the integral of e^(bx²+cx+d) over ℝ equals (π/(-b))^(1/2) e^(d - c²/(4b)), with the principal branch of the square root.

drafts.proof_strategy: Reduce to the Gaussian Fourier transform on the imaginary axis of c and extend by the identity theorem.
sketch_steps: setup: Factor out e^d and set β = -b/π, which has positive real part.
derive: J(c), the integral of e^(bx²+cx), is entire in c.
apply_theorem: For c = -2πit, J(c) is the Fourier transform of a Gaussian, known explicitly.
derive: The two sides agree on the imaginary axis.
conclude: The identity theorem gives equality for all c.

drafts.canonical_statement: Let V be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and b > 0. The integral of e^(-b|v|²) over V equals (π/b)^((dim V)/2). This is the general form of the Gaussian integrals over ℝ and ℝ².

drafts.proof_strategy: Factor the integrand in orthonormal coordinates and use the one-dimensional Gaussian integral.
sketch_steps: setup: An orthonormal basis identifies V with ℝ^n preserving Lebesgue measure.
derive: The integrand factors as the product of e^(-b x_j²).
apply_theorem: Tonelli's theorem splits the integral into n one-dimensional integrals.
conclude: Each equals √(π/b), giving (π/b)^(n/2).

drafts.canonical_statement: Convolution theorem. Let V be a finite-dimensional real inner product space with Lebesgue measure, F f(w) = ∫ e^(-2πi⟨v,w⟩) f(v) dv and (f*g)(x) = ∫ f(t) g(x-t) dt. If f, g are integrable, then F(f*g)(w) = F f(w) F g(w).

sketch_steps: setup: Write the difference quotient of f^ as an integral.
derive: The bound |e^(iθ) - 1| ≤ |θ| gives the integrable majorant 2π|x||f(x)|.
apply_theorem: The dominated convergence theorem applies as h → 0.
conclude: The limit is the Fourier transform of -2πix f(x).

drafts.canonical_statement: Plancherel's theorem. Let V be a finite-dimensional real inner product space, and write F also for the continuous extension to L²(V) of the Fourier transform F f(w) = ∫ e^(-2πi⟨v,w⟩) f(v) dv on Schwartz functions. For Schwartz f, the L² class of f is sent to the L² class of F f, and ‖F f‖₂ = ‖f‖₂ for all f in L²(V).

sketch_steps: setup: For Schwartz f, let h be the conjugate of F f.
apply_theorem: Inversion gives F h = conj f.
apply_theorem: The multiplication formula gives the integral of |F f|² equal to the integral of |f|².
derive: Schwartz functions are dense in L²(V).
conclude: The isometry extends uniquely to L²(V).

sketch_steps: setup: An antiderivative of e^(-2πivw) is e^(-2πivw) / (-2πiw).
derive: The difference of the endpoint values equals -2i sin(2πaw).
conclude: Dividing by -2πiw gives sin(2πaw) / (πw).

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the Poisson summation formula to the Gaussian e^(-πax²).
sketch_steps: setup: Comparison with 1/(πan²) gives absolute convergence.
derive: The Gaussian f(x) = e^(-πax²) and its transform decay faster than |x|^(-2).
apply_theorem: The Gaussian Fourier transform gives f^(t) = a^(-1/2) e^(-πt²/a).
apply_theorem: Poisson summation at x = 0 gives Σ f(n) = Σ f^(n).
conclude: This is the transformation formula.

drafts.canonical_statement: Let V be a finite-dimensional real inner product space. If f on V is a Schwartz function, meaning smooth with |v|^k ‖D^n f(v)‖ bounded for all k and n, then f is integrable with respect to Lebesgue measure and f(v) → 0 as |v| → ∞.

drafts.proof_strategy: The decay bound with k = dim V + 1 gives integrability at infinity and vanishing at infinity.
sketch_steps: setup: Let d = dim V; the Schwartz bounds give M_0 = sup |f| and M_1 = sup |v|^(d+1) |f(v)|.
derive: On the unit ball, |f| ≤ M_0 on a set of finite volume.
derive: Outside it, |f(v)| ≤ M_1 |v|^(-(d+1)), which is integrable.
conclude: So f is integrable, and the same bound gives f(v) → 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: Let V be a finite-dimensional real inner product space. If f on V is a Schwartz function, then F f(w) = ∫ e^(-2πi⟨v,w⟩) f(v) dv is also a Schwartz function.

drafts.proof_strategy: Exchange decay and differentiation through the Fourier transform: each bound comes from the integrability of a Schwartz function.
sketch_steps: setup: Schwartz functions are stable under multiplication by coordinates and partial derivatives, and they are integrable.
derive: Differentiating under the integral gives the derivative of F f as the transform of -2πix_j f.
derive: Integration by parts gives w_j F f as the transform of ∂_j f up to a constant.
derive: So w^α ∂^β F f is a constant times the transform of ∂^α (x^β f).
conclude: The transform of an integrable function is bounded, so F f is Schwartz.

drafts.canonical_statement: Let V be a finite-dimensional real inner product space. For a Schwartz function f on V, the integral of |F f(ξ)|² equals the integral of |f(x)|², where F f(ξ) = ∫ e^(-2πi⟨x,ξ⟩) f(x) dx.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the multiplication formula to f and the conjugate of F f, using inversion.
sketch_steps: setup: F f is Schwartz, so inversion holds for f.
construct: Let h be the conjugate of F f.
derive: Inversion gives F h = conj f.
apply_theorem: The multiplication formula gives ∫ (F f) h = ∫ f (F h).
conclude: This says the integrals of |F f|² and |f|² agree.

drafts.canonical_statement: Fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations. If f on ℝ^n is locally integrable and the integral of g(x) f(x) over ℝ^n is 0 for all smooth compactly supported real g, then f = 0 almost everywhere.
