drafts.proof_strategy: Abelian ideals are solvable, and a nonzero solvable ideal contains a nonzero abelian ideal.
sketch_steps: derive: An abelian ideal is solvable, so it lies in the radical.
contradiction: If the radical is nonzero, some solvable ideal I is nonzero.
derive: The last nonzero derived term of I is a nonzero abelian ideal.
conclude: The two conditions are equivalent.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a Lie algebra L over a commutative ring R is Noetherian as an R-module, then the quotient L/rad L has zero radical.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="noetherian_module"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_quotient"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_radical"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="solvable_lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="zero_lie_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Pull back a solvable ideal of the quotient and use that extensions of solvable by solvable are solvable.
sketch_steps: setup: Noetherianity makes the radical r itself solvable.
construct: Let A be the preimage of a solvable ideal J of L/r.
derive: D^k A lies in r when D^k J = 0, so D^(k+l) A = 0.
derive: A is a solvable ideal, so A lies in r.
conclude: J = pi(A) = 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: With the lower central series C^0 L = L and C^(k+1) L = [L, C^k L] of a Lie algebra, one has [C^i L, C^j L] contained in C^(i+j+1) L for all i, j at least 0.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="subset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_ideal_bracket"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_lower_central_series"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_lower_central_series"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_lower_central_series"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on i for all j, using the Jacobi identity to move the outer bracket.
sketch_steps: setup: Induct on i, with j arbitrary.
derive: For i = 0 this is the definition of C^(j+1) L.
derive: [[a,b],c] = [a,[b,c]] - [b,[a,c]] splits a generator.
conclude: Both terms lie in C^(i+j+2) L by the induction hypothesis.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every Lie subalgebra of a nilpotent Lie algebra over a commutative ring is nilpotent.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nilpotent_lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_subalgebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nilpotent_lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Compare the lower central series of H and L term by term.
sketch_steps: induction: C^k H lies in C^k L for every k.
derive: C^k L = 0 for some k.
conclude: C^k H = 0, so H is nilpotent.

drafts.canonical_statement: If there is a surjective homomorphism from a nilpotent Lie algebra L onto L', over a commutative ring, then L' is nilpotent.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_algebra_hom"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_hom_surjective"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nilpotent_lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nilpotent_lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: A surjection maps the lower central series onto the lower central series.
sketch_steps: induction: f(C^k L) = C^k L' for every k.
derive: C^k L = 0 for some k.
conclude: C^k L' = 0, so L' is nilpotent.

drafts.canonical_statement: If an ideal I of a Lie algebra L over a commutative ring lies in the center and L/I is nilpotent, then L is nilpotent. In particular, L is nilpotent when L/Z(L) is.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="subset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_center"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nilpotent_lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_quotient"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nilpotent_lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: The lower central series enters I, and one more bracket kills it.
sketch_steps: derive: pi maps C^k L onto C^k(L/I).
derive: If C^k(L/I) = 0 then C^k L lies in I.
conclude: C^(k+1) L lies in [L,I] = 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: A nonzero nilpotent Lie algebra over a commutative ring has nonzero center.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nilpotent_lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="not"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="zero_lie_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="not"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="zero_lie_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_center"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: The last nonzero term of the lower central series is central.
sketch_steps: setup: Choose k minimal with C^k L = 0; then k is at least 1.
derive: C^(k-1) L is nonzero.
conclude: [L, C^(k-1) L] = 0 means this term lies in the center.

drafts.canonical_statement: If the derived algebra of a Lie algebra L over a commutative ring lies in the center of L, then L is nilpotent.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="subset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_derived_series"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_center"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nilpotent_lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Compute C^2 L directly.
sketch_steps: derive: C^1 L = [L,L] lies in Z(L).
conclude: C^2 L = [L, C^1 L] = 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a Lie algebra L over a field K has elements x and y with y nonzero and [x,y] = cy for a nonzero scalar c, then L is not nilpotent.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="field"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_bracket"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="not"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nilpotent_lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: A nonzero eigenvalue of ad x contradicts nilpotency of ad x.
sketch_steps: contradiction: Suppose C^n L = 0.
derive: (ad x)^n maps L into C^n L, so it vanishes.
derive: (ad x)^n y = c^n y is nonzero.
conclude: L is not nilpotent.

drafts.canonical_statement: General Leibniz rule for ad. For x, y, z in a Lie algebra over a commutative ring and n at least 0, (ad x)^n [y,z] is the sum over i+j=n of C(n,i) [(ad x)^i y, (ad x)^j z].

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on n using that ad x is a derivation and Pascal's rule.
sketch_steps: setup: D = ad x satisfies D[u,v] = [Du,v] + [u,Dv].
induction: Apply D to the formula for n.
derive: The coefficient of [D^p y, D^q z] is C(n,p-1) + C(n,p) = C(n+1,p).
conclude: This is the formula for n+1.

drafts.canonical_statement: If an element a of a ring A satisfies a^(n+1) = 0, then the map T(b) = ab - ba satisfies T^(2n+1) = 0. In particular ad a is nilpotent for a nilpotent element a.

drafts.proof_strategy: Write ad a as a difference of commuting left and right multiplications and expand.
sketch_steps: setup: T = l - r with l and r commuting and both killed by the power n+1.
derive: Expand T^(2n+1) by the binomial theorem.
derive: In each term one exponent is at least n+1.
conclude: All terms vanish.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a derivation D of a Lie algebra L and x in L, the commutator of D and ad x is ad(Dx). In particular the inner derivations form an ideal of the derivation algebra.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_derivation"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_bracket"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="inner_derivation"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="inner_derivation"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Evaluate the commutator on y and apply the derivation rule.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix y in L.
derive: D[x,y] - [x,Dy] = [Dx,y] by the derivation rule.
conclude: The commutator equals ad(Dx).

drafts.canonical_statement: If D is a nilpotent derivation of a Lie algebra L that is also a Lie algebra over the rationals, then the finite sum exp D = sum of D^k/k! preserves brackets, so exp D [x,y] = [exp D x, exp D y].

drafts.proof_strategy: Divide the Leibniz rule by n! and sum over n.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix N with D^N = 0.
derive: D^n[x,y]/n! is the sum over i+j=n of [D^i x/i!, D^j y/j!].
derive: All sums are finite because D is nilpotent.
conclude: Summing over n gives exp D [x,y] = [exp D x, exp D y].

drafts.canonical_statement: A simple Lie algebra L, meaning non-abelian with only the ideals 0 and L, over a commutative ring satisfies [L,L] = L.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="simple_lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_derived_series"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: The derived algebra is an ideal, and it cannot vanish.
sketch_steps: derive: [L,L] is an ideal, so it is 0 or L.
case_split: [L,L] = 0 would make L abelian.
conclude: Hence [L,L] = L.

drafts.canonical_statement: If submodules N_1 and N_2 of a module over a Lie algebra L are nilpotent L-modules, meaning that C^0 N = N and C^(k+1) N = [L, C^k N] reaches 0, then N_1 + N_2 is a nilpotent L-module.

drafts.proof_strategy: The lower central series of a submodule is additive in the submodule.
sketch_steps: induction: C^k(N_1+N_2) = C^k N_1 + C^k N_2.
derive: The series of N_1 and N_2 vanish for large k.
conclude: The series of N_1+N_2 vanishes at the larger index.

drafts.canonical_statement: Engel's theorem for modules, a generalization of the Lie algebra form. A finite-dimensional module M over a Lie algebra L over a field is nilpotent if and only if every element of L acts on M by a nilpotent endomorphism.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="field"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_module"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals1" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_dimensional"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nilpotent_lie_module"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nilpotent_op"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_action_op"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: One direction uses powers inside the lower central series, the other induction with a common null vector.
sketch_steps: derive: If C^k M = 0 then each X^k maps M into C^k M = 0.
setup: Conversely induct on the dimension of M.
apply_theorem: The common null vector form of Engel's theorem gives v.
derive: By induction C^k(M/Kv) = 0, so C^k M lies in Kv.
conclude: C^(k+1) M = 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: Engel's theorem, common null vector form. If every element of a Lie algebra L over a field acts nilpotently on a nonzero finite-dimensional module M, then there is a nonzero v in M with [x,v] = 0 for all x in L.

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on dimension of the image in End(M) using a maximal proper subalgebra, which is a codimension-one ideal.
sketch_steps: setup: Replace L by its image g in End(M) and induct on dim g.
construct: Take a proper subalgebra h of largest dimension.
apply_theorem: By induction on g/h there is z outside h with [h,z] inside h.
derive: Then g = h + Kz.
derive: W = {m : hm = 0} is nonzero and stable under z.
conclude: A null vector of z in W is killed by all of g.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a Lie subalgebra H of End(V), with the commutator bracket, for a finite-dimensional vector space V over a field consists of nilpotent endomorphisms, then H is a nilpotent Lie algebra.

drafts.proof_strategy: Nilpotent operators are ad-nilpotent, then apply Engel's theorem to the adjoint module.
sketch_steps: derive: T(g) = fg - gf is nilpotent on End(V) when f is nilpotent.
derive: ad of f on H is the restriction of T.
apply_theorem: Engel's theorem makes H nilpotent.

drafts.canonical_statement: For modules M, N over a Lie algebra L and a linear map f from M to N, with (x.f)(m) = [x,f(m)] - f([x,m]), one has x.f = 0 for all x if and only if f is a module homomorphism.

drafts.proof_strategy: Evaluate the action on m and compare.
sketch_steps: setup: Write (x.f)(m) = [x,f(m)] - f([x,m]).
derive: This vanishes exactly when f([x,m]) = [x,f(m)].
conclude: Quantifying over x and m gives the equivalence.

drafts.canonical_statement: For submodules of an L-module define N_0 = N, N_(k+1) = [L, N_k] and N^0 = N, N^(k+1) = {m : [L,m] inside N^k}. For submodules A and B, A_k is contained in B if and only if A is contained in B^k.

drafts.proof_strategy: The case k = 1 is a Galois connection; iterate it by induction.
sketch_steps: derive: [L,A] inside B is equivalent to A inside B^1.
induction: A_(k+1) inside B iff A_k inside B^1 iff A inside (B^1)^k.
conclude: (B^1)^k = B^(k+1).

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on dim L via a codimension-one ideal; the invariance lemma uses a trace computation in characteristic 0.
sketch_steps: setup: Choose an ideal A of codimension one containing [L,L], with L = A + Kz.
apply_theorem: By induction the weight space W of chi on A is nonzero.
derive: [a,[x,w]] = chi(a)[x,w] - chi([x,a])w reduces invariance to chi([x,a]) = 0.
construct: Build a chain U_i spanned by the X^i w, on which elements of A are triangular with diagonal chi.
derive: The trace of [x,a] on U is n chi([x,a]) and also 0.
derive: Characteristic 0 gives chi([x,a]) = 0, so W is stable under z.
conclude: An eigenvector of z in W is a common eigenvector.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Lie's theorem to the radical; irreducibility makes it act by scalars and faithfulness makes it central.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Lie's theorem gives a nonzero weight space W for rad L.
derive: The trace argument shows W is stable under L.
derive: Irreducibility gives W = M, so the radical acts by scalars.
derive: Faithfulness shows the radical is central.
conclude: The center is an abelian ideal, so rad L = Z(L), and the scalar criterion follows.

sketch_steps: derive: Symmetry is tr(XY) = tr(YX).
derive: Expand both sides of the invariance formula.
conclude: tr(YXZ) = tr(XZY) gives equality.

drafts.proof_strategy: Move the bracket with invariance and use that I is an ideal.
sketch_steps: derive: kappa([y,x],z) = -kappa(x,[y,z]) by invariance.
derive: [y,z] lies in I.
conclude: The value is 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: For an ideal I of a finite-dimensional Lie algebra L over a field, the Killing form of I is the restriction of the Killing form of L.

drafts.proof_strategy: The operator maps L into I, so its trace can be computed on I.
sketch_steps: setup: T = ad x ad y maps L into I.
derive: In a basis extending one of I, the remaining diagonal entries vanish.
conclude: tr_L(T) = tr_I(T restricted to I).

drafts.canonical_statement: An element x of an abelian ideal I of a finite-dimensional Lie algebra L over a field satisfies kappa(x,y) = 0 for every y in L.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="field"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals1" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_dimensional"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="abelian_lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="killing_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Show the operator ad x ad y squares to zero.
sketch_steps: derive: T = ad x ad y maps L into I.
derive: T kills I because [y,w] lies in I and I is abelian.
conclude: T^2 = 0, so its trace vanishes.

drafts.canonical_statement: The Killing form of a finite-dimensional nilpotent Lie algebra over a field is identically zero.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="field"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals1" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_dimensional"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nilpotent_lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="killing_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: The product ad x ad y shifts the lower central series and hence is nilpotent.
sketch_steps: derive: T maps C^i L into C^(i+2) L.
derive: T^k vanishes when C^k L = 0.
conclude: A nilpotent operator has trace 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: If the Killing form of a finite-dimensional Lie algebra L over a field is nondegenerate, then L is semisimple, meaning the direct sum of its non-abelian minimal ideals.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="field"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals1" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_dimensional"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="killing_nondegenerate"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="semisimple_lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Split off minimal ideals using orthogonal complements and identify all minimal ideals.
sketch_steps: derive: Abelian ideals vanish because they lie in the kernel of kappa.
derive: For an ideal I, the intersection with its orthogonal is abelian, so L = I + I^perp is direct.
induction: Restrictions stay nondegenerate, so L is a direct sum of minimal ideals S_i.
derive: Each S_i is non-abelian.
derive: Any minimal ideal A has [A,S_i] nonzero for some i, so A = S_i.
conclude: L is the direct sum of its non-abelian minimal ideals.

drafts.canonical_statement: Cartan's criterion for semisimplicity. A finite-dimensional Lie algebra L over a field of characteristic 0 has rad L = 0 if and only if its Killing form is nondegenerate.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use abelian ideals in the kernel in one direction and Cartan's solvability criterion on the kernel in the other.
sketch_steps: derive: If kappa is nondegenerate, abelian ideals vanish.
derive: Then solvable ideals vanish, since they contain abelian ideals.
setup: Conversely let S be the kernel of kappa, an ideal.
derive: The Killing form of S is the restriction of kappa, hence 0.
apply_theorem: Cartan's solvability criterion makes S solvable.
conclude: S lies in rad L = 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: Cartan's criterion for solvability. If a finite-dimensional Lie algebra L over a field of characteristic 0 satisfies kappa(x,y) = 0 for all x in L and y in [L,L], then L is solvable.

drafts.proof_strategy: Prove the trace criterion on End(V) with a rational functional on the eigenvalues of the semisimple part, apply it to ad L, then use Engel's theorem and the extension property of solvability.
sketch_steps: setup: Extend scalars to an algebraic closure; solvability descends.
derive: For g in End(V) with tr([g,g] g) = 0, the trace also vanishes against every z with [z,g] inside [g,g].
construct: For x in [g,g] with semisimple part s and eigenvalues a_i, and a rational functional phi on their rational span, let y act on the eigenvectors by phi(a_i).
derive: ad y is a polynomial without constant term in ad x, so tr(xy) = 0 gives the sum of a_i phi(a_i) = 0.
derive: Applying phi gives phi = 0, so s = 0 and x is nilpotent.
derive: With g = ad L, ad x is nilpotent for x in [L,L] because kappa vanishes on L times [L,L].
apply_theorem: Engel's theorem makes [L,L] nilpotent, hence solvable.
conclude: L/[L,L] is abelian, so L is solvable.

drafts.canonical_statement: If the Killing form of a finite-dimensional Lie algebra L over a field is nondegenerate, then L is the direct sum of any ideal I and its Killing orthogonal complement.

drafts.proof_strategy: The intersection is an abelian ideal, hence zero, and dimensions add up.
sketch_steps: derive: J = I intersect I^perp is an ideal.
derive: kappa([x,y],z) = kappa(x,[y,z]) = 0 shows J is abelian.
derive: Abelian ideals lie in the kernel of kappa, so J = 0.
conclude: Dimension count gives L = I + I^perp, direct.

drafts.proof_strategy: Inner derivations form an ideal with nondegenerate restricted Killing form; its orthogonal complement vanishes.
sketch_steps: setup: ad L is an ideal i of the derivation algebra d, isomorphic to L.
derive: The Killing form of d restricts nondegenerately to i.
derive: So d = i + i^perp is direct.
derive: For D in i^perp, ad(Dx) = [D, ad x] = 0, so Dx = 0.
conclude: i^perp = 0 and every derivation is inner.

drafts.canonical_statement: If the Killing form of a finite-dimensional Lie algebra L over a field is nondegenerate, then [L,L] = L.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show the orthogonal complement of [L,L] lies in the center, which vanishes.
sketch_steps: setup: L = D + D^perp with D = [L,L].
derive: kappa([x,u],v) = kappa(x,[u,v]) = 0 for x in D^perp.
derive: So D^perp lies in the center.
conclude: The center is zero, hence D = L.

sketch_steps: derive: [h,[x,m]] = [[h,x],m] + [x,[h,m]].
conclude: Substituting the eigenvalue relations gives (a+b)[x,m].

drafts.canonical_statement: In the matrix ring over a nonzero commutative ring, for indices i different from j, the elements h = E_ii - E_jj, e = E_ij, f = E_ji satisfy h nonzero, [e,f] = h, [h,e] = 2e and [h,f] = -2f. For two indices this is the standard sl_2 triple.

sketch_steps: derive: The (i,i) entry of h is 1, so h is nonzero.
derive: [e,f] = E_ii - E_jj.
derive: he = e, eh = -e, hf = -f and fh = f.
conclude: The sl_2 relations hold.

derive: 0 = e f^(n+1) m = (n+1)(mu - n) f^n m.
conclude: Hence mu = n.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the e-formula downward for nonvanishing and primitivity of the next vector for vanishing.
sketch_steps: contradiction: A minimal i at most n with f^i m = 0 forces f^(i-1) m = 0.
derive: If v = f^(n+1) m is nonzero, then ev = 0 and hv = (-n-2) v.
contradiction: Primitive eigenvalues are natural numbers, but -n-2 is negative.
conclude: The string has nonzero terms exactly up to n.

sketch_steps: setup: Take an eigenvector m_0 of h.
derive: e^k m_0 has eigenvalue mu_0 + 2k, and these are distinct.
derive: Finite dimension forces e^(k+1) m_0 = 0 with e^k m_0 nonzero.
conclude: v = e^k m_0 is primitive.

sketch_steps: setup: Fix h and set A = ad h - alpha(h), B = h - chi(h).

derive: Iterating gives a binomial sum over [A^i x, B^j m].
conclude: For large N all terms vanish.

sketch_steps: setup: L is the direct sum of finitely many weight spaces.
derive: (ad x)^k maps L_chi into L_(k alpha + chi).
derive: In characteristic 0 these weights are distinct, so the target vanishes for large k.
conclude: ad x is nilpotent.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take a shortest relation and kill one term with a power of x - chi_2(x).
sketch_steps: setup: Each M_chi is a submodule since L is nilpotent.
contradiction: Take a shortest nontrivial relation among distinct weights.
derive: Choose x separating chi_1 and chi_2, and put T = x - chi_2(x).
derive: T^N kills m_2 but not m_1.
conclude: This gives a shorter relation.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the Fitting lemma for one element, show both parts are submodules, and induct on dimension.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The Fitting lemma gives M = M_0(x) + M_1(x) for each x.
derive: Both summands are submodules because ad x is nilpotent.
case_split: If all M_1(x) vanish then M = M_0 and M^+ = 0.
induction: Otherwise apply the claim to N = M_0(x), with N_0 = M_0.
derive: M^+ = N^+ + M_1(x).
conclude: M = M_0 + N^+ + M_1(x) = M_0 + M^+ is direct.

construct: x*m = [x,m] - chi(x) m is a module structure on M_chi.
derive: Each x acts nilpotently for this structure.
conclude: A common null vector is a common eigenvector.

sketch_steps: setup: W = M_chi is a nonzero submodule of dimension d.
derive: x - chi(x) is nilpotent on W, so tr_W(x) = d chi(x).
derive: In characteristic 0, chi = tr_W / d.
conclude: The trace is linear and vanishes on commutators.

drafts.proof_strategy: Decompose M into weight spaces and compute the trace on each using Engel's theorem.
sketch_steps: setup: M is the direct sum of its generalized weight spaces.
derive: On W = M_chi, x = chi(x) + N_x with N_x a nilpotent module action.
apply_theorem: Engel's theorem makes W nilpotent for this action, so N_x N_y is nilpotent.
derive: tr_W(xy) = (dim W) chi(x) chi(y).
conclude: Sum over the weights.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a Cartan subalgebra H, meaning nilpotent and self-normalizing, of a finite-dimensional Lie algebra L over a field, the zero root space L_0(H) equals H.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="field"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals1" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_dimensional"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="cartan_subalgebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="root_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Engel's theorem to L_0(H)/H and use self-normalization.
sketch_steps: derive: H lies in L_0(H) because H is nilpotent.
contradiction: If they differ, H acts nilpotently on the nonzero quotient.
apply_theorem: Engel gives z outside H with [H,z] inside H.
conclude: z normalizes H, contradicting self-normalization.

drafts.canonical_statement: A nilpotent subalgebra H of a finite-dimensional Lie algebra L over a field is a Cartan subalgebra if and only if L_0(H) = H.

drafts.proof_strategy: Engel's theorem for one direction, and the normalizer lies in L_0(H) for the other.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: If H is Cartan, Engel's theorem on L_0(H)/H gives L_0(H) = H.
setup: Conversely let z normalize H.
derive: (ad h)^(k+1) z = (ad h)^k [h,z] = 0 for large k.
conclude: z lies in L_0(H) = H, so H is self-normalizing.

drafts.canonical_statement: For x in a Lie algebra L over a commutative ring, the Engel subalgebra E(x), the set of y with (ad x)^n y = 0 for some n, is its own normalizer.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_normalizer"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="engel_subalgebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="engel_subalgebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: x lies in E(x), so normalizing elements are killed by a power of ad x.
sketch_steps: derive: The Leibniz rule makes E(x) a subalgebra.
derive: x lies in E(x), so [x,y] lies in E(x) for y in the normalizer.
conclude: (ad x)^(n+1) y = 0, so y lies in E(x).

drafts.canonical_statement: A finite-dimensional Lie algebra L over an infinite field has an element x such that the Engel subalgebra E(x) is a Cartan subalgebra.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take E(x) of minimal dimension; a polynomial argument shows every element of E acts nilpotently on E.
sketch_steps: setup: Choose x with E = E(x) of minimal dimension n.
construct: For y in E put z_t = x + ty and let d(t) be the determinant on L/E.
derive: d(0) is nonzero, so d(t) is nonzero for infinitely many t.
derive: For those t, E(z_t) = E, so (ad z_t on E)^n = 0.
derive: As a polynomial identity in t, the coefficient of t^n gives (ad y on E)^n = 0.
apply_theorem: Engel's theorem makes E nilpotent, and E is self-normalizing.

drafts.proof_strategy: The operator ad x ad y shifts weights by alpha + beta, so it is nilpotent.
sketch_steps: setup: L is the direct sum of finitely many weight spaces.
derive: T = ad x ad y maps L_chi into L_(chi + alpha + beta).
derive: Characteristic 0 makes the shifted weights distinct, so T is nilpotent.
conclude: The trace of T vanishes.

drafts.canonical_statement: If the Killing form of a finite-dimensional Lie algebra L over a field of characteristic 0 is nondegenerate and H is a Cartan subalgebra whose ad action has generalized eigenspaces spanning L, then the restriction of the Killing form to H is nondegenerate.

drafts.proof_strategy: Elements of H are orthogonal to the nonzero root spaces automatically.
sketch_steps: setup: L is H plus the nonzero root spaces.
derive: kappa(x, L_alpha) = 0 for x in H and alpha nonzero.
derive: If also kappa(x,H) = 0, then kappa(x,L) = 0.
conclude: Nondegeneracy of kappa gives x = 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: If the Killing form of a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over a field of characteristic 0 is nondegenerate, then a Cartan subalgebra H whose ad action has generalized eigenspaces spanning L is abelian.

drafts.proof_strategy: Weights vanish on [H,H], so kappa pairs [H,H] with H trivially, and kappa is nondegenerate on H.
sketch_steps: setup: L decomposes into weight spaces for H.
derive: Each weight is linear and vanishes on [H,H].
derive: kappa(u,v) is a sum of (dim L_chi) chi(u) chi(v), so it is 0 for u in [H,H].
conclude: Nondegeneracy on H gives [H,H] = 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: If the Killing form of a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over a field of characteristic 0 is nondegenerate and H is a Cartan subalgebra with generalized eigenspaces of ad h spanning L, then [h,x] = alpha(h) x for x in the root space L_alpha and h in H.

drafts.proof_strategy: The nilpotent part of ad h is an inner derivation by an element of H that is Killing-orthogonal to H, hence zero.
sketch_steps: setup: Reduce to diagonalizability of D = ad h.
construct: Let s act by lambda on each generalized eigenspace L^lambda, and put n = D - s; both are polynomials in D without constant term.
derive: [L^lambda, L^mu] lies in L^(lambda+mu), so s and n are derivations.
apply_theorem: Derivations are inner, so n = ad h_n.
derive: n kills H, so h_n normalizes H and lies in H.
derive: ad h_n ad v is nilpotent for v in H, so kappa(h_n,H) = 0.
conclude: h_n = 0, so D = s is diagonalizable and [h,x] = alpha(h) x.

drafts.canonical_statement: Root space decomposition. If the Killing form of a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over a field of characteristic 0 is nondegenerate and H is a Cartan subalgebra with generalized eigenspaces of ad h spanning L, then L is the sum of H and the root spaces of the nonzero roots.

drafts.proof_strategy: Refine generalized eigenspaces to weight spaces and identify L_0 with H.
sketch_steps: derive: Generalized eigenspaces of ad h are stable under the nilpotent subalgebra H.
derive: Refining along elements of H until each has one eigenvalue on each piece gives L as the sum of the L_chi.
conclude: L_0 = H because H is Cartan.

sketch_steps: setup: Take a nonzero x in L_alpha.
contradiction: Suppose L_(-alpha) = 0.
derive: x is orthogonal to every L_beta since alpha + beta is nonzero.
conclude: Nondegeneracy gives x = 0, a contradiction.

sketch_steps: setup: [e,f] lies in L_0 = H.
derive: kappa([e,f],h) = kappa(e,[f,h]) = alpha(h) kappa(e,f).
derive: This equals kappa(kappa(e,f) t_alpha, h).
conclude: Nondegeneracy on H gives the formula.

drafts.proof_strategy: If alpha(t) = 0, a trace on an alpha-string shows every root vanishes at t, forcing t = 0.
sketch_steps: setup: Reduce to alpha(t) nonzero.
contradiction: Suppose alpha(t) = 0 and choose e, f with [e,f] = t.
derive: On the string M through beta, the trace of ad t is 0 and also (dim M) beta(t).
derive: So beta(t) = 0 for every root beta.
derive: kappa(t,h) is a sum containing beta(t), so it vanishes.
conclude: t = 0, contradicting alpha nonzero.

sketch_steps: setup: Take an sl_2 triple attached to alpha.
contradiction: If dim L_alpha is at least 2, choose v nonzero with kappa(v,f) = 0.
derive: Then [f,v] = 0 and [h,v] = 2v.
derive: v is primitive of eigenvalue -2 for the triple (-h,f,e).
conclude: Eigenvalues must be natural numbers, so the dimension is 1.

drafts.proof_strategy: Normalize a pair e, f with nonzero Killing pairing so that [e,f] is the coroot.
sketch_steps: setup: Take e nonzero in L_alpha.
derive: Orthogonality and nondegeneracy give f' in L_(-alpha) with kappa(e,f') nonzero.
construct: Scale so that kappa(e,f) = 2 / alpha(t_alpha).
derive: Then [e,f] = coroot of alpha.
conclude: alpha(h) = 2 gives the remaining relations.

drafts.proof_strategy: Exclude integer multiples at least 2 by an sl_2 string, then use integrality of the pairings.
sketch_steps: derive: For k at least 2 maximal with k gamma a root, x in L_(k gamma) is primitive of eigenvalue 2k.
derive: (ad f)^(k-1) x is a nonzero element of the line L_gamma, so e kills it.
contradiction: The e-formula gives a nonzero value.
apply_theorem: Root strings make 2c and 2/c integers.
derive: So c is one of plus or minus 1/2, 1, 2.
conclude: Multiples by 2 are excluded, so c is 1 or -1.

drafts.canonical_statement: Root string theorem. For a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over a field of characteristic 0 with nondegenerate Killing form, a Cartan subalgebra with generalized eigenspaces spanning L, a nonzero root alpha and a weight beta, there are natural numbers p and q such that L_(beta + n alpha) is nonzero exactly for -q at most n at most p, and beta(coroot of alpha) = q - p.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use primitive vectors at the ends of gaps and at the ends of the string for the triple attached to alpha.
sketch_steps: setup: S, the set of n with L_(beta + n alpha) nonzero, is finite and contains 0.
contradiction: A gap gives primitive vectors with incompatible eigenvalues.
derive: So S is an interval from -q to p.
derive: The top vector has eigenvalue mu = beta(h) + 2p, and its f-string shows beta(h) is at most q - p.
derive: The bottom vector gives beta(h) at least q - p.
conclude: beta(coroot) = q - p.

sketch_steps: case_split: If alpha = 0 the expression is beta.
apply_theorem: Otherwise the root string theorem gives p, q with beta(coroot) = q - p.
derive: n = p - q lies between -q and p.
conclude: beta - beta(coroot) alpha is a weight.

drafts.proof_strategy: Assemble the pairing axiom, reflection stability, spanning, integrality and reducedness.
sketch_steps: setup: Phi is the finite set of nonzero roots.
derive: alpha(coroot) = 2, and reflections preserve Phi.
derive: The Killing form identifies the coroot reflections with the root reflections.
derive: Roots separate H, so roots span the dual of H and coroots span H.
conclude: The root string theorem gives integrality, and proportional roots are plus or minus one another.

sketch_steps: construct: B(x,y) is the sum over k of <x,coroot_k><y,coroot_k>.
derive: B is reflection invariant, so 2B(x,alpha_j) = <x,coroot_j> B(alpha_j,alpha_j).
derive: B_ij is an inner product of integer vectors, with B_ii positive.
derive: a_ij a_ji B_ii B_jj = 4 B_ij^2.
conclude: Cauchy-Schwarz bounds the integer product by 4.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a crystallographic root pairing with finitely many roots over a field of characteristic 0, if i and j differ and <alpha_i, coroot_j> is positive, then alpha_i - alpha_j is a root; if alpha_i is not -alpha_j and the pairing is negative, then alpha_i + alpha_j is a root.

sketch_steps: derive: Roots are closed under negation.
derive: For positive a, the product ab is at most 4, and a = b = 2 forces i = j.
derive: So a = 1 or b = 1, and a reflection gives alpha_i - alpha_j up to sign.
conclude: Applying this to -alpha_j gives the sum statement.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a crystallographic root pairing with finitely many roots over a field of characteristic 0, alpha_i and alpha_j are linearly independent if and only if the product of their two pairings differs from 4.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compute the pairings for proportional roots; for the converse, s_i s_j acts unipotently and produces infinitely many roots.
sketch_steps: derive: If alpha_i = c alpha_j then a = 2c and b = 2/c, so ab = 4.
contradiction: Suppose ab = 4 with independent roots, and let u = s_i s_j.
derive: (u-1) alpha_i = w and (u-1) alpha_j = (b/2) w with w = 2 alpha_i - a alpha_j.
derive: (u-1) w = 0, so u^n alpha_i = alpha_i + n w.
conclude: These are infinitely many distinct roots, a contradiction.

conclude: Independence of simple roots gives a contradiction.

drafts.proof_strategy: Simple roots and coroots are bases of a perfect pairing, so the integer matrix has nonzero determinant.
sketch_steps: derive: Simple roots form a basis of M and simple coroots a basis of N.
derive: The matrix of a perfect pairing in these bases is invertible.
derive: Its integer determinant is nonzero by characteristic 0.
conclude: The Cartan matrix is nondegenerate.

drafts.canonical_statement: For simple roots alpha_i and alpha_j of a base of a root pairing over a field of characteristic 0, the difference alpha_i - alpha_j is not a root.

drafts.proof_strategy: Root expansions in a base have coefficients of one sign.
sketch_steps: case_split: For i = j the difference is 0, which is not a root.
contradiction: For i and j different, suppose the difference is a root.
derive: Its coefficients in the base must all have one sign.
conclude: The coefficients 1 and -1 give a contradiction.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use tr(XY) = tr(YX).
sketch_steps: setup: sl(n,R) consists of the matrices with trace 0.
derive: tr(XY) = tr(YX) by swapping the sum.
conclude: XY - YX lies in sl(n,R).

sketch_steps: setup: sl(n,K) is the kernel of the trace.
derive: The trace is surjective since tr(c E_ii) = c.

sketch_steps: derive: tr A = tr A^T = -tr A.

conclude: The count of pairs i < j is n(n-1)/2.

sketch_steps: setup: Write A in blocks a, b, c, d.
derive: A^T J has blocks c^T, -a^T, d^T, -b^T.
derive: -JA has blocks c, d, -a, -b.

sketch_steps: setup: Write A in blocks a, b, c, d.
derive: Comparing upper right blocks gives d = -a^T.
conclude: tr A = tr a - tr a^T = 0.

sketch_steps: derive: hat(u) x = u cross x.
derive: The commutator applied to x is w(v.x) - v(w.x).
derive: (v cross w) cross x has the same expansion.
conclude: Evaluate on the standard basis.

sketch_steps: setup: U(L) is T(L) modulo x tensor y - y tensor x - [x,y].
construct: f extends to an algebra map F on T(L).
derive: F kills the relations since f preserves brackets.
derive: F induces g with g(iota x) = f(x).
conclude: iota(L) generates U(L), so g is unique.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a vector field V on a Lie group G over a nontrivially normed field, of class C^3 over the reals or complex numbers and analytic otherwise, is invariant under pullback by every left translation, then V equals the left-invariant field X_{V(1)}, where X_v(g) = d(L_g)_1 v.

drafts.proof_strategy: Evaluate the invariance at the identity.
sketch_steps: setup: The pullback is (d(L_g)_x)^(-1) V(gx).
derive: At x = 1 invariance gives V(g) = d(L_g)_1 V(1).
conclude: So V = X_{V(1)}.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a Lie group G modelled on a complete normed space, of class C^3 over the reals or complex numbers and analytic otherwise, with bracket [v,w] = [X_v,X_w](1) on the tangent space at 1, one has X_{[v,w]} = [X_v,X_w]; thus the bracket of left-invariant fields is left-invariant.

sketch_steps: derive: X_v is invariant under left translation by the chain rule.
derive: Pullback by a diffeomorphism commutes with the bracket.
derive: So [X_v,X_w] is invariant.
conclude: It equals X with value [v,w] at 1.

apply_theorem: The Jacobi identity holds for C^2 vector fields.

drafts.proof_strategy: Pair the four numbers by parity and replace each pair by half its sum and half its difference.
sketch_steps: derive: Squares have the parity of their bases, so a+b+c+d is even.
case_split: Rearrange so that a and b have equal parity and c and d have equal parity.
construct: Take (a-b)/2, (a+b)/2, (c-d)/2, (c+d)/2.
conclude: Their squares add up to half of 2m, which is m.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the pigeonhole principle to the residues of a^2 and -1-b^2 with a, b at most (p-1)/2.
sketch_steps: case_split: For p = 2 take a = 1, b = 0, k = 1.
derive: For odd p the squares a^2 with a ≤ (p-1)/2 are distinct modulo p.
derive: The same holds for -1-b^2, and together they form p+1 values, so two coincide.
conclude: Then p divides a^2+b^2+1, and the size bound gives k < p.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take the least positive multiple of p that is a sum of four squares and descend with Euler's identity.
sketch_steps: setup: Some multiple kp with 0 < k < p is a sum of four squares; take the least such m.
case_split: If m is even, halving contradicts minimality.
construct: If m is odd and m > 1, take absolutely least residues y_i of x_i modulo m.
derive: Then the sum of y_i^2 equals rm with 0 < r < m.
apply_theorem: Euler's identity gives (mp)(rm) as a sum of four squares of multiples of m.
contradiction: Dividing by m^2 shows rp is a sum of four squares, contradicting minimality.

drafts.proof_strategy: Reduce to primes by induction on the factorization, using Euler's identity for products.
sketch_steps: case_split: The cases n = 0 and n = 1 are immediate.
setup: For n ≥ 2 write n = pm with p prime.
apply_theorem: The prime case and the induction hypothesis give four-square expressions of p and m.
conclude: Euler's identity combines them, and absolute values give natural numbers.

drafts.proof_strategy: Check residues modulo 8 for k = 0 and descend by 2 using residues modulo 4.
sketch_steps: derive: Squares are 0, 1 or 4 modulo 8, so three of them never add to 7 modulo 8.
induction: For k ≥ 1 assume a solution exists.
derive: Squares are 0 or 1 modulo 4, so a, b, c are all even.
contradiction: Dividing by 4 gives a solution for k - 1.

drafts.proof_strategy: Factor z^2-x^2 for odd x and use that coprime factors of a square are squares.
sketch_steps: derive: Modulo 4 exactly one of x and y is odd; take x odd and y even.
case_split: The case y = 0 gives x = ±1 directly.
derive: For y ≠ 0, (|z|+x)/2 and (|z|-x)/2 are coprime positive integers with product (y/2)^2.
construct: Hence they are m^2 and n^2, which gives the parametrization after fixing the sign of n.
derive: Conversely the identity gives the equation, and a common prime divisor would divide both m and n.
conclude: The two conditions are equivalent.

drafts.canonical_statement: Integers x, y, z satisfy x^2+y^2 = z^2 if and only if there are integers k, m, n such that (x,y) is (k(m^2-n^2), 2kmn) or (2kmn, k(m^2-n^2)) and z = ±k(m^2+n^2).

drafts.proof_strategy: Divide by gcd(x,y) and apply the classification of primitive triples.
sketch_steps: derive: Multiplying the identity by k^2 gives the if direction.
case_split: If x = y = 0, take k = 0.
derive: Otherwise g = gcd(x,y) divides z and the quotient triple is primitive.
apply_theorem: The primitive classification gives m and n.
conclude: Multiplying by g gives the required form with k = g.

drafts.canonical_statement: If integers x, y, z satisfy x^2+y^2 = z^2 and gcd(x,y) = 1, then one of x, y is even and the other is odd.

drafts.proof_strategy: Exclude both even by coprimality and both odd by residues modulo 4.
sketch_steps: case_split: Both even contradicts gcd(x,y) = 1.
contradiction: Both odd gives z^2 ≡ 2 modulo 4, which is impossible.
conclude: Hence the parities differ.

drafts.canonical_statement: If integers x, y, z satisfy x^2+y^2 = z^2 and gcd(x,y) = 1, then gcd(x,z) = gcd(y,z) = 1.

drafts.proof_strategy: A common prime divisor of a leg and the hypotenuse divides the other leg.
sketch_steps: setup: Let a prime q divide y and z.
derive: Then q divides x^2 = z^2 - y^2, hence x.
contradiction: This contradicts gcd(x,y) = 1.
conclude: Swapping x and y gives gcd(x,z) = 1.

drafts.canonical_statement: Let K be a field with 1+t^2 ≠ 0 for all t in K. For x, y in K, the conditions x^2+y^2 = 1 and y ≠ -1 hold if and only if x = 2t/(1+t^2) and y = (1-t^2)/(1+t^2) for some t in K.

sketch_steps: derive: Evaluating the hypothesis at t = 1 shows that 2 is nonzero.
construct: For a point on the circle with y ≠ -1, set t = x/(1+y).
derive: Then 1+t^2 = 2/(1+y), which gives both formulas.
derive: Conversely the formulas satisfy the equation, and y = -1 would force 2 = 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Treat exponents prime to p and the exponent p separately, then combine by writing n = p^a m.
sketch_steps: case_split: For n = 0 both sides are infinite.
derive: If p does not divide m, the cofactor of x-y is congruent to m x^(m-1) modulo p, so it is prime to p.
derive: For exponent p, the cofactor is p y^(p-1) modulo p^2 because p is odd, so it has valuation 1.
induction: Iterating gives the formula for exponents p^a.
conclude: Writing n = p^a m gives the general formula.

drafts.proof_strategy: Replace y by -y in the difference form, using that n is odd.
sketch_steps: derive: For odd n, x^n+y^n = x^n-(-y)^n and x+y = x-(-y).
apply_theorem: The difference form applies to x and -y.
conclude: This is the claimed formula.

sketch_steps: case_split: For n = 0 both sides are infinite.
derive: For odd m the cofactor of x-y is a sum of an odd number of odd terms, so it is odd.
derive: Since 4 | x-y and y is odd, x+y ≡ 2 modulo 4, so squaring adds 1 to the valuation.
conclude: Write n = 2^a m and combine the two facts.

sketch_steps: case_split: For n = 0 both sides are infinite.
derive: Odd squares are congruent modulo 8, so 4 divides x^2-y^2.
apply_theorem: The formula for 4 | u-w gives v_2(x^n-y^n) = v_2(x^2-y^2)+v_2(n/2).
conclude: Factor x^2-y^2 and use v_2(n) = v_2(n/2)+1.

sketch_steps: derive: x^n-y^n = (x-y)S with S the geometric sum.
derive: Modulo p, S is congruent to n x^(n-1).
derive: Since p is prime and divides neither n nor x, p does not divide S.
conclude: Multiplying by a factor prime to p does not change the multiplicity.

conclude: Congruent elements are divisible by p simultaneously.

sketch_steps: setup: Let d be the order of a modulo n.
derive: Division with remainder gives a^k ≡ 1 if and only if d | k.
derive: For i ≤ j, cancelling a^i turns a^i ≡ a^j into a^(j-i) ≡ 1.
conclude: This is equivalent to i ≡ j modulo d.

drafts.proof_strategy: The order divides n; if it were smaller, some n/q would be a multiple of it.
sketch_steps: derive: x^n = 1 shows that the order d is positive and divides n.
setup: Suppose d ≠ n and take a prime divisor q of n/d.
derive: Then d divides n/q, so x^(n/q) = 1.
contradiction: This contradicts the hypothesis.

drafts.canonical_statement: For primes l, q and an integer a, if q | a^l-1 and q does not divide a-1, then q ≡ 1 modulo l.

drafts.proof_strategy: The order of a modulo q divides the prime l and is not 1, so it equals l and divides q-1.
sketch_steps: derive: q does not divide a, so a has an order d modulo q.
derive: d divides the prime l, and d ≠ 1 because q does not divide a-1.
apply_theorem: Fermat's little theorem gives d | q-1.
conclude: Hence l | q-1.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime p and a divisor d of p-1, the number of reduced residues modulo p of order exactly d is φ(d). In particular there are φ(p-1) primitive roots modulo p.

drafts.proof_strategy: Write residues as powers of a primitive root and count exponents with the required gcd.
sketch_steps: setup: Every reduced residue is g^k for a unique k with 0 ≤ k < p-1.
derive: The order of g^k is (p-1)/gcd(k,p-1).
derive: The order is d exactly when k = mj with m = (p-1)/d, 0 ≤ j < d and gcd(j,d) = 1.
conclude: There are φ(d) such j.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime p and a natural number d, the number of reduced residues u modulo p with u^d = 1 equals gcd(p-1, d).
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="P"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="units_power_root_count"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="gcd"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="minus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use a primitive root to turn the equation into a linear divisibility condition on the exponent.
sketch_steps: setup: Write each reduced residue as g^k with g a primitive root.
derive: (g^k)^d = 1 is equivalent to (p-1) | kd.
derive: Dividing by e = gcd(p-1,d), this becomes (p-1)/e | k.
conclude: There are exactly e such k in the range 0 ≤ k < p-1.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime p and a natural number i, the sum of x^i over all reduced residues x modulo p is -1 if (p-1) | i and 0 otherwise, as an element of Z/pZ.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="P"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dvd"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="minus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="units_power_sum"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="unary_minus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="not"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dvd"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="minus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="units_power_sum"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Parametrize the residues by a primitive root and evaluate a geometric sum.
sketch_steps: setup: Write the residues as powers of a primitive root g.
case_split: If (p-1) | i, every term is 1, so the sum is p-1 = -1.
derive: Otherwise g^i ≠ 1, and the geometric sum formula applies.
conclude: The numerator vanishes by Fermat's little theorem.

drafts.canonical_statement: For an odd prime p and a natural number n, the group (Z/p^nZ)^× is cyclic, so primitive roots modulo p^n exist.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="P"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="cyclic_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="zmod_units"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Lift a primitive root modulo p so that h^(p-1) ≢ 1 modulo p^2, then compute its order with the lifting-the-exponent lemma.
sketch_steps: setup: Start from a primitive root g modulo p.
construct: One of g and g+p satisfies h^(p-1) ≢ 1 modulo p^2.
apply_theorem: Lifting the exponent gives v_p(h^((p-1)p^k)-1) = 1+k.
derive: The order d of h modulo p^n is a multiple of p-1 and divides p^(n-1)(p-1).
conclude: The valuation forces d = p^(n-1)(p-1), so h generates the group.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a natural number n, the group (Z/2^nZ)^× is cyclic if and only if n ≤ 2.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="cyclic_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="zmod_units"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="leq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: For n ≥ 3 every odd a satisfies a^(2^(n-2)) ≡ 1 modulo 2^n, which is smaller than the group order.
sketch_steps: case_split: For n ≤ 2 the group has order at most 2.
induction: For odd a and k ≥ 1, a^(2^k) ≡ 1 modulo 2^(k+2).
derive: For n ≥ 3 all element orders are at most 2^(n-2).
conclude: The group has order 2^(n-1), so no element generates it.

drafts.canonical_statement: Gauss's theorem on primitive roots. For a positive integer n, the group (Z/nZ)^× is cyclic if and only if n is 1, 2, 4, or n = p^m or n = 2p^m with p an odd prime and m ≥ 1. The results for odd prime powers and for powers of 2 may be taken as known.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the Chinese remainder theorem to reduce to prime powers; two factors of even order prevent cyclicity.
sketch_steps: case_split: For n = 1, 2, 4 the group has order at most 2.
apply_theorem: The case p^m is known, and CRT reduces 2p^m to it.
case_split: If n is not of the listed form, it is either 2^k with k ≥ 3 or a product ab with coprime a, b ≥ 3.
derive: For coprime a, b ≥ 3, both φ(a) and φ(b) are even.
conclude: Every element then has order at most φ(a)φ(b)/2, so the group is not cyclic.

drafts.canonical_statement: For an odd prime p, an integer a not divisible by p and a natural number n, the multiplicative order of 1+pa modulo p^(n+1) is p^n.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="P"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="Z"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="not"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dvd"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="multiplicative_order"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the lifting-the-exponent lemma to compute v_p(x^(p^k)-1) exactly.
sketch_steps: setup: Put x = 1+pa, so v_p(x-1) = 1.
apply_theorem: Lifting the exponent gives v_p(x^(p^k)-1) = 1+k.
derive: Thus the order divides p^n.
conclude: Smaller powers of p fail, so the order equals p^n.

drafts.canonical_statement: For an odd integer a and a natural number n, the multiplicative order of 1+4a modulo 2^(n+2) is 2^n. In particular 5 has order 2^n modulo 2^(n+2).
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="Z"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="not"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dvd"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="multiplicative_order"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>4</n1:OMI><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the 2-adic lifting formula for 4 | x-1.
sketch_steps: setup: Put x = 1+4a, so v_2(x-1) = 2.
apply_theorem: The 2-adic formula gives v_2(x^(2^k)-1) = 2+k.
derive: Thus the order divides 2^n.
conclude: Smaller powers of 2 fail, so the order equals 2^n.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a positive integer n, the Carmichael function λ(n), the least positive integer m with a^m = 1 for all a in (Z/nZ)^×, divides φ(n).
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="gt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dvd"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="carmichael_lambda"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="euler_phi"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Divide φ(n) by λ(n) and use minimality on the remainder.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Lagrange gives a^φ(n) = 1 for all a in the unit group.
derive: Dividing φ(n) by λ(n) leaves a remainder r with a^r = 1 for all a.
conclude: Minimality forces r = 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: For coprime positive integers a and b, the Carmichael function satisfies λ(ab) = lcm(λ(a), λ(b)).

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the CRT decomposition of the unit group and the characterization of exponents by divisibility.
sketch_steps: derive: All units have m-th power 1 if and only if λ(n) | m.
apply_theorem: CRT decomposes the unit group modulo ab as a product.
derive: Exponent m kills the product exactly when both λ(a) and λ(b) divide m.
conclude: The least such m is the lcm.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a natural number n ≥ 3, the Carmichael function satisfies λ(2^n) = 2^(n-2).

drafts.proof_strategy: Bound the exponent above by squaring induction and below by the order of 5.
sketch_steps: induction: Odd a satisfies a^(2^k) ≡ 1 modulo 2^(k+2) for k ≥ 1.
derive: Taking k = n-2 gives λ(2^n) ≤ 2^(n-2).
apply_theorem: The element 5 has order 2^(n-2) modulo 2^n.
conclude: Hence λ(2^n) = 2^(n-2).

sketch_steps: setup: Write k = φ(n)q+r.
apply_theorem: Euler's theorem gives x^φ(n) ≡ 1 modulo n.
conclude: Hence x^k ≡ x^r modulo n.

sketch_steps: derive: A solution makes gcd(m,n) divide both x-a and x-b, hence a-b.
construct: Write a-b = gc and g = mu+nv.
conclude: Then x = a-muc = b+nvc solves both congruences.

drafts.proof_strategy: Translate congruences into divisibility of a-b and use that common multiples are multiples of the lcm.
sketch_steps: derive: The congruence modulo k means k | a-b.
derive: Since m and n divide L, a congruence modulo L implies both congruences.
conclude: Conversely a-b is a common multiple of m and n, hence a multiple of L.

derive: Its kernel is {1,-1}, which has two elements since p is odd.

sketch_steps: setup: Write ax ≡ ε_x r_x modulo p with 1 ≤ r_x ≤ h and ε_x = ±1.
derive: The map x to r_x is a permutation of {1,...,h}.
derive: Multiplying gives a^h h! ≡ (-1)^μ h! modulo p.
apply_theorem: Euler's criterion identifies a^h with the Legendre symbol.
conclude: Both sides are ±1 and p > 2, so they are equal.

drafts.proof_strategy: Translate the sign in quadratic reciprocity into statements about squares.
sketch_steps: setup: For distinct odd primes the symbols are ±1 and 1 means a square.
apply_theorem: Quadratic reciprocity gives the product of the symbols.
conclude: The parity of the exponent decides whether the symbols agree or differ.

drafts.canonical_statement: For an odd prime p, the number -2 is a square modulo p if and only if p ≡ 1 or 3 modulo 8.

drafts.proof_strategy: Multiply the two supplementary laws and check residues modulo 8.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The supplementary laws give (-1/p) and (2/p).
derive: Their product is computed for each odd residue modulo 8.
conclude: The symbol is 1 exactly for p ≡ 1, 3 modulo 8.

drafts.canonical_statement: Dirichlet's approximation theorem. For a real number ξ and a positive integer n there are integers j, k with 0 < k ≤ n and |kξ-j| ≤ 1/(n+1).

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the pigeonhole principle to the fractional parts of kξ together with 0 and 1.
sketch_steps: setup: Consider the n+2 numbers 0, {ξ}, ..., {nξ}, 1 in [0,1].
derive: Splitting [0,1] into n+1 closed intervals of length 1/(n+1), two of them lie in one interval.
case_split: A pair {aξ}, {bξ} gives k = b-a and j the difference of floors.
case_split: A pair {bξ}, 1 gives k = b and j = ⌊bξ⌋+1.
conclude: In each case 0 < k ≤ n and |kξ-j| ≤ 1/(n+1).

drafts.canonical_statement: For a real number ξ and a positive integer n, there is a rational number q in lowest terms with denominator d ≤ n and |ξ-q| ≤ 1/((n+1)d).
