drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the second and fourth moments of a centered normal variable to the increment.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The increment has the law N(0,|s-t|).
apply_theorem: A centered normal with variance v has second moment v and fourth moment 3v².
conclude: Substituting v = |s-t| gives both formulas.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a real Gaussian process X on [0,∞) has E[X_t] = 0 for all t and Cov(X_s, X_t) = s for s ≤ t, then X is a pre-Brownian motion.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="gaussian_process"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="expectation"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="leq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="covariance"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="pre_brownian_motion"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: A Gaussian law is determined by its mean and covariance.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix finitely many times; the vector is Gaussian by assumption.
derive: Its mean is 0 and its covariance entries are min(t_i, t_j).
apply_theorem: The characteristic function, hence the law, is determined by mean and covariance.

drafts.canonical_statement: If B is a Brownian motion, that is a pre-Brownian motion with almost surely continuous paths, and c > 0, then -B and (c^{-1/2} B_{ct})_{t≥0} are also Brownian motions.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="brownian_motion"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="gt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="brownian_motion"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="unary_minus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="brownian_motion"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="scaled_process"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Check the Gaussian finite-dimensional laws through mean and covariance, and path continuity directly.
sketch_steps: derive: The scaled and reflected processes have Gaussian finite-dimensional laws with mean 0.
derive: Their covariances equal min(s,t).
derive: Path continuity is preserved by composition with t ↦ ct and by negation.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a pre-Brownian motion B and t₀ ≥ 0, the process (B_{t₀+t} - B_{t₀})_{t≥0} is a pre-Brownian motion and is independent of (B_u)_{u≤t₀}.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="pre_brownian_motion"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="geq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="pre_brownian_motion"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="shifted_process"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="indep_shift_past"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Compute covariances of the shifted process with itself and with the past, then extend from finite collections by π-systems.
sketch_steps: derive: The shifted process is Gaussian with mean 0 and covariance min(s,t).
derive: Its covariance with B_u for u ≤ t₀ vanishes.
apply_theorem: Jointly Gaussian uncorrelated blocks are independent.
apply_theorem: The π-system criterion extends independence to the whole processes.

drafts.canonical_statement: The composition of Markov kernels κ from α to β and η from β to γ satisfies (η∘κ)(a,s) = ∫ η(b,s) κ(a,db) for measurable s, and it is again a Markov kernel.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="markov_kernel"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="markov_kernel"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="measurable_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="kernel_apply"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="kernel_comp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="kernel_lintegral_apply"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="markov_kernel"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="kernel_comp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: The formula is the definition of mixing; total mass 1 follows by integrating 1.
sketch_steps: setup: The composition mixes η against κ(a, -).
derive: On the whole space the integrand is 1, so the total mass is 1.
derive: Measurability in a follows from approximation by simple functions.

drafts.canonical_statement: Composition of kernels is associative, ξ∘(η∘κ) = (ξ∘η)∘κ, which is the kernel form of the Chapman–Kolmogorov relation.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="kernel_comp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="kernel_comp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="kernel_comp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="kernel_comp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Extend the composition formula to nonnegative functions and apply it to f = ξ(·,s).
sketch_steps: derive: The composition formula extends to nonnegative measurable functions by simple-function approximation.
derive: Applying it to c ↦ ξ(c,s) writes the left side as an iterated integral.
conclude: The inner integral is (ξ∘η)(b,s), giving the right side.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a Markov kernel κ and a measure π satisfy detailed balance, meaning the integral of κ(x,B) over A equals the integral of κ(x,A) over B for all measurable A and B, then π is invariant for κ.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="markov_kernel"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="kernel_detailed_balance"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="measure_bind"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Take A to be the whole space in the detailed balance condition.
sketch_steps: derive: Detailed balance with A the whole space gives ∫ κ(x,s) π(dx) = ∫_s κ(x, whole space) π(dx).
conclude: Since κ is Markov, the right side is π(s).

drafts.canonical_statement: For a finite prior π on a nonempty standard Borel space Θ and a finite kernel κ from Θ to X, the posterior kernel κ† makes the joint law of (x,θ) built from the data marginal κπ and κ† equal to the swap of the joint law of (θ,x) built from π and κ. The disintegration theorem is taken as known.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="standard_borel_nonempty"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_measure"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_kernel"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="measure_comp_prod"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="measure_bind"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="posterior_kernel"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="swap_image"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="measure_comp_prod"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: The posterior is the disintegration of the swapped joint law over the data marginal.
sketch_steps: setup: Form the joint law π⊗κ and swap its components.
derive: The first marginal of the swapped law is the data marginal κπ.
apply_theorem: The disintegration theorem on the standard Borel space Θ gives the posterior kernel.
conclude: Evaluating on rectangles gives the measure-theoretic Bayes formula.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a finite prior π on a nonempty standard Borel space Θ, a finite kernel κ from Θ to X and a measurable loss ℓ(θ,y) in [0,∞], the Bayes risk, the infimum of the average risk over all Markov-kernel estimators, is at least ∫ inf_y ∫ ℓ(θ,y) κ†(x,dθ) (κπ)(dx). The outer integral is a lower integral, since the infimum need not be measurable.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="standard_borel_nonempty"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_measure"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_kernel"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="measurable_uncurried_loss"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="leq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="integrated_min_posterior_loss"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="bayes_risk"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Rewrite the average risk through the posterior and bound the integral against ρ(x,·) by the infimum.
sketch_steps: derive: Bayes in kernel form and Tonelli rewrite the average risk as an integral against the posterior and the estimator.
derive: Since ρ(x,·) is a probability measure, the inner integral is at least the infimum over y, and the outer integral is read as a lower integral because the infimum need not be measurable.
conclude: Taking the infimum over ρ gives the lower bound for the Bayes risk.

drafts.canonical_statement: For nonzero polynomials f and g over an integral domain, deg(fg) = deg f + deg g and the leading coefficient of fg is the product of the leading coefficients of f and g.

sketch_steps: setup: Let m, n be the degrees and a, b the leading coefficients of f, g.
derive: Coefficients of fg above degree m+n vanish.
derive: The coefficient of X^(m+n) equals ab.

sketch_steps: setup: Let n be the degree of f and a its leading coefficient.
derive: Both polynomials have zero coefficients above degree n.
derive: The coefficient of X^n in g vanishes, so f+g has coefficient a there.
conclude: Hence f+g has degree n and leading coefficient a.

drafts.canonical_statement: For polynomials f and g over an integral domain, the degree of the composite f(g) equals deg f times deg g, with the zero polynomial given degree 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Expand f(g) as a sum of a_i g^i and isolate the unique term of top degree mn.
sketch_steps: case_split: If f or g is constant, then f(g) is constant and both sides are 0.
setup: Otherwise write f as the sum of a_i X^i with a_m nonzero, so f(g) is the sum of a_i g^i.
derive: Over a domain, a_i g^i has degree i n for nonzero a_i.
conclude: The term a_m g^m alone has degree mn, so f(g) has degree mn.

drafts.canonical_statement: A polynomial over an integral domain A is a unit of A[X] if and only if it is a constant polynomial whose value is a unit of A.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply additivity of degree over a domain to an equation fg = 1.
sketch_steps: setup: Suppose fg = 1 in A[X].
derive: Additivity of degree forces deg f = deg g = 0.
derive: So f = r and g = s are constants with rs = 1.
conclude: Conversely a unit constant has its inverse as a constant polynomial.

drafts.canonical_statement: A polynomial over a commutative ring A is nilpotent in A[X] if and only if all of its coefficients are nilpotent in A.

drafts.proof_strategy: The coefficient of X^(nk) in f^k is the k-th power of the top coefficient, so the top coefficient is nilpotent and can be removed by induction.
sketch_steps: derive: If all a_i are nilpotent, then f is a finite sum of nilpotent terms.
setup: Conversely write f with terms up to degree n and take k at least 1 with f^k = 0.
derive: The coefficient of X^(nk) in f^k is a_n^k, so a_n is nilpotent.
derive: Then f - a_n X^n is a nilpotent polynomial with terms up to degree n - 1.
conclude: Induction on n shows every a_i is nilpotent.

drafts.canonical_statement: A polynomial over a commutative ring A is a unit of A[X] if and only if its constant coefficient is a unit of A and all its other coefficients are nilpotent.

drafts.proof_strategy: Combine "unit plus nilpotent is a unit" with an induction on the degree that removes the top coefficient of a unit polynomial.
sketch_steps: derive: If a_0 is a unit and the other coefficients are nilpotent, then f is a unit plus a nilpotent.
construct: A finite geometric sum gives the inverse of a unit plus a nilpotent.
setup: Conversely let fg = 1; comparing constant terms shows a_0 and b_0 are units.
induction: Comparing the coefficient of X^(n+m-r) gives a_n^(r+1) b_(m-r) = 0 for r up to m.
derive: The case r = m shows a_n is nilpotent, so f - a_n X^n is again a unit.
conclude: Induction on n shows every a_i with i at least 1 is nilpotent.

drafts.proof_strategy: Subtract the two expressions and compare degrees, using that a monic factor preserves the leading coefficient.
sketch_steps: setup: Let q = q_1 - q_2, so gq = r_2 - r_1.
contradiction: If q is nonzero, monicity of g gives deg(gq) = deg g + deg q at least deg g.
derive: But r_2 - r_1 has degree less than deg g.
conclude: Hence q = 0 and then r_1 = r_2.

drafts.proof_strategy: Prove existence by induction on deg f by removing the top term, and uniqueness by comparing degrees.
sketch_steps: induction: Induct on deg f; the case deg f < deg g is immediate with q = 0.
construct: Otherwise subtract a b^(-1) X^(m-n) g to lower the degree of f.
derive: The inductive hypothesis gives a division of the lowered polynomial and hence of f.
contradiction: Two divisions give g(q-q') = r'-r, impossible by degree unless q = q'.
conclude: Therefore the pair (q, r) exists and is unique.

drafts.canonical_statement: For an integral domain A, the polynomial ring A[X] is a principal ideal ring if and only if A is a field.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="integral_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="principal_ideal_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="polynomial_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="is_field"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use a polynomial of least degree for one direction, and for the other analyse a generator of the ideal (a, X).
sketch_steps: setup: If A is a field, take a nonzero element g of least degree in an ideal I.
derive: Division by g gives a remainder in I of smaller degree, so it vanishes and I = (g).
setup: Conversely, for nonzero a in A let d generate (a, X).
derive: Since d divides a, it is a constant, and since d divides X, it is a unit.
conclude: Thus 1 = au + Xv; setting X = 0 shows a is a unit.

drafts.canonical_statement: The ideal (2, X) of Z[X] is not principal.

drafts.proof_strategy: A generator would divide 2 and X, hence be a unit, but 1 is not in (2, X) by evaluating at 0.
sketch_steps: setup: Suppose f generates the ideal (2, X).
derive: Since f divides 2, it is an integer c.
derive: Since c divides X, comparing coefficients gives c = 1 or c = -1.
contradiction: Then 1 = 2u + Xv, and X = 0 gives 1 = 2u(0), which is impossible.
conclude: Therefore (2, X) is not principal.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a polynomial f over a commutative ring and its formal derivative f' satisfy uf + vf' = 1 for some polynomials u and v, then f is squarefree, that is, g^2 dividing f forces g to be a unit.

drafts.proof_strategy: A repeated factor of f also divides the derivative, hence divides 1.
sketch_steps: setup: Write f = g^2 h.
derive: The product rule gives that g divides the derivative of f.
derive: So g divides uf + vf' = 1.
conclude: Hence g is a unit and f is squarefree.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use a generator of the ideal (f, g); over an algebraically closed field a nonconstant generator would give a common root.
sketch_steps: derive: Evaluating uf + vg = 1 at a common root gives 0 = 1.
setup: Conversely let d generate the ideal (f, g) of the principal ideal domain K[X].
case_split: d = 0 would make every element of K a common root.
case_split: A nonconstant d has a root by algebraic closedness, and that root is common to f and g.
conclude: So d is a nonzero constant and 1 lies in (f, g).

drafts.canonical_statement: If monic polynomials f and g over a commutative ring divide each other, then f = g.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="polynomial_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="polynomial_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="monic_polynomial"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="monic_polynomial"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dvd"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dvd"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: A monic factor preserves leading coefficients and adds degrees, so the cofactor must be the constant 1.
sketch_steps: case_split: The zero ring is trivial.
setup: Write g = fh and f = gk with h and k nonzero.
derive: Monicity makes degrees add, so deg h = 0.
derive: The leading coefficient of fh is h, and it equals 1.
conclude: Therefore g = f.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a polynomial f over a commutative ring A and a in A, the polynomial f(X + a) is irreducible if and only if f is irreducible.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="polynomial_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="irreducible_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="poly_comp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="poly_var"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="poly_const"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="polynomial_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="irreducible_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="polynomial_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Translation of the variable is a ring automorphism of A[X], and automorphisms preserve irreducibility.
sketch_steps: construct: Define the ring homomorphism sending h to h(X + a).
derive: Substitution of X - a is its inverse, so it is an automorphism.
translate: A ring automorphism preserves units and factorizations.
conclude: Hence f and f(X + a) are irreducible together.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every irreducible polynomial in R[X] has degree at most 2.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="irreducible_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="polynomial_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="R"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="leq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="poly_degree"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Take a complex root by the fundamental theorem of algebra and produce a real factor of degree at most 2.
sketch_steps: setup: f has positive degree, so it has a complex root z.
case_split: If z is real, then X - z divides f, so f has degree 1.
construct: If z is not real, then q = (X - z)(X - conj z) has real coefficients.
derive: The remainder of f by q has degree at most 1 and the nonreal root z, so it vanishes.
conclude: Irreducibility makes f a constant multiple of q, of degree 2.

drafts.canonical_statement: If p is a prime ideal of a commutative ring A, then the ideal pA[X] generated by p in A[X] is a prime ideal of A[X].
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prime_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prime_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_extension_to_polynomials"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="polynomial_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Identify pA[X] with the kernel of coefficient reduction onto the domain (A/p)[X].
sketch_steps: construct: Let π be coefficient reduction from A[X] onto (A/p)[X].
derive: A polynomial lies in pA[X] exactly when all coefficients lie in p.
translate: Hence pA[X] is the kernel of π.
derive: The quotient is (A/p)[X], a polynomial ring over a domain.
conclude: A quotient that is a domain means pA[X] is prime.

drafts.canonical_statement: Gauss's lemma in content form. Over a GCD domain with a chosen normalized gcd, the content c(h), which is the normalized gcd of the coefficients of h, satisfies c(fg) = c(f)c(g).

drafts.proof_strategy: Factor out the contents, apply Gauss's lemma on primitive polynomials and use c(ah) = normalize(a)c(h).
sketch_steps: case_split: The case f = 0 or g = 0 is immediate.
setup: Write f = c(f)f_1 and g = c(g)g_1 with f_1, g_1 primitive.
apply_theorem: Gauss's lemma says f_1 g_1 is primitive.
derive: Pulling out constants gives c(fg) = normalize(c(f)c(g)).
conclude: Contents are normalized and normalization is multiplicative, so c(fg) = c(f)c(g).

drafts.proof_strategy: Clear denominators in the cofactor and use multiplicativity of content to show the denominator divides it.
sketch_steps: setup: Write q = ph in K[X] and clear denominators to get aq = ph_1 with h_1 in A[X].
apply_theorem: Gauss's lemma says contents are multiplicative up to units.
derive: Since p is primitive, the content of h_1 is the content of aq up to a unit.
derive: So a divides every coefficient of h_1, and h_1 = a h_2.
conclude: Cancelling a gives q = p h_2 in A[X].

drafts.proof_strategy: The roots of g are roots of f, hence integral; its coefficients are symmetric functions of them lying in K.
sketch_steps: setup: Pass to a splitting field L of f over K, where g splits.
derive: Each root of g is a root of the monic f, so it is integral over A.
derive: Coefficients of g are symmetric functions of these roots, hence integral.
apply_theorem: They lie in K, so integral closedness puts them in A.
conclude: Therefore g is a monic polynomial over A.

drafts.canonical_statement: For elements a and b of an integral domain, (a) = (b) if and only if a and b are associated.

drafts.proof_strategy: Mutual divisibility gives a = axy, and cancellation in a domain makes the cofactors units.
sketch_steps: derive: If a = bu with u a unit, then a and b lie in each other's principal ideals.
setup: Conversely write a = bx and b = ay.
case_split: If a = 0 then b = 0.
derive: Otherwise a(1 - xy) = 0 gives xy = 1 in a domain.
conclude: So x is a unit and a, b are associated.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every nonzero element of a Noetherian integral domain is a unit times a finite product of irreducible elements.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take a maximal principal ideal among counterexamples and split it into two strictly larger principal ideals.
sketch_steps: setup: Suppose S, the set of nonzero elements without such a factorization, is nonempty.
apply_theorem: The Noetherian property gives a maximal element (a) among the ideals generated by S.
derive: The element a is neither a unit nor irreducible, so a = bc with b and c nonunits.
derive: Cancellation gives strict inclusions of (a) in (b) and (c), so b and c factor.
contradiction: Then a also factors, contradicting that a lies in S.

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on the number of factors; a prime factor on one side divides, hence is associated to, a factor on the other side.
sketch_steps: setup: Write p_1...p_r = u q_1...q_s with u a unit and induct on r.
case_split: If r = 0 then s = 0, because irreducibles are not units.
derive: Primality of p_1 gives that p_1 divides some q_j, and irreducibility of q_j makes them associated.
derive: Cancel p_1 in the domain to obtain a shorter equation.
conclude: The inductive hypothesis gives r = s and the matching.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare exponents in the prime factorizations of a and b, taking minima.
sketch_steps: case_split: If a or b is zero, the other element works.
setup: Write a and b with the same pairwise nonassociated irreducibles p_i and exponents e_i, f_i.
construct: Let d be the product of p_i to the power min(e_i, f_i).
derive: Unique factorization shows a common divisor has exponents at most min(e_i, f_i).
conclude: Hence every common divisor divides d.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every nonzero prime ideal of a unique factorization domain contains a prime element.

drafts.proof_strategy: Factor a nonzero element of the ideal and apply primality of the ideal to the factors.
sketch_steps: setup: Take a nonzero a in the prime ideal p; a is not a unit.
derive: Factor a as a unit times irreducibles q_1, ..., q_n with n at least 1.
derive: Since p is prime and contains no unit, some q_i lies in p.
conclude: Irreducibles are prime in a unique factorization domain, so q_i is the required element.

drafts.canonical_statement: A unique factorization domain is integrally closed in its field of fractions.

drafts.proof_strategy: Write x in lowest terms and clear denominators in the integral equation, so an irreducible factor of the denominator would divide the numerator.
sketch_steps: setup: Let x = a/b be integral over A, with a and b having no common irreducible factor.
derive: Multiplying the integral equation by b^n shows b divides a^n.
contradiction: An irreducible factor p of b is prime, so it would divide a.
conclude: Hence b is a unit and x lies in A.

sketch_steps: setup: Choose d with (a, b) = (d).
derive: Membership of d in (a, b) gives d = ax + by.
derive: Membership of a and b in (d) gives d divides a and b.
conclude: Any common divisor divides ax + by = d.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a nonzero element p of a principal ideal domain, p is irreducible if and only if (p) is a maximal ideal.

drafts.proof_strategy: Translate factorizations of p into principal ideals containing (p).
sketch_steps: setup: Assume p is irreducible and let (p) lie in an ideal I = (q).
derive: Writing p = qr, either q is a unit and I is the whole ring, or r is a unit and I = (p).
setup: Conversely assume (p) is maximal and p = ab.
case_split: Maximality gives (a) = A or (a) = (p).
conclude: In the second case cancellation makes b a unit, so p is irreducible.

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on the finite index set, multiplying Bezout relations to show s_k is coprime to the product of the others.
sketch_steps: induction: Induct on the size of t; the empty product is 1.
setup: Let t be t' with k added and r the product of s_j over t'.
derive: Multiplying x_j s_k + y_j s_j = 1 over j gives X s_k + Y r = 1.
derive: Then z = X s_k z + Y r z, and s_k r divides both terms.
conclude: Hence the full product divides z.

drafts.canonical_statement: A formal power series over a commutative ring is a unit if and only if its constant coefficient is a unit.

drafts.proof_strategy: Solve fg = 1 coefficient by coefficient using the inverse of the constant term.
sketch_steps: derive: If fg = 1, the constant terms give a_0 b_0 = 1.
construct: Conversely define b_n recursively using the inverse of a_0.
derive: The recursion says exactly that all higher coefficients of fg vanish.
conclude: Hence fg = 1.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a formal power series f over a commutative ring, X^n divides f if and only if the coefficient of X^m in f vanishes for all m < n.

drafts.proof_strategy: Multiplication by X^n shifts coefficients by n.
sketch_steps: translate: Multiplying by X^n shifts every coefficient up by n.
derive: So a multiple of X^n has zero coefficients below degree n.
construct: Conversely shift the coefficients of f down by n to get h.
conclude: Then f = X^n h.

drafts.canonical_statement: For an element a of a commutative ring, the formal power series identity (sum over n of a^n X^n)(1 - aX) = 1 holds.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare coefficients; the series telescopes.
sketch_steps: setup: Let g be the series with coefficients a^n.
derive: The constant term of g(1 - aX) is 1.
derive: The coefficient of X^(n+1) is a^(n+1) - a a^n = 0.
conclude: Therefore g(1 - aX) = 1.

drafts.canonical_statement: For formal power series over an integral domain, ord(fg) = ord f + ord g, where the order is the least index of a nonzero coefficient and the order of 0 is infinity.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="integral_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="power_series_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="power_series_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="power_series_order"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="power_series_order"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="power_series_order"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: The lowest coefficient of the product is the product of the lowest coefficients, which is nonzero in a domain.
sketch_steps: case_split: If f or g is zero, both sides are infinite.
setup: Let m and n be the orders of f and g.
derive: Coefficients of fg below degree m+n vanish.
derive: The coefficient of X^(m+n) is a_m b_n, nonzero in a domain.
conclude: Hence ord(fg) = m + n.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every nonzero formal power series f over a field K can be written as f = X^n u with n a nonnegative integer and u a unit of K[[X]].

drafts.proof_strategy: Factor out the lowest power of X; the remaining series has invertible constant term.
sketch_steps: setup: Let n be the least index of a nonzero coefficient of f.
construct: Shift coefficients down by n to get u with f = X^n u.
derive: The constant term of u is nonzero, hence invertible in K.
conclude: The recursive inverse shows u is a unit.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a valuation v on a commutative ring with values in a totally ordered commutative group with zero, if v(a) and v(b) differ, then v(a + b) = max(v(a), v(b)).
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="krull_valuation"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="max_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the ultrametric inequality to a + b and to b = (a + b) + (-a).
sketch_steps: derive: v(-1) squares to 1 in a totally ordered group, so v(-x) = v(x).
setup: Assume v(a) < v(b) by symmetry.
derive: The ultrametric inequality gives v(a + b) at most v(b).
derive: Applied to b = (a + b) + (-a), it gives v(b) at most v(a + b).
conclude: Thus v(a + b) = v(b), the maximum.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a valuation v on a field K with values in a totally ordered commutative group with zero and nonzero x in K, both v(x) ≤ 1 and v(x^(-1)) ≤ 1 hold if and only if v(x) = 1; so the units of the valuation ring of v are exactly the elements of value 1.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use v(x^(-1)) = v(x)^(-1) and order-compatibility in the value group.
sketch_steps: derive: v(x) v(x^(-1)) = 1, so v(x^(-1)) is the inverse of v(x).
derive: If v(x) = 1, both values equal 1.
derive: If both are at most 1, then multiplying gives 1 at most v(x).
conclude: So v(x) = 1, which describes the units of the valuation ring.

drafts.canonical_statement: For an integral domain A, the elements of A are totally ordered by divisibility if and only if the ideals of A are totally ordered by inclusion.

drafts.proof_strategy: Translate between divisibility and inclusion of principal ideals, and choose an element witnessing non-inclusion.
sketch_steps: setup: Assume divisibility is total and I is not contained in J; pick a in I outside J.
derive: For b in J, b cannot divide a, so a divides b.
derive: Thus b lies in I, so J is contained in I.
translate: Conversely compare the principal ideals (a) and (b).
conclude: Inclusion of these ideals gives one of the divisibilities.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a Noetherian integral domain A has the property that a divides b or b divides a for all a and b in A, then A is a principal ideal domain.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="integral_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="noetherian_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="or"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dvd"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dvd"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="principal_ideal_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Finite generation plus total divisibility lets one generator divide all the others.
sketch_steps: setup: Every ideal is finitely generated, I = (a_1, ..., a_n).
induction: By total divisibility, some a_i divides all generators.
derive: Then I is generated by that a_i.
conclude: So every ideal is principal.

drafts.canonical_statement: If ϖ is an irreducible element of a discrete valuation ring A and x is a nonzero element of A, then x = u ϖ^n for some nonnegative integer n and some unit u.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="discrete_valuation_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="irreducible_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="unit_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Factor x into irreducibles and observe that all irreducibles generate the unique maximal ideal.
sketch_steps: setup: A principal ideal domain is a unique factorization domain, so x factors into irreducibles.
derive: Every irreducible generates a maximal ideal, which must be the unique maximal ideal m.
derive: So every irreducible factor is associated to ϖ.
conclude: Collecting units gives x = u ϖ^n.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a Dedekind domain, if I is a nonzero ideal and J and L are ideals with IJ = IL, then J = L.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dedekind_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="zero_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_product"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_product"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Multiply by an ideal I' with II' principal, then cancel the nonzero generator in the domain.
sketch_steps: setup: Choose a nonzero c in I.
apply_theorem: In a Dedekind domain containment means divisibility, so II' = (c) for some ideal I'.
derive: Multiplying IJ = IL by I' gives (c)J = (c)L.
conclude: Cancelling c in the domain gives J = L.

drafts.canonical_statement: For ideals I and J of a Dedekind domain, (I + J)(I ∩ J) = IJ.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dedekind_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_product"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_sum"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="intersect"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_product"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: In terms of prime exponents, the sum takes minima and the intersection takes maxima.
sketch_steps: case_split: The case I = 0 or J = 0 is immediate.
setup: Factor I and J into primes with exponents a_p and b_p.
apply_theorem: Containment is divisibility, so I + J has exponents min(a_p, b_p).
derive: Likewise the intersection has exponents max(a_p, b_p).
conclude: Adding min and max gives a_p + b_p, so the product is IJ.

drafts.canonical_statement: A Dedekind domain with only finitely many prime ideals is a principal ideal domain.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dedekind_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prime_ideals_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="principal_ideal_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use the Chinese remainder theorem to build an element with exactly the prime exponents of a given ideal.
sketch_steps: setup: Factor a nonzero ideal I as the product of p_i^(e_i) over the finitely many nonzero primes.
construct: Pick a_i in p_i^(e_i) outside p_i^(e_i+1).
apply_theorem: The Chinese remainder theorem gives a congruent to a_i modulo p_i^(e_i+1) for all i.
derive: The exponent of p_i in (a) is exactly e_i, and no other prime occurs.
conclude: Hence (a) = I.

drafts.canonical_statement: A Dedekind domain is a unique factorization domain if and only if it is a principal ideal domain.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dedekind_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="unique_factorization_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="principal_ideal_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: In a unique factorization domain, a nonzero prime contains a prime element whose principal ideal must be maximal, hence equal to it.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: A principal ideal domain is a unique factorization domain.
setup: Conversely take a nonzero prime ideal p of A, which contains a prime element q.
derive: The nonzero prime (q) is maximal in a Dedekind domain, so p = (q).
apply_theorem: Every nonzero ideal is a product of primes.
conclude: Products of principal ideals are principal, so A is a principal ideal domain.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every element a of a finite associative ring with identity, not necessarily commutative, is a unit or satisfies ab = 0 for some nonzero b.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="is_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="or"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="unit_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: If no right annihilator exists, left multiplication by a is injective, hence bijective on a finite set, which produces a two-sided inverse.
sketch_steps: setup: Assume ab = 0 has no nonzero solution b.
derive: Left multiplication by a is injective.
derive: On a finite set it is surjective, so ab = 1 for some b.
derive: a(ba) = a gives ba = 1 by injectivity.
conclude: Hence a is a unit.

drafts.canonical_statement: For elements a and b of a ring with identity, not necessarily commutative, 1 - ab is a unit if and only if 1 - ba is a unit.

drafts.proof_strategy: Write down the explicit inverse 1 + b(1-ab)^{-1}a and verify it on both sides.
sketch_steps: setup: Let u be the inverse of 1 - ab, so u - abu = 1 and u - uab = 1.
construct: Put v = 1 + bua.
derive: (1 - ba)v = 1 by factoring b(u - abu)a.
derive: v(1 - ba) = 1 by factoring b(u - uab)a.
conclude: The roles of a and b are symmetric, so the equivalence follows.

drafts.canonical_statement: If ab = 1 in a ring with identity, not necessarily commutative, then ba is idempotent; if moreover ba ≠ 1, then ba ≠ 0, 1 - ba ≠ 0 and ba(1 - ba) = 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compute (ba)^2 using ab = 1 and rule out ba = 0 by expanding (ab)(ab).
sketch_steps: setup: Put e = ba.
derive: e^2 = b(ab)a = e.
case_split: If e ≠ 1, then e(1 - e) = 0 and 1 - e ≠ 0.
contradiction: If e = 0, then 1 = a(ba)b = 0, which forces e = 1.
conclude: So e is a nonzero zero divisor when e ≠ 1.

drafts.canonical_statement: A nonzero commutative ring is a field if and only if its only ideals are the zero ideal and the whole ring.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nontrivial_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="is_field"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="or"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="zero_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="unit_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: A nonzero element of an ideal in a field generates the unit ideal; conversely (a) = A gives an inverse of a.
sketch_steps: setup: Let A be a nonzero commutative ring.
derive: In a field, a nonzero ideal contains a unit, so it is A.
derive: If only 0 and A are ideals, then (a) = A for a ≠ 0.
conclude: So a has an inverse and A is a field.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every ring homomorphism preserving 1 from a division ring, in particular from a field, to a nonzero ring is injective.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="division_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="is_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nontrivial_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ring_hom"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="injective"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: A nonzero element in the kernel would be invertible and force 1 = 0 in the target.
sketch_steps: setup: Reduce injectivity to showing the kernel is zero.
contradiction: If f(a) = 0 with a ≠ 0, then 1 = f(a)f(a^{-1}) = 0 in B.
conclude: Hence the kernel is zero and f is injective.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a nonnegative integer n, the ring Z/nZ is an integral domain if and only if n = 0 or n is prime, where Z/0Z = Z and the zero ring is not a domain.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="integral_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="zmod_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="or"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="P"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: A proper factorization of n gives zero divisors; for prime n use that a prime dividing ab divides a factor.
sketch_steps: case_split: Treat n = 0 and n = 1 directly.
derive: If n = kl with 1 < k, l < n, the classes of k and l are zero divisors.
derive: If n is prime and n divides ab, then n divides a or b.
conclude: So Z/nZ is a domain exactly when n = 0 or n is prime.

drafts.canonical_statement: An element (a, b) of a product ring A x B is a unit if and only if a is a unit of A and b is a unit of B.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="is_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="is_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="unit_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ordered_pair"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ring_product"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="unit_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="unit_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Multiplication in the product is componentwise, so inverses correspond componentwise.
sketch_steps: setup: The identity of A x B is (1, 1).
derive: An inverse (c, d) of (a, b) gives inverses c of a and d of b.
derive: Conversely (a^{-1}, b^{-1}) is an inverse of (a, b).
conclude: The two conditions are equivalent.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a and b are commuting nilpotent elements of a ring with identity, not necessarily commutative, then a + b and ab are nilpotent.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="is_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nilpotent_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nilpotent_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nilpotent_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nilpotent_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use the binomial theorem for commuting elements; every term has a high power of a or of b.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix m and n with a^m = 0 and b^n = 0.
derive: Since ab = ba, (ab)^m = a^m b^m = 0.
apply_theorem: Expand (a + b)^(m+n) by the binomial theorem.
derive: Each term has i ≥ m or m + n - i > n, so it vanishes.
conclude: Therefore a + b and ab are nilpotent.

drafts.canonical_statement: If an element a of a ring with identity, not necessarily commutative, satisfies a^n = 0, then 1 - a is a unit with inverse the sum of a^i for i from 0 to n - 1.

drafts.proof_strategy: Telescope the geometric sum on both sides.
sketch_steps: setup: Put s equal to the sum of a^i for i < n.
derive: (1 - a)s telescopes to 1 - a^n.
derive: s(1 - a) telescopes to 1 - a^n as well.
conclude: Since a^n = 0, s is the two-sided inverse of 1 - a.

sketch_steps: setup: Let e satisfy e^2 = e.
derive: e(1 - e) = e - e^2 = 0 and (1 - e)e = 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: A square factor produces an explicit nilpotent class; for squarefree n every prime factor of n divides a whenever n divides a power of a.
sketch_steps: case_split: Assume first that n = p^2 m.
construct: The class of pm is nonzero and its square vanishes.
setup: Now let n = p_1 ... p_r with distinct primes.
derive: If n divides a^k, each p_i divides a.
conclude: Hence n divides a and the class of a is zero.

drafts.proof_strategy: A prime dividing a power divides the base; conversely compare prime powers of n with a^n.
sketch_steps: setup: Suppose n divides a^k and p is a prime factor of n.
derive: Then p divides a.
setup: Conversely factor n into prime powers p_i^{e_i}.
derive: Each e_i ≤ n, so p_i^{e_i} divides a^n.
conclude: Coprimality gives n | a^n, so the class of a is nilpotent.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply x^2 = x to x + x and to x + y.
sketch_steps: setup: Assume x^2 = x for every x.
derive: Squaring x + x gives x + x = 0.
derive: Squaring x + y gives xy + yx = 0.
conclude: Since xy + xy = 0, we get xy = yx.

drafts.proof_strategy: The ideals (e) and (1 - e) are comaximal with zero intersection, and (1 - e)a + eb is an explicit preimage.
sketch_steps: setup: Put I = (e) and J = (1 - e).
derive: e + (1 - e) = 1 gives I + J = A.
derive: e(1 - e) = 0 gives I ∩ J = 0.
construct: The element (1 - e)a + eb maps to the pair of classes of a and b.
conclude: The natural map to the product is an isomorphism.

drafts.proof_strategy: Split the binomial expansion of (a + (1 - a))^(2n-1) into two orthogonal parts.
sketch_steps: setup: Pick a with f(a) = e, so a(1 - a) is nilpotent, with n-th power zero.
apply_theorem: Expand 1 = (a + (1 - a))^(2n-1) by the binomial theorem.
construct: Let e be the sum of the terms with i ≤ n - 1 and e2 the rest.
derive: e e2 is a multiple of (a(1 - a))^n, so it is 0 and e is idempotent.
derive: Under f only the term a^(2n-1) survives, so f(e) = e prime.
conclude: e is an idempotent lift.

drafts.canonical_statement: For ideals I and J of a commutative ring, the product IJ is contained in the intersection of I and J.

drafts.proof_strategy: Each generator ab lies in both ideals by absorption.
sketch_steps: setup: IJ consists of finite sums of products ab with a in I and b in J.
derive: Absorption gives ab in I and ab in J.
conclude: Finite sums stay in the intersection.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show that each pair of generators lies in the other ideal.
sketch_steps: derive: a + bq and b lie in (a, b).
derive: a = (a + bq) - bq and b lie in (a + bq, b).
conclude: The two ideals coincide.

drafts.proof_strategy: If neither ideal contains the other, the sum of an element of each lies in neither.
sketch_steps: derive: If one ideal contains the other, the union is the larger ideal.
setup: Otherwise pick x in I outside J and y in J outside I.
contradiction: x + y lies in the union, but it can lie in neither I nor J.
conclude: Hence the ideals are comparable.

sketch_steps: setup: Put U equal to the union of the I_n.
derive: Elements x in I_m and y in I_n both lie in I_k with k = max(m, n).
derive: Hence x + y lies in U, and U absorbs left multiplication.

drafts.proof_strategy: Membership in J/I of the class of x is equivalent to membership of x in J; for maximality use the ideal correspondence.
sketch_steps: setup: Let π be the projection to A/I.
derive: π(x) lies in J/I if and only if x lies in J, because I ⊆ J.
derive: The primality condition transfers through the surjection π.
apply_theorem: Ideals of A/I correspond to ideals of A containing I.
conclude: Maximality transfers through this correspondence.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a subring S of a commutative ring A containing 1 and an ideal I of A, the quotient S/(S ∩ I) is isomorphic to the image of S in A/I, that is, to (S + I)/I.

sketch_steps: construct: Restrict the projection A → A/I to f on S.
derive: The kernel of f is S ∩ I.
derive: The image of f is the set of classes of elements of S, which is (S + I)/I.
apply_theorem: The first isomorphism theorem gives the claim.

drafts.proof_strategy: Expand the product of two expressions of 1; powers follow by induction on the exponents.
sketch_steps: setup: Write 1 = x + y and 1 = x2 + z with x, x2 in I, y in J, z in K.
derive: Multiplying gives 1 in I + JK.
induction: Apply this repeatedly to get I + J^n = A.
induction: Apply it again in the first variable to get I^m + J^n = A.

drafts.proof_strategy: Expand products of elements of I ∪ J; each product has at least m factors in I or at least n factors in J.
sketch_steps: setup: (I + J)^(m+n) is spanned by products of m + n elements of I ∪ J.
derive: Each such product lies in I^k J^(m+n-k) for some k.
case_split: If k ≥ m it lies in I^m = 0; otherwise it lies in J^n = 0.
conclude: Hence (I + J)^(m+n) = 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Multiply by the idempotents (1, 0) and (0, 1) to separate the components.
sketch_steps: construct: Let I be the a with (a, 0) in L and J the b with (0, b) in L.
derive: I and J are ideals.
derive: (a, b) = (a, 0) + (0, b) gives I x J ⊆ L.
derive: Multiplying by (1, 0) and (0, 1) gives L ⊆ I x J.
conclude: L = I x J.

drafts.proof_strategy: The relation (1, 0)(0, 1) = 0 forces a prime ideal to contain exactly one of the two idempotents.
sketch_steps: setup: Write L = I x J using the idempotents (1, 0) and (0, 1).
derive: Since (1, 0)(0, 1) = 0, exactly one idempotent lies in a prime L.
case_split: If (0, 1) is in L, then L = I x B and I is prime; the other case is symmetric.
derive: Conversely p x B and A x q satisfy the definition of a prime ideal.
conclude: This gives the classification.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every prime ideal of a finite commutative ring is a maximal ideal.

drafts.proof_strategy: The quotient is a finite integral domain, hence a field.
sketch_steps: setup: A/p is a finite integral domain.
derive: Multiplication by a nonzero x is injective, hence surjective.
derive: So x has an inverse and A/p is a field.
conclude: Therefore p is maximal.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a field K of characteristic zero, there is exactly one ring homomorphism from Q to K.

sketch_steps: construct: Define f(a/b) = (a·1)(b·1)^{-1}, using that b·1 ≠ 0 in characteristic zero.
derive: The value is independent of the representation and f is a ring map.
setup: Let g be any ring homomorphism from Q to K.
derive: g agrees with n·1 on integers and hence with f on fractions.
conclude: f is the only homomorphism.

drafts.proof_strategy: Values on classes are forced by f(1) = 1; existence comes from the universal property of the quotient of Z.
sketch_steps: derive: Any homomorphism sends the class of k to k·1, which gives uniqueness.
derive: Taking k = n gives n·1 = 0.
construct: If n·1 = 0, the map k to k·1 from Z kills nZ.
conclude: It induces a homomorphism from Z/nZ.

drafts.canonical_statement: The identity map is the only ring homomorphism from R to R preserving 1.

drafts.proof_strategy: The map fixes the rationals and preserves order because nonnegative reals are squares; density of the rationals finishes.
sketch_steps: derive: f fixes every rational number.
derive: Nonnegative reals are squares, so f preserves order.
contradiction: If f(x) ≠ x, a rational between x and f(x) contradicts monotonicity.
conclude: f is the identity.

drafts.proof_strategy: Define the map on coefficients by substitution; A and X generate A[X], which gives uniqueness.
sketch_steps: construct: Put f(sum a_i X^i) = sum φ(a_i) s^i.
derive: Commutativity of B shows that f preserves products.
setup: Let f2 be another homomorphism with the same values on A and X.
derive: f2 agrees with f on every polynomial, since A and X generate A[X].
conclude: f exists and is unique.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a commutative ring A and a in A, the kernel of the evaluation homomorphism from A[X] to A sending f to f(a) is the ideal (X - a).

drafts.proof_strategy: Factor X^i - a^i and sum up to write f - f(a) as a multiple of X - a.
sketch_steps: derive: Multiples of X - a vanish at a.
derive: X^i - a^i is divisible by X - a for each i.
derive: Hence f - f(a) is divisible by X - a.
conclude: If f(a) = 0, then f lies in (X - a).

drafts.canonical_statement: For a commutative ring A and a in A, the quotient A[X]/(a, X) is isomorphic to A/(a).

drafts.proof_strategy: Compose evaluation at zero with the projection to A/(a) and compute the kernel.
sketch_steps: construct: Let φ send f to the class of f(0) in A/(a).
derive: φ is surjective, by looking at constants.
derive: The kernel of φ is (a, X).
apply_theorem: The first isomorphism theorem gives the isomorphism.

drafts.canonical_statement: For an element a of an integral domain A that is neither zero nor a unit, the ideal (a, X) of A[X] is not principal; this generalizes the fact that (2, X) is not principal in Z[X].

drafts.proof_strategy: A generator divides a, so it is constant, and it divides X, so it is a unit; evaluating at zero then makes a a unit.
sketch_steps: setup: Suppose (a, X) = (d).
derive: d divides the nonzero constant a, so d is a constant c.
derive: c divides X, so comparing coefficients of X shows that c is a unit.
contradiction: Then 1 = au + Xv, and X = 0 makes a a unit.
conclude: Hence (a, X) is not principal.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a commutative ring A, the ideal (X) of A[X] is prime if and only if A is an integral domain, and it is maximal if and only if A is a field.

drafts.proof_strategy: Identify A[X]/(X) with A by taking constant terms and apply the quotient characterizations.
sketch_steps: construct: Let φ take the constant term of a polynomial.
derive: φ is surjective with kernel (X), so A[X]/(X) is isomorphic to A.
apply_theorem: An ideal is prime exactly when its quotient is a domain.
apply_theorem: An ideal is maximal exactly when its quotient is a field.

drafts.canonical_statement: For an ideal I of a commutative ring A, the quotient A[X]/IA[X] is isomorphic to (A/I)[X], where IA[X] is the ideal of A[X] generated by I.

drafts.proof_strategy: Reduce coefficients modulo I; the kernel consists of polynomials with all coefficients in I.
sketch_steps: construct: Let φ reduce all coefficients modulo I.
derive: φ is a surjective ring homomorphism.
derive: The kernel consists of the polynomials with coefficients in I, which is IA[X].
apply_theorem: The first isomorphism theorem gives the claim.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a monic polynomial f and a nonzero polynomial g over a commutative ring, fg is nonzero and deg(fg) = deg f + deg g.
