drafts.proof_strategy: The coefficient of X^(m+n) in fg is the leading coefficient of g because f is monic.
sketch_steps: setup: Let m = deg f, n = deg g and let b be the leading coefficient of g.
derive: The coefficients of fg vanish above degree m + n.
derive: The coefficient of X^(m+n) equals 1·b = b, which is nonzero.
conclude: Hence fg is nonzero of degree m + n.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take a nonzero annihilator of minimal degree; the top nonannihilating coefficient would produce one of lower degree.
sketch_steps: derive: A nonzero constant annihilator makes f a zero divisor.
setup: Conversely take g nonzero of minimal degree with fg = 0.
contradiction: If some a_i g ≠ 0, take the largest such r; then a_r b_m = 0 and a_r g is a smaller annihilator.
derive: So a_i g = 0 for every i.
conclude: The leading coefficient c of g satisfies cf = 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a nonzero polynomial f over a nonzero commutative ring A and a in A, there are a nonnegative integer m and g in A[X] with f = (X - a)^m g and g(a) ≠ 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Divisibility by powers of the monic polynomial X - a is bounded by the degree; take the largest power and use the factor theorem.
sketch_steps: derive: (X - a)^k | f forces k ≤ deg f, because X - a is monic.
setup: Let m be the largest k with (X - a)^k | f and write f = (X - a)^m g.
contradiction: If g(a) = 0, the factor theorem gives a higher power dividing f.
conclude: So g(a) ≠ 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a polynomial f over a commutative ring A and a in A, (X - a)^2 divides f if and only if f(a) = 0 and f'(a) = 0, where f' is the formal derivative; this generalizes the real case.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the factor theorem twice, together with the product rule for the formal derivative.
sketch_steps: derive: If f = (X - a)^2 g, the product rule gives f(a) = f'(a) = 0.
setup: Conversely write f = (X - a)g by the factor theorem.
derive: The product rule gives f'(a) = g(a), so g(a) = 0.
conclude: Applying the factor theorem to g gives (X - a)^2 | f.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a is a root of a nonzero polynomial f over an integral domain of characteristic zero, then the multiplicity of a as a root of f' is one less than its multiplicity as a root of f, where a non-root has multiplicity zero.

drafts.proof_strategy: Differentiate f = (X - a)^m g and check that the cofactor of (X - a)^(m-1) does not vanish at a.
sketch_steps: setup: Write f = (X - a)^m g with g(a) ≠ 0 and m ≥ 1.
derive: f' = (X - a)^(m-1) h with h = mg + (X - a)g'.
derive: h(a) = m g(a) ≠ 0, because the characteristic is zero and A is a domain.
conclude: The multiplicity of a in f' is exactly m - 1.

drafts.canonical_statement: The formal derivative of polynomials f and g over a commutative ring satisfies the product rule (fg)' = f'g + fg'.

drafts.proof_strategy: Both sides are bilinear, so it suffices to check monomials.
sketch_steps: setup: The derivative is linear over A, so both sides are bilinear in f and g.
derive: For monomials both sides equal (m + n)X^(m+n-1).
conclude: Bilinearity gives the rule for all polynomials.

drafts.canonical_statement: If the formal derivative of a polynomial f over an integral domain of characteristic zero vanishes, then f is constant.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare coefficients of f'; multiples by positive integers are injective in characteristic zero domains.
sketch_steps: setup: Write f as the sum of a_i X^i.
derive: f' = 0 gives i a_i = 0 for i ≥ 1.
derive: In a characteristic zero domain this forces a_i = 0.
conclude: f equals its constant term.

drafts.proof_strategy: In characteristic p, only exponents divisible by p survive when f' vanishes.
sketch_steps: derive: The derivative of b_j X^(pj) has factor p, so it vanishes.
setup: Conversely f' = 0 gives i a_i = 0 for every i ≥ 1.
derive: If p does not divide i, the image of i is nonzero, so a_i = 0.
construct: Put g equal to the sum of a_(pj) X^j.
conclude: Then f = g(X^p).

sketch_steps: setup: Write f = g^2 h.
derive: The product rule gives f' = g(2g'h + gh').
conclude: Hence g divides f'.

drafts.canonical_statement: If polynomials f and g over an infinite integral domain A satisfy f(a) = g(a) for all a in A, then f = g.

drafts.proof_strategy: The difference has infinitely many roots, which is impossible for a nonzero polynomial over a domain.
sketch_steps: setup: Put h = f - g.
derive: Every element of A is a root of h.
contradiction: A nonzero polynomial over a domain has finitely many roots.
conclude: Hence h = 0.

conclude: The induction hypothesis for g gives the claim.

drafts.proof_strategy: A polynomial with n roots equals c times the product of the X - r_i, and expanding the product gives the elementary symmetric polynomials.
sketch_steps: setup: Let g be the product of the X - r_i.
derive: g divides f and has the same degree, so f = cg.
derive: Expanding g gives coefficients (-1)^(n-k) e_(n-k).
conclude: Multiply by c.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a polynomial f over a commutative ring A, a in A and a nonnegative integer k, if c_k is the coefficient of X^k in f(X + a), then k! c_k equals f^(k)(a), where f^(k) is the k-th formal derivative.

drafts.proof_strategy: Check monomials using the binomial theorem and the formula for iterated derivatives.
sketch_steps: setup: Both sides are additive and A-linear in f, so take f = X^n.
derive: The binomial theorem gives c_k = binom(n, k) a^(n-k).
derive: The k-th derivative at a equals n(n-1)...(n-k+1) a^(n-k).
conclude: k! binom(n, k) equals this product, which gives the identity.

drafts.proof_strategy: In a factorization of a monic polynomial the leading coefficients are units, so the factors can be normalized to be monic.
sketch_steps: derive: The only monic unit of A[X] is 1.
derive: Irreducibility directly gives the condition on monic factorizations.
setup: Conversely let f = gh with leading coefficients u and v.
derive: uv = 1, so u and v are units and g, h can be made monic.
conclude: The condition forces g or h to be a unit.

drafts.proof_strategy: Middle binomial coefficients vanish for k = 1; induct on k and write x = (x - y) + y for the difference.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Expand (x + y)^p by the binomial theorem.
derive: The middle coefficients are divisible by p, so they vanish in A.
induction: Raising to the p-th power repeatedly gives the formula for p^k.
derive: Applying the sum formula to x = (x - y) + y gives the difference formula.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a polynomial f, the sum of a_i X^i, over a commutative ring A of prime characteristic p, one has f^p equal to the sum of a_i^p X^(ip).

drafts.proof_strategy: The p-th power map is additive in A[X], so it can be applied term by term.
sketch_steps: setup: A[X] also satisfies p·1 = 0.
apply_theorem: In such a ring (u + v)^p = u^p + v^p.
induction: The p-th power of a finite sum is the sum of p-th powers.
conclude: Apply this to the monomials a_i X^i.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a ring homomorphism f from A to B preserving 1, with B nonzero, if A has characteristic m and B has characteristic n, then n divides m.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply f to the relation m·1 = 0 and use the divisibility characterization of the characteristic of B.
sketch_steps: setup: In B, k·1 = 0 holds exactly when n divides k.
derive: f(m·1) = m·1 in B and m·1 = 0 in A.
conclude: Therefore m·1 = 0 in B and n divides m.

drafts.proof_strategy: Translate membership in principal ideals into divisibility and use the defining property of the least common multiple.
sketch_steps: setup: Let l = lcm(a, b).
translate: x lies in (a) ∩ (b) exactly when x is a common multiple of a and b.
derive: This holds exactly when l divides x.
conclude: So (a) ∩ (b) = (l).

drafts.proof_strategy: Write the ideal as (p) and read off the prime element condition from the prime ideal condition.
sketch_steps: setup: Write P = (p).
case_split: If p = 0, then P is the zero ideal.
derive: Otherwise p is a nonunit because P is proper.
derive: p | ab means ab in P, so p | a or p | b.
conclude: Thus p is a prime element.

drafts.proof_strategy: The union of the chain is principal, and its generator already lies in some member of the chain.
sketch_steps: derive: The union U of the chain is an ideal.
setup: Write U = (a) and choose N with a in I_N.
derive: For n ≥ N, U ⊆ I_N ⊆ I_n ⊆ U.
conclude: The chain is constant from N on.

drafts.proof_strategy: A generator of (a, b) is a common divisor, hence a unit.
sketch_steps: derive: If ax + by = 1, a common divisor divides 1.
setup: Conversely write (a, b) = (d).
derive: d is a common divisor, so it is a unit.
conclude: Therefore 1 lies in (a, b).

drafts.proof_strategy: Take a nonzero element of minimal degree, divide by it, and normalize; two monic generators differ by a constant equal to 1.
sketch_steps: setup: Choose g nonzero in I of minimal degree.
derive: Division with remainder shows I = (g).
construct: Scale g to the monic polynomial f.
derive: Two monic generators divide each other and so differ by a constant, which must be 1.
conclude: The monic generator exists and is unique.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a unique factorization domain A with fraction field K, a primitive polynomial f in A[X] is irreducible in A[X] if and only if it is irreducible in K[X]; this generalizes the case of Z and Q.

drafts.proof_strategy: A factor constant in K[X] is a unit by primitivity; a nontrivial factorization over K descends to A[X] by Gauss's lemma.
sketch_steps: derive: Irreducibility over K gives irreducibility over A because constant factors of a primitive polynomial are units.
setup: Conversely suppose f = gh over K with both degrees positive.
construct: Write g = α g_0 and h = β h_0 with g_0 and h_0 primitive in A[X].
apply_theorem: By Gauss's lemma g_0 h_0 is primitive, so f = u g_0 h_0 with u a unit of A.
contradiction: This is a nontrivial factorization of f in A[X].

drafts.canonical_statement: An irreducible polynomial of positive degree over an integral domain A is primitive, that is, every element of A dividing all coefficients is a unit.

drafts.proof_strategy: Factor out the common divisor; the cofactor cannot be a unit because the degree is positive.
sketch_steps: setup: Suppose c divides all coefficients and write f = cg.
derive: Irreducibility makes c or g a unit of A[X].
derive: Units of A[X] are constants, so g is not a unit since deg f > 0.
conclude: Therefore c is a unit of A.

sketch_steps: case_split: For f = 0 take c = 0 and g = 1.
setup: Otherwise let c be a greatest common divisor of the coefficients of f.
construct: Write a_i = c b_i and put g equal to the sum of b_i X^i.
derive: If d divides all b_i, then cd divides c, so d is a unit.
conclude: g is primitive and f = cg.

sketch_steps: translate: x lies in (a) exactly when a divides x.
translate: (a) is proper exactly when a is not a unit.
derive: The prime ideal condition becomes the prime element condition.
conclude: Since a is nonzero, the two notions coincide.

sketch_steps: translate: (a) ⊆ (b) means b divides a, and (a) proper means a is a nonunit.

setup: Conversely take a factorization a = bc.
derive: If (b) = (a), cancellation shows that c is a unit.
conclude: Thus a is irreducible.

derive: Terms with i ≤ n - 1 are divisible by b, so b | c_n a^n and b | c_n.

drafts.proof_strategy: Check the Eisenstein conditions at the prime p and pass to the fraction field by Gauss's lemma.
sketch_steps: setup: f = X^n - a is monic, hence primitive.
derive: The lower coefficients lie in (p), and the constant term is not in (p^2).
apply_theorem: Eisenstein's criterion gives irreducibility in A[X].
apply_theorem: Gauss's lemma transfers irreducibility to K[X].

drafts.canonical_statement: For an integer d and elements x, y of Z[sqrt d], the norm N(a + b sqrt d) = a^2 - d b^2 satisfies N(xy) = N(x)N(y), and N(x) equals x times its conjugate; here Z[sqrt d] is the ring of pairs (a, b) with sqrt(d)^2 = d, and d may be a square.

drafts.proof_strategy: Direct computation in coordinates.
sketch_steps: setup: Write x = a + b sqrt d and y = u + v sqrt d.
derive: x times its conjugate equals a^2 - d b^2.
derive: Expanding N(xy) in coordinates gives (a^2 - d b^2)(u^2 - d v^2).

drafts.canonical_statement: For an integer d and x in Z[sqrt d], x is a unit if and only if |N(x)| = 1, where N(a + b sqrt d) = a^2 - d b^2; here Z[sqrt d] is the ring of pairs (a, b) with sqrt(d)^2 = d, and d may be a square.

drafts.proof_strategy: Multiplicativity sends units to units of Z; conversely the conjugate gives an inverse.
sketch_steps: derive: If xy = 1, then N(x)N(y) = 1 in the integers, so N(x) = ±1.
derive: If N(x) = ±1, then x times ± its conjugate is 1.
conclude: The two conditions are equivalent.

drafts.canonical_statement: For an integer d and x in Z[sqrt d], if |N(x)| is a prime number, then x is irreducible, where N(a + b sqrt d) = a^2 - d b^2; here Z[sqrt d] is the ring of pairs (a, b) with sqrt(d)^2 = d, and d may be a square.

drafts.proof_strategy: A factorization of x factors the prime |N(x)| in the integers.
sketch_steps: setup: Units of Z[sqrt d] are the elements of norm ±1.
derive: x is not a unit, since |N(x)| is prime.
derive: x = yz gives |N(y)| |N(z)| = |N(x)|.
conclude: One factor has norm ±1, so it is a unit.

drafts.canonical_statement: The units of the ring of Gaussian integers Z[i] are exactly 1, -1, i and -i.

drafts.proof_strategy: Units have norm 1, and a^2 + b^2 = 1 has only four integer solutions.
sketch_steps: setup: Use the multiplicative norm N(a + bi) = a^2 + b^2.
derive: A unit has norm 1.
derive: a^2 + b^2 = 1 forces x to be 1, -1, i or -i.
conclude: These four elements are indeed units.

drafts.canonical_statement: For an integer d ≥ 3, the element 2 of Z[sqrt(-d)] is irreducible but not prime, so Z[sqrt(-d)] is not a unique factorization domain; this generalizes the case d = 5.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="Z"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="geq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>3</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="irreducible_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="int_adjoin_sqrt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="unary_minus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="not"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prime_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="int_adjoin_sqrt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="unary_minus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="not"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="unique_factorization_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="int_adjoin_sqrt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="unary_minus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: The norm has no value 2 when d ≥ 3, which gives irreducibility; an explicit product divisible by 2 depending on the parity of d shows that 2 is not prime.
sketch_steps: setup: Use the norm N(a + b sqrt(-d)) = a^2 + d b^2.
derive: The value 2 is not attained because d ≥ 3.
derive: Hence 2, of norm 4, is irreducible.
case_split: For even d use sqrt(-d)^2; for odd d use (1 + sqrt(-d))(1 - sqrt(-d)).
derive: 2 divides these products but not the factors, so it is not prime.
conclude: Irreducibles are prime in a unique factorization domain, so the ring is not one.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime number p congruent to 3 modulo 4, the quotient Z[i]/(p) is a field.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="P"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nat_mod"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>4</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>3</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="is_field"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="quotient_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="gaussian_int"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="principal_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: The congruence shows that p is not a sum of two squares, so p is irreducible in the principal ideal domain Z[i].
sketch_steps: derive: p is not a unit, because N(p) = p^2.
contradiction: A proper factorization gives p = a^2 + b^2, impossible modulo 4.
apply_theorem: Z[i] is Euclidean, hence a principal ideal domain.
derive: An irreducible element generates a maximal ideal.
conclude: Therefore Z[i]/(p) is a field.

drafts.canonical_statement: The ring A[[X]] of formal power series over an integral domain A is an integral domain, and X is a prime element of it.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="integral_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="integral_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="power_series_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prime_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="power_series_x"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="power_series_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Compute the lowest coefficient of a product; divisibility by X is vanishing of the constant term.
sketch_steps: setup: Let m and n be the orders of nonzero f and g.
derive: The coefficient of X^(m+n) in fg is f_m g_n, which is nonzero.
translate: X | f means that the constant term of f vanishes.
conclude: Since A is a domain, X | fg gives X | f or X | g.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every ideal of the ring K[[X]] of formal power series over a field K is the zero ideal or (X^n) for some nonnegative integer n.

drafts.proof_strategy: Every nonzero series is X^k times a unit, so an ideal is determined by the smallest power of X it contains.
sketch_steps: derive: A nonzero series has the form X^k u with u a unit.
setup: For I ≠ 0 let n be the least k with X^k in I.
derive: Any nonzero g = X^m v in I gives X^m in I, so m ≥ n.
conclude: Hence I = (X^n).

derive: f' = g' gives (n + 1)(f_(n+1) - g_(n+1)) = 0.
derive: Injectivity gives f_(n+1) = g_(n+1).

drafts.proof_strategy: Compute the coefficients of the product with the binomial theorem applied to (1 - 1)^n.
sketch_steps: setup: Write the coefficient of X^n as a sum over i + j = n.
derive: The sum equals (1 - 1)^n / n! by the binomial theorem.
conclude: It is 1 for n = 0 and 0 otherwise.

sketch_steps: setup: x lies in the Jacobson radical exactly when 1 + xy is a unit for all y.
setup: A power series is a unit exactly when its constant term is a unit.
derive: Constant multipliers y give f(0) in J(A).
derive: The constant term of 1 + fg is 1 + f(0)g(0), a unit.
conclude: The two conditions are equivalent.

sketch_steps: setup: The (r, s) entry of the product is a sum over t.
derive: A term survives only if t = j = k, r = i and s = l.
conclude: This gives (ab)E_il when j = k and 0 otherwise.

drafts.proof_strategy: Commuting with matrix units forces the off-diagonal entries to vanish and the diagonal entries to agree.
sketch_steps: setup: Compare PE_ij and E_ij P at position (i, j).
derive: This gives P_ii = P_jj.
derive: Comparing PE_jj and E_jj P at (i, j) with i ≠ j gives P_ij = 0.
conclude: So P = rI, and scalar matrices commute with everything because A is commutative.

drafts.canonical_statement: The square matrix ring over a field K, indexed by a nonempty finite set, is a simple ring, that is, it is nonzero and its only two-sided ideals are 0 and the whole ring.

drafts.proof_strategy: Multiply a nonzero matrix on both sides by matrix units to produce all matrix units in the ideal.
sketch_steps: setup: Take a nonzero P in a two-sided ideal I with P_ij ≠ 0.
derive: E_pi P E_jq = P_ij E_pq.
derive: Since P_ij is invertible, every E_pq lies in I.
conclude: The identity is the sum of the E_pp, so I is the whole ring.

sketch_steps: derive: (QP)_ij is a combination of the entries P_tj, so L is a left ideal.
setup: Pick k ≠ j.
construct: Take P = E_kk in L and Q = E_kj.
conclude: PQ = E_kj is not in L, so L is not a right ideal.

drafts.proof_strategy: The left ideal Ax gives a left inverse of each nonzero x; applying this to the left inverse shows it is two-sided.
sketch_steps: derive: In a division ring a nonzero left ideal contains 1.
setup: Conversely Ax = A for nonzero x gives yx = 1.
derive: For a ≠ 0 take ba = 1 and cb = 1.
derive: c = c(ba) = (cb)a = a, so ab = 1.
conclude: Every nonzero element is a unit.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the class equation of the unit group and compare with the value of a cyclotomic polynomial at q.
sketch_steps: setup: Let Z be the center with q elements and n the dimension of D over Z.
derive: Centralizers have size q^d with d | n.
apply_theorem: The class equation reads q^n - 1 = q - 1 + sum (q^n - 1)/(q^d - 1).
derive: For n ≥ 2 the integer Φ_n(q) divides every other term, hence q - 1.
contradiction: But |Φ_n(q)| > q - 1, since |q - ζ| > q - 1 for each primitive n-th root ζ.
conclude: Hence n = 1 and D = Z is commutative.

drafts.proof_strategy: The conjugate divided by the norm gives the inverse; i and j do not commute.
sketch_steps: setup: For x ≠ 0 put N = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 > 0.
derive: x times its conjugate equals N on both sides.
construct: Take y equal to the conjugate of x divided by N.
derive: ij = k and ji = -k differ.
conclude: H is a noncommutative division ring.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a real quaternion x = a + bi + cj + dk, one has x^2 = -1 if and only if a = 0 and b^2 + c^2 + d^2 = 1; in particular x^2 = -1 has infinitely many solutions in H.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="real_quaternions"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="unary_minus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="quaternion_re"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="quaternion_im_i"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="quaternion_im_j"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="quaternion_im_k"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Compute x^2 in coordinates and compare components.
sketch_steps: derive: x^2 = (a^2 - b^2 - c^2 - d^2) + 2a(bi + cj + dk).
case_split: If a ≠ 0, then b = c = d = 0 and a^2 = -1, which is impossible.
derive: So a = 0 and b^2 + c^2 + d^2 = 1.
conclude: The converse is the same formula, and the unit sphere is infinite.

drafts.canonical_statement: Let J be the Jacobson radical of a ring A with identity, not necessarily commutative, defined as the intersection of all maximal left ideals. An element x lies in J if and only if 1 + yx has a left inverse for every y in A; this generalizes the criterion for commutative rings.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="is_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ring_jacobson_radical"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: A proper left ideal containing 1 + yx lies in a maximal left ideal; conversely M + Ax = A produces an invertible element of M.
sketch_steps: setup: Suppose x lies in J and 1 + yx has no left inverse.
contradiction: A(1 + yx) lies in a maximal left ideal M containing yx, so 1 lies in M.
setup: Conversely suppose x is not in a maximal left ideal M.
derive: M + Ax = A gives m = 1 - tx in M.
contradiction: m has a left inverse, so 1 lies in M.

drafts.canonical_statement: If every element of a left ideal I of a ring with identity, not necessarily commutative, is nilpotent, then I is contained in the Jacobson radical, the intersection of all maximal left ideals.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="is_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="left_ideal_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nilpotent_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="subset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ring_jacobson_radical"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: For x in I the element yx is nilpotent, so 1 + yx is invertible by the geometric series.
sketch_steps: setup: x lies in J(A) when 1 + yx has a left inverse for all y.
derive: For x in I, yx lies in I and is nilpotent.
derive: The geometric sum gives an inverse of 1 + yx.
conclude: Thus I ⊆ J(A).

drafts.canonical_statement: The Jacobson radical of the polynomial ring A[X] over an integral domain A is zero.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="integral_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="jacobson_radical"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="polynomial_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="zero_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="polynomial_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: For nonzero f the polynomial 1 + Xf has positive degree, so it is not a unit.
sketch_steps: setup: f in the radical makes 1 + fg a unit for every g.
derive: Units of A[X] over a domain are constants.
contradiction: For f ≠ 0 the polynomial 1 + Xf has degree deg f + 1 ≥ 1.
conclude: Hence the radical is zero.

drafts.canonical_statement: The nilradical of a commutative ring is contained in its Jacobson radical.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="subset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nilradical_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="jacobson_radical"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Maximal ideals are prime, and a prime ideal containing x^n contains x.
sketch_steps: setup: Let x^n = 0 and let M be a maximal ideal.
derive: M is prime and contains x^n, so it contains x.
conclude: x lies in the intersection of all maximal ideals.

drafts.canonical_statement: The Jacobson radical of a left Artinian ring with identity, not necessarily commutative, is a nilpotent ideal.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="is_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="left_artinian_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ring_jacobson_radical"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="zero_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: A stable power I of J with I^2 = I would admit a minimal left ideal L with IL ≠ 0, and then a = xa contradicts the invertibility of 1 - x.
sketch_steps: setup: The chain of powers of J stabilizes at I = J^n with I^2 = I.
setup: If I ≠ 0, choose a minimal left ideal L with IL ≠ 0.
derive: Choose a in L with Ia ≠ 0; minimality gives Ia = L.
derive: Hence a = xa with x in J.
contradiction: 1 - x has a left inverse, so a = 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: A left Artinian ring with identity, not necessarily commutative, is semisimple if and only if its Jacobson radical is zero, where semisimple means that it is a sum of simple modules as a left module over itself.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="is_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="left_artinian_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="semisimple_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ring_jacobson_radical"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="zero_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: The radical kills every simple left ideal; conversely finitely many maximal left ideals intersect in 0, which embeds A into a sum of simple modules.
sketch_steps: derive: J annihilates each simple left ideal, because J lies in the kernel of a ↦ as.
derive: Since 1 lies in a finite sum of simples, J = 0.
setup: Conversely take a minimal finite intersection of maximal left ideals.
derive: It equals J = 0.
apply_theorem: A embeds in a semisimple module, and submodules of semisimple modules are semisimple.

drafts.canonical_statement: The Hopkins-Levitzki theorem. A left Artinian ring with identity, not necessarily commutative, is left Noetherian.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="is_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="left_artinian_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="left_noetherian_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Filter A by powers of its nilpotent radical; each layer is a semisimple Artinian module, hence of finite length.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: J is nilpotent and A/J is semisimple.
derive: Each J^i / J^(i+1) is a semisimple Artinian module.
derive: Such a module is a finite direct sum of simples, hence Noetherian.
induction: Extensions of Noetherian modules are Noetherian.
conclude: A is left Noetherian.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every left ideal I of a semisimple ring A with identity, not necessarily commutative and a sum of simple modules as a left module, has the form I = Ae for an idempotent e.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="is_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="semisimple_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="left_ideal_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="idempotent_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="left_principal_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Decompose 1 along a complement of I; the I-component is the required idempotent.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: I has a complement L, so A = I ⊕ L.
setup: Write 1 = e + f with e in I and f in L.
derive: For x in I, xf lies in I ∩ L = 0, so x = xe.
conclude: Hence I = Ae and e is idempotent.

drafts.canonical_statement: The center of a simple ring, a nonzero ring with identity whose only two-sided ideals are 0 and the whole ring, is a field.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="is_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="simple_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="is_field"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ring_center"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: A nonzero central element generates a nonzero two-sided ideal, so it is invertible, and its inverse is central.
sketch_steps: setup: Let z be a nonzero central element.
derive: Az is a nonzero two-sided ideal, so Az = A.
derive: Thus z has an inverse y in A.
derive: ya = y(az)y = y(za)y = ay shows that y is central.
conclude: The center is a field.

drafts.proof_strategy: Decompose A into isotypic pieces and compute End(A) = A^op with Schur's lemma.
sketch_steps: setup: A is a finite direct sum of simple left ideals, grouped into isomorphism classes.
apply_theorem: Schur's lemma gives division rings D_i' and vanishing Hom between different classes.
derive: End(A) is the product of the matrix rings M_(d_i)(D_i').
derive: End(A) is isomorphic to the opposite ring of A.
conclude: Taking opposites and transposes gives the product of matrix rings over division rings.

drafts.canonical_statement: The Wedderburn-Artin theorem for simple rings. A left Artinian simple ring is isomorphic to a matrix ring over a division ring.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="is_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="left_artinian_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="simple_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="gt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="division_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ring_isomorphic"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="matrix_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: A simple Artinian ring has zero Jacobson radical, so it is semisimple, and simplicity leaves only one factor.
sketch_steps: derive: J is a proper two-sided ideal, so J = 0.
apply_theorem: An Artinian ring with J = 0 is semisimple.
apply_theorem: The Wedderburn-Artin theorem gives a product of matrix rings.
derive: Two or more factors would yield a proper nonzero two-sided ideal.
conclude: Therefore A is a single matrix ring.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a field k and a finite group G with |G| nonzero in k, the group algebra k[G] is a semisimple ring; this is Maschke's theorem in ring form.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="is_field"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ring_nat_cast"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="semisimple_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Average a k-linear projection onto a left ideal over the group to make it A-linear.
sketch_steps: setup: Let L be a left ideal and π a k-linear projection of A onto L.
construct: Put π'(x) = |G|^{-1} sum over g of g π(g^{-1} x).
derive: π' is a projection onto L.
derive: Reindexing the sum shows that π' is A-linear.
conclude: The kernel of π' is a complementary left ideal, so A is semisimple.
